exp.7:1:
Jesus says he feels compassion for the people. They have been with him for three days and now have nothing to eat. The word "compassion" speaks of a deep sorrow over the suffering of others, a feeling that moves a person to act. "Have nothing to eat" means they have no food left.

He speaks in a remote area before a large crowd that was listening to him. He himself calls his disciples and lays out the problem. He explains that if he sends them away hungry, they will grow weak on the road, since some of them have come from far away. The disciples answer with doubts, because they cannot see how to get bread in the desert. This is the account of the second multiplication of loaves in Mark.

For today: Jesus notices concrete needs, not only spiritual ones. We can ask him to give us eyes to notice who around us is hungry or worn out, and to help with something simple and real.
exp.3:11:
The verse says that some look, but do not truly see, and listen, but do not really understand. At the end, it speaks of turning back to God and receiving forgiveness.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples and others close to him, who ask him about the parable of the sower. He explains that to them it is given to know the mystery of the kingdom, while for those on the outside everything comes in parables. Jesus quotes the prophet Isaiah (Isaiah 6). Interpreters debate the exact meaning of "that" in this verse: some see it as a judgment on hardness of heart, others as the result of not wanting to listen.

Today, it is not enough to hear the Word; we must listen to it with humility. Before reading the Bible, ask God for a heart ready to understand and to obey.
exp.13:26:
Jesus tells his disciples that this very night they will all be "made to stumble" because of him. That old word means to trip, to fall, or to pull away out of fear or disappointment. He quotes a prophecy: "I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep will be scattered" (here "scattered" means spread apart).

Jesus speaks after the Last Supper, on the way to the Mount of Olives. He knows he will be arrested and that his friends will run away. The quotation comes from the prophet Zechariah 13:7. Jesus does not scold them; he warns them so they do not lose their faith. Right after this he promises that he will rise again and will wait for them in Galilee.

For today: all of us can fail, even with good intentions, as Peter did. But Jesus already knows our weakness and does not let us go. If you stumble, do not stay far from him: come back, because his promise still stands.
exp.13:71:
Here is what the text says: right when Peter finished denying Jesus, the rooster crowed for the second time. Then Peter remembered what Jesus had told him: that he would deny Him three times before the rooster crowed twice. The phrase "thinking on this" can also be understood as meaning that he burst into tears or that he was broken when he realized what he had done. Either way, he was weeping.

Mark tells this on the night Jesus was arrested. Peter was in the courtyard of the high priest, and several people told him he was a follower of Jesus. Out of fear, he denied it with curses and oaths. Earlier, Peter had insisted that he would never leave Him. Jesus had warned that he would fail, and so it happened.

For today: when we fail, there is no need to hide the pain. Remembering Jesus's word can lead us to sincere repentance, not despair. We can weep, acknowledge our fault, and return to Him, trusting in His mercy.
exp.9:8:
This verse says that marriage is a union that God himself makes, and that no person should separate it. The word "joined" means united or brought together, and "asunder" means separate or divide.

Jesus speaks with some Pharisees who wanted to test him by asking whether it was lawful for a husband to divorce his wife. He takes them back to the beginning, to what God did from creation, and quotes Genesis about the man and the woman who become one flesh. Later, at home, he explains more to his disciples. Christians understand in different ways how to apply this in difficult cases, such as abuse or abandonment.

For today: value your marriage as something serious and sacred. Nurture the union with kind words, forgiveness, and prayer, and do not let others, pride, or resentment harm it. If you are going through a crisis, seek pastoral help and wise counsel.
exp.1:3:
Mark says that four men wanted to bring a paralyzed man to Jesus, but the crowd was so large that they could not get near him. So they went up onto the roof, removed part of it, and opened a hole. Through it they lowered the mat on which the sick man was lying. "Bed" is the mat or cot; "crowd" is the throng; "uncovered the roof" means they took it apart.

Mark tells what happened in a house in Capernaum, where Jesus was teaching the word and people filled the space right up to the door. The paralyzed man's friends did not give up in the face of the obstacle. Roofs in those days were usually flat and made of materials that could be opened. Mark makes clear that Jesus noticed their faith, and that led him to act.

Today we can learn not to give up when something stands in our way of coming to Jesus, or of bringing others to him. Think of someone who needs help or comfort, and pray for that person or stand with them with courage and love.
exp.6:9:
Jesus recalls what Moses wrote in the law: "Honour thy father and thy mother," and also that whoever spoke a curse against father or mother was to die. In this text, "curse" means speaking with contempt or dishonour, and "die the death" is an old way of saying the penalty was death.

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees and some teachers of the law, who were criticising his disciples for not following certain traditions about washing. He answers that they, by keeping human customs, were setting aside a clear command of God. He quotes this commandment to show how seriously God takes it.

For today: think of one concrete way to honour your parents or the older adults in your family, such as speaking to them respectfully, helping them, or listening to them. Let no custom or religious excuse keep you from doing it.
exp.15:2:
These verses tell how the women were walking toward Jesus' tomb and asking one another who would roll away the stone from the entrance for them. "Roll away" here means to roll or move aside. The "tomb" is the sepulchre.

The speakers are Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. They had bought spices to anoint Jesus' body, as was the customary sign of respect. They knew the stone was very large, and the text does not say they had thought of a solution. Yet the next verse shows that when they arrived, the stone had already been rolled away.

We often worry about obstacles we have not yet faced. The women kept walking in spite of their doubt, and they found the way open. Take the step you can take today, trusting God, and do not let fear of what lies ahead hold you back.
exp.3:34:
Jesus says to his disciples, "Let us pass over unto the other side." That same day, as evening came on, he proposes that they cross the Sea of Galilee. The words "pass over" and "the other side" in this verse are the ones that matter here; they simply mean the far shore of the lake.

Jesus speaks after teaching the crowd in parables and explaining everything privately to his disciples. He himself takes the initiative to cross the lake. The verses that follow tell of a great storm that arose, so Jesus' command led them into a difficult crossing. The text does not say why he wanted to cross at that moment.

When we feel that we are following Jesus and storms still come, this does not mean we have taken the wrong road. We can trust that he is with us in the boat and that his word remains sure.
exp.3:1:
This verse says that Jesus taught them many things by means of parables, which are simple stories drawn from everyday life to explain deeper truths. The word "teaching" here means instruction, and the phrase about what he said in his teaching introduces what follows.

Jesus is speaking to a large crowd beside the Sea of Galilee. He got into a boat and sat down in it so that everyone on the shore could see and hear him. Mark tells us that this is one more of his teachings, and right after this Jesus begins the parable of the sower. Why he chose to speak this way is explained in the texts that follow, and some scholars understand it in different ways.

For today: when you read the Bible, go slowly, like someone listening to a story and asking what God wants to say to their heart. Ask him to give you attentive ears.
exp.11:28:
Jesus answers the question about the most important commandment by quoting the Shema, the central prayer of Israel: "Hear, O Israel, the Lord our God, the Lord is one." He says that there is one true God, and that Israel must listen to him with attention. "Hear" means "listen." A "commandment" is an order or teaching from God.

A scribe, that is, a teacher of the Law, saw that Jesus had answered the Sadducees well and asked him which commandment was the first. Jesus does not invent anything new: he goes back to the words of Deuteronomy 6:4-5, which every Jew knew and repeated every day. In this way he shows that everything begins with recognizing who God is.

For today: before asking God for anything or striving to obey him, let us begin the day by remembering that he is the only God and deserves the first place. A moment of silence and attention to him can put everything else in order.
exp.11:30:
Jesus says that the second most important commandment is like the first: to love your neighbour as yourself. The phrase "is like" means "is similar to" it. "Neighbour" refers to the person near you, the one who crosses your path. He also states that there is no commandment greater than these two.

Jesus is speaking with a scribe, a teacher of the law, who asked him which was the first commandment of all. Jesus joins two texts from the Old Testament: Deuteronomy 6:4-5 and Leviticus 19:18. Then the scribe agrees and says that this love is worth more than the sacrifices in the temple.

Today you can practise it this way: think of someone close to you who is going through a hard time and do a concrete act of kindness for them, such as calling them, listening to them calmly, or helping them with something simple. In this way your love for God becomes visible.
exp.4:36:
Jesus did not let anyone go with him to Jairus's house except three of his disciples: Peter, James (Santiago) and John, the brother of James.

The account is told by Mark. Jairus, the leader of the synagogue, had just received word that his daughter had died. Jesus told him not to be afraid and to keep believing. Then Jesus chose this small group to go in with him. It is not stated clearly why he chose these three. Some think it was so that they would be close witnesses to what was about to happen. These three also appear at other important moments, such as the transfiguration.

For today: when you are in a time of grief or fear, Jesus does not ask you for a crowd of supporters, but for trust in him. And God often uses a few faithful, close people to walk with you.
exp.7:0:
In those days, a great crowd had gathered again around Jesus, and the people had nothing to eat. Then Jesus called his disciples to speak with them.

This is the start of the second feeding of the bread in Mark. The narrator tells us that Jesus takes the initiative: he sees the need and gathers his disciples before acting. In the verses that follow he explains that he feels compassion, because the people had been with him for three days. Some scholars believe this scene is different from the one with the five thousand; others see it as a parallel account.

For today: Jesus notices the concrete needs of people, not only their spiritual ones. We can ask him for attentive eyes to notice who around us is hungry, lonely or tired, and ask him how to help with what we have.
exp.12:6:
Jesus says that when his disciples hear of wars and of reports of wars, they should not be frightened or distressed. The word "turbéis" in the source means "be alarmed," so the translation keeps that sense: do not be alarmed. He says that such things "must needs be," meaning they are going to happen, and he adds that the end will not come yet.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the Mount of Olives, who had asked him about the signs of the future. First he warned them against the deceptions of false Christs. Now he teaches them that wars and crises are not, by themselves, a sign that the end has arrived. Interpreters disagree about how this is fulfilled, but Jesus's advice is clear: do not live in panic.

When the news fills us with fear, we can pray and trust that God still guides history. Then, instead of being carried away by fear or by alarmist predictions, we remain faithful to Christ and live with peace and hope.
exp.13:45:
This verse tells that the men who came with Judas seized Jesus and arrested him. "To lay hands on" means to take hold of someone by force, and the phrase has to do with grabbing him and holding him fast.

Mark tells what happened in the garden of Gethsemane, at night. Judas, one of the twelve disciples, had agreed on a signal with the crowd sent by the religious leaders: a kiss. With that gesture of affection he pointed out Jesus so that they would take him. Mark is not the one speaking here; he is only narrating. Jesus had already announced that he would be handed over, and he does not resist with violence.

For today: sometimes we are betrayed or treated unjustly, even by people close to us. Jesus teaches us not to answer with evil, but to trust God and keep calm. Ask God to give you peace and wisdom in those moments.
exp.3:13:
Jesus explains here the first detail of the parable of the sower: the one who sows scatters the word, that is, God's message. The phrase is brief and simple. It does not say who the sower is in particular, but focuses on what is sown: the word. The verses that follow show that this message falls on different kinds of hearts.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, apart from the crowd. He has just told the parable and asks them whether they understand it, because it is the key to understanding the others. He himself explains each part to them, so that they can see how people respond to the message of the kingdom.

Today we can ask ourselves how we receive the word of God. Before worrying about others, it is good to read it carefully and to ask God for a willing heart. And if we share it, we can do so with patience, trusting that God makes the seed grow.
exp.2:19:
The explanation says the crowd gathered again in such large numbers around Jesus that neither he nor his disciples could even eat. The word "crowded" means a multitude pressing together into one place. "Bread" here stands for food in general.

Mark tells this right after Jesus chose the twelve apostles and entered a house. The people were looking for healing, help, and teaching. The next verse shows the reaction: his relatives thought he had lost his senses, perhaps from exhaustion, and went out to take charge of him. Interpreters explain this in different ways, but all of them see great pressure.

For today: serving others is beautiful, but we also need rest and food. Ask God for wisdom to help with love, without neglecting your body or your family.
exp.14:15:
The explanation says that the Roman soldiers led Jesus inside the building called the Praetorium, which was the governor's residence or barracks. "Hall" here refers to the inner courtyard or enclosure. "Call together" means they summoned one another to gather. The "band" was a group of Roman soldiers; in theory it could number around six hundred, although here it probably refers to those who were available.

Mark tells the events with restraint. Pilate had already given in to the crowd, released Barabbas, and handed Jesus over to be crucified, after having him flogged. Now the soldiers, charged with the execution, gather together and prepare to mock Him. The verses that follow show this: they put a purple robe on Him and a crown of thorns.

Jesus endured the contempt and humiliation without answering with vengeance. When someone mocks you or treats you unjustly, remember that Christ went through that first. You can ask Him for the strength to respond with patience and gentleness.
exp.2:24:
Jesus says that a house, that is, a family, in which its members fight against one another cannot stay standing. Here "house" can also be understood as a lineage or an entire family, and "stand" means to remain firm and not fall apart.

Jesus speaks to the teachers of the law, who were accusing him of casting out demons by the power of the prince of demons. He answers them with simple examples, called parables: a divided kingdom and a divided house both fall apart. In this way he shows that their accusation makes no sense, since Satan would not be fighting against himself.

For today: if there is friction in your home or in your church, seek peace before the division grows. Listen, ask for forgiveness and forgive, and remember that unity protects what God has given you.
exp.13:22:
He says that Jesus took the cup, gave thanks to God, and passed it to his disciples. All of them drank from it. The word "cup" here is the one in the verse; the Greek-style phrasing in the source is not needed for the reader.

It is the night before the crucifixion, during the Passover meal. Mark tells what Jesus did with his twelve disciples. Shortly before, he had spoken of one of them who would betray him. Even so, the cup was shared with everyone. Soon Jesus will explain that it represents his blood, poured out for many.

For today: when you take part in the Lord's Supper, do it with gratitude and not out of habit. Jesus gave thanks even knowing the suffering that was coming. You too can thank him, remembering that his giving of himself was for you.
exp.10:26:
They came back to Jerusalem again. As Jesus was walking in the temple, the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders came up to him. The chief priests were the priests with the most authority. The scribes were teachers who were experts in the Law. The elders were respected leaders of the people. Jerusalem is Jerusalem.

The one telling the story is Mark. This happens one day after Jesus drove out the sellers from the temple. The leaders come to call him to account, since they felt responsible for the temple. The verses that follow show that they wanted to question his authority. The verses before this speak about faith and forgiveness in prayer, and here the scene shifts to a conflict.

When someone questions what God is doing, we can respond calmly, as Jesus did. And before we pray, it is good to check whether we are holding on to resentment and to hand it over to God.
exp.0:37:
Jesus answers his disciples by telling them to go to the nearby towns, so that he can preach there too. He explains that this is the reason he came. The word "nearby" is the sense of the phrase, and the old-fashioned spelling of "to" is simply the way the text was written in its time.

Jesus is the one speaking. He has just spent a night in prayer and healing in Capernaum, and Simon and the others find him and say that everyone is looking for him. Jesus does not stay where he is already popular; he wants more people to hear the message of the kingdom. Some understand "for this I have come" to refer to leaving Capernaum, and others to his whole mission. Both ideas fit.

For today: do not measure your life only by what people applaud or expect from you. Ask God for clarity about your purpose, and have the courage to step out of what is comfortable in order to serve and share his hope with others.
exp.14:32:
When the sixth hour came, that is, noon, darkness fell over the whole land until the ninth hour, or about three in the afternoon. The word "darkness" here simply means the absence of light. The text does not say what caused it, nor whether it covered the entire world or only the region, since the word for "land" can be understood in either sense.

Mark tells us what happens while Jesus is on the cross. Before this, the religious leaders and the other men being crucified had been mocking Him. Then, in this darkness, Jesus cries out, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" Many Christians see in that darkness a sign of the solemn weight of that moment, although the text does not explain it.

When you find yourself living through dark hours, remember that Jesus knows that pain. You can speak to Him honestly, without pretending to be strong, and trust that God has not forgotten you.
exp.13:15:
They went to the city, that is, Jerusalem, and everything happened just as Jesus had told them. The phrase "they made ready the passover" means that they prepared the Passover meal: they obtained the lamb, the unleavened bread, and what was needed for the table.

Mark tells this as narrator. Jesus had already given them precise instructions: they would find a man carrying a pitcher of water, and he would lead them to a large upper room already furnished. This takes place shortly before the Last Supper and the betrayal by Judas. Some think Jesus had arranged this in advance, and others that he knew it supernaturally. The text does not make this clear.

For today: trust the word of Jesus and obey step by step, even when we cannot see the whole path. Often, as we obey, we discover that God had already prepared what was needed.
exp.1:1:
As soon as word got out that Jesus was at home, so many people gathered that there was no room left, not even outside the door. The word "straightway" means right away, and the phrase "around him" describes how the crowd surrounded him. While everyone pressed in around him, Jesus preached the word to them, that is, he announced God's message.

Mark tells this in Capernaum, where Jesus had already healed and taught, and that is why the people were looking for him. Here the narrator is Mark, and he wants to show that Jesus did not draw crowds only through miracles; his main work was teaching. This detail also sets up the next scene, where some men have to open the roof to bring someone to him.

For today: let us seek Jesus eagerly, even when there are obstacles. And when we gather together, let us give first place to his word, not only to what suits us or moves us.
exp.11:21:
This verse ends the story told by the Sadducees: seven brothers married the same woman, one after another, and none of them had children. In the end the woman also died. "Seed" means descendants, children. "Last of all" means at the end.

The ones speaking are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They cite the Jewish law of levirate marriage, which required a dead man's brother to marry the widow so that she would have descendants. With this exaggerated story they want to make the hope of rising again look ridiculous and to put Jesus in a difficult position.

For today: when a question seeks to mock faith, Jesus teaches us to return to the Bible and to trust in the power of God, which is greater than our reasoning. Studying the Scriptures with humility keeps us from error.
exp.11:8:
Jesus asks a question and then answers it himself. The owner of the vineyard will come, will bring an end to those wicked farmers, and will hand the vineyard over to others. The word "destroy" here means that he will punish them severely. "Husbandmen" are the people who work the land.

Jesus is speaking in the temple to the religious leaders, who were questioning him. He tells them a parable: the vineyard represents Israel, the farmers represent its leaders, and the son who was killed represents Jesus himself. The leaders understood that he was speaking about them. Many see in this a warning of judgment and a sign that others would receive the responsibility of the kingdom of God.

Everything we have comes from God, and we are stewards, not owners. Today you might ask yourself: do I use my time, my gifts, and my influence to honor God and serve others, or only for my own benefit?
exp.7:13:
This verse tells us that the disciples had forgotten to bring bread for the journey. They had only one loaf for everyone in the boat. "Had forgotten" means they had not remembered to prepare food before setting out.

The author, Mark, recounts the moment just after Jesus, with sadness, refused the Pharisees' request that He give them a sign. Jesús left the Pharisees and crossed the lake with his disciples. This detail about the bread sets up what follows: Jesus warns them about the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod, and they think He is speaking about having no bread. They do not understand that He is speaking of something spiritual.

For today: sometimes we worry so much about what we lack that we fail to listen to what God is telling us. Before we become anxious, let us pause and remember that Jesus has already cared for us before.
exp.7:20:
Jesus asks his disciples a question: "How is it that ye do not understand?" In other words, "Why do you still not grasp this?" The word "baskets" refers to large baskets, and the verb form used there is an old way of saying "understand," so rewrite that point as simply the verb "understand" in the verse above.

Jesus speaks with his disciples in the boat. They have just been worried because they had only one loaf of bread, and He reminds them of the two feedings, when twelve and seven baskets were left over. He shows them that if He had provided so much before, He could also care for them now. Soon after, He heals a blind man, and many see in this an image of how the disciples needed to open the eyes of their understanding, although the text does not say so explicitly.

Today, when you worry about what you lack, remember the times God has already sustained you. That grateful remembrance strengthens trust.
exp.9:30:
Jesus says that many who now seem the most important will be last, and that many who now seem last will be first. The words that the reader sees in this verse, "first" and "last," are the ones explained here: those who go ahead in importance or honor are the first, and those who come at the end are the last.

Jesus speaks with his disciples after a rich young man went away sad, unwilling to give up his riches. Peter had said that they had left everything behind. Jesus promises that God rewards what is given up for him, though with persecutions. Then he warns that God does not measure worth as the world does. Right after, he announces his death in Jerusalem, where he himself will humble himself.

Today we can serve without competing or comparing ourselves with others. What the world applauds may not be worth anything before God, and what no one sees, he remembers. Serve with humility and trust in his justice.
exp.8:41:
It says that whoever causes one of these little ones who believe in Jesus to stumble into sin would be better off if a heavy millstone were hanged about his neck and he were cast into the sea. "Offend" means to make someone stumble or turn them away from their faith. A millstone was a huge, heavy stone used for grinding grain.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after they argued about who was the greatest and wanted to stop someone who was not part of their group. Earlier he had placed a child in the midst of them. These "little ones" may be children or simple, humble believers; they are understood in both ways. With this strong image, Jesus shows how much he values the weak.

For today: take care with your example and your words, especially with those who are just beginning in the faith or are vulnerable. Ask yourself whether what you do encourages people to draw near to God or places a stumbling block in their way.
exp.5:0:
He went out from there and came to his own country, and his disciples followed him. The explanation says that Jesus left the place where he had been, which was Jairus's house in Capernaum, and went to his own home region, the town where he grew up. His disciples went with him.

The narrator here is Mark. Almost everyone understands that "his own country" refers to Nazareth, although the text does not name it. Mark tells this to show that Jesus did not arrive alone, but as a teacher with his followers. What follows shows that the people of his hometown received him with amazement and also with unbelief.

For today: sometimes it is harder to be accepted by those who know us best. If Jesus went through this, we can trust that he understands when our family or friends do not understand our faith. Let us keep being faithful, with love and patience.
exp.10:1:
Jesus sends two of his disciples to the village that lies ahead of them. He tells them that as soon as they enter it, they will find a colt tied there, a young donkey, on which no one has ever sat. They are to untie it and bring it to him.

Jesus speaks as he approaches Jerusalem, near the Mount of Olives, a few days before his death. He is going to enter the city riding on a young donkey, like a humble and peaceful king. Many believe this recalls the prophecy in Zechariah 9:9. That the animal had never been used before suggests that it was set apart for a sacred purpose.

For today: Jesus knows what is coming and guides with attention to detail. We can obey step by step, even when we do not understand everything, trusting that he knows what he is doing.
exp.12:31:
It says that no one knows the exact day or hour of that final event. Not even the angels in heaven know it, nor the Son; only the Father does.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after describing signs and difficult events that would come. They wanted to know when all of this would happen. He does not give them a date; instead, he asks them to stay alert. That the Son says he does not know the day is a mystery; many understand it as part of his humility in becoming a man, and others explain it in other ways.

We can stop making calculations about dates and live each day faithfully. If today you take care of your prayer, your work, and the people around you, you will be ready, without fear and trusting in the Father.
exp.14:23:
It says that, after they had nailed Jesus to the cross, the soldiers kept his clothing. Since there were several pieces, they cast lots, something like rolling dice, to decide what each one would take. The words "garments" and "lots" have been used here to refer to his clothes and to a random drawing.

Mark tells the events like a narrator, without commenting on them. It was customary for the soldiers in charge of an execution to divide up the condemned person's belongings. Many Christians see here a fulfillment of Psalm 22:18, though Mark does not quote it in this passage. Jesus was stripped of everything, amid mockery and pain.

For today: While some were gambling over his clothing, Jesus was giving his life for them. Today it is also easy to be close to what is sacred without noticing what is happening. Take a moment today to thank him for what he did for you.
exp.8:33:
They kept silent when Jesus asked them what they had been talking about. They said nothing because, on the way, they had been arguing with one another about which of them was the greatest.

Mark tells this as Jesus and his disciples are heading toward Capernaum. Shortly before, Jesus had told them about his death, and they did not understand. While he spoke of suffering and serving, they were thinking about having a place of honor. Their silence shows shame. Jesus corrects them by teaching that whoever wants to be first must be the servant of all.

Today we can ask ourselves what fills our minds when no one is listening to us. If we discover pride or a desire to stand out, we can ask God for a humble heart and look for a concrete way this week to serve someone without expecting recognition.
exp.1:4:
This verse says that Jesus saw the faith of the men who brought the paralyzed man. Then he spoke to the sick man tenderly, and told him that his sins were forgiven. Jesus looks beyond what is visible.

Jesus is in a crowded house in Capernaum. Four men opened the roof to bring their friend near. Jesus surprises everyone by offering forgiveness first, not healing. The scribes think that only God can forgive sins, and they are right; Jesus wants to show that he acts with divine authority. Some scholars see here a message about who Jesus is.

Today we can bring others to Jesus through prayer and sincere help. And let us remember that Jesus first attends to the deepest need of the heart: forgiveness and peace with God.
exp.11:3:
This verse tells that the owner of the vineyard sent another servant to the tenant farmers. They treated him worse than the first: they threw stones at him, struck him on the head, and sent him back dishonored. "Shamefully handled" means treated with disgrace and contempt. "Stoning him" means that they threw stones at him.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, before the religious leaders, and tells this parable. The vineyard represents Israel, and the servants represent the prophets whom God sent again and again. Many understand that the beloved son points to Jesus himself. The leaders understood that he was speaking about them.

For today: God keeps speaking with patience, and we can harden ourselves against his voice. Let us ask him for a humble heart to hear his correction, even when it comes through ordinary people or at uncomfortable moments, and to treat well those who bring us his message.
exp.14:28:
The verse tells that the people passing by the cross insulted Jesus. They hurled hard words at him, shaking their heads in mockery, and reminded him of what was said he had claimed about destroying the temple and building it again in three days.

The speakers are ordinary people who were walking along the road near the place of crucifixion. They were mocking a statement Jesus had made earlier, which some understood wrongly (John 2:19-21 explains that he was speaking about his body). They thought that if he truly had power, he could come down from the cross. Without realizing it, they showed that they did not understand his mission.

For today: when others mock your faith or judge you without understanding, remember that Jesus also endured mockery. Trust that God works even in what looks like defeat, and respond with patience and humility.
exp.2:33:
Jesus looks with affection at the people sitting around him, who are listening to him, and he calls them "my mother and my brothers." He is not rejecting his family; he is showing that there is a very deep spiritual bond.

Jesus is teaching in a house full of people. His mother and his brothers arrive and send for him, perhaps worried about him (verse 21 says some people thought he was out of his mind). Jesus takes the moment to teach who truly makes up his family: those who do the will of God, as verse 35 says.

Today, being part of Jesus' family does not depend on surnames or traditions, but on listening to his word and obeying it. Ask yourself: what concrete step of obedience can I take today? And treat other believers as true brothers and sisters, with care and support.
exp.0:18:
This verse tells us that Jesus went a little farther on and saw James (Santiago) and his brother John, the sons of Zebedee. They were in the boat, that is, in the small vessel, and were mending their nets, meaning they were repairing them or getting them ready to fish again.

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. Jesus has just called Simon and Andrew, who left their nets to follow him. Now Jesus approaches another pair of brothers who were also fishermen. The verses that follow say that he called them and they went after him, leaving their father and the hired men in the boat.

For today: Jesus often calls us in the middle of ordinary life, while we work or go about our daily routine. You can stay attentive to his voice in your routine and ask him what step of obedience he wants you to take today.
exp.5:1:
He says that when the sabbath day came, Jesus began to teach in the synagogue of his own people. Many who heard him were astonished, that is, greatly amazed. They kept asking where all of this came from: such wisdom, and those mighty works done by his hands.

Mark tells us that Jesus returned to his home region, probably Nazareth, accompanied by his disciples. The ones speaking are the neighbors who had known him since childhood. Their amazement did not lead them to believe; the following verses show that they were offended, that is, they stumbled over him, because they saw him only as the carpenter they knew. Jesus replies that a prophet is often less honored in his own country.

For today: let us not allow custom or prejudice to keep us from recognizing what God is doing. Sometimes He works through people who are humble or familiar to us. Let us ask for a humble and open heart, so that we may listen with faith.
exp.9:33:
This verse says that Jesus will be mocked, whipped, spat upon, and killed, but that on the third day he will rise again. "Mock" means to make fun of someone with contempt. "Scourge" means to strike with a whip. Jesus announces it in detail, hiding nothing.

He speaks to his twelve disciples, whom he takes aside, as they journey toward Jerusalem. They were walking along afraid and full of fear. This is the third time in this Gospel that he tells them of his suffering. Even so, James and John soon ask him for a favor, which shows that they did not fully understand what he was saying.

For today: Jesus walked toward suffering knowing how it would end, and he trusted God's plan. When you face something difficult, you can remember that pain does not have the last word. Ask God for courage and hope to keep going forward.
exp.2:5:
The explanation says that the Pharisees went out of the synagogue and at once made a plan with the Herodians to find a way to kill Jesus. The phrase "took counsel" means they made a plan together. "Kill him" means to put him to death.

Mark, the narrator, tells what happened after Jesus healed a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath. Jesus asked whether it was lawful to do good or harm on that day, and they kept silent. The Herodians were supporters of the family of Herod. Normally they did not get along with the Pharisees, but they joined together against Jesus. Scholars believe they did so for political and religious reasons, although the text gives no further details.

For today: when the truth makes us uncomfortable, we can harden ourselves instead of changing. Ask God for a humble heart that values doing good, and that does not defend its rules above people.
exp.12:20:
Jesus says that, in times of great distress, some people will say, "Look, here is the Christ," or "he is there." His instruction is clear: "do not believe them." The words "ó" and "fué" are old spellings of "o" and "fue."

Wait, the sentence about "ó" and "fué" explains old spellings in the source wording, which the reader never sees, so it must be deleted.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives as he warns them about what is coming. After describing days of great suffering, he wants to prepare them so they will not be deceived. Interpreters disagree about how all of this is fulfilled: some see it in the destruction of Jerusalem, others in the end of the age, and others in both.

Today we can be wary of anyone who promises a special Christ, hidden, or limited to a place or a leader. Let us know Jesus well through the Scriptures, so that his voice guides us and we are not carried away by every spectacular novelty.
exp.14:27:
The verse says that what Scripture had announced was fulfilled: Jesus was numbered among the wicked. The two thieves crucified beside him are the ones meant here.

Mark, the narrator, notes that this was no accident. The phrase comes from Isaiah 53:12, the passage about the suffering servant. It should be said that some ancient manuscripts do not include this verse, and for that reason several modern translations omit it or place it in a footnote. Jesus himself quoted these words in Luke 22:37.

Jesus, though without sin, was treated as a criminal and placed between two wrongdoers. God did not lose control: every detail of the cross pointed to an ancient promise.

For today: if you feel unjustly judged or misunderstood, remember that Jesus knows that pain and was willing to take the place of the guilty out of love.
exp.7:21:
This verse tells that Jesus and his disciples arrived at Bethsaida. There some people brought him a blind man and begged him to touch him. The phrase about them begging him is about how they kept asking him insistently to put his hands on the man so that he would be healed.

It is Mark who narrates. Jesus had just rebuked his disciples for not understanding the miracle of the loaves, even though they had seen it with their own eyes. Many interpreters see in this healing, which happens in two steps, an image of how the disciples were slowly opening their eyes to understand who Jesus was. This is a possible reading, although the text does not state it directly.

For today: we learn from those friends, who did not stay still and brought the blind man to Jesus. We can pray and intercede for someone who needs help, and accompany them with love, trusting that Jesus cares for each person.
exp.0:33:
He healed many who were sick with all kinds of diseases, and he drove out many demons. It also says that he would not let the demons speak, because they knew who he was.

Mark tells what happened in Capernaum, on a Saturday evening, when the sun went down and the Sabbath ended. Then the people could bring him their sick, and the whole city gathered at the door. Mark is the narrator. Scholars explain in several ways why Jesus silenced the demons; many think he did not want his identity announced too soon, or announced by evil spirits.

For today: Jesus welcomes everyone who comes tired and wounded. You can bring him your pains with confidence, and also look for quiet moments to pray, as he did.
exp.5:29:
This verse tells that the apostles returned to where Jesus was. They gathered around him, meaning they came together at his side. They reported to him everything they had done and everything they had taught.

Earlier, Jesus had sent them out two by two to preach, heal, and drive out demons (Mark 6:7-13). Now they come back to give him an account. Just before this, the story mentioned the death of John the Baptist, and his disciples had buried him. Afterward, Jesus invites them to rest in a quiet place, because there were so many people that they could not even eat in peace.

For today: after serving others, take some time to tell Jesus in prayer how things went for you, your joys and your weariness. He listens, and he also knows when you need rest.
exp.2:11:
This verse says that Jesus repeatedly and firmly ordered the unclean spirits not to make him known. The word translated here as "straitly charged" means that he rebuked them or commanded them with severity. The idea is that he made them promise not to reveal who he was.

Mark tells us that many sick people pressed toward Jesus in order to touch him and be healed. The unclean spirits, when they saw him, cried out that he was the Son of God. What they said was true, but Jesus did not want that testimony. Scholars offer several explanations: to prevent misunderstandings about his mission, or because he would not accept a witness coming from evil spirits. He himself would reveal who he was in his own time and in his own way.

For today: it is not enough to say correct things about Jesus. What he wants is for us to truly follow him and make him known through a life that reflects him, with humility and sincerity.
exp.13:37:
Jesus tells his disciples to stay awake and pray, so that they will not fall into temptation. The word "watch" means to stay alert, and the phrase "ready" means willing and eager; the body is weak. In other words, the heart wants to obey, but human strength fails.

Jesus is in Gethsemane, troubled, shortly before his arrest. He has just prayed to the Father with deep surrender, and he finds Peter and the others sleeping. He speaks to them with tenderness, not only with rebuke: he recognizes their good intention, but also their weakness. They were facing a very hard trial, and their eyes, heavy with sleep, show their exhaustion.

For today: do not rely only on your good intentions. Set aside a moment each day, even a brief one, to pray and ask God for strength before pressure or temptation arrives.
exp.13:3:
It says that some of those present were indignant within themselves at what the woman had done. They asked why this ointment had been wasted. Ointment is a fragrant perfume or aromatic oil, and the flask was a container made of a fine stone.

This takes place in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a few days before Jesus' crucifixion. A woman pours a very valuable perfume over his head. Those who complain look at the cost and think of the poor. Mark does not name them; he only says "some." Jesus will respond by defending the woman.

We can be quick to judge the devotion of others, believing we know better how God should be loved. Today it is worth pausing before we criticize and asking what is in the heart of the one who gives. It is also worth asking ourselves what we are willing to offer Jesus with generosity.
exp.9:2:
Jesus answers the Pharisees' question with another question. He asks them what Moses commanded, and he asks them to say what Moses taught on the subject.

The Pharisees wanted to test him with a question about divorce, a subject that was widely debated at that time. Jesus does not answer right away with his own opinion. Instead, he leads them to the Scripture they knew. In this way he shows that they already had the answer at hand, and he will then explain God's purpose.

For today: when someone brings us a difficult question, before we argue with opinions, let us return to the Word of God. Let us ask what Scripture actually says and what God's purpose was from the beginning.
exp.5:22:
Here the text says that Herod, the king, made a vow in front of all his guests. He promised the girl that he would give her whatever she asked, even up to half of his kingdom. "Swore" means that he confirmed it with a solemn promise. The phrase "up to half of my kingdom" is an exaggerated way of saying that he would place no limits on his generosity.

It speaks of Herod Antipas, at his birthday party. He was among officials and important people, and the young woman's dancing had pleased him greatly. He wanted to show off with a great promise. Even so, he did not think about the consequences, and his mother Herodias took the opportunity to ask for the death of John the Baptist.

For today: before promising something, think carefully about what you say. Words spoken out of pride or to look good before others can lead us to do unjust things. It is better to speak with wisdom and always seek what is right.
exp.11:31:
A scribe, that is, a teacher of the Law, answers Jesus that he agrees with him. He says, "Well, Master," and confirms that Jesus spoke the truth: God is one, and there is no other besides him.

Jesus had just quoted the two most important commandments: to love God with all your being and to love your neighbor. The scribe had heard him debate with other groups and wanted to know which commandment came first. Here he does not argue but sincerely acknowledges what Jesus taught. Then Jesus tells him that he is not far from the kingdom of God.

Today we can learn from this humble attitude. Recognizing the truth when we hear it, even when it comes from someone else, brings us closer to God. Let us pause today to ask ourselves whether we truly love God and others.
exp.14:36:
This verse says that Jesus cried out with a loud voice and died.

Mark tells of the final moment of the crucifixion here. Some of those present had misunderstood Jesus' words and thought he was calling for Elijah. Mark does not explain the reason for the cry; scholars understand it in several ways. What follows shows its effect: the temple veil is torn, and the Roman centurion recognizes that Jesus is the Son of God.

For today: Jesus did not die defeated, but gave up his life with purpose. When you feel weak or confused, remember that his death opened the way to God. You can come to him with confidence, just as you are.
exp.5:33:
Jesus got out of the boat and found a large crowd waiting for him. He felt compassion, that is, a deep sorrow for them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd, lost and without guidance. Then he began to teach them many things.

Jesus and his disciples were looking for a quiet place to rest. But the people saw them leave, ran on foot along the shore, and arrived first. Mark tells us that Jesus was not bothered at losing his rest. He chose to meet the people's need. His first response was to teach them, before giving them bread, which comes later in the account.

Today, when someone interrupts your plans with a real need, pause for a moment and look at it with the eyes of Jesus. Perhaps you can listen, counsel with the Word, or walk alongside them, instead of feeling annoyed.
exp.12:7:
Jesus says there will be wars between nations and kingdoms, earthquakes in various places, famines and troubles, that is, uproar and unrest. Then he calls all of this "the beginnings of sorrows," an image of the pains of childbirth: signs that begin and announce something more, but that are not yet the end.

Jesus speaks privately to his disciples, on the Mount of Olives, after they heard him announce the destruction of the temple. They asked him when it would be. He wants them not to be frightened or led astray by false messiahs. Interpreters disagree about how much of this refers to the year 70 AD and how much to the end of time.

When the news is frightening, do not be carried away by panic or by anyone who promises easy answers. Trust in Christ, pray, and keep serving faithfully.
exp.4:8:
In this verse, Jesus asks the spirit that was tormenting the man what his name is. The answer is "Legion," and it is explained: "for we are many." A legion was a unit of the Roman army, made up of thousands of soldiers. So the name speaks of a great number of spirits.

Jesus is speaking with the unclean spirit that controlled this man. He had already commanded it to come out, and the spirit, frightened, begged him not to torment it. By asking the name, Jesus reveals the seriousness of the case. Some think that "Legion" indicates a very large number, and others that it speaks only of strength and power. The Bible does not give the exact number.

For today: however great the problem we face, Jesus has authority over it. No burden is too heavy for Him. We can come to Christ with confidence and ask for His help.
exp.13:12:
Jesus sends two of his disciples into the city, Jerusalem, to prepare the Passover supper. He tells them that they will meet a man carrying a pitcher of water, and that they should follow him. A pitcher is a large vessel for carrying water. The words "will meet you" mean that the man will come out to meet them.

Jesus speaks a few days before his death. The disciples have just asked him where they want to celebrate the Passover. Mark has just mentioned that the leaders were looking for a way to hand him over. Jesus gives precise directions, perhaps to protect the place. Some think he had already arranged this with someone, and others see supernatural knowledge; the text does not make it clear. Carrying water was a common task for women, so seeing a man do it would be an easy sign to recognize.

For today: God cares about the details. When you cannot see the whole path, take the next step in simple obedience, trusting that He goes ahead of you.
exp.13:43:
Judas, the one who handed Jesus over, had agreed on a signal with the crowd that came to arrest him. He told them that whomever he kissed, that was Jesus. They were to seize him, that is, arrest him, and lead him away carefully guarded so that he would not escape.

Mark, who tells the story, reports this in the garden of Gethsemane. Judas was one of the twelve disciples, and he came with armed men sent by the religious leaders. A kiss was a normal greeting of respect toward a teacher, and Judas used it to hide his betrayal. Judas's inner motives are not explained here.

For today: we should examine our hearts so that our words and gestures of affection are sincere. Jesus, even while betrayed, continued on the path of giving himself up out of love for us.
exp.8:1:
It says that six days after Jesus spoke to his disciples, he took Peter, James (Santiago) and John up a high mountain, away from the rest. There he was "transfigured", that is, his appearance visibly changed in front of them.

Mark is the one who tells the story, and he recounts it right after Jesus spoke about his cross and promised that some would see the kingdom of God come with power. Many understand this scene as a foretaste of that glory; others think of the resurrection or of other events. The text does not say which mountain it was, and people have discussed which one it would be.

For today: after speaking about suffering, Jesus gave his friends a glimpse of his glory. When the road gets hard, set aside time alone with God; there hope is renewed.
exp.12:27:
Jesus tells us to look at the fig tree to learn something. When its branches become tender and it puts out leaves, everyone knows that summer is near.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after announcing the destruction of the temple, hard times, and his coming in glory. They had asked him when all of that would happen. He uses this simple picture to teach them to be alert to the signs. How to understand "these things" and "this generation" is interpreted in several ways among Christians.

For today: just as we pay attention to the seasons, we can live awake and attentive to God, with faith and without fear, trusting that Jesus will fulfill what he promised.
exp.13:17:
Jesus and his disciples are sitting at the table, eating the Passover supper. At that moment Jesus says, very seriously, that one of them is going to hand him over. The words "sat down at the table" and "eat" simply mean that they were eating. "Hand over" means to betray, to put him into the hands of his enemies. And what is most painful is that the traitor is someone who eats with him.

Jesus speaks shortly before his arrest. The disciples had prepared the Passover supper, which remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Jesus knows what is coming and says so openly. The disciples are saddened, and each one asks himself, "Is it I?" Mark does not explain here the whole reason for the betrayal; he only shows Jesus' pain.

For today: Jesus knows our weaknesses and still invites us to his table. Instead of looking at the failings of others, we can ask ourselves humbly, "Lord, am I being faithful to you?" And we can ask him for help to follow him wholeheartedly.
exp.15:11:
This verse tells that the risen Jesus showed himself to two disciples who were walking toward the countryside, that is, out of the city. It says he appeared "in another form," or in other words, with an appearance different from the one they knew, so they did not recognize him right away. Many connect this with the more detailed account in Luke 24, the road to Emmaus, although the text does not state this directly.

Mark's account summarizes Jesus' appearances after the resurrection. Earlier, Mary Magdalene had brought the news, and the disciples, sad and weeping, did not believe her. Now these two travelers also give their testimony, and once again the response is doubt. Mark shows that unbelief was common among the first followers. It is worth mentioning that some ancient manuscripts do not include these final verses of Mark.

When God works in ways we do not expect, we can pass by without recognizing him. Ask the Lord for attentive eyes, and do not dismiss what others tell you about his work without examining it with humility.
exp.10:8:
This verse tells us that the people walking ahead of Jesus and those following behind were shouting joyfully, "Hosanna!" This word comes from Hebrew and means something like "save us now," and it was also used as a cry of praise. They said that blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord, that is, sent by God.

The ones speaking are the disciples and the crowd that accompanied Jesus as he entered Jerusalem riding on a colt, which is a young donkey. They spread their cloaks and branches as a sign of honor, as was done for a king. Many saw in Jesus the long-awaited Messiah, a descendant of David.

For today: before asking anything of Jesus, take a moment to praise him and to acknowledge him as your Lord. Receiving him with a sincere heart is better than following the crowd out of habit or emotion alone.
exp.9:7:
Jesus says that the man and the woman who marry stop being two separate lives and become "one flesh." This speaks of a very deep union: of the body, of shared life, and of the family they form together. The word "so then" in the verse means "therefore." And "one flesh" does not mean that they lose their personality, but that their lives are joined together in a special way.

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees, who asked him whether it was lawful for a husband to divorce his wife. He does not answer with a rule from Moses, but returns to God's original plan in Genesis, when he created the man and the woman. In this way he shows that marriage has a higher purpose than mere convenience.

For today: if you are married, care for the unity with your spouse. Consult each other on decisions, speak with sincerity, and do not let other interests separate you. If you are not married, value and respect the marriages of others.
exp.11:40:
He says that Jesus sat opposite the offering chest, which was a place in the temple where people deposited their money. From there he watched how each person gave. Many rich people put in large amounts. "Chest" here refers to a box or container for offerings, not to a boat or the ark of the covenant.

Jesus had just warned against the teachers of the law who sought honors and took advantage of widows while appearing to be pious. Now, in the temple, he watches those who give. Mark prepares us for the contrast: a poor widow appears, and Jesus will teach his disciples what God values in an offering.

Today we can remember that God looks not only at the amount, but at the heart. Before we give, serve, or pray, let us ask ourselves: am I doing it to be seen, or out of sincere love for God?
exp.0:3:
Mark presents John the Baptist in the wilderness. He was baptizing and announcing a baptism of repentance. "Repentance" means turning around, returning to God. "Forgiveness" means pardon. Thus, the baptism showed that the person wanted to leave their sin behind and receive God's forgiveness.

Mark, the narrator, explains that John fulfills what Isaiah had announced: a messenger who prepares the way of the Lord. That is why John calls the people to confess their sins, because Jesus is about to appear. The wilderness, far from the noise of the crowds, helped people stop and listen.

Today we can prepare the way of the Lord with honesty. Take a few minutes to tell God in prayer what you need to correct, without excuses, and trust that He forgives. Then take one concrete step of change, such as asking forgiveness from someone.
exp.7:29:
This verse says that Jesus firmly charged his disciples not to tell anyone who he was. The word "charged" in the verse above is the same idea as the source's comment, so no separate explanation is needed here.

Jesús had just asked his disciples who the people thought he was, and then who they themselves believed him to be. Peter answered, "You are the Christ." Right after that, Jesus asked them to keep silent. Many people were thinking of a Messiah who would triumph with political power. Jesus, however, began to explain that he would suffer, be rejected, die, and rise again. Scholars explain this silence in several ways, but the context suggests he wanted to prevent misunderstandings about his mission.

For today: knowing Jesus does not consist only in repeating the right titles. We must learn to follow him as he really is, including on the path of humility and service.
exp.3:8:
Jesus ends the parable of the sower with an invitation: whoever has ears to hear, let him hear. He means more than the physical ear; he means listening carefully and with a willingness to obey. The word "hear" here means receiving and putting into practice what is said.

Jesus is teaching a crowd beside the Sea of Galilee. He has just described how the seed falls on different kinds of ground and only in good soil does it bear fruit. With this phrase he invites them to consider which of those kinds of ground resembles their own heart. Later, in private, he explains the meaning to his disciples.

For today: before you open the Bible or listen to a teaching, ask God for an attentive and willing heart. Then choose one specific thing you have heard and put it into practice this week.
exp.12:3:
Four of the disciples, Peter, James, John and Andrew, ask Jesus two things: when the event he spoke of about the temple will happen, and what sign will show that everything is about to be fulfilled.

Jesús had just said that the great temple in Jerusalem would be thrown down. The disciples, sitting with him on the Mount of Olives across from the temple, ask him privately. They want to know more. Jesús does not give them a date, but begins with a warning: that no one should deceive them. Scholars debate how this answer relates to the destruction of the temple and to the end of the age.

Today, before we worry about dates and signs, Jesus invites us to stay alert and not to believe just anyone who speaks in his name. Knowing his Word well protects us from deception.
exp.12:8:
Jesus warns his disciples: "Take heed to yourselves", that is, be watchful and alert. He tells them they will be handed over to councils (Jewish courts), beaten in the synagogues, and brought before governors and kings for his sake. This will be a witness, an opportunity to make Christ known.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, before his crucifixion. He explains that wars and disasters are not yet the end, but only the beginning of sorrows. He wants to prepare them so that they will not be frightened or lose their faith when persecution comes. Then he promises that the Holy Spirit will give them what to say.

Today, if we face mockery or rejection for following Jesus, we can see it as an opportunity to bear witness, trusting that God accompanies us and gives us wisdom.
exp.0:41:
This verse tells us that, as soon as Jesus said, "I will; be thou clean," the leprosy left the man at once. The phrase "as soon as he had spoken" in the verse above is the one that gives the sense of "as soon as he finished speaking." "Straightway" means "immediately," and "he was cleansed" means that he was made healthy and clean.

A leper had knelt before Jesus and said to him: "If thou wilt, thou canst make me clean." Jesus, moved with compassion, touched him and healed him with his word. In that time, leprosy (or similar skin diseases) separated a person from others. For that reason, this healing was also a restoration to life in community.

Today we can come to Jesus with sincerity, even with our most hidden wounds or those that bring shame. He does not turn away from us. We can ask him with confidence and leave the answer in his hands.
exp.13:32:
Jesus takes Peter, James, and John with him, the three closest to him. The text shows Jesus openly revealing what he feels.

Mark tells this in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before Jesus is arrested. Shortly before, Peter had promised that he would never deny him, and all the disciples said the same. Now Jesus leaves the others behind and asks these three to stay close to him, because the hour of his suffering is near.

For today: you do not have to pretend to be strong before God. Jesus felt fear and anguish, and still he prayed. You can bring your fear to God honestly, and also seek out trusted people to stand with you in difficult moments.
exp.9:31:
They were on the road going up to Jerusalem, and Jesus was walking ahead of them. The people were astonished and uneasy. Those who followed him were afraid. Then Jesus took the twelve disciples aside and began to tell them what was going to happen to him.

The one who tells the story is Mark. Jesus had just spoken about what it costs to follow him and about God's reward, even when it comes with persecution. Now he draws near to Jerusalem, and in the verses that follow he announces his betrayal, his death, and his resurrection. The text does not say exactly why they were afraid; it is likely that they sensed something serious was coming.

For today: Jesus does not hide how hard the way is. We can follow him with fear, but without letting go of his hand, trusting that he goes ahead of us and that his road ends in life.
exp.7:3:
The disciples answer Jesus with a question: from where could anyone get enough bread to feed so many people in such a remote place? The verse asks how a man could satisfy these people with bread here in the wilderness. Here the wilderness means a lonely place, far from towns.

Jesus had just said that he felt compassion for the crowd, that they had been with him for three days and had nothing to eat. The disciples speak looking only at what seems impossible. It is striking that Jesus had already fed a crowd before (Mark 6), and still they hesitate. Some think this shows how easy it is to forget what God has already done.

For today: when a need seems too great, do not stay only with what you do not have. Remember what God has already done for you, and bring to Jesus the little you have, like the seven loaves.
exp.8:45:
It says there is a place of judgment, called "Gehenna," where the "worm" does not die and the fire is not put out. Gehenna was the Greek name for the valley of Hinnom near Jerusalem, which Jesus uses as a picture of final punishment. "Occasion to fall" means whatever makes us stumble and sin. The verse is repeated several times in this passage.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. He has just warned them about causing others to stumble, and he uses strong, deliberately exaggerated language to show how serious sin is. No one thinks Jesus is asking for literal self-mutilation; the images teach that it is worth giving up anything in order not to lose life with God. Christians understand in different ways what that punishment is like, but all of them see the seriousness of the warning.

For today: think about which habit, friendship, or content makes you stumble, and decide today, with God's help, to stay away from it.
exp.12:33:
Here Jesus compares his coming to a man who goes on a long journey and leaves his house in the care of his servants. He gives them authority and gives each one a task. To the doorkeeper, the one who guards the door, he commands that he stay alert. ("Watch" means to keep awake, not to become careless.)

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, while teaching them about the future. He has just said that no one knows the day or the hour of his return. That is why he uses this comparison: while the Lord is out of sight, each person has a responsibility and must stay awake.

For today: do not live waiting in fear, but in faithfulness. Ask yourself what task God has given you in your family, your work, or your church, and carry it out today with care and with love.
exp.14:29:
Mark 15:30 says that some people were mocking Jesus on the cross and calling out to him to save himself by coming down from it. The mockery is repeated here in an ironic way: they ask for a miracle, but without faith, only to ridicule him.

The ones speaking were passersby, and they did it while shaking their heads in contempt. They remembered what had been said about Jesus: that he would destroy the temple and raise it up in three days. For them, seeing Jesus nailed to the cross proved that his words were false. They did not understand that his surrender was part of God's plan.

Often we believe that God only acts when he takes away pain or gives us quick ways out. Jesus remained on the cross out of love. When you face mockery or suffering for doing what is right, remember that faithfulness to God does not always look like success.
exp.13:36:
This verse tells that Jesus returned from the place where he had been praying and found his disciples asleep. He spoke to Peter and called him by his earlier name, Simon. He asked him whether he was sleeping and whether he had not been able to stay awake even one hour. The word "watch" in the verse means to stay awake and alert. Where the verse says "findeth," it means "found."

Jesus is in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before his arrest. He had just prayed with great anguish, asking the Father to take the cup of suffering away from him, a picture of the suffering that was coming. He had asked Peter, James, and John to stay with him. His question is a rebuke, but it also shows his sorrow at being left alone.

For today: when life becomes hard, do not wait until you feel strong to pray. Set aside a simple, steady moment to speak with God, and ask a trusted person to pray with you.
exp.11:18:
The Sadducees say to Jesus that Moses left a law: if a married man died without having children, his brother was to marry the widow and have children with her, so that the name of the dead man would not be lost. The phrase "raise up seed" means to give descendants, to have children for the dead brother. "Seed" here means the same thing: children.

The Sadducees were a religious group who did not believe in the resurrection. They cite the law found in Deuteronomy 25:5-10. They are not asking with sincere searching, but are constructing an exaggerated case, with seven brothers, to make the idea of rising from the dead look ridiculous and to put Jesus in a difficult position.

For today: sometimes we use the Bible to win arguments instead of to know God. Before we ask or debate, let us examine our hearts. Let us come to the Word with humility, willing to be corrected and to discover what God truly wants to teach us.
exp.10:16:
Jesus teaches the people in the temple. He quotes Scripture: the temple was meant to be a house of prayer for all peoples, not only for Israel. He says that they have made it a "den of thieves," that is, a hideout where those who abuse others or take advantage of people take refuge.

Jesus has just entered Jerusalem and drives out those who were buying and selling in the temple. His words combine Isaiah 56:7 and Jeremiah 7:11. Some think the rebuke points to unjust business dealings; others think the trading took the place where foreigners could pray. The religious leaders become angry and look for a way to kill him.

For today: take care that your life and your church have God at the center. Ask yourself whether prayer, honesty, and welcome for others have their place, or whether other interests have pushed them aside.
exp.8:46:
It says that if your eye causes you to sin, it is better to tear it out than to lose your life with God. "Stumbling block" means something that makes you trip or sin. "Hell" is the name of the place of final judgment; "cut it out" means tear it out. Entering the kingdom with one eye is preferable to being thrown in with two.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after warning them about causing others to stumble. He uses exaggerated language, typical of the teachers of his time, to show how serious sin is. Most interpreters think he is not commanding self-mutilation, but rather firmly removing everything that pulls us away from God. How to understand the fire and the worm is debated, but all agree that it is a serious warning.

Today, identify what leads you to sin, for example certain content or a harmful friendship, and make a concrete decision to step away from it.
exp.9:15:
This verse shows Jesus embracing the children. He takes them up in his arms, puts his hands upon them, and blesses them, that is, he asks for God's favor and care over their lives. The phrase "he blessed them" indicates that he did it with affection, again and again, with each child.

The disciples had tried to keep the children away from the people who were bringing them to Jesus, and he became indignant with them. He explained that the kingdom of God belongs to those who are like children, and that it must be received with trust and without personal merit. After this moment, a rich man approaches to ask what he must do to inherit eternal life.

For today: come near to God without trying to impress him, with simplicity and trust. And make sure the children around you feel welcomed, valued, and blessed.
exp.13:7:
Jesus says that this woman did what was within her reach. She went ahead and perfumed his body as preparation for his burial. The phrase "she is come aforehand" means that she did it before the appointed time. "To anoint" means to pour perfume or oil on someone.

Jesus speaks in Bethany, at a supper, while some criticize the woman for the cost of the perfume. He defends her. Shortly afterward Judas goes to betray him. Some understand that she knew what was coming; others, that Jesus gave her gesture a deeper meaning than she herself had in mind. The text does not make this clear.

Today, don't wait until you have a lot to serve God. Do with love what you can, even if others do not understand it. And do not let pass the opportunity to show affection to the person closest to you right now.
exp.13:18:
It says that, when they heard that one of them would betray him, the disciples became sorrowful. Each one, separately, asked Jesus: "Is it I?" The phrase about being sorrowful means feeling grief or pain, and the phrase about "one by one" means each one in turn.

Jesus is having supper with the twelve, the night before his death. He has just announced that one of those who eat with him will betray him. The disciples do not point to anyone; rather, they ask themselves, which shows that they took the warning seriously and did not feel entirely sure of themselves.

For today: instead of thinking right away about the failings of others, we can ask God to examine our own heart. A sincere question like "Is it I?" keeps us humble and attentive, and leads us to depend on the grace of Jesus.
exp.3:4:
Another part of the seed fell on rocky ground, that is, on soil with stones and only a thin layer of earth on top. The seed sprouted quickly ("sprang up") because the soil was shallow. "Rocky ground" refers to soil full of rock, and "quickly" means right away.

Jesus is teaching a crowd beside the Sea of Galilee. He uses this parable of the sower to explain how different people receive his message. Later in this same chapter, he himself explains that this kind of ground represents those who receive the word with joy but without firm roots.

Today it invites us to examine the depth of our faith. A quick enthusiasm is not enough; we need roots. We can cultivate them through daily prayer, constant reading of the Bible, and Christian community, so that our faith can withstand difficulties.
exp.5:50:
He says that Jesus got into the boat where his disciples were, and at that moment the wind died down. They were completely overwhelmed, nearly unable to react, and they marveled at what they saw. The word "boat" here refers to a small fishing boat.

Mark tells this after the feeding of the loaves. The disciples were rowing at night against the wind, and Jesus came walking on the sea. They were frightened because they thought it was a ghost, but He said to them, "It is I; do not be afraid." The next verse explains that they had not understood the matter of the loaves, because their hearts were hardened or closed.

Today, when a storm frightens you, remember what Jesus has already done for you. His presence can bring peace, even when you do not yet understand everything that is happening.
exp.14:25:
This verse says that over Jesus' cross there was a written sign that stated the reason for his condemnation. The sign read "THE KING OF THE JEWS," and it named the charge against him.

Mark, as the narrator, tells us that the Roman soldiers crucified Jesus. It was Roman custom to display the crime of the condemned person in plain view. The charge is connected to what Pilate had asked him: whether he was the king of the Jews. For the authorities it was a mockery and a political accusation, but Mark shows, with irony, a truth they did not understand. Jesus is truly King.

For today: Jesus reigns in a way that is different from the world's way, through self-giving and love. We can ask ourselves whether we allow him to be King in our decisions, and trust that his path of humility is the right path.
exp.4:15:
This verse says that the people who had seen everything told those who came along. They explained to them what had happened to the man who had been possessed, and also what had happened with the pigs.

The ones speaking are the witnesses, probably the men who tended the pigs and others who saw the scene. Jesus had just freed this man, and the animals had rushed into the sea. The people who came were frightened and wanted explanations. But the story that follows shows that, even after hearing it, they asked Jesus to leave. The text does not say exactly why, although fear and the loss of the animals may be part of the reason.

For today: telling what one has seen is important, but so is how we respond. We may see the work of God and become afraid that it will disturb our comfort. Let us ask God for an open heart to receive Jesus, even when he sometimes unsettles us.
exp.8:11:
Jesus answers his disciples that Elijah does indeed come first and "restores all things," that is, he prepares and puts the people in order for God. Then he asks them a separate question: if that is so, why do the Scriptures say that the Son of man must suffer many things and be "set at nought," that is, despised and rejected?

Jesus speaks with Peter, James, and John after coming down from the mountain of the transfiguration. They were confused by the idea of rising from the dead and by what the scribes taught about Elijah. Jesus explains to them that the Messiah would not come in immediate glory, but would first pass through suffering. In the following verse he says that Elijah has already come, and many understand this to refer to John the Baptist.

For today: God sometimes carries out his plans by paths different from those we expect. Trust in him even when his work passes through pain or humility.
exp.8:23:
This verse shows a father crying out with all his heart. He says that he does believe in Jesus, but he admits that his faith is weak and asks for help to believe more. The sentence about the wording needs care: the verse reads "straightway" and "cried out," so I will rewrite that comment in those terms. "Straightway" means "immediately," and "cried out" means "shouted loudly."

A desperate father has brought his son, who has suffered since childhood from an evil spirit. The disciples were not able to heal him. Jesus tells him that all things are possible for the one who believes, and the man answers honestly: he trusts, but he also has doubts. Jesus does not reject him, and shortly afterward he heals the boy.

For today: you do not have to pretend to have perfect faith. You can tell God honestly what you believe and what it costs you to believe, and ask him to strengthen your trust in him.
exp.8:48:
