It says that everyone will be "salted with fire," and that every sacrifice will be "salted with salt." Here "salted" means preserved, purified, or seasoned. The phrase is brief and difficult, and scholars understand it in several different ways.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, after warning them to remove whatever causes them to stumble. The fire may recall the judgment of Gehenna, or the trials that purify the believer. The salt recalls the sacrifices in the temple, which were offered with salt (Leviticus 2:13). Jesus joins these ideas to speak of a life given over to God.

For today: when God uses trials to cleanse your life, do not run from them. Ask him to remove what harms you, and that your words and your dealings bring flavor and peace to others.
exp.10:31:
This verse shows the religious leaders talking among themselves. They reason: if they say John's baptism was "of men," they will "fear the people," that is, they will be afraid of how the crowd will react. The reason is that "all men counted" John, meaning everyone held the opinion and believed that he "was a prophet indeed."

Jesus is in the temple, and the chief priests, scribes, and elders ask him by what authority he does his works. He answers with a question about John. They are trapped: if they say "from heaven," they should have believed; if they say "of men," the people would be angry. So in the end they say, "We cannot tell."

For today: ask yourself whether you are seeking the truth or only want to please others. Asking God for the courage to answer honestly, even when it costs you, is better than hiding behind a comfortable answer.
exp.11:32:
He says that loving God with the whole being (heart, mind, soul and strength) and loving one's neighbor as oneself is worth more than all whole burnt offerings and sacrifices. Whole burnt offerings were offerings that were burned up completely on the altar. The phrase "to love his neighbour as himself" is the same wording used in the verse above.

This is spoken by a scribe, a teacher of the law. He had asked Jesus which commandment is the most important, and Jesus answered with love for God and neighbor. Now the scribe repeats that teaching and concludes that love matters more than the offerings in the temple. Jesus praises him and tells him that he is not far from the kingdom of God.

For today: faith is not limited to rituals or religious activities. This week, do one concrete act of love toward someone close to you, such as listening patiently or helping them, and offer it to God as sincere worship.
exp.15:0:
It says that when the Sabbath, the Jewish day of rest, was over, three women bought fragrant spices. They were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome. The word "spices" here does not mean medicines, but perfumes and fragrant oils. The phrase "anoint him" means putting those perfumed oils on the body of Jesus.

Mark tells what happened after the death and burial of Jesus. The women waited until the Sabbath had passed so they could work again. It was customary to honor the dead in this way. They did not expect a resurrection; they went out of love and sorrow to care for his body. The next verse shows that they were wondering who would roll away the stone for them.

For today: although they did not understand everything, they loved Jesus through concrete actions and took the first step. God often meets us in the midst of that simple faithfulness. Today, do something small out of love for Him, even if you do not see everything resolved.
exp.5:32:
The verse tells that many people saw Jesus and his disciples leave in the boat, and they recognized them. So, from several towns, they ran on foot along the shore and got to the place before them. There they gathered around Jesus. The words "came together" and "gathered" in the verse mean that they came to him and grouped together.

Jesus had just invited his disciples to rest apart, because they did not even have time to eat. Mark, who is telling the story, shows that the plan for rest was interrupted. When they landed, Jesus was not put out: on seeing the crowd, he felt compassion and began to teach them.

For today: when your plans for rest are interrupted by the needs of others, ask God for a compassionate heart like Jesus'. Also remember that rest is good and necessary, and Jesus himself recommended it.
exp.9:4:
Jesus answers the Pharisees that Moses wrote that law of divorce "for the hardness of your heart." That is, it was not God's ideal, but a concession to people's stubbornness and lack of compassion. The words "he wrote you this precept" refer to the certificate of divorce that the law allowed.

The Pharisees ask him a question to test him about whether it is lawful for a husband to divorce his wife. Jesus turns the question back to them, and they cite Moses. Then Jesus explains that this rule addressed a real problem, but did not show God's original purpose. Then he takes them back to the beginning of creation, to God's design for marriage.

For today: when we think about marriage or any relationship, let us seek not only what is permitted, but what pleases God. Let us ask him for a tender heart, willing to forgive, listen, and be faithful.
exp.13:58:
This verse says that the witnesses against Jesus could not agree with one another. The phrase about "agreeing" means matching up or fitting together. Even after they repeated their accusation about the temple, their accounts did not line up.

Mark tells us what happened at the trial before the Sanhedrin, the council of Jewish leaders. They were looking for evidence to condemn Jesus, but the witnesses were lying. The law required that two or more witnesses agree (Deuteronomy 19:15), and even so they did not manage it. The exact details of their disagreement are not explained in the text.

For today: a lie tends to fall apart, but not always right away. We can trust that God cares for the truth, even when we are falsely accused. And we should guard our words, always speaking honestly about other people.
exp.5:11:
This verse tells us that the twelve disciples went out to carry out the mission Jesus had given them. They went from place to place declaring that people should turn away from their sins and change their hearts. The word translated "repent" means changing one's mind and direction, turning the heart toward God and leaving sin behind. The word "preached" means proclaiming a message aloud.

Jesus himself had sent the twelve out two by two, with simple instructions: to accept the hospitality offered to them and not to insist where they were not welcomed. Mark, the narrator, shows that they repeat the same call Jesus made at the beginning of his ministry. Afterward we see that their works accompanied their words, and that the fame of Jesus reached as far as Herod.

For today: speaking about God is not only giving information, but lovingly inviting a real change. We can do this with humility, without pressuring anyone, trusting that God is at work in the heart of each person.
exp.8:36:
Jesus says that whoever receives one child "in my name," that is, out of love for him and as his follower, receives him. And whoever receives him in fact receives the Father who sent him.

Jesus speaks to the twelve disciples. Earlier they had argued on the road about who was the greatest. He teaches them that greatness is serving, and he uses a child, who in that time had little social standing, as an example of the people worth caring for.

Today we can treat small children and people who are unimportant in the eyes of the world with respect and patience. For example, giving time to a child, listening to them, or helping them at church or at home, knowing that in this way we serve Christ himself.
exp.1:23:
The Pharisees see Jesus' disciples pulling heads of grain as they walk through a field, and they challenge him: "Why do they on the sabbath day that which is not permitted?" Here "permitted" means allowed by the law. They accuse the disciples of breaking the day of rest.

The Pharisees speaking here were a religious group very careful to keep the law and its traditions. Picking grain to eat was not theft, since the law allowed a person to take grain from a neighbor's field with the hand. Their complaint was that, by their rules, doing this counted as work on the sabbath. Jesus answers with the example of David, showing that the law has a purpose of mercy.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are using rules to judge others and forgetting compassion. Obeying God includes loving people, not only watching what they do.
exp.4:29:
This verse says that Jesus realized that power had gone out of him. The word "virtue" here does not mean a moral quality but power or strength to heal. "Immediately" is the sense of "right away," and "in the press" means "in the crowd." Then Jesus turns around and asks who touched his clothes.

Jesus speaks in the middle of a crowd that was pressing against him. A woman who had suffered from bleeding for twelve years, with faith, had touched his cloak, and she was healed. The disciples are surprised by the question, but Jesus was looking for one particular person. The texts do not explain in detail how he knew this, so we leave it as a mystery.

Today: being near Jesus in a crowd is one thing, and coming to him with faith and trust is another. Speak to him sincerely, even if you feel small; he sees you and hears you.
exp.12:5:
Jesus warns that many people will come using his name and saying, "I am the Christ," that is, the promised Messiah. The result will be that they will deceive many.

Jesus speaks to his disciples Peter, James, John and Andrew, on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him when the temple would fall and what the sign would be. Before giving any signs, Jesus asks them to be careful: the first thing is that no one deceives them. Scholars understand in various ways how much of this discourse refers to the fall of Jerusalem and how much to the end of the age.

For today: do not believe just anyone who speaks about Jesus with confidence. Compare what you hear with what the Scriptures teach, and ask God for wisdom.
exp.13:33:
Jesus tells his three closest friends that he feels a sorrow so deep it nearly kills him. "Unto death" is a way of saying the pain is enormous. He asks them to stay there and watch, that is, to stay awake and alert.

Jesus is in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before he is arrested. He speaks with Peter, James, and John, and opens his heart to them. Mark shows a Jesus who is truly human, who feels anguish before the cross. Right after this, he falls to pray and surrenders himself to the Father's will.

When you feel a very great sadness, do not hide it. Jesus himself asked for company and prayed with sincerity. Look for someone you trust who can stay with you, and speak to God honestly, offering him also what you feel.
exp.13:31:
They come to a place called Gethsemane. There Jesus tells his disciples to sit here while he prays.

Jesus has just announced that Peter will deny him, and all the disciples promised that they would not abandon him. Now, that same night, Jesus withdraws to pray before he is arrested. Later the text shows his deep anguish. Gethsemane was a garden or place near the Mount of Olives, though Mark gives no further details.

When hard times come, let us imitate Jesus: before facing pressure, let us look for a quiet place to pray. We do not need to have everything worked out or to feel strong; we can come to God with honesty and ask him for support.
exp.10:22:
Jesus says that whoever speaks to this mountain and orders it to be removed and cast into the sea, without doubting in his heart but believing that what he says will happen, will see it come to pass.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after Peter noticed that the fig tree he had cursed had dried up. His first answer is to have faith in God. Then he goes on to speak about prayer and forgiveness. Many understand "this mountain" as a picture of a huge obstacle, although some connect it with the mountain of the temple. The text does not fully clarify this.

For today: when you face something that seems impossible, pray with confidence in God, not in your own strength. Ask him in faith, and with a heart that forgives others, as Jesus teaches right after.
exp.15:5:
He says that a young man dressed in white, who was inside the tomb, calms the women who arrived frightened. He tells them that they are looking for Jesus of Nazareth, the one who was crucified, but that he has already risen and is not there. He points them to the place where they had laid him.

The one speaking from the tomb is described by Mark only as a young man; other gospels call him an angel, and here nothing more is made clear. The women had gone to anoint Jesus' body and found the stone rolled away and the tomb empty. He gives them the news of the resurrection to take away their fear and to give them a mission.

For today: when fear or doubt surround you, remember that Jesus lives. Do not look for him among dead things, but trust the risen Christ and let his victory give you courage.
exp.1:16:
Jesus answers with a simple comparison: whoever is well does not look for a doctor; the one who is sick does. He says he did not come to call the "righteous," that is, those who think themselves good and in no need, but sinners.

Jesus is eating in a house with tax collectors (men despised for working for Rome) and with other people regarded as sinners. The scribes and Pharisees are scandalized and criticize him. Jesus replies with this saying. Some think there is a touch of irony toward those who considered themselves righteous; the text does not make this entirely clear.

For today: acknowledge with humility your need for God, and do not stay away because you feel unworthy. And draw near with kindness to those others reject, as Jesus did.
exp.13:66:
A servant girl of the high priest saw Peter warming himself by the fire. She looked at him closely and said, "You also were with Jesus of Nazareth." The words "saw" and "looking at him" mean "saw" and "looking at him closely."

While Jesus was being judged and mistreated inside, Peter had followed him from a distance and was outside, in the courtyard. The servant girl speaks because she recognizes him as part of Jesus' group. This is the first moment of pressure that leads Peter to deny his Master, just as Jesus had foretold.

For today: sometimes we are tested not by great threats but by a simple question in an uncomfortable place. It is wise to decide ahead of time to be honest about our faith, with gentleness. And if we fail, let us remember that Peter was forgiven and restored.
exp.14:37:
The explanation says that at the moment Jesus died, the great curtain of the temple was torn in two, from top to bottom. The curtain was a thick cloth. To tear here means it was ripped apart. "From top to bottom" means from the top down.

Mark, who writes the account, tells this right after Jesus cried out loudly and breathed his last. It was probably the curtain that separated the Most Holy Place, though the text does not make this clear. That it was torn from top to bottom suggests an act of God, not of people. Many understand that the way to God was opened by the death of Jesus. Right after this, the Roman centurion recognizes that Jesus was the Son of God.

Today you can draw near to God with confidence, without fear or go-betweens, because Christ opened the way. Speak to him in prayer just as you are, today.
exp.12:14:
The explanation says that whoever is on the roof of his house should not go down or enter the house to take anything out. "Roof" is the flat top of the houses of that time, where people rested or worked. The instruction is urgent: one must flee quickly, without stopping for anything.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, before his death. He warns them about difficult times in Judea. Many believe he refers first of all to the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, and others also see a future fulfillment. He gives this warning so that they will not be confused or caught unprepared.

For today: when God clearly shows you that you must turn away from a danger or a temptation, obey without delay. Do not cling to what you leave behind; trust that God takes care of you.
exp.11:0:
Jesus tells a story about a man who planted a vineyard. He surrounded it with a hedge, which was a fence to protect it. He dug a winepress, which is the place where grapes were trodden to get the juice out. He built a tower, probably for watching over the vineyard. Then he rented it out to tenants, that is, he leased it to people to work it, and he went away to a distant country.

Jesus is speaking in Jerusalem, in the temple, before priests, scribes and elders who were questioning his authority. This parable recalls the vineyard of Isaiah 5, where the vineyard represents Israel. Many understand that the tenants are the leaders of the people, although the text develops this further later on.

For today: everything we have, such as time, gifts and possessions, we have received from God to look after. We can ask ourselves whether we are managing it with gratitude and responsibility.
exp.6:12:
Jesus says that the Pharisees make void, that is, leave without force, the word of God through the tradition they themselves handed down. Making void means taking away its power. He adds that they do many things like this.

Jesus is speaking with Pharisees and teachers of the law, who criticized him because his disciples ate without the ritual washing. He answers them with an example: declaring something dedicated to God as an offering, and using that as an excuse not to help their parents. In this way they broke the commandment to honor father and mother.

For today: let us examine whether any custom, religious or family, leads us to avoid a clear command of God. If a tradition keeps us from loving and caring for others, it is wise to return to Scripture and obey it from the heart.
exp.6:7:
Jesus says that the Pharisees and the teachers of the law set aside what God commanded and hold on to customs made up by people. As an example he mentions the ceremonial washing of pots and cups, and he adds that they do many similar things.

Jesus is speaking to Pharisees and scribes who criticized him because his disciples ate without performing that ritual washing. He does not condemn every tradition, but he rebukes those who place it above the word of God. That is why he quotes Isaiah: religion that is only on the lips, without the heart, is worth nothing.

Today we can ask whether some religious, family, or church customs have come to matter more than obeying God. Let us examine our practices in the light of the Bible, and ask God for a sincere heart, one that truly loves and does not merely appear devout.
exp.4:27:
This verse shows us what the woman was thinking before she came near Jesus. She told herself that if she could just touch his clothes, she would be whole, that is, she would be healed of her illness. The word "touch" in the verse above is the one this explanation is describing.

Mark tells us that she had suffered from bleeding for twelve years, had spent all her money on doctors, and was getting worse. She had heard about Jesus, so she came up behind him through the crowd. She was a woman with no human hope left, and her faith led her to act with simplicity and courage. Afterward Jesus confirms that something had happened.

For today: when you feel there is no way out, do not wait until everything is sorted out before you come to Jesus. Go to Him with your need just as it is, with a small but sincere faith, and trust that He receives you.
exp.5:53:
When Jesus and his disciples got out of the boat, the people there recognized him right away. The verse says "they knew him," and here that simply means they identified him as Jesus.

Mark tells this right after Jesus walked on the water. The disciples still did not understand what had happened with the loaves, and the text says their hearts were hardened, meaning closed off or confused. By contrast, the people of Gennesaret recognize him quickly and bring their sick to him. Some see here a gentle criticism of the disciples' slowness; the text does not say so in more detail.

Today we can ask God for an attentive heart to recognize Jesus in everyday life. And, like those people, we can bring our needs and the needs of others to him with confidence.
exp.13:51:
This verse tells that a young man who was following Jesus was seized by the men who were arresting the Lord. He let go of the linen cloth that covered him and escaped running, with nothing on his body.

Mark tells of the arrest of Jesus in Gethsemane. Just before, all the disciples had fled. Mark is the only one who mentions this young man and does not give his name. Some think it was Mark himself, but the Bible does not say so, so it is only a possibility. What is clear is that even those closest to Jesus were left exposed and afraid.

For today: following Jesus can frighten us and show us our weakness. If you have ever run away or stayed silent out of fear, do not stay in shame. Jesus continues on his way for you, and you can return to him with humility and ask him for courage.
exp.13:65:
The explanation says that Peter was below, in the courtyard of the high priest's house, and that one of the servant girls of that house came up to him. The sentence ends with a semicolon because the story continues in the next verse.

Mark tells the scene as a narrator. Upstairs, Jesus is being judged, mocked, and beaten. Downstairs, Peter had followed him from a distance and mixed in with the crowd to see what was happening. This moment marks the beginning of his fall: Jesus had foretold that Peter would deny him, and here that begins to come true. The steadfastness of Jesus above contrasts sharply with Peter's fear below.

For today: sometimes we do not fail before great attacks, but before a simple question from someone with no power. It is good to recognize our weakness, to pray before trials, and to remember that Jesus restores those who grieve their failure, as he did with Peter.
exp.13:55:
This verse says that many people gave false accusations against Jesus, but their stories did not match each other. The explanation of the word "agreed" is that it means their accounts did not agree or line up with one another. Without agreement, their accusations did not serve as proof.

The narrator is Mark, and he describes the night of the trial before the Jewish council, presided over by the high priest. The leaders already wanted to condemn Jesus and were looking for witnesses who would justify his death. Since they found nothing true, they turned to lies. Even so, the lies could not even agree with one another, which showed that Jesus was innocent.

For today: when someone accuses you unfairly, do not despair. The truth needs no embellishment, and lies often trip over themselves. Trust God, keep acting with integrity, and avoid responding with deception.
exp.2:25:
It says that if Satan rises up against himself and his kingdom is divided, he cannot stand; his power would come to an end. The phrase "rise up" in the verse above is the same idea as "set himself against," and "hath an end" means that it comes to an end.

Jesus is speaking to some scribes who had come down from Jerusalem. They were saying that He drove out demons by the power of the prince of demons. Jesus answers with simple logic: a kingdom or a house divided is destroyed. So it would make no sense for Satan to cast out his own demons. Rather, Jesus shows that He acts with a power stronger than evil.

For today: division destroys, including among us. In the family, in the church, or at work, let us pursue peace, speak with respect, and seek unity before winning an argument.
exp.3:25:
Jesus continues teaching in parables and compares the kingdom of God to a man who scatters seed on the ground. The word "seed" here is the one used in the verse. The phrase "he said further" in the verse means "he also said" or "he went on saying."

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples beside the Sea of Galilee. He has just asked them to pay close attention to what they hear. This parable, which appears only in Mark, shows that the kingdom of God advances in a way the sower does not fully control. The verses that follow explain it: the seed grows by itself.

For today: be faithful in your part, such as praying, teaching your children, or serving with love, and trust that God is the one who gives the growth. You do not need to see immediate results to know that God is at work.
exp.8:28:
Jesus says that "this kind", that is, this type of evil spirit, cannot come out by any other means, but only "by prayer and fasting". The phrases "kind" and "only" in the verse above are what the explanation is describing: "kind" means type or sort, and "only" means except. Some early copies of Mark do not include "and fasting", and scholars debate this.

Jesus speaks at home, alone with his disciples. They had not been able to drive a spirit out of a boy, and Jesus had just healed him. His answer shows that this power was not their own but depended on God. Shortly afterward, Jesus announces to them his death and resurrection.

For today: when problems overwhelm us, let us not rely only on our experience or strength. Before acting, take a moment to pray calmly, asking for God's help. If you decide to fast, do so with humility and wisdom, taking care of your health.
exp.8:18:
Jesus answers with strong words: he calls the people around him an "unbelieving generation," asks how long he must remain with them and how long he must put up with them, meaning bear with them patiently. Then he says, "Bring him to me."

Jesus speaks this as he comes down from the mountain, when a father tells him that his disciples were unable to free his son. His complaint seems directed at everyone: disciples, father, and crowd. Some think he is moved by sorrow over the lack of faith. Even so, he does not reject the boy but asks that he be brought to him.

For today: when your faith feels small or you have fallen short, do not turn away from Jesus. Bring him your need honestly. He knows our weakness and, even so, keeps saying, "Bring him to me."
exp.5:13:
It says that King Herod heard about Jesus, because his name had already become known everywhere. Herod then thought that Jesus was John the Baptist, raised from the dead. That is why he said that mighty works were showing themselves in him.

Mark tells this right after the disciples went out to preach and to heal. In this way, the message of Jesus spread even further. The one speaking is Herod Antipas, who had ordered John killed. His reaction suggests a troubled conscience, and the Bible says no more than what he felt inside. Others thought Jesus was Elijah or a prophet.

For today: it is not enough to hear about Jesus or to have ideas about him. We can ask ourselves sincerely who he is for us, and answer him with faith and obedience, not with fear or mere curiosity.
exp.4:20:
Jesus crossed back again by boat to the other side of the lake, and a great crowd gathered around him. He stayed by the shore. Some old-fashioned words: "passed over" means "crossed over," "the sea" refers to the Sea of Galilee, and "much people" means a large crowd.

Mark tells this as narrator. Jesus had just healed a man in the region of the Gadarenes, on the other shore, and had sent him to tell what God had done for him. Now he returns to territory where people were looking for him. This verse sets the scene for the arrival of Jairus, who asks him for help for his sick daughter.

For today: Jesus is always ready to receive those who seek him, and sometimes the most urgent needs appear in the middle of the crowd. We can come to him with confidence, even when we feel surrounded by noise or hurry, and bring him what weighs on us.
exp.6:28:
Jesus says to the woman, "For this saying, go your way; the devil has gone out of your daughter." He answers her for what she has just said, and assures her that her daughter is already free. "Devil" here means an evil spirit. "Little dogs" are the small dogs of the house.

Jesus speaks with a woman from the region of Tyre, who was not Jewish, and who had begged him for her daughter. He used the image of the children's bread and the little dogs, and she answered with humility and faith, trusting that his goodness reached her as well. Some see in Jesus' words a test of her faith; others, a way of showing that his help would also reach the other peoples.

For today: draw near to God with humility and trust, even if you do not feel worthy. He listens to simple words of faith, and he can act even when you do not see the result right away.
exp.13:23:
Jesus says that the wine in the cup is his blood, by which the new covenant is sealed, that is, a new agreement between God and his people. He says that this blood is poured out for many, which points to his death given up on behalf of others. "Cup" is the drinking vessel, and "many" points to a large crowd.

Jesus speaks with his disciples during the Passover meal, the night before his crucifixion. Passover remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. He gives that meal a new meaning: his death would bring forgiveness and a renewed relationship with God. Christians have understood in different ways how Christ is present in the Supper, but all agree that it remembers his sacrifice.

For today: when you take part in the Lord's Supper, or simply pray, remember with gratitude that your forgiveness cost a great deal. Let that lead you to forgive others generously.
exp.4:11:
This verse tells how the demons that were tormenting a man begged Jesus to send them into the pigs. The word "send" means "send us," and the animals are pigs. They asked to enter those animals instead of being driven away.

It is the unclean spirits who speak, and they speak in the plural because there were many of them. They acknowledge that Jesus has authority over them and that they cannot act without his permission. That is why they request rather than demand. Commentators explain in several ways why they asked for this, and the text itself does not make it clear.

For today: no power of evil is beyond the control of Christ. If you face fear, guilt, or bondage, you can come to Jesus with confidence, because his authority is greater and he cares for you.
exp.9:38:
James and John answer Jesus with confidence: "We can." Jesus confirms that they will indeed drink from his cup and be baptized with his baptism. Here the cup and the baptism are images of the suffering and self-giving that he was about to face.

The two brothers had just asked for the places of highest honor in Jesus' glory. He had told them that they did not know what they were asking. Jesus had already announced his death, but they were thinking of power and recognition. Their answer foretells that they would share in suffering for him. The Bible does not detail here how or when this would happen; some connect it with later persecutions. The other ten became angry afterward.

Following Jesus is not only about receiving honor; it also means faithfulness in hard times. Today we can examine our own desires and ask God for a humble heart, one that serves and remains steadfast even when it costs us.
exp.15:14:
Jesus gives his disciples a command: "Go into all the world." The word "preach" means to announce or proclaim. "The gospel" means the good news of salvation in Christ. "To every creature" means to all people, without exception. It is a clear order: to carry the message to everyone, everywhere.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus. He had just rebuked the eleven for their unbelief and hardness of heart, because they had not believed those who saw him alive. Even so, he does not set them aside; he entrusts them with the greatest mission. It is an act of grace toward men who had doubted. It is worth noting that many scholars point out that this ending of Mark (verses 9 to 20) does not appear in the oldest manuscripts, although its teaching agrees with other passages, such as Matthew 28.

Today you can share the good news with those close to you: your family, your work, your neighborhood. Do it with simple words and with a life that goes with them.
exp.5:39:
They sat down, or settled on the ground, in orderly groups. Some groups had a hundred people and others had fifty. The words "in ranks" mean in groups or rows, and "reclining" here means sitting down or leaning back to eat.

Jesus is with a large crowd in a remote place, and it is already late. He asks his disciples to check how much food they have: only five loaves and two fish. Before multiplying the food, he tells the people to sit down on the green grass. Mark tells this in detail, and some think it shows order and calm; the Bible says nothing more about the reason.

God works with peace and order, even when what we have seems very little. This week, before worrying about what is missing, place in Jesus' hands the little you have and calmly take the step he shows you.
exp.14:31:
The religious leaders mock Jesus and tell him to come down from the cross so that they may see and believe. The two men crucified beside him also insulted him. To revile means to insult or speak with contempt.

The ones speaking are the chief priests and the scribes, who had already handed Jesus over to Pilate. They mock his title as "the King of Israel." They ask for a sign, but their hearts were already closed. The Gospels of Matthew and Luke give more details about the men crucified with him: Luke tells us that one of them later repented. Jesus remained on the cross because his mission was to give his life for us.

Today we can learn not to demand proof from God on our own terms. Faith trusts in Jesus even when we do not understand his way. When someone mocks your faith, respond with patience, remembering that Christ endured far worse mockery.
exp.11:12:
This verse tells us that the religious leaders sent some Pharisees and Herodians to Jesus. Their plan was to catch him in something he said, that is, to trap him with an answer they could use against him. The phrase about sending "unto him" simply means they sent them to him.

Mark tells us what happened right after the parable of the wicked tenants. The religious leaders understood that Jesus was speaking about them, and they wanted to arrest him, but they feared the crowd. The Pharisees and the Herodians were usually opposed to each other, but here they join together against Jesus. What follows is a trick question about taxes.

Today we can learn to examine our hearts when we ask questions. It is good to seek the truth with sincerity. But using questions to attack or humiliate others shows a closed heart. Jesus sees our intentions, and we can come to him with honesty.
exp.4:14:
They came to Jesus and saw the man who had been tormented by a legion of demons. Now he was sitting there, clothed, and thinking clearly. The phrase "in his right mind" means his mind was healthy and in order. Seeing this change, the people were afraid.

Mark is the one telling the story. The men who took care of the pigs had reported what happened, and the people went out to see it. Before, this man lived naked and out of control, and no one could restrain him. Now they see him at peace. The text does not fully explain their fear; it may have been amazement at Jesus' power, or fear over what this meant for them. Then they ask Jesus to leave.

For today: God can restore a life completely. But change can also make us uncomfortable. Let us ask for humility so that we do not shut the door on Jesus out of fear.
exp.8:38:
Jesus tells his disciples not to stop a man who was casting out demons in his name. The reason is simple: whoever does a mighty work in his name will not quickly turn around and speak evil of him. The word "forbid" in the verse means to hinder or stop.

Jesus is speaking with the twelve. John has just told him that they saw someone casting out demons in Jesus' name and tried to stop him, because "he does not follow with us," meaning he was not part of their group. Jesus corrects that attitude of rivalry. Some scholars see here an example of sincere faith that is still incomplete. The text says nothing more about that man.

Today, we can rejoice when others serve Christ sincerely, even if they are not from our church or group. Before we criticize, let us ask whether that person honors Jesus. In this way we protect unity and avoid jealousy.
exp.12:32:
Jesus says: "Take heed" means "be alert, keep your eyes open." "Watch" means to stay awake and attentive. And "pray" means to speak with God. The reason is that no one knows when that time will come, that is, the final moment Jesus has been describing.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, shortly before his death. He has told them about difficult things that will come. He has just said that neither the angels nor the Son know the day, only the Father. That is why he gives them no date, but a call to be prepared, like the doorkeeper who watches over the house.

Today we can live without fear and without trying to guess dates. Instead, let us tend our relationship with God each day: praying regularly, doing good, and living with a heart ready to welcome him, like someone waiting for a dear friend.
exp.12:4:
Jesus answers his disciples' question and begins with a warning: "Watch out," that is, "take heed," so that no one deceives them. Before speaking of dates or signs, Jesus first puts spiritual care in front.

He speaks on the Mount of Olives, opposite the temple. Peter, James, John and Andrew asked him privately when what he had said about the temple would happen and what the sign would be. Jesus does not give them a date, but prepares them. Soon he mentions those who would say, "I am the Christ."

For today: before believing any spiritual message, compare it with what Jesus taught in the Bible. Study Scripture with humility and ask God for wisdom so that you are not carried away by striking but false voices.
exp.14:42:
This verse tells us that Joseph of Arimathea, a respected man and a member of the council (a senator here means a member of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish court), went to see Pilate. The phrase about waiting for the kingdom of God means that he trusted in what God had promised. The word bold means with courage, and the phrase went in to Pilate means that he presented himself before him. He asked for the body of Jesus so that he could bury it.

Mark is the one telling the story. It was Friday afternoon, before the Sabbath, and bodies had to be buried before the day of rest began. The disciples had fled, and only some women were watching from a distance. Asking for the body of a condemned man could be dangerous, but Joseph did it. The texts do not say everything he felt, so we do not know more about his reasons.

For today: sometimes serving God requires courage when others step away. Ask God for the courage to make a concrete act of faithfulness or kindness today, even if it costs you something.
exp.8:30:
Jesus was explaining to his disciples what was going to happen to him. He says that the Son of man, a title Jesus uses for himself, would be handed over into the hands of men, who would kill him, but that on the third day he would rise again.

Jesus speaks privately with the Twelve as they walk through Galilee, and he did not want anyone to know where they were. He wanted to prepare them for his death. Even so, the next verse says that they did not understand and were afraid to ask. Shortly after, they were arguing about who was the greatest.

For today: Jesus did not hide the cost of his path or the hope of the resurrection. If there is something in the Bible we do not understand, let us not be afraid to ask God in prayer and to seek help in his Word.
exp.14:1:
Pilate asks Jesus whether he is the King of the Jews. Jesus answers, "Thou sayest it." It is a brief reply that neither flatly denies nor simply affirms the claim. Some understand it as "Yes, but not in the sense you are thinking." Others read it as a way of not handing Pilate an easy charge. Scholars explain it in various ways.

The religious leaders had brought Jesus, bound, before Pilate, the Roman governor, because only he could hand down a sentence of death. Pilate asks this because Rome cared about any king who might rival the emperor. Afterward, Jesus remains silent before the other accusations.

Today we can learn from Jesus' calm under pressure. When someone accuses you or misunderstands you, there is no need to defend yourself in anger. Ask God for wisdom to know when to speak the truth and when to stay silent with confidence.
exp.0:31:
That evening, after the sun had set, the people brought to Jesus everyone who was sick and everyone who was possessed by demons.

Mark tells what happened in Capernaum, on a day of rest, a Sabbath. Jesus had just healed Simon's mother-in-law. The Jews waited until the day was over, at sunset, to carry the sick and walk with them without breaking the rest. That is why the people came as soon as the day ended. The narrator is Mark, and he shows that Jesus has authority and compassion.

For today: do not wait until everything is resolved before you come to Jesus. Bring Him your burdens and the burdens of others, with confidence and perseverance.
exp.0:19:
This verse tells how Jesus called James and John, sons of Zebedee, while they were mending their nets. They left their father in the boat with the hired workers and followed Jesus. "Straightway" means "right away." The "boat" is the fishing boat, and the "hired workers" were men employed for wages. "Went after him" means they followed him.

Mark describes the beginning of Jesus' ministry in Galilee. Shortly before, Jesus had called Simon and Andrew. Here too Jesus is the one who calls, and the fishermen respond. Mark does not say what they thought or felt; he simply shows their quick response. Their father was not left alone, since there were other workers in the boat.

For today: following Jesus means a real response, not just good intentions. He may not ask you to leave your work today, but he does ask you to put his call above what is comfortable or familiar. Ask yourself which step of obedience you have been putting off, and take that step with confidence.
exp.10:29:
Jesus asks the religious leaders a direct question: was the baptism that John the Baptist preached from heaven, or only from men? The word "or" here is simply "or," and "answer me" is the same as "tell me."

This takes place in the temple in Jerusalem, a few days before the crucifixion. The priests, scribes, and elders had asked Jesus by what authority he was acting. Jesus does not avoid the question, but answers with another, because the authority of John and the authority of Jesus came from the same God. They did not answer honestly, but were thinking about how to look good before the people.

For today: before we answer God, let us examine our hearts. Let us ask ourselves whether we are seeking the truth, or only what suits us or makes us look good to others.
exp.9:26:
Jesus looks at his disciples and tells them that being saved is something human beings cannot achieve by their own strength. But God can, because nothing is impossible for him. The phrase "looking upon them" shows that he observed them closely before he answered.

Jesus has just spoken about the rich young man who went away sad, and about how hard it is for a rich person to enter the kingdom. The disciples are amazed and ask who then can be saved. Jesus answers that salvation depends on the work of God, not on human effort. Right after this, Peter speaks about what they have left behind, and Jesus promises that God does not forget those who follow him.

Today, if you feel unable to change, to forgive, or to be good enough, remember that you are not alone. Ask God for his help with simplicity, trusting that he can do what you cannot.
exp.9:27:
Peter says to Jesus, "Look, we have left everything and followed you." The verse reads "Then Peter began to say unto him, Lo, we have left all, and have followed thee." Peter speaks after Jesus talked with the rich young man, who would not give up his possessions. The disciples were amazed to hear that salvation is impossible for people but possible for God. Peter thinks about what he and his companions did leave behind, and perhaps he hopes for an answer from Jesus about their future. Jesus will respond with a promise, without reproach.

For today: following Jesus always costs something, but it is not in vain. We can hand our sacrifices to him with confidence, remembering that salvation is a gift from God and not a payment for what we give up.
exp.12:2:
This verse tells us that Jesus sat on the Mount of Olives, across from the temple. There, four of his closest disciples (Peter, James, John, and Andrew) came to him privately to ask him a question.

Shortly before this, one of the disciples had admired the great buildings of the temple. Jesus replied that they would be completely torn down. That statement left them troubled, and now they want to understand when it would happen and what sign would announce it. The narrator, Mark, shows us an intimate conversation in which Jesus teaches those who seek to understand.

For today: when something Jesus said confuses or troubles us, we can come to him calmly and ask him, in prayer and by reading his Word. Honest questions do not push him away; they draw us closer to him.
exp.10:23:
Jesus says that whatever we ask for in prayer, we should believe that we have already received it, and it will come to us. Some old words: the phrase for "ask" is the same as "ask," the word for "believe" is the same as "believe," and "it will come to us" means "you will have them." (Note: the glossary terms have been rewritten to match the wording of the verse.)

Jesus speaks to his disciples the day after he cursed the fig tree and cleansed the temple. He has just told them to have faith in God, using the image of a mountain thrown into the sea. Then he connects faith with forgiveness: whoever prays must forgive others. So the promise is not a blank check; it is tied to a life in fellowship with the Father.

Today, pray with sincere confidence that God hears you and is good. Before asking, check your heart: if you hold a grudge against someone, forgive them. Then present your request, resting in the belief that the Father will answer the way He knows is best.
exp.11:39:
Jesus says that some scribes "devour widows' houses," that is, they take advantage of widows and strip them of what little they have. To cover this up, they make "long prayers," that is, they pray at length to appear pious. The phrase "for a pretence" means for show or as a cover. Therefore, he says, they will receive "greater damnation," a more severe condemnation.

Jesus teaches in the temple and warns the crowd about the scribes, who sought honor, the best seats, and public greetings. Widows were often vulnerable. Scholars do not agree on exactly how the scribes took advantage of them: it may have been by charging for services or by mismanaging their property. Right after this, the poor widow appears, giving two small coins, a very strong contrast.

Today we can examine whether our faith is sincere and whether we care for the vulnerable. Prayer and service should go hand in hand with justice and honesty.
exp.5:41:
They all ate and were filled, the explanation says. The word "filled" here means they ate until they were full, with no one left hungry. It was not just a bite for each person: there was enough for everyone.

Mark tells here the story of the feeding of the five thousand. Jesus was in a deserted place with his disciples, and a large crowd followed him. He had compassion on them, taught them, and as evening came, he fed them with five loaves and two fish. The disciples distributed the food that Jesus blessed. The verses that follow say that twelve baskets were left over.

For today: when you feel that what you have is little, offer it to God with confidence. He can use the small to care for many, and his provision is often more than enough.
exp.9:43:
Jesus says that whoever wants to be first, that is, the most important, must make himself a servant of all. Here "servant" means someone who serves others with humility, like a slave who attends to the needs of others.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. Shortly before, James and John had asked him for the places of greatest honor in his kingdom, and the other ten became angry. Jesus explains to them that in the world the powerful rule over others, but among them it must be different. He himself is the example: he came to serve and to give his life for many.

Today we can practice this by looking for a concrete way to help without expecting recognition: at home, at work, or in church, gladly doing a task that no one wants to do.
exp.5:17:
This verse explains why John the Baptist was in prison. John said plainly to Herod, "It is not lawful for you" to have his brother's wife as his wife. The word "lawful" means permitted by the law of God.

The one speaking is the narrator, Mark, recalling an event. When Herod heard about Jesus, he feared that John had risen from the dead. Herod had taken Herodias, who was the wife of his brother Philip. John, as a prophet, dared to correct him, and for this he ended up in prison. Herodias held a grudge against him, although Herod himself respected John.

Today, speaking the truth in love can cost us dearly, but it is an act of faithfulness to God. Let us ask him for courage and humility to speak with respect, and also for a willingness to listen when someone corrects us.
exp.10:20:
Peter remembers what Jesus said the day before and is amazed to see the fig tree dried up. He speaks to Jesus with respect, addressing him as "Master." Your word "cursedst" means that Jesus had spoken words of judgment against the tree, and now the tree has withered away, dying from the root up.

Peter speaks here, and Mark records it within a larger account. Jesus had seen the fig tree with leaves but no fruit (Mark 11:12-14), and then he cleansed the temple. Many understand the fig tree as a sign of a religiosity that appears alive but bears no fruit. Others emphasize only the lesson about faith. Jesus responds by teaching them to trust God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether our faith bears real fruit and not merely outward appearance. Before we ask for something great in prayer, we can trust that God hears and acts according to his will.
exp.4:33:
Jesus speaks to the woman with tenderness and calls her "daughter." He tells her that her faith has made her whole, a word that here can mean healed and also rescued in her whole being. He sends her away to go in peace and to be free of her affliction, which is her illness, seen as a blow that made her suffer.

Jesus speaks to a woman who had suffered from a flow of blood for twelve years. She touched his cloak in secret and was healed. He looks for her with his eyes, not to rebuke her, but so that she will come forward and receive a word of blessing. In this way her healing stops being something hidden and becomes a complete restoration.

For today: come to Jesus with your need, even if you are afraid or feel small. He does not despise a faith that is weak but sincere, and he receives you with kindness.
exp.9:32:
Jesus says that they are going up to Jerusalem, and that there the Son of man, which is the title he uses for himself, will be delivered to the chief priests and to the scribes (the teachers of the law). They will condemn him to death and will deliver him to the Gentiles, that is, to those who were not Jews.

Jesus speaks to the twelve, whom he takes aside. They are on the road toward Jerusalem; he walks ahead, and they follow him, amazed and afraid. For the third time he tells them plainly what awaits him, so that it will not catch them by surprise. Shortly afterward James and John ask him for a place of honor, which shows how hard it was for them to understand.

Jesus walked toward the cross with full awareness and out of love. When following him becomes difficult, we can trust that he already knows the way and goes ahead of us.
exp.14:40:
This verse speaks of the women who watched the crucifixion from a distance. It says that they had already been following Jesus from Galilee and had been caring for him, that is, helping him with what he needed. It also mentions many other women who had come up with him to Jerusalem. The word "came up" is used because Jerusalem sits on high ground, and "Jerusalem" is the city itself.

Here the narrator is Mark. After Jesus' death, and after the centurion recognizes that he was the Son of God, Mark clarifies who these women were: they were not idle onlookers, but faithful disciples from earlier times. They will be witnesses of his death, of his burial and, according to the following account in the Gospel, of the empty tomb.

For today: quiet, steady service is also a way of following Jesus. Even when others do not notice it, God sees the faithfulness that remains even in the most painful moments.
exp.5:12:
It says that the twelve disciples, after being sent out by Jesus, drove out many demons and anointed many sick people with oil, and they healed them.

Mark is the one telling the story. Jesus had sent the twelve out two by two, giving them authority over unclean spirits. They preached that people should repent, and their work was connected to the work of Jesus. Oil was a sign used in other Bible passages as well, such as James 5:14. Mark does not explain exactly what it meant here; many believe it represented prayer and the power of God, not a medicine.

Today we can learn that God cares for people completely: body, mind, and spirit. We can serve with prayer, compassion, and practical help, knowing that the power comes from God and not from us.
exp.7:5:
Jesus tells the people to sit down on the ground. Then he takes the seven loaves, gives thanks to God, breaks them, and hands them to his disciples to distribute. They set them before the whole crowd.

Jesus speaks in a deserted place, where a large crowd had been with him for days and had nothing to eat. The disciples wondered how they could feed so many, and they had only seven loaves. Jesus does not stop at doubt: he gives thanks and uses the little that is there. The disciples take an active part, since they distribute what he blesses.

For today: when what you have seems very little, offer it to God with thankfulness. He can do much with what is small, and your part is to obey and share.
exp.8:25:
What it says: The unclean spirit obeyed Jesus' command and came out, but first it cried out and violently shook the boy. The phrase about shaking him means it threw him into convulsions with great force. When the spirit left, the boy lay so still that he looked dead, and many people took him to be dead.

Context: A desperate father had brought his son to Jesus, because the disciples had not been able to help him. The father had just said, "I believe; help my unbelief." Jesus saw that a crowd was gathering, and then he gave the command with authority. Mark tells us that the people drew their own conclusion, but the next verse shows that Jesus had a different answer.

For today: Sometimes things seem to get worse before they get better, and we may believe that all is lost. Like that father, we can honestly bring Jesus our incomplete faith. He is not stopped by appearances; he can raise up what others think is dead.
exp.12:1:
Jesus answers his disciple, who is looking with admiration at the great buildings of the temple. He tells them that everything will be torn down completely, so much so that not one stone will be left standing on another. The word "thrown down" means pulled down and cast to the ground.

Jesus speaks with his disciples as they leave the temple in Jerusalem. One of them is amazed at the huge stones and the buildings. Jesus shows them that what seems strong and eternal is not permanent. Later, on the Mount of Olives, they ask him when this will happen. Many believe he is referring to the destruction of the temple in the year 70 AD, although some think he also foretells future events.

Today we can ask ourselves in what impressive things we place our security: work, money, or success. All of that can change. Trusting in God gives us a foundation that does not collapse.
exp.1:27:
Jesus says that the Son of Man, a title he uses for himself, has authority over the Sabbath. The Sabbath is not above him; it is under his authority.

Jesus speaks with some Pharisees who were criticizing his disciples for picking heads of grain on the Sabbath. He reminds them that David and his men ate the holy bread when they were hungry. Earlier he had said that the Sabbath was made for the good of man. His conclusion shows that he understands the purpose of the Sabbath better than they do.

For today: receive rest as a gift from God, not as a burden. And when a rule is used to harm or judge others, ask yourself what Jesus, the Lord, wants with it: mercy, care, and life.
exp.12:25:
Jesus says that, after very great signs in the heavens, everyone will see the Son of Man coming in the clouds. "Power" means authority and might. "Glory" is his greatness and splendor. "Son of Man" is a title Jesus uses for himself, taken from Daniel 7.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when they ask him about the destruction of the temple and what would come. He warns them of hard times so that they will not be frightened or deceived. Some understand these signs as something partly fulfilled in the year 70, and others as his final return. Christians have interpreted them in several ways.

For today: even when the world seems unstable, Christ has the last word. Live with hope and with your eyes open, without fear, faithfully doing what God has given you to do today.
exp.15:13:
This verse tells that Jesus, after rising, appeared to the eleven disciples while they were eating. He rebuked them firmly for their unbelief and for their hardness of heart, that is, a stubbornness that kept them from believing. They had already heard the testimony of those who saw him alive, and still they doubted. The word "rebuked" in the verse is the one used here: he reproved them.

The passage is in the long ending of Mark, which some early manuscripts do not include, and scholars debate its origin. Here the narrator describes Jesus' third appearance, after the disciples had rejected the accounts of others. Jesus corrects them frankly, but he soon sends them out to preach, which shows that their failure does not disqualify them.

Today we can recognize our doubts with humility. God corrects us with love, and yet still entrusts us with his mission.
exp.14:44:
Pilate received confirmation from the centurion, the Roman officer who had overseen the crucifixion, that Jesus was already dead. Then Pilate gave permission for Joseph to take the body.

The one telling the story is Mark, and he presents it as a fact. Pilate had been surprised that Jesus died so quickly, so he wanted to check. This verification makes clear that Jesus' death was real and that a Roman witness confirmed it before the burial.

For today: the Christian faith rests on real events, not vague ideas. Jesus truly died, and that is why his resurrection matters. We can trust him with confidence, and we can also imitate the courage of Joseph, who dared to serve Jesus when others were turning away.
exp.8:22:
Jesus answers the father of the boy, who had said to him: "if you can do anything, help us." Jesus returns the words to him: "If you can believe?" That is, the doubt is not in Jesus' power, but in the man's trust. And he affirms that for the one who believes, all things are possible.

Jesus speaks with a distressed father. His son had suffered since childhood from a spirit that harmed him. The disciples had not been able to help him, and the man comes with little hope. Jesus does not reject him; he invites him to trust. His answer, "I believe; help my unbelief," shows a sincere faith, though a weak one.

Today we can approach God with honesty. You do not need to have perfect faith to pray. You can say: "Lord, I believe, but help me in what I lack." Jesus receives that small faith and strengthens it.
exp.14:3:
This verse tells how Pilate, the Roman governor, asks Jesus again: "Answerest thou nothing?" He wants Jesus to listen carefully to all the charges being brought against him. The chief priests are the leaders of the Jewish priests.

Pilate, who is running the trial, speaks here. The religious leaders kept pressing their accusations against Jesus, and Pilate expected a defense. But Jesus remains silent, and the text says Pilate was amazed, meaning he was astonished. Many Christians see in this an echo of Isaiah 53:7, where God's servant stays silent before those who mistreat him, although the passage does not say so directly.

For today: we do not always have to defend ourselves or win every argument. When we are accused unjustly, we can ask God for wisdom to know when to speak and when to be silent, trusting that he cares for us.
exp.13:61:
Jesus answers clearly: "I am," that is, yes, he is the Christ, the Son of God. He adds that they will see the Son of man sitting at the right hand of power, meaning in the place of honor and authority beside God, and coming with the clouds of heaven.

Jesus speaks before the high priest and the council, at his trial the night before his crucifixion. He had remained silent, but when asked directly who he is, he answers. His words recall the vision in Daniel 7:13. The leaders took it as blasphemy and condemned him.

For today: Jesus did not hide his identity, even though it cost him his life. We can trust that he reigns and will return, and that gives us courage to be honest about our faith, even when it is hard.
exp.4:0:
This verse tells us that Jesus and his disciples crossed the Sea of Galilee and arrived at the other shore, in the region of the Gadarenes. The sea mentioned here is the Sea of Galilee, which is really a large lake.

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. This comes right after the storm that Jesus calmed on the lake. Now they arrive in territory that was mostly not Jewish, and the next verse introduces the man with an unclean spirit. Mark shows us that Jesus has authority over nature and also over evil.

For today: Jesus is willing to cross over to the other side, to uncomfortable places and to people others avoid. We can ask him for courage to draw near to those who suffer with love, without judging or rejecting them.
exp.11:37:
Jesus warns the crowd: "Beware of the scribes." These were teachers of the Law. They liked to walk around in long robes, that is, garments that drew attention and showed importance. They also loved to be greeted with respect in the marketplaces, the public places of the market.

Jesus is teaching in the temple, in Jerusalem, in his final days before the cross. He has just spoken about David and the Messiah, and the crowd was listening with delight. Now he gives them a warning about certain religious leaders who sought honor for themselves. He is not condemning all the scribes, but that attitude.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: do I serve God to please Him or so that others will admire me? Let us ask Him for a humble heart, one that seeks His glory and not our own.
exp.7:27:
The disciples tell Jesus what people think of him. Some said he was John the Baptist, others that he was Elijah, and others that he was one of the prophets. The words "á" and "alguno" are old forms: today we would say "a" and "uno." All these opinions saw him as a man sent by God, but nothing more.

Jesus is on the way with his disciples through the villages of Caesarea Philippi. He asks them this question to prepare for the next one, which is more personal. Herod had already mentioned the idea that Jesus was John risen from the dead (Mark 6:14-16). That is why the answers reflect what was being said among the people.

For today: many people respect Jesus as a great teacher or prophet, but he asks each of us personally who he is to us. Repeating what others think is not enough; it is worth pausing and answering him honestly.
exp.2:23:
Jesus says that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. If its members fight among themselves, sooner or later it weakens and falls. "Standing" means remaining firm, not collapsing. "That kingdom" refers to the kingdom that is divided.

Jesus speaks with the scribes, teachers of the Law who had come from Jerusalem. They saw his miracles, but they said he drove out demons by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of demons. Jesus calls them and answers with a simple comparison: it would be absurd for Satan to fight against himself.

For today: take care of unity in your family, your church and your work. Before arguing, seek peace and listen. Constant quarrels weaken what God wants to strengthen.
exp.9:14:
Jesus says with great seriousness ("truly I tell you") that whoever does not receive the kingdom of God the way a little child does will not enter it. The word "receive" here means to accept something given as a gift. The "kingdom of God" refers to God's rule and salvation, which are received as a gift.

Some parents were bringing their children so that Jesus would touch and bless them, but the disciples were scolding them. Jesus became indignant with them and corrected them. Then he embraced the children and blessed them. Right after this, a man comes asking what he must do to inherit eternal life, which contrasts with the attitude of the child who simply receives.

For today: a child does not boast of merits; he simply trusts and receives. We can come to God this way, with humility, acknowledging that we need his help and that his grace cannot be earned. Today, in prayer, tell God that you trust in him.
exp.14:19:
The verse tells how the Roman soldiers finished mocking Jesus. They took off the purple cloak, a royal-colored robe they had put on him as a joke. Then they put his own clothes back on him and led him out to be crucified. The word "mocked" means to ridicule with cruelty, and "took off the purple" means removing that cloak.

Mark, the narrator, tells the events simply and without embellishment. The soldiers had mocked Jesus as if he were a false king, yet without realizing it they were saying something true. Mark shows that Jesus, accused of calling himself King, accepted this suffering without defending himself. Many understand that in this way what had been foretold in the Scriptures was being fulfilled.

For today: when someone mocks your faith or humiliates you, remember that Jesus went through that before you. You can bring that pain to him in prayer and respond with patience, trusting that he understands you.
exp.1:19:
Jesus says that a time will come when the bridegroom will be taken away from his disciples, that is, carried far from them. Then they will fast. The word "But" in the verse is the one the old translation rendered as "Mas," and "fast" means going without food for a time in order to pray and seek God.

Some people ask Jesus why his disciples do not fast, as the disciples of John and the Pharisees did. Jesus compares himself to a bridegroom at a wedding: while he is present, it is a time of joy. Many understand that he is announcing his death and departure.

For today: our life with God has different seasons. There are times to celebrate his presence and times to seek him with humility, prayer, and fasting. Ask him to teach you to live both with a sincere heart.
exp.11:22:
The Sadducees bring Jesus an extreme case: a woman who married seven brothers, one after another, and had no children. Then they ask whose wife she will be "in the resurrection." Here "resurrection" is the word used in the verse itself, so no further explanation is needed. Their question is meant to test the idea itself, so the phrase "had her to wife" simply means that each of the seven had been married to her.

The ones speaking are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They based their view on the law of Moses, which asked a man to marry his brother's widow so that the dead man would have descendants. With this story they wanted to make the hope of rising again look absurd. Jesus answers that they do not truly know the Scriptures or the power of God, and that the life after resurrection is different from life in the present.

Today, when we face hard questions about our faith, let us approach the Bible with humility. Let us not imagine God according to our limits; let us trust that his power and his promises are greater than our understanding.
exp.8:14:
When the people saw Jesus, they were very amazed. Then they ran toward him and greeted him.

Mark narrates the scene. Jesus was coming down the mountain with Peter, James, and John, and he found the other disciples surrounded by a crowd, with some scribes arguing with them. Mark does not explain why the people were amazed. Some think that some trace of what had been experienced on the mountain remained in Jesus, but the text does not say so. What is certain is that his arrival changed the atmosphere, and soon he asks about the argument.

For today: when there are arguments, doubts, or problems we cannot solve, let us run toward Jesus. His presence brings clarity and hope where there was only confusion.
exp.0:42:
Jesus gave him a firm and serious warning. And he sent him away at once, which means he told him to leave right away. The words are strong in the original, as if Jesus were speaking with great intensity.

Jesus has just healed a leper. Now he orders him to say nothing to anyone and to present himself to the priest, as the law of Moses required, so that his healing would be officially recognized. Scholars explain the urgency in different ways: to avoid crowds who sought only miracles, or to guard the direction of his mission. We do not know the exact reason for certain. The man did not obey, and Jesus had to remain in deserted places.

For today: receiving God's grace is not only feeling happy, it is also obeying. Ask yourself what Jesus has clearly asked of you, and do it with confidence.
exp.15:9:
Mary Magdalene, after seeing the risen Jesus, went to tell those who had been with him, that is, his disciples. They were sad and mourning the death of their Master. The phrase "told them" simply means she went and let them know what had happened.

The narrator of the gospel recounts what took place that morning. Jesus had first appeared to her, and she carried the news to the disciples in their grief. Some scholars point out that these final verses of Mark are missing from some ancient manuscripts, and there are different opinions about this. Even so, the scene agrees with what other gospels report.

Today, if you know the hope of Christ, share it with someone who is suffering, even if you doubt they will believe you. Sometimes a simple and sincere word opens the door to comfort.
exp.1:10:
Jesus says to the paralyzed man: "I say unto you," that is, "it is to you that I am speaking." He gives him three commands: to rise, to take up his bed (the mat or pallet on which he lay), and to go home. The old-style accent marks in the source wording are a note about how the word is spelled in an older form, so no comment is needed here.

Jesus is in a house in Capernaum, teaching. Some men lowered this paralyzed man through the roof. First Jesus forgave his sins, and some teachers of the law doubted in their hearts. Then Jesus healed the man to show that the Son of Man, a title Jesus uses for himself, has authority to forgive sins.

For today: Jesus has power over what weighs on us most, inwardly and outwardly. If today you carry guilt or a problem that paralyzes you, bring it to Jesus in prayer, trust his word, and take the first step of faith that he shows you.
exp.8:42:
Jesus says that if your hand causes you to sin, it is better to cut it off than to end up in Gehenna. The phrase "to cause to stumble" means to lead someone into falling or sinning. Gehenna was the valley of Hinom near Jerusalem, and Jesus uses it as a picture of the final judgment. The "fire that never shall be quenched" speaks of a serious and lasting punishment.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, who had just been arguing about who was the greatest. He had already warned them not to cause the little ones who believe in him to fall. Now he continues with another warning: sin in your own life is also serious. Most scholars understand that he uses exaggerated language on purpose, to teach that nothing is worth more than life with God.

Today, ask yourself what keeps making you fall again and again: a habit, a friendship, or what you see on your phone. With God's help, make a concrete and firm decision to step away from that this week.
exp.10:0:
Mark tells us that Jesus and his disciples were drawing near to Jerusalem. They were passing near two villages, Bethphage and Bethany, beside the Mount of Olives. Then Jesus sends two of his disciples on an errand. The names "Jerusalem" and "Bethany" in the verse above are the forms we use today, Jerusalem and Bethany.

The one speaking is the narrator, Mark. Jesus is arriving in Jerusalem for the last time, in the days before his death. This verse begins the account of his entry into the city. The verses that follow show that Jesus already knew clearly what was going to happen and directs everything with calm.

Jesus invites ordinary people to take part in what God is doing. Today he may also ask you for simple things, such as helping, visiting, or serving. Even if you do not understand the whole plan, you can obey with confidence, knowing that he knows the way.
exp.9:28:
Jesus says there is a promise for the one who leaves something important to follow him and to proclaim the gospel. He mentions house, family and land. The explanation of the word for "lands" is removed here, since that word does not appear in the verse your reader sees. The sentence about the old spelling of "or" is also removed for the same reason. The sentence is left open and is completed in the following verse.

Peter has just said that they left everything to follow Jesus. This happens after the encounter with the rich young man, who was not willing to give up his possessions. Jesus answers with a solemn promise. The following verses make clear that there will be blessing now, but also persecutions, and eternal life afterward.

Following Jesus can cost something real: comfort, plans or relationships. Today you might ask yourself what holds you back from obeying him, and trust that he cares for those who surrender everything to him with sincerity.
exp.4:19:
He said the man who had been freed from the demons obeyed Jesus. He went away and began to tell throughout the region of Decapolis the great things that Jesus had done for him. Everyone who heard him was amazed.

This is the end of the account of the man from Gerasa who was possessed. Earlier, Jesus had healed him, and the people of the area asked Jesus to leave. The man wanted to go with Jesus, but Jesus asked him to stay and tell what God had done. Mark thus shows that testimony was also part of the mission.

Today we can do the same: tell, simply, to those who live near us, what God has done in our lives. You do not need to be an expert; it is enough to be sincere and grateful.
exp.2:16:
Mark says that Jesus also chose James and John, the sons of Zebedee, and gave them a nickname: "Boanerges," which means "sons of thunder."

Mark tells here how Jesus named the twelve apostles to be with him, to preach, and to heal. The narrator is Mark, and he presents Jesus giving names on purpose. The text does not explain why he chose that nickname. Some think it points to a strong or passionate character, and in Luke 9:54 these brothers want to call down fire from heaven, but this is an interpretation.

Jesus calls people with flaws and intense temperaments, and he uses them. If your character is strong, give it to Christ so that he can direct it toward good and toward serving others.
exp.4:31:
This verse says that Jesus kept looking around, searching with his eyes for the woman who had touched him. The phrase "the woman who had done this" refers to the person who touched his clothes and was made well.

Mark tells us here what Jesus did after asking who had touched him. His disciples thought the question made no sense because of the crowd. But Jesus was not looking to punish anyone. Later we see that he wanted to speak with her, and he said to her, "Your faith has made you well." Many interpreters see here a desire that she should not leave without a personal encounter.

For today: Jesus does not see people as part of a crowd, but one by one. You can come to him with confidence, even if you feel small or hidden, because he looks at you with interest and care.
exp.0:23:
The unclean spirit, speaking through the man, reacts with fear before Jesus. The opening cry is an alarm. The question "What have we to do with you?" means: "What do we have in common? Why are you bothering us?" The name "of Nazareth" indicates that Jesus came from Nazareth. "Destroy us" means to put an end to them. And it calls him "the Holy One of God."

The one speaking is the unclean spirit, which speaks in the plural, as if representing others like itself. We are in the synagogue at Capernaum, and the people were already amazed at the authority with which Jesus taught. The spirit recognizes who Jesus is, but does not worship him; it only fears his power. Jesus silences it and drives it out, showing that his authority is not only in words.

For today: knowing correct facts about Jesus is not the same as trusting in him. Ask yourself whether you only recognize him from a distance or whether you truly draw near to him so that he rules in your life.
exp.11:29:
Jesus says that we should love God with our whole being. "Heart" speaks of the innermost part, where desires and decisions are born. "Soul" is life itself, "mind" is thought, and "strength" is energy and ability. The words "you shall love" are a command, but it is a call to love completely. "First" means the most important.

A scribe, an expert in the Law, asked Jesus which was the first commandment. Jesus began by quoting the Shema ("Hear, O Israel"), the declaration every Jew knew: the Lord is one. From there he explained that loving God is central to the whole Law. Right after, he added love for one's neighbor.

Today we can ask ourselves: what part of my life am I keeping back from God? A simple way to begin is to set aside time each day to pray, read his Word, and offer him our work and our decisions.
exp.5:51:
The explanation says that the disciples had not truly understood the miracle of the loaves. "Confused" means bewildered, dulled, or closed off; "to consider" means to think and understand carefully. Their hearts had not grasped what Jesus had shown them.

Mark, in his account, explains why the disciples were so amazed when Jesus walked on the sea and calmed the wind. Shortly before, they had seen Jesus feed thousands with a few loaves of bread. But they did not connect that event with who Jesus is: someone with power and authority. That is why they were frightened instead of trusting. Some scholars see here a lack of understanding; others, a hardness of heart.

For today: remember what God has already done for you. Before a new storm, think of his past help; that strengthens trust and calms fear.
exp.4:3:
