This verse tells that the man possessed by an unclean spirit had often been bound with shackles (iron rings for the feet) and with chains. But he would snap the chains and break them apart. The quoted words in the source refer to breaking them into small pieces, and to restraining or subduing him. Nobody had the strength to hold him.

Here the writer, Mark, describes the man's situation before he met Jesus. Jesus had just crossed the lake and arrived in the region of the Gadarenes. Mark emphasizes that this man lived alone, among the tombs, and that no one could help him. In this way the power of Jesus, who can set him free, is made to stand out even more.

For today: there are problems that people cannot control by their own strength or by the strength of others. Bring that situation to Jesus with confidence, because He has authority where we cannot.
exp.14:6:
This verse introduces a man named Barabbas. He was in prison together with others who had taken part in a riot, that is, a rebellion against authority. A murder had been committed during that uprising.

Mark, who is telling the story, explains who Barabbas was so that the choice Pilate puts before the crowd can be understood. It was the custom to release a prisoner at the feast of Passover. Historians have no other source outside the Gospels that confirms this custom, so we do not know more details. Pilate sets Jesus, who was innocent, against a well-known guilty man.

For today: Barabbas was set free while Jesus was going to the cross. This reminds us that God's grace reaches those who do not deserve it. Today we can give thanks for that forgiveness and treat with mercy those who fail us.
exp.8:17:
It says that an evil spirit attacks this man's son without warning: it throws him into violent convulsions (the phrase about it tearing him apart means it wrenches him and throws him with force), foam comes from his mouth, he grinds his teeth, and the boy grows weaker and weaker. The father tells that he asked Jesus' disciples to cast out that spirit, but they could not.

A distressed father speaks, from among the crowd. Jesus had just come down from the mountain and found the disciples arguing with others. The man explains his problem and acknowledges the disciples' inability. Then Jesus responds with sorrow over the lack of faith and asks that the boy be brought to him.

For today: when you feel drained before a problem you cannot solve, bring it to Jesus honestly, as this father did. You do not need to pretend you have everything under control.
exp.11:35:
Jesus quotes Psalm 110:1. David, guided by the Holy Spirit, says that the Lord spoke to my Lord and asked him to sit at his right hand until he puts his enemies under his feet. A footstool is a low stool where the feet rest, a picture of complete victory.

Jesus is teaching in the temple and asks how the scribes can say that the Christ is the son of David. If David himself calls him Lord, the Messiah is more than a human descendant. Jesus shows that the Messiah has a higher dignity, and Christians have seen here his divine lordship.

For today: if Jesus reigns at God's right hand, we can trust that his final victory is certain. When you feel pressured or afraid, remember that he is already Lord and that your life is in his hands.
exp.10:2:
Jesus tells his two disciples what to say if anyone asks them why they are untying the young donkey. They are to say, "The Lord has need of it," and the owner will let it go at once. The explanation of the old wording is removed here since those terms do not appear in the verse your readers see; the verse uses "need" and "straightway," and the sense is the same.

Jesus speaks near Jerusalem, on the way to his final entry into the city. He arranges everything calmly and gives clear instructions. Some think he had already arranged this with the owner; others see here a supernatural knowledge. The text does not make this clear. In any case, the disciples are only to obey and trust.

For today: when God asks us for something simple, even when we do not understand everything, we can obey with confidence. And what we have, even the smallest thing, can serve Jesus if we give it up gladly.
exp.2:2:
Jesus speaks to a man who had a withered hand, that is, a hand that was paralyzed or without strength. He asks him to stand up in the middle of the synagogue, where everyone can see him.

Jesus is in the synagogue on the Sabbath. Some people were watching him closely, looking for a reason to accuse him if he healed on the Sabbath. Instead of hiding the miracle, Jesus makes it public. In this way he shows that compassion matters more than criticism, and then he asks whether it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath. They remain silent.

For today: Jesus does not ignore the one who suffers, even when people are watching with bad intentions. We can ask him for courage to do good simply, without letting the fear of criticism stop us.
exp.7:4:
Jesus asks his disciples a simple question: how many loaves do they have? They answer that they have seven. The explanation of the old wording that was translated as "to feed until satisfied" and the word meaning "have" is removed, since the reader's verse uses "How many loaves have ye?" and "Seven," and the word "have" already appears there.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples in a deserted place, next to a crowd that has been with him for some time and has no food. He feels compassion and does not want to send them away hungry. The disciples doubt that it is possible to feed them there. Jesus does not begin with a miracle, but by asking what they already have on hand. He will later use those seven loaves.

For today: when a need seems bigger than your resources, do not stop at what is missing. Honestly acknowledge how little you have, place it in the hands of Jesus, and trust that He can do much with it.
exp.0:15:
As Jesus walked along the shore of the Sea of Galilee, he saw Simon and his brother Andrew. They were casting their net into the water, because they were fishermen.

Mark is the one telling the story. Jesus has just begun his public work in Galilee, announcing that the kingdom of God was near and calling people to turn from their sins and believe. Now Jesus begins to call his first disciples. Mark tells us they were working, in the middle of their ordinary lives, when Jesus found them.

For today: Jesus often calls us in the middle of everyday life, at work or in our routine. We can live each day alert to his voice, ready to answer him with faith and obedience, without thinking that we must wait for some special moment to follow him.
exp.4:24:
The explanation says that there was a woman who had suffered a flow of blood for twelve years. In today's language, she had bleeding that would not stop, a chronic and very draining illness.

Mark is the one who tells the story. Jesus is on his way to the house of Jairus, whose daughter is dying, and a large crowd presses around him. In the middle of that rush this woman appears, almost unnoticed. According to the law of Moses (Leviticus 15), her condition made her ceremonially unclean, so she probably lived isolated and ashamed. Mark presents her without a name and without power, to highlight her need.

For today: there is no pain or problem so long or forgotten that Jesus does not see it. If you have been carrying something for years, come to him with sincerity, even if it is with timidity, and tell him everything in prayer.
exp.3:29:
Jesús hace dos preguntas a quienes lo escuchan: ¿con qué se puede comparar el reino de Dios? ¿Qué ejemplo sirve para explicarlo? Una parábola es una historia sencilla que usa cosas de la vida diaria para enseñar una verdad. Una comparación es algo que se parece a otra cosa.

Jesús está hablando a la multitud junto al mar de Galilea, y les enseña con parábolas. Justo antes habló de la semilla que crece sola hasta la cosecha. Ahora busca otra imagen, la de la semilla de mostaza, para mostrar que el reino de Dios comienza pequeño y luego crece.

Para hoy: no te desanimes si lo que Dios hace en tu vida o en tu iglesia parece pequeño. Sigue sembrando con fidelidad, oración y paciencia, y confía en que Dios da el crecimiento a su tiempo.
exp.8:16:
In this verse, a man from the crowd answers Jesus's question. He addresses Jesus as "Teacher" and explains that he has brought his son, who has a dumb spirit. This means the boy was under the influence of a spirit that kept him from speaking. "I have brought unto thee" is an older way of saying "I have brought you" in the sense of "I have brought him to you."

Here speaks an anguished father. Jesus had just come down from the mountain and found his disciples arguing with others. The father had first sought help from the disciples, but they had not been able to heal his son. So now he comes directly to Jesus.

Today we can learn from this father: when a situation overwhelms us, the best thing is to bring it honestly to Jesus. He is not troubled by our need. We can present with confidence the people we love and their sufferings, even when other resources have failed us.
exp.3:6:
It says that another part of the seed fell among thorns. The thorns grew up, pressed in on the plant until it was choked, and in the end it produced no fruit. "Choked" here means smothered, cut off from the air and room it needs to live. The word "fell" in the verse is the same as the verb "fell" used in the explanation's own wording.

Jesus is teaching a crowd with the parable of the sower. Later in this same chapter, he explains to his disciples that the thorns stand for the worries of this world, the deceitfulness of riches, and the desires for other things (Mark 4:18-19). The seed is the word of God.

For today: look at what is growing in your life alongside the word of God, such as worries, debts, or ambitions. Remove one that is taking time away from God, and give that space to reading the Bible and praying.
exp.12:15:
He says that the person who is working in the field, when that moment of danger arrives, must not go back home for his garment. The "garment" was the cloak or outer coat that people took off so they could work more freely. The old spelling "Á" is the form of "a," and "huída" is "huida."

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he announces what will happen to Jerusalem and the temple. He gives them an urgent warning: when the sign comes, they must flee without delay. Interpreters disagree about whether he speaks only of the year 70 A.D., of the end of time, or of both.

For today: when God shows you clearly that you must leave behind something harmful or dangerous, do not stay looking for excuses or for things that hold you back. Obey promptly and trust that He will take care of you.
exp.4:10:
This verse says that near the mountain there was a large herd of pigs eating grass. "Pigs" are swine, "herd" is a large group of animals, and "feeding" means they were eating out in the field.

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. Jesus has just spoken with a man tormented by many evil spirits, who said their name was "Legion." They begged Jesus not to send them out of the region. Mark mentions the pigs because the demons will soon ask to enter them. Pigs were unclean animals to the Jews, and it is not known for certain why Mark gives so much detail; what is clear is that Jesus has authority over these spirits.

For today: there is no force so great that Jesus does not control it. If something overwhelms you, bring it to him in prayer with confidence.
exp.9:41:
Jesus calls his disciples and reminds them of something everyone knew: those who are regarded as rulers of the nations "lord it over" them, that is, they command with authority and dominate others. Those who are great among them "exercise authority," or in other words, wield power over the people.

Jesus speaks to the Twelve after James and John asked for the places of honor at his side. The other ten became angry, and they probably also wanted those positions. Jesus gathers them together to correct everyone, not just the two. He shows them that their way of understanding greatness must be different from the way of the world.

Today we can ask ourselves how we use our influence, whether at home, at work, or in the church. This week, look for a concrete way to serve someone without expecting recognition.
exp.4:32:
Here the story is told of the woman who had touched Jesus' cloak and realized that He was looking for her. She felt great fear and trembled, because she knew she had been healed. Then she came forward, knelt before Him, and told Him the whole truth. "Falling down before" means bowing all the way to the ground as a sign of respect.

The Evangelist Mark recounts that this woman had been ill with a flow of blood for twelve years. She approached Jesus in secret, among the crowd. According to the law of Moses, her condition made her ritually unclean, so her fear of being discovered is understandable. Jesus asked who had touched Him, not to shame her, but to bring her into a personal encounter with Him. Then He called her "daughter" and blessed her.

When God calls us, we should not hide. We can come to Jesus with sincerity, even with fear, and tell Him the whole truth. He receives with tenderness those who come with faith.
exp.14:21:
Mark tells us that the soldiers bring Jesus to a place called Golgotha. The same evangelist explains that this name means "the place of a skull." Golgotha is an Aramaic word, and the phrase "which is, being interpreted" here means that the name is translated for the reader.

Here the narrator, Mark, is writing for readers who did not know Aramaic. Jesus has already been mocked and stripped of the purple robe, and Simon of Cyrene has carried his cross. It is not known for certain why the place had this name: some think it was a hill shaped like a skull, others that it was a place of executions. The Bible does not make this clear.

Jesus went to the hardest and most shameful place, and he did so out of love. Today we can draw near to him with confidence when we feel pain, shame or guilt, because he knows suffering and does not abandon us. Today, give thanks to him for what he suffered for you.
exp.4:9:
The unclean spirit kept begging Jesus earnestly that he would not send them away from that region. The explanation of "begged" as asking with urgent pleading and humility is dropped, since the reader's verse reads "besought" and the word is not being explained here. The reference to the territory where they were, in the region of the Gadarenes, is kept in plain terms: the spirits were in the area of the Gadarenes.

The spirit speaking is the one that controlled a man, and it calls itself "Legion" because there were many of them. Jesus had already commanded it to come out of the man. The spirits recognize that Jesus has authority over them and ask for a limit. It is not stated with certainty why they wanted to stay in that region; some think they wanted to keep operating in that place.

For today: Jesus has authority over every kind of evil, and nothing escapes Him. If something is oppressing you, go to Him with confidence and without fear, because He commands and cares for you.
exp.2:30:
This verse tells us that Jesus' mother and brothers arrived. They stayed outside the house and sent someone in to call him. The phrase "sent to him" means they sent him a message. The phrase "calling him" means they were asking him to come out.

Mark tells this after some people accused Jesus of having an unclean spirit. A few verses earlier (3:21) it says his family went out to take hold of him, because they said he was out of his mind. We do not know exactly what each person was thinking, and interpreters explain it in different ways. What we do see is that the family was outside, while the crowd was inside, close to him.

For today: we can come close to Jesus with humility and listen to him, instead of staying at a distance and expecting him to come to our plans. Being near him matters more than any family tie or position.
exp.9:39:
Jesus says that sitting at his right hand and at his left, the places of greatest honor, is not something he hands out as he pleases. Those places belong to those for whom they have been prepared, that is, for those already readied or destined for them.

Here Jesus is speaking with James and John, who asked him for those places of honor in his glory. He warns them that they do not understand what they are asking, for the road to glory passes through suffering. Jesus speaks of the cup he will drink and the baptism he will undergo, images of his suffering. The other ten disciples became angry when they heard this, and that shows that all of them were struggling with the desire to be great.

For today: instead of seeking places of honor, trust that God knows who is to receive them and how each person is being prepared, and serve with humility, without comparing yourself with others.
exp.4:26:
She says that this woman, after hearing what was being told about Jesus, came up from behind through the crowd and touched his garment. The word "garment" here means the outer clothing, the cloak. The crowd is the throng of people surrounding him. She did not confront him face to face; she came near with discretion.

The one telling the story is Mark, recounting an event. The woman had suffered from bleeding for twelve years, had spent everything on physicians, and was getting worse. According to the law of Moses, that condition made her ceremonially unclean, so she was probably avoiding contact with people. That is why she approaches from behind. What she had heard about Jesus awakened her faith.

For today: when you feel there is no way out, come to Jesus with whatever you have, even a small and fearful faith. You do not need perfect words or to feel worthy; it is enough to come to Him with trust.
exp.10:25:
Jesus says that if we do not forgive others, our heavenly Father will not forgive us either. The word forgive here is the verb in its plain form, and the word trespasses means the wrongs or sins we commit against God and others.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples on the road to Jerusalem, right after teaching them about faith and prayer. He shows them that praying with confidence goes together with having a clean heart toward others. Some ancient manuscripts do not include this verse, which is why many modern translations leave it out, but the same teaching appears in Matthew 6:14-15 and in the verse before this one.

For today: before you pray, ask yourself whether you are holding a grudge against anyone. Hand it over to God and choose to forgive, remembering how much he has forgiven you.
exp.13:48:
Jesus says to those who have come to arrest him that he was with them every day, teaching in the temple in plain view of everyone, and they never laid hands on him. He says that all of this happens so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.

Jesus speaks in the garden of Gethsemane, just after Judas betrays him and one of his followers strikes the servant of the high priest. Jesus rebukes the manner of the arrest: at night and with weapons, as if he were a robber. He does not say which passage of Scripture he has in mind; many think of prophecies such as Isaiah 53. Shortly afterward, all the disciples flee.

For today: even when injustice seems to win, we can trust that God is still at work. Respond without violence and with truth, trusting that his purpose is greater than what we can see.
exp.5:38:
Jesus asked the disciples to have the people sit down in groups on the green grass. The word "sit down" here means settling in to eat, as was the custom at that time. "Groups" means in groups or in rows. The green grass shows that the place had fresh grass.

Jesus speaks with his disciples in front of an enormous crowd that had followed him to a remote place. It was already late and there was no food. The disciples saw the problem as impossible, but Jesus put them to work. Before performing the miracle, he asked them to arrange the people calmly. Some see the green grass as a detail of the scene; the text does not explain more.

When you face a need that seems very large, do not just stand there looking at what is missing. Take the simple step that Jesus puts before you, with obedience and trust, and leave in his hands what you cannot resolve.
exp.14:17:
The Roman soldiers begin to greet Jesus with mockery. The greeting used the Latin word for "hail," and it was the kind of cheer people gave the emperor Caesar. The soldiers copied that greeting to make fun of Jesus, whom they called "King of the Jews."

Context: Pilate had already ordered Jesus to be flogged. Inside the Praetorium, the governor's headquarters or palace, the soldiers dressed him in purple and placed a crown of thorns on his head to mock his title. Without realizing it, they spoke a truth: Jesus is King, though not in the way they understood.

For today: Jesus endured mockery and contempt without returning evil for evil. When someone laughs at your faith or treats you badly for following him, you can remember that your Lord went through this first. Ask him for patience and for a heart that responds with humility and love.
exp.6:10:
Jesus says that the Pharisees and scribes taught that if someone declared "Corban" (an offering dedicated to God) over their possessions, they were no longer obligated to use them to help their parents. The word "Corban" means a gift given to God, and "by whatsoever thou mightest be profited by me" refers to whatever benefit a person might otherwise have received from another. The phrase "you say" is how the verse introduces what these teachers said.

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees and some teachers of the law, who were criticizing him because his disciples did not follow certain traditions of the elders. He responds by showing that a human custom could cancel the commandment to honor one's father and mother. Scholars debate exactly how this practice worked, but Jesus' point is clear.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we use some religious excuse to avoid loving in concrete ways. Honoring God includes caring for, visiting, and helping our family according to our means.
exp.6:34:
At once his ears were opened, and the restraint on his tongue was released, which means the thing that kept him from speaking. From that moment he spoke well and clearly.

Mark tells what Jesus did. He took the man aside, away from the crowd, touched him, and looking up to heaven said, "Ephphatha," which means "be opened." Afterward he asked that no one be told, but the people could not keep quiet. Many were amazed, and his words recall promises from the prophet Isaiah about the deaf and the mute being healed.

For today: Jesus cares about each person, not only about crowds. Bring honestly to him whatever has shut you in or silenced you, such as fear or sadness. And when you receive his help, give thanks and tell it with humility.
exp.5:7:
Jesus told his disciples to take nothing for the journey except a staff. A staff is a walking stick. The "scrip" is a travel bag, and the "purse" here refers to the belt where money was kept, not even coins or bread.

Jesus speaks to the twelve, right after he was rejected in Nazareth. He sends them out two by two with authority over unclean spirits. By asking them to travel light, he taught them to depend on God and on the hospitality of the people. Some think it was also a sign of urgency in his message.

For today: we do not need to have everything worked out in order to obey God. Take the step he shows you, trust his provision, and let go of what gets in your way so you can serve with freedom.
exp.6:31:
It tells that a group of people brings to Jesus a man who could not hear and who had great difficulty speaking. The word "stammering" here can mean that he could barely talk or that he spoke with great effort. The people who bring him ask Jesus to put his hand on him, as a sign of blessing and healing.

This is a story from Mark. Jesus has just left the region of Tyre, passes through Sidon, and reaches the area of the Decapolis, near the Sea of Galilee. The ones who speak are the man's friends or family. It is not he who asks for help; others bring him. Afterward, Jesus takes him away from the crowd and heals him in a very personal way.

For today: think of someone who cannot come to God on their own because of their pain or weariness. You can carry them in prayer, with simple faith, as these friends did. Praying for others is a real act of love.
exp.1:8:
Jesus asks the teachers of the law: which is easier to say, "Your sins are forgiven you," or "Get up, take your bed, and walk"? The word "bed" in the verse refers to the mat or small cot on which the sick man was lying.

Jesus speaks to some scribes who, in their hearts, accused him of blasphemy because only God can forgive sins. Jesus knew their thoughts. That someone has been forgiven cannot be checked by looking, but healing a paralyzed man can be seen. With the healing, Jesus shows that he has real authority to forgive sins.

For today: Jesus does not only care for our visible wounds, but also for our deepest need for forgiveness. Today you can come to him with confidence, knowing that he has authority to forgive you and raise you up.
exp.14:18:
The explanation says the soldiers struck Jesus on the head with a reed, spat on him, and kneeled before him as if they worshipped him. "Struck" means hit, and "kneeling" means on their knees. It was a cruel mockery, not sincere worship.

Mark tells what the Roman soldiers did after Pilate handed Jesus over to be crucified. They dressed him in purple and put a crown of thorns on him to ridicule the accusation that he was "King of the Jews." Without knowing it, they were mocking the true King, and Mark tells it soberly, without embellishment.

For today: Jesus endured contempt without repaying evil for evil. When someone mocks you or humiliates you, you can ask God for patience and respond with gentleness, remembering that Christ understands you in your pain.
exp.0:39:
A man with leprosy comes to Jesus, kneels down, and begs him. He says, "If you are willing, you can make me clean." The words "begging him" mean pleading with him earnestly; "kneeling down" means going down on his knees; "make me clean" means healing me of the leprosy.

The one speaking is this leper. Jesus was traveling through Galilee, preaching and casting out demons. At that time, the law of Moses required that people with leprosy live apart from others (Leviticus 13). For this reason, the man coming close to Jesus was an act of great need and faith. He trusts in Jesus' power, though he is not sure of his willingness.

Today we too can come to Jesus honestly, even with our wounds and shame. We can ask him with humility, trusting in his power and his good heart, and leave the outcome in his hands.
exp.0:28:
This verse tells us that Jesus left the synagogue in Capernaum and went to the house of Simon and Andrew. James (Santiago) and John were with him.

Here the narrator, Mark, presents Jesus in action. He has just taught with authority and freed a man with an unclean spirit, and the people are amazed. Mark shows a change: Jesus moves from a public place to a simple home, where he will soon heal Simon's mother-in-law. Many believe this was Simon's house in Capernaum, though the text gives no further detail.

For today: Jesus is not only present in the temples and in the great moments; he also enters our homes and our everyday lives. Invite him into your home and your family concerns, trusting that he cares about them.
exp.3:9:
When Jesus was alone, those who were around him, together with the twelve disciples, asked him about the parable of the sower. The verse does not record an exact question, only that they wanted to understand what he meant.

Jesus had just taught a crowd with the parable of the seed falling on different kinds of ground. He ends by saying, "He that hath ears to hear, let him hear." Afterward, in private, some close followers ask him for an explanation. He answers that they have been given to know the mystery of the kingdom, and then he quotes the language of Isaiah about seeing without understanding. Scholars explain the exact meaning of that statement in several different ways.

For today: if something in the Bible is not clear to you, do not just leave the doubt there. Draw near to Jesus in prayer and study, and ask sincerely, alongside other believers.
exp.11:43:
Jesus says that the others gave "out of their abundance," that is, out of what they no longer needed. But this widow, being poor, gave "everything she had." The word "living" can also be rendered as "means of support" or "what is needed to live." The "mites" were coins of very little value, and the Reina-Valera says two of them were worth a maravedí.

Jesus speaks with his disciples in the temple in Jerusalem, near the treasury where the offerings were placed. He watched how the people gave. The rich were putting in large amounts, but Jesus does not look only at the quantity. He looks at the heart and at the personal cost of the giving. In this way he teaches his disciples what truly matters to God.

For today: God values sincerity and trust more than the amount. You can give your time, your help, or your money generously, even if it is little, trusting that God takes care of you. Do not compare yourself with others.
exp.5:35:
The disciples ask Jesus to send the crowd away so they can go into the farms and the nearby villages to buy bread, because there was no food in that place. "Send them away" is the same as telling him to dismiss them.

The disciples are speaking. Jesus had spent the day teaching a large crowd, moved by compassion, because the people were wandering like sheep without a shepherd. It was already late and they were in a deserted place. The disciples see the problem and propose a sensible solution, but one that keeps the need at a distance from them. Jesus will answer with something different: "You give them something to eat."

When we see a need, we sometimes first think of sending it somewhere else. Jesus invites us to draw near, to place in his hands what little we have, and to trust that he can use it to help others.
exp.13:41:
Jesus tells his disciples to get up and come with him. The old-fashioned wording in the source is simply the way an older English version would say "stand up," so here we just say "get up." The phrase about the one who hands him over refers to the person who betrays him, meaning the one who puts him in the hands of his enemies. And the phrase about being near means that the betrayer is already drawing close.

Jesus speaks in the garden of Gethsemane, after praying alone three times while the disciples fell asleep. He already knows what is coming and does not run away. Rather, he rises to meet what the Father has allowed. Soon Judas arrives with a crowd armed with weapons.

For today: when we face something hard, we can pray first and then move forward with courage and peace, trusting that God is still in control, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.1:20:
He says that no one sews a patch of new, unshrunk cloth onto an old garment. If someone does, the patch shrinks when washed, pulls on the old cloth, and the tear becomes worse than before. A patch of new cloth is strong, unwashed fabric; a patch is the piece sewn on to mend a garment; the tear is the rip itself.

Jesus is speaking with some people who were asking why his disciples did not fast. He answered that while the bridegroom is present, it is a time for celebration. Then he uses this comparison to show that what he brings is something new and does not fit into simple repairs of the earlier customs. Scholars discuss the exact details, but the central idea is clear.

For today: let us not treat Jesus as a patch for our old life, but let him truly renew us. Let us ask him for a heart willing to change, rather than simply adding a little faith to what we already do.
exp.0:14:
Jesus announces four things: the time set by God has arrived (the time is fulfilled), the kingdom of God is very near, and because of this people must turn from their sins and believe the good news. Turning from sins means changing one's mind and direction, and believing means trusting. Gospel means good news.

Jesus speaks at the beginning of his ministry in Galilee. John the Baptist was already in prison, and Jesus comes out of his time of testing in the desert to proclaim God's message. With "the time is fulfilled" he shows that what the prophets promised begins to come true in him. Right after this he calls his first disciples.

For today: do not put off your response to God. Today you can recognize where you need to change direction and trust again in the good news of Jesus. Say to him simply: "Lord, I turn to you and I believe in you."
exp.11:23:
Jesus answers some men who are questioning him: "Are you not therefore wrong, because you do not know the scriptures, nor the power of God?" The word "erred" here means "are wrong," and "power" is the word for the might of God.

The people speaking with Jesus are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They brought up an invented case about a woman who married seven brothers, in order to make that hope look ridiculous. Jesus shows them that their mistake came from misunderstanding both the Word and what God is able to do.

For today: when we have doubts or very fixed ideas about the faith, it is good to return to the Bible with humility and remember that God can do more than we imagine.
exp.10:27:
The religious leaders ask Jesus: "By what authority do you do these things? Who gave you this authority?" The word "authority" here means the power or right to act. "These things" refers to what Jesus did the day before in the temple, when he drove out those who were buying and selling.

The chief priests (the leading priests), the scribes (teachers of the Law), and the elders (leaders of the people) are the ones speaking. They had authority over the temple, and they felt challenged. Their question seems more like an attempt to trap Jesus than a sincere search for the truth. Jesus answers with a question of his own about John the Baptist, and in doing so he reveals what is in their hearts.

For today: before we question God or others, let us examine whether we truly want the truth or only want to defend our own comfort. Let us ask God for a humble heart, ready to listen and to obey.
exp.11:19:
This verse begins a story that the Sadducees make up as an example. It says there were seven brothers. The first one married and died without having children. The word "seed" in the verse means offspring, that is, children.

The ones speaking are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They based their question on the law of Moses about the practice in which, if a man died without children, his brother would marry the widow to continue the family line. With this extreme case they wanted to make the idea of rising from the dead look ridiculous and to test Jesus.

For today: when someone asks us questions with bad intent or traps, we can come to Jesus with humility. He answers with truth and shows us that God's Word and his power are greater than our doubts.
exp.5:52:
This verse tells us that Jesus and his disciples finished crossing the lake. They arrived in the region of Gennesaret, an area along the Sea of Galilee, and they brought their boat in to shore, that is, they tied up the boat and stepped onto the land.

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. Shortly before this, Jesus had walked on the water and calmed the wind. The disciples were astonished, because they had not understood the matter of the loaves, when Jesus fed the crowd. Their hearts were dull and confused, closed to what they had seen. Even so, Jesus brought them safely to the other shore.

For today: even when it is hard for us to understand what God is doing, He continues to guide us with patience until we reach our destination. We can trust Him and remember his past works so that our faith grows stronger.
exp.6:36:
The explanation says the people were greatly astonished, that is, filled with wonder. They recognized that Jesus "has done all things well," and gave an example: he makes the deaf hear and the mute speak. The words "á" and "oir" are the old spelling of "a" and "oír".

Those who speak are the ones who saw the healing of a deaf man who could barely talk, in the region of the Decapolis. Jesus had asked them not to tell anyone, but they could not keep quiet. Their amazement reflects what the prophet Isaiah said about the time when God would restore his people (Isaiah 35:5-6). Some see here a sign that Jesus is the Messiah.

Today we can notice the good that God has done in our lives and tell it with gratitude. If he opened ears and loosened tongues, he can also help us listen to his voice and speak of him with simplicity.
exp.13:47:
Jesus asks those who have come to arrest him whether he is a thief, since they have come out with swords and clubs. The word "come out" in the verse above refers to their having come all the way there, and "take me" means to arrest me. It is a question that makes plain how unjust that treatment is.

Jesus speaks in the garden of Gethsemane, just after Judas betrays him with a kiss. A crowd sent by the religious leaders arrives armed, at night and in secret. Jesus reminds them that he taught openly in the temple every day and they never arrested him there. He does not resist, because he accepts that this is happening so that the Scriptures would be fulfilled.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, you can respond with calm and truth, without violence or revenge. Jesus trusted God's plan even in the most difficult moment, and you too can hand over your fears and your experiences of injustice to him.
exp.9:46:
Mark tells us that Bartimaeus, a blind man, heard that Jesus of Nazareth was passing by. Then he began to cry out, asking for help. He calls him "Son of David," a title that spoke of the king God had promised. "Have mercy on me" means "have compassion on me, help me." The words "heard" and "began to cry out" are old forms that mean "when he heard" and "shout."

Bartimaeus was a beggar sitting beside the road at the edge of Jericho. He could not see Jesus, but he had heard about him. For this reason he recognizes Jesus as the Messiah and asks him urgently for help. Just before this, Jesus had said that he came to serve and to give his life for many.

Today we can imitate Bartimaeus: when we are in need, let us call out to Jesus sincerely, without shame, and without waiting until we are better off. He hears us.
exp.0:21:
The people were astonished at what Jesus taught. "Teaching" means what he taught. "Authority" means power or the right to command. The "scribes" were the teachers of the Jewish Law. Jesus did not speak as they did, but with an authority of his own.

Mark tells what happened in the synagogue in Capernaum, on a Sabbath, shortly after Jesus called his first disciples. Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. The scribes used to rely on what other teachers had said before them. Jesus, by contrast, taught with firmness, and that authority soon shows itself when an unclean spirit obeys him.

For today: it is not enough to admire Jesus; we must let his words guide us. This week, read a passage from the Gospels and ask yourself what concrete change Jesus is asking of you.
exp.13:10:
The chief priests were glad when Judas offered to hand Jesus over to them. They promised to give him money, and Judas began looking for a good opportunity to do it. The verse says they were glad, and it says they promised to give him money.

Mark is the one telling the story. Just before this, a woman had anointed Jesus with very costly perfume, and Jesus defended her act as something beautiful. Right after that, Mark sets up the contrast: Judas, one of the twelve, goes to the religious leaders who wanted to stop Jesus. The text does not fully explain his motives; money is mentioned, but nothing more is said.

For today: Let us guard our hearts, because a person can stay close to Jesus and still let something else weigh too heavily. Let us ask Him to keep us faithful and sincere with Him.
exp.13:30:
Peter insists even more strongly. Peter's words mean that he is set on his claim and will not let it go. The phrases about dying with Jesus and not denying him are rendered in the verse above, so no further comment is needed on them. The other disciples say the same thing.

Jesus has just warned them that they will all fall away that night. Peter does not accept his Master's word and declares that he will be faithful, even to the point of death. Jesus had already told him that he would deny him three times. Shortly afterward, in Gethsemane, Jesus is in anguish, and the disciples are unable to stay with him.

For today: sincere love needs humility. Peter truly loved Jesus, but he trusted in his own strength. Instead of boasting about our faith, let us ask God for help every day, and remember that Jesus restores those who fail and return to him.
exp.11:7:
It says the tenants seized the owner's son, killed him, and threw him out of the vineyard. The word "seized" is not in the verse your reader sees, so I'll use the verse's own wording: they took him, killed him, and cast him out of the vineyard. This is the harshest moment of the parable: they reject the son and remove him from the place as though he did not belong there.

Jesus is speaking in Jerusalem, in the temple, to the religious leaders who were questioning his authority. He tells this parable of the vineyard, in which the owner sends servants and finally his son. Many understand that the tenants represent the leaders of Israel and the son represents Jesus himself. He speaks of his own rejection, and the verses that follow connect it with the stone the builders rejected that God makes the chief one.

For today: God has entrusted us with things that are not ours, such as life, time, and gifts. Let us examine whether we truly listen to Christ or prefer to keep control for ourselves.
exp.4:4:
This verse describes the constant suffering of a man tormented by unclean spirits. Day and night he wandered through the mountains and among the tombs, crying out and hurting himself with stones.

Here the narrator, Mark, presents the most severe case of bondage that Jesus encounters. No one had been able to subdue this man, not even with chains. Mark stresses his desperation so that the power of Jesus may be seen more clearly, since in the following verse Jesus meets him and sets him free.

Today, this passage reminds us that no person is beyond the reach of Christ. If we know someone who is suffering and hurting himself or herself, we can approach them with compassion, pray for them, and help them seek support, without judging them and without giving up.
exp.4:7:
This verse explains why the man was crying out in such fear. Jesus had already been telling the spirit: "Come out of the man." "Unclean" means impure, something that harms and pulls a person away from God. The earlier verse's phrase that means "I solemnly beg you" is not needed here; the verse itself says "Come out of the man, thou unclean spirit," so the reader can follow the command directly.

The narrator, Mark, makes clear what happened before the cry. Jesus arrived in the region of the Gadarenes and met a tormented man. The spirits recognized Jesus and were afraid, because they knew He had authority over them. Some scholars think the man and the spirit speak as if mixed together, and the text does not fully explain this.

For today: no darkness, vice, or fear is stronger than the word of Jesus. If you carry something that binds you, come to Him with confidence, and also seek the support of brothers and sisters in your church.
exp.9:20:
Jesus looked at this man with love and pointed out the one thing he still lacked: to sell what he had, give the money to the poor, and follow him. The explanation notes that the words "loved him" are the same as the words in the verse, so the wording of the verse is reflected here, and that Jesus also spoke to him. He promised treasure in heaven. The phrase "take up the cross" appears in this version and expresses the cost of being a disciple.

Jesus speaks with a rich man who asked him how to inherit eternal life. The man said he had kept the commandments since his youth. Jesus did not scold him but looked at him with love and went to the depths of his heart. What he had had become the most important thing to him, and he went away sad.

Today we can honestly ask ourselves what we find hard to let go of in order to follow Jesus. It may be money, comfort, or something else. Let us give it to God with trust, knowing that his call is born of love.
exp.0:13:
When John the Baptist was put in prison, Jesus returned to the region of Galilee and began to proclaim the good news of the kingdom of God.

Mark, the narrator, tells how Jesus had just come through the wilderness, where he was tested. Now his public ministry begins. John's arrest, the one who prepared the way, marks the start of this new stage. The text does not explain every detail of that change, but it shows that God's message goes forward even when his messengers suffer.

For today: even when there are difficult moments or losses around you, God is still at work. Ask him for courage to share with simplicity the hope you have received, without waiting for perfect conditions.
exp.0:9:
This verse tells what happened just as Jesus came up out of the water after being baptized. "Straightway" means "immediately," and the word "saw" is the one used in the verse above. Jesus saw the heavens opened and the Spirit descending upon him like a dove. Some understand that only Jesus saw this; the text puts it that way, though other Gospels tell it with some differences.

Mark is the one narrating. John the Baptist had just announced that someone greater would come to baptize with the Holy Spirit. This scene shows that Jesus is that messenger sent by God. Immediately the Father speaks from heaven, and so we see the Father, the Son, and the Spirit acting together.

For today: Jesus began his work knowing he was loved by God and guided by his Spirit. We can remember that God loves us as his children before we do anything, and ask him each day to guide us by his Spirit.
exp.6:24:
This verse tells us that a woman, whose little daughter was troubled by an unclean spirit (that is, an evil spirit), heard that Jesus was nearby. As soon as she heard about him, she went looking for him and fell at his feet. The phrase "as soon as" in this verse is a rendering of the same idea as "immediately" or "no sooner than."

Jesus had just taught that what defiles a person comes out of the heart, not from what they eat. Afterward he went to the region of Tyre and Sidon, a land of Gentiles, and wanted to go unnoticed, but he could not. Mark is the one who tells the story, and he presents this woman as a foreigner who comes forward with urgency.

When something overwhelms us, we can do what she did: come to Jesus without delay and with humility. We do not need perfect words or a sense that we are worthy; it is enough to come to his feet and place before him what hurts us most.
exp.13:0:
It was two days before the Passover and the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which were very important Jewish celebrations. The chief priests and the scribes were looking for a way to arrest Jesus by deceit, that is, with cunning and in secret, in order to kill him. To arrest him means to take him into custody.

Mark, the narrator, places us in Jesus' last days in Jerusalem. The religious authorities saw him as a threat to their influence. They feared the people, who admired Jesus, so they wanted to act without causing an uproar. While they plan evil, Mark prepares the contrast with the woman who will anoint Jesus.

For today: when someone acts out of envy or fear, they can end up doing unjust things. Let us examine our hearts and ask God to deliver us from envy, so that we always act with honesty and truth.
exp.3:40:
The disciples felt a very great awe and reverence. They asked one another who Jesus was, because even the wind and the sea obeyed him. The phrase "they feared exceedingly" does not speak only of fear of the storm, but of a holy awe before his power. "The sea" refers to the Sea of Galilee.

The disciples are going with Jesus in a boat when a strong storm arrives. Jesus was sleeping; they wake him, he calms the wind, and then he asks them about their faith. Mark presents here a key question of his Gospel: who is Jesus? The disciples do not yet fully understand, and the text does not detail their thoughts any further.

Today, when a storm frightens you, remember who is in the boat with you. Before carrying your worries alone, bring them to Jesus in prayer. Trusting him does not remove the storm at once, but it reminds you that he has authority over what surrounds you and that he is near you.
exp.7:14:
Jesus gives his disciples a firm command: "Take heed," that is, "watch yourselves," and "beware," meaning "be on your guard," against the leaven of the Pharisees and the leaven of Herod. Leaven is what makes bread dough rise; here it works as an image of something that spreads little by little.

Jesus speaks in the boat with his disciples, after a conflict with the Pharisees who had asked him for a sign. They were only thinking that they had no bread, and they did not understand the warning. Jesus uses leaven as a symbol of an influence that spreads. Many believe he is referring to hardness of heart and unbelief; the text does not go into more detail.

Today we can ask ourselves what ideas or attitudes influence our hearts without our noticing. It is good to compare what we hear with the words of Jesus and to ask him for an attentive heart, ready to believe.
exp.7:37:
Jesus says that whoever is ashamed of him and of his teachings, in this unfaithful and sinful generation, will also be a source of shame for the Son of man when he returns. The word "adulterous" in the verse means unfaithful to God, abandoning him for other loyalties. The word "gain" refers to winning or profiting. "Son of man" is the title Jesus uses for himself.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, shortly after announcing that he would suffer and die, and after inviting them to take up the cross to follow him (Mark 8:34-37). He warns them that following him has a cost, and that eternal life is worth more than any gain or approval this world can offer.

For today: when it is uncomfortable or when you are mocked for your faith, do not hide it. Look for an opportunity this week to be honest about your trust in Jesus, with love and respect, without fear of what others may think.
exp.0:32:
It says that all the people of the city gathered in front of the door of the house. "Gathered" means they came together as a crowd, and "crowded at the door" shows that they pressed in outside, waiting for Jesus.

Mark tells what happened in Capernaum, on a Sabbath, after Jesus healed Simon Peter's mother-in-law. At sunset the Sabbath ended, and the people felt free to bring their sick. That is why they came with so many who needed help. Mark is the one telling the story, and he wants to show that Jesus has power and compassion, and that the news about him spread quickly.

For today: like those people, we can come to Jesus with our burdens and the burdens of others. If you know someone who is suffering, bring them to Christ in prayer, with confidence and without growing weary.
exp.10:19:
The explanation says that, as they passed by again in the morning, the disciples saw that the fig tree was dried up from the roots. It was not just that the leaves looked bad: the tree had died completely. "From the roots" means the damage went down to the very depths.

Here Mark speaks as the narrator. The day before, Jesus had cursed that fig tree for having no fruit (Mark 11:12-14). Between those two moments, Jesus cleansed the temple, and the religious leaders were looking for a way to kill him. Many understand the fig tree as a sign about a religion without fruit, though others see it mainly as a lesson about faith.

For today: Jesus teaches us to trust God. Ask Him with sincerity, and at the same time examine whether your life bears real fruit and not just appearance.
exp.14:5:
At that feast, the explanation says, Pilate had the custom of releasing a prisoner to the people, whichever one they asked for. The word "whomsoever" simply means "whoever," and "released" means "set free." It is a brief explanation of a custom of the time.

The one telling this is Mark, who is narrating the trial of Jesus before Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate had already been amazed at Jesus' silence. Now Mark presents this custom because it will be key: the crowd will ask for Barabbas to be released and not Jesus. Historians have little information outside the Bible about this practice, so it is best not to say more than the text states.

For today: Jesus remained silent and accepted the path of the cross while others decided his fate. We can remember that his silence was not weakness but surrender. Today we can give thanks to him and ask ourselves whether we follow Christ or the crowd.
exp.13:20:
Jesus says that his death will happen just as the Scriptures foretold. But he warns, with sorrow, that it will go very badly for the one who hands him over. "Woe" expresses grief and judgment. "It would have been good for that man if he had never been born" shows how serious that betrayal is. "Is betrayed" means that someone will put him into the hands of his enemies.

Jesus speaks with his twelve disciples during the Passover supper, shortly before he is arrested. They are saddened and ask, "Is it I?" Jesus knows what is coming, and yet he remains calm. By saying "as it is written," he shows that his path to the cross is no accident. Even so, the responsibility of the one who betrays him remains real.

For today: instead of pointing at others, we can ask ourselves with humility whether our hearts are drifting away from Christ, and ask him to keep us faithful.
exp.2:15:
This verse begins the list of the twelve apostles and names Simon first. It says that Jesus gave him the name Peter. The word for "surnamed" in the verse above means "named" or "gave a name to," and this is the word the verse uses for what Jesus did. Peter means "rock" (in Aramaic, Cephas).

Mark tells us that Jesus went up the mountain and chose twelve to be with him, to go out and preach, and to have authority over diseases and demons. Simon heads the list, just as he does in the other New Testament lists. Mark does not explain here why Jesus gave him that name. Other gospels, such as Matthew 16:18, connect it to a later moment.

Jesus calls people by name and sees in them more than they see in themselves. Peter was imperfect, yet Jesus gave him a new identity. Today you can trust that God does not define you by your failures, but by what he can do in you. Place yourself in his hands today.
exp.2:7:
This verse lists the places people came from to seek Jesus: Jerusalem, Idumea, the other side of the Jordan, and the area of Tyre and Sidon. It was a "great multitude," drawn because they heard "what great things he did." "Came unto him" means they went toward him.

Mark, as narrator, tells us that Jesus withdrew to the sea with his disciples, because the Pharisees and the Herodians were already plotting to kill him. While some leaders rejected him, crowds from distant regions, even from non-Jewish areas like Tyre and Sidon, were coming to him. Idumea was a region south of Judea.

For today: the fame of Jesus drew many people, and today too there are those who seek him out of need. We can approach him with confidence, bringing him our real burdens, and remember that his invitation has no borders. Let us ask him to give us a heart that seeks him, not only for what he does, but for who he is.
exp.12:36:
What Jesus taught his four closest disciples was not meant only for them, but for everyone. To watch means to stay awake, alert, and ready. He is giving a short, direct command that closes the whole discourse.

Jesus is speaking on the Mount of Olives with Peter, James, John, and Andrew. He has spoken to them about hard times and his return, and he has said that no one knows the day or the hour. Just before this verse, he tells the parable of a master who goes away on a journey and leaves his servants and the doorkeeper waiting for his return. He ends by extending the call to everyone who hears.

Today we can live with spiritual alertness: praying each day, obeying God in small things, and not putting off what he asks of us. Being ready is not living in fear, but living with faithfulness and hope.
exp.0:29:
The explanation says that Simon's (Peter's) mother-in-law was in bed, with a fever. The word for fever here is a common, everyday one. The phrase that tells us they spoke to Jesus about her right away is rendered with the word "anon" in the verse; the explanation simply means they told him about her immediately.

Mark tells us that Jesus had just left the synagogue in Capernaum, where he had taught and healed a man with an unclean spirit. Now he arrives with his first disciples at the house of Simon and Andrew. Those who speak to Jesus are probably the people of the house, although the text does not make this clear. They do not ask for anything explicitly; they simply inform him of the need.

For today: we can do what they did, telling Jesus plainly what is happening to someone we love. An elegant prayer is not necessary; it is enough to present the need to him with confidence.
exp.13:21:
This verse tells how, while they were eating, Jesus took bread, gave thanks to God for it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples. He said: "Take, eat; this is my body." Some words in the wording you are reading are older: the phrase "take, eat" is what the words "take" and "eat" in the verse above convey, and the old forms are simply the familiar English of the same command.

Jesus speaks with the twelve during the Passover meal, shortly before he is arrested. He had just announced that one of them would betray him. Even so, he shares the bread with all of them. With this gesture, he signals that his body will be given up. Christians understand in different ways how Christ is present in this bread, but all of them remember it as a central act.

For today: when you take part in the Lord's Supper, do so with gratitude and humility, remembering that Jesus gave himself up for you, even knowing that they would abandon him.
exp.11:1:
He says that the owner of the vineyard, when the time of the harvest came, sent a servant of his to the workers who tended it. His purpose was to receive a share of the fruit that belonged to him. The vineyard had been leased to them, which means it had been rented out to them in exchange for a portion of the harvest.

Jesus tells this parable in Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion, to religious leaders who were questioning his authority. The vineyard is usually understood to be Israel (Isaiah 5), the owner as God, and the servants as the prophets who were sent. The workers represent the leaders who were supposed to care for the people.

For today: everything we have comes from God, and we are stewards, not owners. We can ask ourselves whether we respond with humility when God speaks to us, even through people or corrections we did not expect.
exp.8:20:
Jesus asks the boy's father how long it has been since this began to happen to him, and the man answers, "From childhood." The old words here are "há" (has been) and "aconteció" (happened). The young man's suffering went back a long way.

Jesus has just come down from the mountain and finds a crowd, some disciples who were unable to help, and a desperate father. Although the spirit is already tormenting the boy in front of everyone, Jesus does not act at once. He asks a calm question. Scholars often see compassion here: Jesus gives the father room to tell his pain and his story.

For today: Jesus is not hurried in the face of your old or recurring suffering. You can tell him calmly what you have carried for years, without hiding anything. He listens, understands, and remains compassionate.
exp.7:33:
Jesus invites the crowd and his disciples to follow him. He says that whoever wants to come after him must let go of himself, that is, stop putting his own desires first. He must also take up his cross, meaning he must be willing to suffer and bear rejection for following him. And then, follow me: walk with him every day.

Jesus has just announced that he will suffer and die. Peter rebuked him, thinking the way people think, and Jesus corrected him firmly. Now Jesus widens the message to everyone: the Master's way is one of surrender and sacrifice, and his followers walk it with him. In that time the cross was a symbol of execution, so his hearers understood that this was something very serious.

Today, following Jesus can mean choosing his way even when it costs: forgiving when it hurts, being honest even when you lose something, or serving without seeking applause. Ask yourself today: where must I say "no" to myself in order to say "yes" to Jesus?
exp.13:68:
This verse tells that the servant girl of the high priest saw Peter again and began to say to those who were standing nearby, "This is one of them." Peter had been identified once before and had denied it. Now she is speaking to the bystanders, which makes the situation more dangerous for him.

It is the night Jesus was arrested. Peter had gone into the courtyard to follow closely what was happening to his Master. The servant girl had already pointed him out once, and he denied it. Now he is pressed again, and this time the accusation is made openly to others. Peter is afraid, and soon he will deny Jesus once more.

For today: the pressure of people around us can make us silent about our faith. Peter fell, but Jesus restored him afterward. If we fail today, we can return to Him with humility. And if we can, let us ask for courage before the test.
exp.14:46:
The explanation says that two women, Mary Magdalene and Mary the mother of Joses, were watching the place where the body of Jesus was laid. The word "beheld" means that they looked on closely and with attention, and "where he was laid" refers to the place where they were putting his body.

Mark, as narrator, tells what happened after the death of Jesus. Joseph of Arimathea had already buried the body and closed the tomb with a stone. These women had followed Jesus and now were witnesses of his burial. Their looking is important because later they would return to that same tomb (Mark 16:1-2). Some think Mark stresses this so that it is clear they did not mistake the tomb.

For today: sometimes the only thing we can do in the midst of grief is to remain faithful and present. God can use that simple faithfulness, even when we do not yet understand what is coming.
exp.13:25:
He says that Jesus and his disciples, after finishing the Passover supper, sang a hymn and then went out toward the Mount of Olives, a hill east of Jerusalem. "Went out" means they left that place. "Had sung" means they had already sung.

Mark, in telling the story, recounts what happened right after the Last Supper. Jesus had just spoken of his blood poured out and of the new covenant. Many understand that the hymn was the psalms sung at Passover (Psalms 113 to 118), but the text does not say this precisely. Jesus knew what was coming: the abandonment of his friends and the cross.

For today: even when Jesus faced his hardest moment, he sang. When a trial comes, we can praise God and trust in Him, without waiting for everything to be resolved.
exp.10:5:
Here the account tells us that the two disciples answered those who were there in exactly the way Jesus had told them to answer. And they let them go. A young donkey is a little colt, and "let them go" means they allowed them to take it away.

Jesus was approaching Jerusalem and sent two disciples for a colt that no one had ever ridden. He told them what to say if anyone asked. According to the account, Jesus said they should answer that the Lord needs it (v. 3). Some see here a special knowledge on Jesus' part; others think there may have been a prior arrangement. The text does not make this clear.

For today: the disciples obeyed even though the task seemed strange and risky. We can trust Jesus' word and take the step He asks of us, even when we do not understand everything.
exp.2:3:
Jesus asks those who were watching him a direct question: on the Sabbath, is it right to do good or to do evil, to save a life or to destroy it? The words "lawful" and "to kill" in the verse above are the ones this part of the explanation is about, so the question is simply whether doing good or doing harm is what is permitted, and whether saving a life or taking one is what is allowed. They stayed silent and did not answer.

Jesus is in a synagogue, and some men are watching him to see whether he will heal a man with a withered hand, so that they can accuse him. He places the man in the middle and confronts them with this question. Their silence shows that they do not want to discuss the matter honestly. Shortly afterward, the text says that Jesus was grieved at the hardness of their hearts, and that they began to plan his death.

For today: do not use rules or religion as an excuse for ignoring someone who is suffering. Ask yourself humbly whether your attitude helps people, or whether it only defends your comfort or your pride.
exp.3:12:
Jesus asks his disciples whether they do not understand the parable of the sower. The phrase "to notice" means "to realize." If they do not grasp this one, they will not be able to understand the other parables either. It is a question meant to make them think, almost a wake-up call.

Jesus speaks to the twelve and to others who were nearby. He had just told the parable of the sower, and they asked him about its meaning. He had told them that it was given to them to know the mystery of the kingdom. This parable is like a key to understanding the others, and right away he explains its meaning.

For today: do not be ashamed to ask when you do not understand the Bible. Ask God to open your heart, and humbly seek out Jesus and other believers who can help you understand his Word.
exp.14:8:
Pilate asks the crowd whether they want him to release Jesus. He calls him "King of the Jews," a title that appears throughout the trial scene. The phrase "Will ye that I release unto you" means "Do you want me to set free for you?" (or "Do you want me to release him to you?"), and "Will ye" simply means "Do you want?"

Pilate speaks to the people who came to ask for the customary pardon of the festival. Mark explains that Pilate knew the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy. It seems Pilate hoped the people would choose Jesus instead of Barabbas, a prisoner accused of rebellion and murder. But the priests stirred up the crowd in another direction.

For today: let us not be swept along by the opinion of the majority or by the envy of others. Let us ask God for courage to defend what is right, even when the atmosphere around us goes against it.
exp.2:4:
This verse shows Jesus looking around at the people near him with anger, yet also with grief over the hardness of their hearts. Then he tells the man to stretch out his hand, and when he does, it is made well.

The explanation's three quoted words are not in the verse above, so the sentences that define them are removed.

Jesus is in a synagogue on a Sabbath. The Pharisees were watching him closely so they could accuse him if he healed. He asks them whether it is lawful to do good on the Sabbath, and they remain silent. His anger is not born of resentment but of seeing that they would rather keep a rule than preserve a person's life. After this, they begin to plan his death.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we sometimes place our customs or ideas above compassion. God invites us to have a tender heart, one that rejoices when someone receives help, and to act with love without waiting for everything to be comfortable.
exp.11:4:
The explanation says that the owner of the vineyard kept sending servants to the tenant farmers. One of them was killed, and many others were beaten or killed.

Jesus tells this parable in Jerusalem to the religious leaders, shortly before his crucifixion. The vineyard represents Israel (as in Isaiah 5), and the owner represents God. Many understand the servants to be the prophets, who were often rejected. The tenant farmers are the leaders who refused to answer to God. Jesus shows them his patience and also their hardness of heart.

Today we can ask ourselves how we respond when God corrects us, whether through his Word or through other people. His patience is an invitation to listen with humility and to turn back to him before hardening our hearts.
exp.8:32:
Jesus and his disciples arrive in Capernaum. Once they are inside the house, Jesus asks them a direct question: "What was it that ye disputed among yourselves by the way?" The old word "disputed" in this verse means arguing or quarreling with words.

Jesus had just told them that he would be handed over, would die, and would rise again. They did not understand, and they were afraid to ask him. Meanwhile, they had been arguing about who was the greatest among them. Jesus already knew what they had been talking about; his question invited them to be honest. His answer afterward was that whoever wants to be first must be a servant of all.

Today, Jesus also knows our thoughts and motives. Instead of hiding our pride or ambition, we can bring them to him with honesty and ask him for a humble heart that seeks to serve others before seeking to stand out.
exp.14:12:
They cried out again, and their shouts called for Jesus to be crucified. "They cried out again" means that they shouted once more. Calling for him to be crucified means asking that he be put to death nailed to a cross, a very cruel Roman punishment.

Pilate had just asked what should be done with Jesus, whom they called the King of the Jews. The chief priests had stirred up the crowd to ask for the release of Barabbas. So the crowd, influenced by their leaders, shouts against Jesus. Mark shows that Jesus was rejected unjustly, even though Pilate himself could see that he had done no wrong.

For today: it is easy to be swept along by what the majority shouts or by leaders who pressure us. Before repeating an opinion or joining a group, it is wise to stop, think, and ask God for the courage to defend what is right.
exp.0:17:
Simon and Andrew, as soon as Jesus called them, left their nets and went after him. The explanation notes that the word translated "straightway" means "immediately" or "at once." "Forsook" means "having left behind." "Followed him" speaks of going with him as disciples, not merely walking behind him.

Mark tells of the beginning of Jesus' ministry in Galilee. Walking beside the sea, Jesus invited two fishermen to follow him and promised to make them fishers of men. Mark does not explain why they answered so quickly; he only shows that Jesus' word had authority over them. Some think they may have already known him, but this text does not say so.

Following Jesus involves letting something go. It may not be your work, but it may be some security, habit, or fear that holds you back. Ask God today to show you which net you need to leave behind so that you can obey him promptly.
exp.15:10:
This verse tells us that the disciples heard that Jesus was alive and that Mary Magdalene had seen him, but they did not believe it. The word "alive" simply means that he was living, and the phrase "did not believe" means that they doubted the news.

Mark tells what happened after the resurrection. Jesus first appeared to Mary Magdalene, and she went to tell the disciples, who were sad and mourning his death. Mark does not hide their unbelief, and he goes on to say that they did not believe two others who saw him as well. Some scholars think this shows the honesty of the account.

Today, if you sometimes find it hard to believe or to trust, you are not alone. The first disciples doubted too. Bring your doubts to God honestly, and keep seeking the truth with humility.
exp.8:2:
What it says: When Jesus was transfigured, his clothing became shining, a white so intense it was like snow. Mark adds that no one on earth who washed and whitened cloth could make it that white.

Context: Mark, who is writing, tells what Peter, James, and John saw on a high mountain. Jesus had just spoken about the kingdom of God coming with power. This scene lets them see, for a moment, the glory of Jesus. The text does not say which mountain it was, and tradition has proposed several.

For today: Jesus is greater than we sometimes imagine. When you feel tired or confused, take a moment to remember his glory and his power. Read it in the Gospels and ask him to strengthen your trust in him.
exp.12:30:
Jesus says that everything that seems most firm, heaven and earth, will one day stop existing as we know them. But his words will never fail to come true or lose their value. "Pass away" means that they will come to an end or disappear.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. He has been telling them about signs and hard times, and they want to know what will come. Scholars understand in different ways what is meant by "this generation" and "these things," but they all agree that Jesus wants to give assurance: what he said can be trusted, even though no one knows the day or the hour.

Today, when the news or life fills you with fear and uncertainty, lean on the words of Jesus. Read a passage from the Gospels each day and trust that what he promises is more solid than anything you see.
exp.2:34:
Jesus says that whoever does God's will is, to him, like a brother, a sister, or a mother. The old wording that his readers would have seen does not appear in the verse you are reading, so there is nothing more to explain about it. God's will is what God wants and asks of us.

Jesus is speaking in a house full of people. His mother and his brothers had arrived and sent word for him from outside (Mark 3:31-32). Earlier, some of his relatives thought he had lost his mind (3:21). Jesus looks at the people listening to him and calls them his family. He is not rejecting his mother; he is showing that his true family is united by obeying God, not only by blood.

For today: it is not enough to admire Jesus or to say that we believe in him. This week, choose one specific thing that God asks of you, such as forgiving someone, helping someone in need, or being honest, and do it with joy. In this way you live as part of his family.
exp.3:14:
Jesus explains that some people are like the path beside the field. God's word falls on them, but as soon as they hear it, Satan comes and takes it away from their hearts. "Taketh away" means snatches away, and the word "was" in the verse above is the same as "was" in today's English.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples after telling the parable of the sower. He explains its meaning because they did not understand it. He says this parable is the key to understanding all the others. The seed is the word, and the different kinds of ground represent how each person's heart responds.

For today: do not let what you hear from God be lost. After reading the Bible or listening to a teaching, write down one idea, think about it during the day, and ask God to help you put it into practice.
exp.7:9:
He says that Jesus, right after sending the crowd away, got into the boat with his disciples and came to the region of Dalmanutha. "Straightway" means "immediately," and the "boat" here is a fishing boat on the Sea of Galilee. Nobody knows for certain where Dalmanutha was; Matthew 15:39 mentions Magdala, and some think it is the same area or a nearby one, but this is not confirmed.

The one telling the story is Mark. Jesus had just fed about four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish. This verse is a brief transition: one miracle of provision ends and a new encounter begins, in which the Pharisees ask him for a sign, even though they had already seen many.

For today: God has already shown us his faithfulness in many ways. Instead of demanding more proof, we can remember what he has done and follow Jesus with confidence, even when the path suddenly changes.
exp.3:0:
Mark tells us that Jesus began teaching again beside the sea of Galilee. So many people gathered that he got into a small boat and sat in it, a little way out from the shore. The crowd stayed on the beach, facing him. Some older or unusual words in the source are explained by the sentence that follows: "the sea" is the lake of Galilee, and "boat" is a small vessel.

The narrator is Mark, and the main character is Jesus. Mark says "again" because Jesus had already taught in that place before. Many think the boat helped everyone see and hear him better, though the text does not say so. What follows is the parable of the sower.

For today: if Jesus looked for a way for the people to hear him well, we too can prepare a quiet time free of distractions to listen to his Word with attention.
exp.1:13:
As Jesus was passing by, he saw Levi, the son of Alphaeus, sitting in the tax booth, that is, the place where taxes were collected. Jesus said to him, "Follow me," and Levi got up and followed him.

Jesus had just healed a paralyzed man in Capernaum and had taught the crowd again by the sea. Tax collectors were looked down on, because they worked for Rome and sometimes collected more than they should. Many believe that Levi is the same person as Matthew, although the text here does not say so. Afterward, Jesus eats in Levi's house, and the religious leaders are scandalized.

Jesus calls the one whom others despise. If today you feel you do not deserve his call, remember that he invites you just as you are. Responding promptly, leaving behind what gets in the way, is the first step to following him.
exp.7:23:
Jesus has touched the blind man's eyes, and he begins to see, but not clearly. He says he sees people, though they look like trees walking. He can make out shapes and movement, but not yet the details. "I see men, for they look like trees, walking" means: I see large shapes that are moving.

The blind man speaks, the one whom Jesus led out of the village. Mark is the only one who tells this healing in two stages. Some believe it teaches that the disciples also understand little by little; others think it only shows a method of Jesus. The Bible does not explain this clearly.

For today: if your faith or your understanding of God is still blurry, do not lose heart. Keep coming to Jesus with sincerity, asking him to help you see more clearly, and trust that he finishes what he begins.
exp.14:43:
Mark tells us that Pilate was surprised that Jesus had already died. So he called the centurion, the Roman officer in charge of the soldiers at the crucifixion, and asked him whether Jesus was really already dead.

Mark is the one narrating. Joseph of Arimathea, a respected member of the Jewish council, had just asked Pilate for Jesus' body. Pilate wanted to be sure before handing it over. Crucifixion normally took much longer to cause death, which is why this surprised him. The centurion's confirmation shows that Jesus' death was real and verified.
