For today: our faith rests on real events, not on vague ideas. Jesus truly died, and that is why his resurrection has such power. We can trust Him with confidence, and we can also be encouraged, like Joseph, to act with courage out of love for Christ.
exp.4:2:
This verse says that the man lived among the tombs, as if that were his home. The word "dwelling" is an old way of saying "house" or "place where he lives." In addition, no one could restrain him, not even with chains. He was a man who was rejected, isolated, and beyond the control of the people around him.

Mark is not recounting a speech, but narrating what Jesus found when he arrived in the region of the Gadarenes. He describes the seriousness of the case in detail to show that no human power could help him. In this way the reader is prepared to see Jesus's power over evil.

For today: when a person or a situation seems impossible to change, let us remember that Jesus does draw near. We can pray for those who live isolated, and treat them with compassion, not with fear or contempt.
exp.1:18:
Jesus answers with a simple question: can the guests at a wedding fast while the bridegroom is with them? He himself answers that they cannot. "Bridegroom" means the man getting married, and "the children of the bridechamber" are the wedding guests. While the bridegroom is present, it is a time to celebrate.

Some people asked why the disciples of John and of the Pharisees fasted, while Jesus' disciples did not. Jesus presents himself as the bridegroom. His presence brings joy, like a feast, and so it was not a time for sorrow or mourning. Then he speaks of a day when he will be taken away from them, and then they would fast. Many understand this as a reference to his death.

Today we can live with joy and gratitude because Christ is near. If we fast, let it be to seek him sincerely, not to fulfill a custom or to appear devout.
exp.6:32:
This verse tells how Jesus took a deaf man who also had a speech impediment away from the crowd. There, he put his fingers in the man's ears and, after spitting, touched the man's tongue. The phrase "taking him aside" means that he led him to a private place.

The one acting here is Jesus, and Mark is the one who tells the story. The man's friends had brought him to Jesus and asked him to lay his hand on him. Jesus responds in a more personal way: he uses gestures that the man, who could not hear, could understand. Some believe that in this way Jesus was treating him with gentleness; the text does not explain why he used saliva, so it is better not to claim more than the text says.

For today: Jesus does not treat people as a number in the crowd. When someone is suffering, it is worth coming close to them in private, with patience and tenderness. We can also bring our personal wounds to Jesus, confident that he attends to us with care.
exp.1:6:
The scribes think to themselves: "Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming. Who can forgive sins but God alone?" "Blasphemies" means words that insult God or that claim for oneself what belongs only to God.

The ones speaking are some scribes, teachers of the Law. Jesus had just told the paralyzed man that his sins were forgiven. They were right that only God forgives, but they did not recognize that Jesus was acting with divine authority. Jesus answers them by healing the man, to show who He is.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we truly recognize who Jesus is. He is concerned not only with our visible needs, but also with the deepest one: forgiveness. If you carry guilt, bring it to Jesus with confidence, for only God forgives, and He offers that forgiveness.
exp.4:12:
Jesus gives the evil spirits permission to enter the pigs. They leave the man and go into a herd of about two thousand animals, which rushes down a steep slope into the sea and drowns.

Jesus has just arrived in the region of the Gadarenes and has freed a man tormented by a host of demons. The spirits beg him not to send them away and ask to enter the pigs. Jesus has authority over them, and they can do only what he allows. Interpreters explain in various ways why he permitted it; the text does not make this clear.

For today: evil has limits, and Jesus holds final authority. If you feel bound by fear or by things that control you, come to him with confidence. His power sets people free and restores them to a healthy life, like the man who was found sitting, clothed, and in his right mind.
exp.5:55:
This verse tells that wherever Jesus went, into villages, cities, or the countryside, people laid the sick out in the streets, in the squares where everyone passed by. They begged him to let them touch, even just, the edge of his garment. All who touched him were made well.

The sentence that explained the old words has been left out, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

It is a summary by the narrator, Mark, about Jesus' ministry in the region of Gennesaret, after he crossed the lake with his disciples. The people recognized him at once and ran to bring him their sick. It shows the simple faith of the people and the compassionate power of Jesus. The text does not say that the garment had any power of its own; the healing came from Jesus.

Today, we can come to Jesus with our needs, even when our faith is small. We can also bring others to him in prayer, as these people did with their sick.
exp.4:17:
The explanation says that when Jesus was getting into the boat to leave, the man who had been tormented by a demon begged him to be allowed to stay with him. The word the source uses for "tormented" here means troubled or afflicted, and the reference is to the boat in which Jesus had crossed the lake.

Mark tells this after Jesus freed the man and the pigs rushed down the steep bank. The local people, frightened, asked Jesus to leave. The man, grateful and perhaps afraid to be left alone in that setting, wanted to stay close to the one who had set him free. Jesus had a different plan for him: to tell his testimony in his own land.

For today: wanting to be close to Jesus is good, but sometimes he calls us to serve him right where we live. Think about who in your family or among your friends needs to hear what God has done in your life, and tell them simply.
exp.14:38:
The explanation says that a Roman officer, the centurion, was standing in front of Jesus and saw how he died: he cried out loudly and breathed his last. The verse's wording for dying is "gave up the ghost," so that phrase is explained as meaning to stop breathing, to die. On seeing this, the man declared that Jesus was truly the Son of God.

The speaker is the centurion, a pagan soldier in charge of the execution. Mark has just told that the curtain of the temple was torn. His statement is the clearest confession in the whole Gospel, and it comes from a foreigner. It is not certain how much he understood by "Son of God"; some scholars see it as full faith and others as an initial astonishment.

For today: God can touch the heart of the person we least expect. Look with humility at Jesus' sacrifice and do not dismiss anyone, because anyone can recognize it.
exp.10:10:
This verse tells us that Jesus came to Jerusalem and went into the temple. There he looked carefully at everything around him. Since it was already late, he went out to Bethany with the twelve disciples. The explanation of the old wording is not needed here, since the verse uses plain words.

Mark tells what follows the triumphant entry without giving Jesus any words to say. When the crowd was shouting and welcoming him as the king who came in the name of the Lord, Jesus does not make a speech after all that applause. He quietly observes the temple. Mark does not explain what he was thinking. The next day Jesus will return and act there, so this careful look seems to prepare for what is coming.

For today: before acting or speaking, take time to look calmly and prayerfully. Jesus shows us how to pay close attention to what is happening in our lives and in the church, without letting ourselves be carried away only by the emotion of the moment.
exp.5:42:
It says that after everyone had eaten until they were satisfied, the disciples gathered up what was left over: twelve baskets full of pieces of bread, and also leftover pieces of the fish. "Gathered up" is the sense of the verb here, and the baskets were woven wicker containers.

Here the narrator, Mark, is telling what Jesus did. He had blessed five loaves and two fish, and with them he fed a crowd in a remote place. Mark notes that far more was left over than there had been at the start. Some see in the twelve baskets a sign pointing to the twelve tribes of Israel, but the text does not say so, so this is one possible interpretation.

For today: God does not only give what is needed, but often gives in abundance. We can place in his hands the little we have, trusting that he can multiply it, and also take care of what he gives us without wasting it.
exp.11:17:
These verses tell that some Sadducees came to Jesus. They were a religious group that denied the resurrection of the dead. They came to ask him a question. The phrase "come unto him" only means that they arrived where Jesús was, and "asked him" introduces what they will say next.

Mark tells this during Jesus' final days in Jerusalem. Earlier, some Pharisees and Herodians had tried to trap him with the question about the tax to Caesar. Now it is the Sadducees, a different group, who test him. They accepted above all the books of Moses, and they will use a difficult case to mock the idea of rising from the dead.

For today: when we have doubts about the faith, it is good to ask with humility in order to learn, not to win an argument. Jesus answers with patience even those who question him with bad intentions.
exp.11:14:
Jesus realizes that the people speaking to him are not sincere. He asks them why they are testing him, and he asks for a coin so he can see it. Here "testing" means putting someone to the test with bad intent, and "hypocrisy" means pretending to feel or believe something you do not.

Pharisees and Herodians, who normally did not get along, join together to trap Jesus. They flatter him first and then ask him a question about paying the tax to the Roman emperor. Any answer could get him into trouble, either with the people or with the authorities. Jesus knows their intentions and does not fall into the trap.

God sees beyond our pretty words. Today we can ask ourselves whether our questions and the way we speak with God and with others are sincere. He prefers an honest heart to a perfect speech.
exp.14:33:
Jesus cries out with a loud voice around the ninth hour, that is, three in the afternoon. He speaks the words "Eloi, Eloi, lama sabachthani?", which mean: "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" "Forsaken" means left alone, without help. To "reproach" someone meant to insult them.

He speaks from the cross, after three hours of darkness over the land. He quotes Psalm 22:1, a psalm that begins with pain and ends with trust in God. Christians understand this cry in several ways: as Jesus' real suffering as he bears our sin, and also as a prayer that points to that whole psalm. Some of those present misunderstood it and thought he was calling for Elijah.

If you feel alone or without answers today, you can speak to God honestly, even with your pain. Jesus himself prayed this way, and he understands what you feel.
exp.8:13:
He said that Jesus came to where the other disciples were and saw a large crowd around them. He also saw some scribes, who were teachers of the law, arguing with them. Some words are old: "came" is the word here, "saw" is the word here, "a large crowd" means a multitude, and "arguing" means discussing or debating.

Mark tells what happened when Jesus came down from the mountain with Peter, James and John, where he had been transfigured. Before that he had been speaking about Elijah and about his own suffering. On arriving, he finds an atmosphere of argument. The text does not state the exact subject here, but the story that follows shows that the disciples had not been able to help a sick child.

For today: when there is tension or arguments over things that are beyond us, let us not stay only debating. Let us bring the matter to Jesus, who arrives calmly and asks what is happening.
exp.1:22:
This verse tells how Jesus was walking through fields of grain on the Sabbath day, and as they went along, his disciples began to pick the heads of grain. A field of grain is simply a field that has been planted and cultivated, and the heads of grain are the top parts of the plant where the kernels grow.

Mark tells this as the start of an argument. Just before, Jesus spoke about a new patch on an old garment and new wine in old wineskins, to show that what he brought could not be fitted into old forms. The Pharisees, who watched the Sabbath very strictly, complained that his disciples were doing what was not permitted. Jesus answers by pointing to David.

For today: obedience to God is not only following rules, but understanding the heart of God, who cares for people. Before judging others, let us ask what God truly intends through his commands.
exp.14:39:
This verse says that some women were still watching the crucifixion of Jesus, but from a distance. It names three of them: Mary Magdalene, another Mary (the mother of James and Joses), and Salome. The words "the less" most likely distinguish this James from another man with the same name, perhaps by age or height.

Here the narrator, Mark, speaks. He has just told of Jesus' death and the centurion's declaration. He then points out that there were faithful witnesses. The verses that follow explain that these women had followed and served Jesus from Galilee. About the exact identity of Salome and of this Mary, the biblical texts give few details.

For today: sometimes our faith feels fearful or distant, but God values faithful presence. These women could not change what was happening, but they stayed. Stay close to Jesus and to those who suffer, even if all you can do is accompany them.
exp.11:25:
Jesus asks his listeners whether they have not read in the book of Moses what God said to him from the bush: "I am the God of Abraham, and the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob." The "bush" is the shrub that burned without being consumed, where God appeared to Moses (Exodus 3). You are wrong, and you do not understand, are the words Jesus uses to show how they had gone astray.

The one speaking is Jesus, and he is answering the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They had put to him a complicated case about a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus shows them that they are mistaken because they do not understand the Scriptures or the power of God. He uses a text from Moses because the Sadducees gave special value to the first books of the Bible.

For today: God remains faithful to those who trust in him, even beyond death. You can face your losses and fears with hope, and read the Bible with humility to know God better.
exp.3:31:
It says that the mustard seed, after it is sown, grows and becomes the greatest of the garden plants. It puts out branches so large that the birds of the air can make their nests under its shade. Here "garden plants" means herbs or vegetables from the garden, and "dwell" means to live or rest.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd by the Sea of Galilee, and he uses a parable to explain what the kingdom of God is like. He contrasts its very small beginning with a surprisingly large end. Some think the birds represent the peoples who find shelter in the kingdom, although the text does not explain this directly.

For today: do not despise small beginnings. A kind word, a faithful prayer, or an act of service may seem like little, but God can make them grow in ways you do not imagine. Do your part with steadiness, and trust that he gives the growth.
exp.3:35:
They had sent the crowd away, and Jesus and his disciples set out in the boat with him, just as he was, without any further preparation, right as he was after teaching. "Sent away" means dismissed or sent home. Other small boats also went with them.

Jesus had spent the day teaching in parables beside the Sea of Galilee. When evening came, he himself proposed crossing to the other side. Mark does not say who was in the other boats or what happened to them; he only mentions that they were there. What follows is the storm, and the disciples were obeying an order from Jesus.

Today, sometimes we obey God and storms still come. Following Christ does not guarantee a calm path, but he is in the boat with us. When something hard comes, remember that you are not alone and that he invited you to keep going.
exp.8:37:
John tells Jesus that they saw a man casting out demons in Jesus' name. Because this man was not part of the group of disciples, they told him to stop.

John speaks right after Jesus had placed a child among them and taught about humility and simplicity. Before that, the disciples had been arguing about who was the greatest. John seems concerned to protect his place as part of the group closest to Jesus. Jesus answers that they should not forbid him, because whoever acts in his name will not easily become his enemy.

Today we can rejoice when others serve Christ, even if they belong to another church or do not think exactly as we do on everything. Before criticizing, let us ask whether they honor Jesus, and let us celebrate the good that is done in his name.
exp.3:27:
This verse says that the earth produces fruit by itself, without the sower knowing how. First the tender blade comes up, then the ear, and at last the full grain inside the ear. The phrase "of herself" in the verse above is the same idea as "by itself," and "bringeth forth fruit" means "produces fruit."

Jesus is speaking to the crowd in parables. With this story he teaches how the kingdom of God works: the man sows the seed and waits, but the growth happens in a way he does not control and does not fully understand. Then comes the harvest. Some scholars see here a message about patience and others about the inherent power of God's word; the text does not explain this further.

For today: do faithfully what is yours to do, such as prayer, serving, or sharing the Word, and trust that God makes things grow in his time. Do not be discouraged if you do not see quick results.
exp.1:0:
He tells that Jesus returned to Capernaum after some days away. People found out that he was "at home". That phrase could refer to a house where he was staying, perhaps Peter's, although the text does not say so with certainty. "It was noised" means that the news spread.

Mark is the one narrating. Earlier, Jesus had traveled through Galilee preaching and healing, and his fame was growing. So when people learned he had come back, they gathered quickly. This verse sets up the next scene, where four men bring a paralyzed man so that Jesus can heal him.

For today: Jesus is willing to receive those who seek him, even in everyday life and at home. We can come to him simply, and also help others come to him, as those four friends will do.
exp.6:22:
This verse sums up the list before it: all those evil things, such as evil thoughts, deceit, theft, and pride, come from within a person. That is where what truly makes someone unclean before God begins. The words "shameless conduct" refer to behavior without decency, and "evil eye" to envy or ill will.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples. The Pharisees had criticized him because his disciples ate without washing their hands according to tradition. Jesus answers that what enters through the mouth does not make a person impure; the deeper problem lies in the heart.

For today: instead of blaming only our circumstances or other people, we can ask God each day to examine and cleanse our hearts, and to take care of what we feed into our thoughts.
exp.7:30:
Jesus begins to explain to his disciples that it was necessary for him, the Son of Man, to suffer greatly. He says he would be rejected by the elders, the chief priests, and the teachers of the law (the scribes). He also announces that they would kill him and that he would rise again after three days.

Peter had just confessed that Jesus is the Christ. Now Jesus shows them what kind of Messiah he would be: one who suffers before the glory. He says it plainly, and Peter reacts with rebuke, because he expected a different path.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we accept Jesus only when everything is easy, or also when his path includes sacrifice. Trusting God sometimes means accepting what we do not understand, knowing that he has a purpose and the final word.
exp.10:15:
This verse says that Jesus would not allow anyone to carry any object through the temple. The word "vessel" here does not mean only a small container, but any item, container, or tool that someone carried from one place to another. The verse's word "suffer" means allow.

Mark tells us what Jesus did when he entered the temple in Jerusalem. He had just driven out the sellers and the money changers. Some had been using the temple courtyard as a shortcut for their business and errands. Jesus wanted to restore the place to its purpose: to be a house of prayer for all nations. The religious leaders became angry and began looking for a way to kill him.

Today we can ask ourselves which everyday things, though they seem normal, take away reverence from our time with God. Let us make room to pray without rush or distraction.
exp.13:53:
And Peter followed him from a distance, that is, without getting very close. He went as far as the courtyard of the house of the high priest, who was the most important religious leader. There he sat with the guards (the attendants or helpers) and warmed himself by the fire.

The one telling the story is Mark, who describes the night Jesus was arrested. The disciples had fled in fear, and Jesus was being taken before the Jewish leaders. Peter, who had promised not to abandon him, wanted to see what was happening, but without exposing himself too much. Mark lets us see his mix of loyalty and fear.

For today: following Jesus from a distance is easy, but it does not transform us. We can ask ourselves whether in some area, such as work or friendships, we keep our distance out of fear. Ask God for courage to draw closer to Jesus and to be faithful.
exp.1:5:
This verse says that there were some scribes sitting in that place. The scribes were men who copied and taught the Law of Moses. They were reasoning in their hearts, that is, in the innermost part of their minds, without saying anything out loud.

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. Jesus had just told the paralyzed man that his sins were forgiven. The scribes heard that and began to question it in silence. They thought Jesus was speaking as though he were God. Mark shows us that Jesus knew what they were thinking, even though they did not say it.

For today: God knows our quietest thoughts. Instead of keeping doubts or criticisms in our hearts, we can bring them honestly to Jesus and ask him to teach us to see with faith.
exp.0:44:
He says that the man who had been healed of leprosy, as he went out, began to tell everyone what had happened to him and to spread the news. Because of this, Jesus could no longer enter the cities openly; He stayed in deserted places, and even so, people came to Him from everywhere. The words "publish it" and "spread the matter" mean to announce and spread the news. "Openly" means "in plain sight of everyone."

Mark tells this after Jesus healed the leper and asked him to say nothing, but to present himself to the priest. The man did not obey that part. Scholars explain in various ways why Jesus asked for silence; one idea is that He was avoiding crowds that were only looking for miracles.

For today: thanking God is good, but obeying Him is part of that thanks. Let us speak of what He has done, and let us do it with wisdom and attention to what He asks of us.
exp.5:3:
Jesus says that a prophet is honored everywhere except in his own country, among his relatives, and in his own house. The word "dishonored" here means that people do not respect or value him. "Country" refers to his hometown.

Jesus speaks in the synagogue at Nazareth, where he grew up. The people are amazed at his wisdom and his miracles, but they see him only as the carpenter, the son of Mary, and they know his family. For this reason they were offended, that is, they stumbled and would not accept him. This lack of faith limited what Jesus did there, and he marveled at their unbelief.

For today: let us not allow custom or what we think we know about someone to close our hearts. God can speak through people who are very familiar to us and who seem ordinary. Let us listen with humility and faith.
exp.1:21:
No one puts new wine into old wineskins. The wineskins were bags made of animal leather used to store wine. Over time the old leather hardened and lost its stretch. New wine kept fermenting and expanding, so it would burst the old skin, and both the wine and the skin would be lost. That is why new wine is poured into new skins.

Jesus speaks with some people who asked him why his disciples did not fast like the disciples of John and the Pharisees. He answers with three images: the bridegroom with his guests, the patch, and the wine. He shows that his arrival brings something new that does not fit into rigid religious forms. Interpreters explain in various ways exactly what the wineskins represent, but all of them see a contrast between the new and the old.

Today, ask God for a heart willing to learn. Do not cling to customs just because they have always been done that way.
exp.1:14:
This verse tells us that Jesus was sitting down to eat in Levi's house. Many tax collectors and sinners were with them, people who collected taxes and had a bad reputation. They were at the table together with Jesus and his disciples, because there were many who followed him.

Mark describes what happened right after Jesus called Levi, a tax collector, and Levi followed him. The house seems to be Levi's, though the text simply says "in his house." Tax collectors were looked down on for collecting taxes for Rome. Soon after, the Pharisees criticized this meal, and Jesus answered that he came to call sinners.

Jesus did not wait for people to be perfect before drawing near to them. We can follow his example today: invite to your table someone who feels far from God, and treat them with respect and kindness.
exp.13:14:
Jesus says that the owner of the house will show them a large room upstairs, already furnished and ready. The word "upper room" is an older term for a dining room or hall on the upper floor. The disciples were to get everything ready there for the Passover supper.

Jesus speaks to two disciples whom he sends to Jerusalem, shortly before his arrest. He is going to celebrate the Passover with the twelve. He gives them very specific signs: a man carrying a jar of water and the owner of a house. Mark does not explain whether Jesus had arranged this beforehand or knew it in some other way; the text only shows that everything happened as he said.

For today: Jesus knows what is coming and attends to the details. We can obey step by step, even without seeing the whole way, trusting that he has already prepared what is needed.
exp.14:45:
Mark tells us that Joseph of Arimathea bought a linen cloth. He took down Jesus' body from the cross, wrapped him in the cloth, and placed him in a tomb cut into the rock. Then he rolled a large stone across to close the entrance.

Mark, as narrator, has just described Jesus' death. Pilate confirmed with the centurion that Jesus was already dead and gave the body to Joseph. This man, according to the same chapter, was waiting for the kingdom of God. The account shows that Jesus truly died and was buried with care. The next verse mentions women who saw where he was laid, and this prepares the account of the resurrection.

For today: Joseph acted with courage and generosity when others had kept their distance. We can serve with love and without expecting recognition, even when doing so costs us.
exp.6:26:
Jesus tells the woman that the children must eat first, because it is not right to take the children's bread and throw it to the little dogs. The word "filled" means eating until one is satisfied. The "little dogs" are puppies or small dogs, the kind kept at home. "Throw it to" means the same as "cast it unto."

Jesus speaks to a woman who is a Greek, from the region of Syrophoenicia, that is, not a Jew. She asks him to free her daughter. By "the children" is understood Israel, the people to whom Jesus was sent first. Some see in his words a test of her faith; others, a way of explaining the order of his mission. The text does not say the tone in which he spoke, but the ending shows that her faith was received.

Today we can draw near to God with humility and perseverance, even when we do not understand everything. He responds to sincere faith, wherever it comes from.
exp.15:8:
The verse says that Jesus rose very early on the first day of the week, Sunday morning, and that the first person he appeared to was Mary Magdalene, the woman from whom he had earlier driven out seven demons. The word "but" is used in the sense of "however" here, and "appeared first" means that he showed himself to her first.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Mark. He comes right after the scene at the empty tomb, where the women fled overcome with fear. It should be noted that many ancient manuscripts do not include Mark 16:9-20, and scholars debate its origin. Even so, this passage agrees with what other gospels report, such as John 20.

For today: Jesus first revealed himself to someone with a past of suffering and frailty. No one is so marked by their history that they cannot be reached by him. If you carry a painful past, remember that Christ often draws near precisely to those he has already healed and restored.
exp.0:30:
He came near to Simon's mother-in-law, who was lying sick in bed with a fever. He took her by the hand and lifted her up. At once the fever left her, and she began to serve them.

The account follows a day of teaching by Jesus in the synagogue in Capernaum. Mark is the one telling the story. When they arrived at Simon's (Peter's) house, the disciples told him about the sick woman and asked for his help. It is a simple, private moment, before the people of the town come looking for healing in the evening.

For today: we can bring to Jesus the needs of the people we love, as the disciples did. And when we receive his help, our natural response can be to serve others with gratitude, not out of obligation.
exp.7:10:
The verse tells that some Pharisees came to Jesus and began to question him. They were asking him for a sign from heaven, that is, a spectacular miracle that would come directly from God. The word translated "question with him" in the verse above carries the sense of arguing persistently, and their attitude was one of putting him to the test, not out of faith but with bad intent.

The context is that Jesus had just fed about four thousand men with a few loaves and fish, and had arrived in the region of Dalmanutha. The Pharisees had already seen his miracles, but they wanted another proof. Jesus, according to the passage that follows, sighed deeply with sorrow, refused to give them that sign, and left.

For today: faith does not come from demanding proofs from God on our own terms. We can bring our doubts to him honestly, but it is wise to examine whether we are truly seeking the truth or only looking for an excuse not to believe.
exp.2:31:
This verse tells us that Jesus was inside a house, surrounded by people sitting around him. Someone tells him that his mother and brothers were outside and were looking for him. The word "multitude" here refers to the crowd that was listening to him.

Those who speak are the people who were close to Jesus. Earlier, some had said that he had an unclean spirit, that is, that he was out of his mind or possessed. His family probably came worried about him, although the text does not explain all their reasons. Jesus will use this moment to teach something deeper about who his true family is.

For today: Jesus invites us to put him and his word first, even above the closest ties. Today you can make room to listen to him, and also to love the community of believers as your own family.
exp.15:19:
This verse closes the Gospel of Mark. It says that the disciples went out and preached the message everywhere, while the Lord worked alongside them. He confirmed what they said with the signs that accompanied them. "Working with them" means that Jesus was acting at their side, and "confirming" means giving proof that the message was true.

Here the author summarizes what happened after Jesus went up into heaven. The disciples obeyed his command to carry the gospel. It is worth noting that many scholars point out that verses 9 to 20 of Mark do not appear in some of the oldest manuscripts, and for that reason their origin is debated. Even so, the church has read them for centuries.

For today: when you share your faith, trust that you do not do it alone. The Lord continues to accompany those who speak of him with simplicity and obedience.
exp.7:17:
Jesus asks his disciples some pointed questions. He tells them they have eyes and ears, yet they are not seeing or understanding what they have lived through with him. The verse's words "see" and "hear" describe their failure to perceive who is standing in front of them.

Jesus speaks with his disciples in the boat. They were arguing with one another because they had forgotten to bring bread. But they had already seen Jesus multiply loaves twice, and many baskets were left over. Their worry showed that they had not grasped who Jesus is or the extent of his power. Earlier he had warned them about the yeast of the Pharisees, and they thought only of physical bread. Some scholars see here a loving correction, not a simple scolding.

When we worry about what we lack, let us remember how God has cared for us before. Remembering his faithfulness helps us trust him today.
exp.3:39:
Jesus asks his disciples why they are so afraid and why they still lack trust in him.

Jesus speaks after calming the storm on the Sea of Galilee. The disciples, who were in the boat, woke him in great distress, thinking they were going to die. Jesus calmed the wind and the sea, and then he spoke to them. His question does not seem like an insult, but an invitation to trust more, although some read it as a gentle rebuke.

For today: when storms come into your life, you can bring your fear honestly to Jesus. He does not mock your distress, and he invites you to remember that he is with you in the boat.
exp.7:16:
Jesus realizes that his disciples are arguing because they have no bread. He asks them several questions: Why are you arguing about this? Do you not yet perceive or understand? Do you still have a hardened heart? To argue with anger means to quarrel heatedly. A hardened heart speaks of a closed heart, slow to understand.

Jesus had just warned them to beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod, that is, of their harmful influence. The disciples thought he was speaking of material bread. He reminds them that he had already multiplied the loaves for thousands of people, and twelve baskets were left over. They were to trust him.

Today we can worry so much about what we lack that we forget what God has already done. When you feel anxious about a need, remember how God has cared for you before and trust him.
exp.12:26:
Jesus says that when the Son of Man comes, he will send his angels to gather his chosen ones, that is, those who belong to him. He will gather them from the four winds, meaning from every direction, from the farthest end of the earth to the farthest end of heaven. The phrase "from the uttermost part" simply means "from the very edge" or "from the farthest limit."

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him about the future, and he warns them of difficult times. This verse closes his description of his coming in power and glory. Christian interpreters explain the order and timing of these events in different ways, but all agree that Christ will come and gather his people.

Today, this verse invites us to live with hope and not with fear. None of those who belong to Christ will be lost from sight. We can trust in him and remain faithful, loving others with patience.
exp.8:7:
Verse 8 says that suddenly, when Peter, James and John looked around, they no longer saw Moses or Elijah, who had appeared talking with Jesus. Only Jesus remained with them.

Mark tells the story of the transfiguration. The disciples were frightened, and Peter spoke without really knowing what to say. Then a cloud covered them, and the Father said: "This is my beloved Son; hear him." After that voice, the scene is left with Jesus alone. Many understand that this shows Jesus is the center and goal of the Law and the Prophets, represented by Moses and Elijah, although the text does not explain it in those words.

For today: when there are intense experiences, confusion, or many voices around you, turn your gaze to Jesus and listen to him in his Word. He remains with you when everything else passes away.
exp.9:6:
This verse says that when a man marries, he leaves the home and the dependence on his parents to be united with his wife. The word "cleave" (in the older text, "shall be joined to") means to join firmly, like being glued together. It does not speak of ceasing to honor one's parents, but of changing one's primary loyalty.

Jesus is speaking with some Pharisees who asked him about divorce. He takes them back to Genesis, to what God planned from the beginning, before Moses allowed a certificate of divorce because of the hardness of the human heart. Here he quotes Genesis 2:24.

For today: if you are married, make sure your spouse is your priority after God. Talk with your partner before making important decisions, and set healthy, respectful limits with relatives who want to direct your marriage.
exp.4:37:
He comes to the house of Jairo, the leader of the synagogue, that is, the official in charge of the gatherings held there. There he sees the uproar, a great noise and confusion, with people weeping and wailing loudly, expressing their grief out loud.

Mark tells the scene. Jairo had asked Jesus to heal his daughter, but news arrived that she had already died. Jesus told him not to be afraid and only to believe. He took with him only Peter, James and John. On arriving, he finds the house full of mourning, as was customary in that culture at a death.

For today: when everything around you is noise, fear and sadness, remember that Jesus enters into the middle of pain. You can bring Him your situation and keep trusting Him, even when others see only the end.
exp.15:4:
The explanation says that the women entered the tomb and saw a young man sitting on the right side, dressed in a long white robe. They were frightened. The word for "young man" here means a young person, and the phrase about their reaction means they felt great fear and amazement. Although Mark calls him a young man, the message he gives suggests he was a being sent by God, and many understand him to be an angel, though the text does not say so directly.

Mark's account tells how the women went early to anoint the body of Jesus. They were worried about the large stone, but they found it had been rolled away. The narrator, Mark, is the one speaking at this point, and right away the young man tells them that Jesus has risen and sends them to tell the disciples and Peter.

For today: we often face problems that seem enormous, like that stone, and God has already been at work before we arrive. We can take the step of faith with humility, even with fear, trusting that He goes ahead of us.
exp.9:24:
Jesus uses an exaggerated comparison: it is easier for a camel, a large animal, to go through the tiny opening of a needle than for a rich person to enter the kingdom of God. He means that, by one's own effort, this is impossible.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples after a rich man walked away sad, because he would not give up his possessions to follow him. Earlier, Jesus had made clear that the difficulty lies in trusting in riches. The disciples are amazed and ask who then can be saved. Jesus answers that for men it is impossible, but not for God. Some have proposed explanations about a gate called the "eye of the needle," but there is no firm evidence for that.

For today: examine where you place your security, whether in your possessions or in God. Whether you have much or little, hand it over to him and trust in his grace, which saves.
exp.9:47:
Many people, it says, scolded Bartimaeus and ordered him to be quiet. But he, instead of staying silent, cried out all the more: "Thou Son of David, have mercy on me." Where the explanation says "reñían," meaning they rebuked or scolded him, the word "charged" in the verse covers this, so the sentence is kept as written. The phrase about shouting even louder means that he cried out the more a great deal.

Bartimaeus was a blind beggar sitting by the road as Jesus was leaving Jericho. When he heard that Jesus was passing by, he began to ask for help. "Son of David" was a title that acknowledged Jesus as the promised Messiah. The crowd may have been hushing him out of annoyance or because they did not think he mattered. Even so, Jesus stopped and called him.

When others discourage you from seeking God, do not stay silent. Keep praying with sincerity and humility, trusting that Jesus hears the cry of anyone who asks him for mercy.
exp.8:35:
Jesus takes a small child, places him in the middle of the disciples, and embraces him. Then he is going to speak to them. "He placed him" means he set him there, and "taking him in his arms" means that he held him close with affection.

Jesus and the twelve are in Capernaum, in a house. On the way, the disciples had argued about who was the greatest among them, and they fell silent when asked about it. Jesus had just taught them that being first means serving everyone. Now he uses a child as a living example: in that time, a child had no standing or influence.

For today: value and treat with tenderness the people others regard as unimportant, such as children, the elderly, and the poor. Serving them with humility is serving Christ, and that is worth more than seeking recognition.
exp.13:57:
These words were spoken by false witnesses at Jesus' trial. They accuse him of having said that he would destroy the temple made by human hands and that in three days he would build another one not made by hands, that is, not built by people.

It is night, before the Sanhedrin, and they are looking for evidence to condemn him. The text says that their testimony was false and did not agree. Jesus did speak of a temple in John 2:19, but there he said, "Destroy this temple," and John explains that he was speaking of his body and his resurrection. The witnesses twisted his words.

For today: when you are misunderstood or falsely accused, remember that Jesus went through the same thing. Trust that God knows the truth, and always try to speak with honesty.
exp.10:28:
Jesus answers the religious leaders with a proposal: he will ask them one question, and if they answer him, he will tell them by what authority he does what he does. The word "authority" in the verse above means the right or power to act, and the question he puts to them is about that authority.

This takes place in the temple in Jerusalem, a day after Jesus drove out the sellers. The chief priests, the scribes, and the elders confront him. Jesus does not avoid the issue, but he asks them about the baptism of John. His question reveals whether they were seeking the truth sincerely or only wanted to trap him.

For today: before we ask hard questions of God or of others, let us examine our hearts. Do we truly seek the truth, even when it costs us to change, or do we only want to defend what we already think? Let us ask God for honesty and humility to listen.
exp.15:18:
The verse says that Jesus, after speaking with his disciples, was taken up into heaven and sat down at the right hand of God. The wording of the older text is easy to follow in the verse above, so no comment on old words is needed here.

Mark tells here the ending of his Gospel. The risen Jesus has just given his disciples the mission to proclaim the good news, and he spoke of the signs that would accompany believers. Then he ascends, and the disciples go out to preach. It should be noted that many scholars point out that this ending of Mark (16:9-20) does not appear in the oldest manuscripts, and churches interpret it in different ways.

For today: Jesus reigns with authority, and although we do not see him, he continues working with his people. This encourages us to share his message with confidence, without depending only on our own strength.
exp.0:1:
Mark says that what happens with John the Baptist had already been announced in the Scriptures. God promises to send a messenger ahead, to prepare the way, that is, to make it ready and clear before someone important arrives. The word "before thy face" means before your presence.

Mark opens his gospel presenting Jesus as the Son of God. Here he explains that John is the promised messenger. He attributes the whole quotation to "Isaiah," although the first part seems to come from Malachi 3:1 and the second from Isaiah 40:3. Some scholars believe Mark joined both texts under the name of the best-known prophet.

For today: God prepares hearts before he acts. We can prepare the way for him with humility and repentance, and trust that his promises are fulfilled in his own time.
exp.5:43:
This verse says that the people who ate the bread and the fish numbered five thousand men. The figure refers to the men; Matthew 14:21 clarifies that this count did not include women and children, so the total crowd was probably larger.

Here the narrator, Mark, tells how Jesus fed the crowd with five loaves and two fish. Jesus had seen the people as sheep without a shepherd, and first he taught them. Then he gave them food. The number highlights that the miracle was real and large, and that food was left over.

For today: God does not see people as a faceless mass; he knows their needs. Place in his hands whatever little you have, time, help, or a kind word, and trust that he can do much with it.
exp.6:8:
Jesus tells the Pharisees and scribes that they set aside, that is, make void, God's commandment in order to keep their own tradition. He says "Full well" with irony: "What a fine way you have of setting aside what God commands!" Here "tradition" refers to the customs and rules that were handed down from generation to generation.

Jesus is speaking with the religious leaders who criticized him because his disciples ate without performing the ritual washings. He answers that they have placed human rules above the word of God. Right away he gives an example: under the pretext of declaring their possessions dedicated to God, some were avoiding helping their parents, even though Moses commanded that parents be honored.

Today it is worth asking ourselves whether any religious custom or pious excuse leads us to neglect what God clearly asks, such as loving and caring for our family.
exp.6:4:
The Pharisees and scribes ask Jesus why his disciples do not follow "the tradition of the elders." That tradition was customs that Jewish teachers had handed down from generation to generation. "Unwashen hands" means hands not washed according to the ritual, not necessarily dirty ones.

The ones speaking are religious leaders, probably come from Jerusalem according to verse 1. They do not accuse the disciples of breaking the law of Moses, but of breaking a rule added by men. Jesus answers firmly, quoting Isaiah: God looks at the heart, not merely at outward appearances or human customs.

Today we can ask ourselves: am I guarding my religious customs more than my sincere love for God and for people? Before judging others over details, let us ask God for a humble and obedient heart.
exp.7:34:
Jesus says that whoever clings to their life, that is, whoever lives only to protect themselves and keep what is theirs, will end up losing it. On the other hand, whoever gives up their life for Jesus and for the gospel (the good news of the kingdom) will find it. The word "life" here can also be understood as "soul" or the whole person, as seen in the following verse.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples. He has just announced that he will suffer and die, and he rebuked Peter for rejecting that path. Now he explains that following him also means denying oneself and taking up the cross.

Today we can ask ourselves: what am I holding back for myself? Perhaps Jesus is inviting you to forgive, to serve, or to be honest even when it costs you. Trust that giving everything to him is the path to true life.
exp.12:16:
It says it will be very hard for women who are pregnant and for those who are nursing their babies. The phrase "with child" refers to those who are expecting a child, and "give suck" refers to those who are nursing. "Woe!" expresses pity and grief rather than a punishment.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, and warns them of a great distress that is coming. Many understand that it refers first to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70 AD, and some also see a future fulfillment. Jesus tells them to flee quickly, and mothers with small children would have more difficulty escaping.

For today: God looks after the most vulnerable, and we should do the same. Today you can help a mother, or someone frail, with a concrete gesture of care and companionship.
exp.5:4:
It says that Jesus could not do any mighty work there. He healed only a few sick people, laying his hands on them. Mark does not say that he lacked power, but that something limited him in that place.

Jesus was in Nazareth, his hometown. His neighbors knew him as the carpenter, the son of Mary, and they knew his family. For that reason they were offended, that is, they stumbled over him and rejected him. Jesus reminded them that a prophet is without honor in his own country. Then Mark says that Jesus marveled at their unbelief. Afterward he kept teaching and sent out the twelve.

For today: let us not allow habit or prejudice to close our hearts. If we believe we already know Jesus, we may miss what God wants to do. Let us come to him with humility and trust.
exp.13:9:
Judas Iscariot, one of Jesus' twelve disciples, went to the chief priests, the religious leaders of the temple. He went to hand Jesus over to them, that is, to put Jesus into their hands. The word "princes" here means leaders or heads, and the word "to" is written in an older form.

Mark is the one telling the story. Just before this, a woman had poured perfume over Jesus, and He praised her act as a preparation for His burial. Then the account shows a contrast: while she gave what she had, Judas went to those who wanted to arrest Jesus. Mark does not explain his motives here; the verses that follow only say that the priests promised to give him money.

Today we can remember that a person can be close to Jesus and still turn away from Him. It is good to ask Him to examine our hearts, and to respond to Him with sincere devotion.
exp.7:2:
Jesus says that if he sends the people away without eating, they will faint on the way. He explains that some of them came from far away. "Fasting" means without having eaten anything. "Faint" means they will grow weak or collapse from exhaustion.

Jesus speaks with his disciples. A great crowd has been with him for three days, listening to him in a remote place, and they now have no food. He himself says he feels compassion. For this reason he does not want to send them away hungry. The disciples respond with doubts, because they see little bread and a great many people. This prepares the miracle of the feeding of the multitude.

For today: Jesus attends to the real needs of people, not only their spiritual ones. We can imitate him by paying attention to whoever is tired or in need around us, and helping them with whatever we have, even when it seems like little.
exp.1:17:
This verse tells us that the disciples of John the Baptist and the disciples of the Pharisees had the custom of fasting, that is, of going without food for a time as a sign of devotion to God. Some people come to Jesus and ask him why his disciples do not do the same.

Jesus had just eaten with tax collectors and sinners, and the religious leaders were criticizing him. Now another comparison arises: Jesus and his followers looked different from other religious groups. The Bible does not make clear exactly who asked this question; the text only says that they came. Jesus will answer with the image of a wedding.

Today we can remember that religious practices, such as fasting, have value when they come from a sincere heart and not from habit or from comparing ourselves with others. Before judging how another person serves God, it is good to ask ourselves what God is doing in each case.
exp.7:36:
Jesus asks a question to make us think: what could a person give in exchange for their soul? "Exchange" here means something one could trade or pay to buy back. "Soul" can be understood as a person's life or their whole being. The question implies that nothing in this world has that value, and once a soul is lost, there is no way to buy it back again.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and to the crowd, after announcing his cross. He explains that following him costs something, but that turning away from him out of fear or in order to gain things means losing everything. Then he warns about being ashamed of him and of his words.

Today, before deciding something important, ask yourself what costs you more: giving up a gain, or failing to remain faithful to Christ. Ask him for courage to follow him with honesty, even when others mock you.
exp.11:33:
Jesus sees that the scribe answered wisely and tells him, "You are not far from the kingdom of God." After this, no one dared to ask him any more questions. The word "dared" in the verse means the same as "ventured," and "wisely" means with good understanding.

Jesus had been tested by several religious groups. This scribe asked him which commandment was the most important, and Jesus spoke of loving God and loving one's neighbor. The scribe agreed and understood that this love is worth more than sacrifices. Jesus does not say that he is already inside the kingdom, but near it. Some believe he still lacked following Jesus; the text does not make this clear.

Being near God is not the same as entering. If today you understand well what God asks, take the step of obeying him and following Jesus with all your heart.
exp.14:34:
Some of the people standing near the cross heard Jesus cry out, and they said, "Look, he is calling for Elijah." The phrase that the verse renders "when they heard it" is simply the same idea as "hearing him," and the words "look" and "behold" in the verse both draw attention to what they were seeing and hearing.

The ones speaking were some of the bystanders. Jesus had cried out in Aramaic, "My God, my God," and those words sound a lot like the name Elijah, which is why they understood him that way. It is not known for certain whether this was a sincere mistake or mockery. Jews expected that Elijah would come to help the righteous who were in trouble.

For today: sometimes we misunderstand the pain of others, or their prayers, because we do not listen carefully. Let us approach them with humility and compassion, without mocking, and truly listen to the one who is suffering.
exp.11:2:
The explanation says that the tenants seized the servant the owner of the vineyard had sent them, beat him, and sent him back with nothing. The word "but" in the verse is rendered as "but," and "empty-handed" means without the fruit he had come to collect.

Jesus is speaking to the religious leaders of Jerusalem, shortly before his crucifixion. He tells this parable to show how God sent his messengers, the prophets, again and again, and many of them were rejected. Many understand that the vineyard represents Israel and the owner is God, though the parable also speaks to the response to Jesus himself.

For today: God speaks to us with patience, sometimes through people we do not expect. Ask yourself whether there is some voice, correction, or biblical counsel that you have been rejecting, and ask for a humble heart to listen.
exp.3:37:
He was in the back of the boat, asleep on a cushion, which is a pillow. The disciples woke him and asked him, "Master, don't you care that we are going to drown?" The word "perish" in the verse means they are about to die.

The ones speaking are the disciples, frightened by a strong storm that was filling the boat with water. Some of them were fishermen and knew the sea, so the danger seemed real. Jesus was sleeping, probably from exhaustion after teaching the crowd. Afterward he calmed the wind and the sea, and asked them why they were afraid and had so little faith.

For today: when storms arrive in your life, you can tell Jesus your fear with honesty. He is not bothered by your cry. Also, remember that being with him in the boat is already a reason to trust, even when you do not understand his silence.
exp.10:21:
Jesus answers Peter with a short sentence: "Have faith in God." It is a direct invitation to trust God. The phrase "says to them" is the present tense used to narrate events, and "have" is a gentle command, meaning "you should have."

Jesus speaks with his disciples on the road to Jerusalem, a day after he cursed the fig tree. Peter is amazed to see it dry from the roots. Jesus does not dwell on the event but directs their attention toward God. Then he speaks of the mountain and of prayer. Some understand the fig tree as a sign of the lack of fruit in the temple, but scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: before asking for something in prayer, begin by remembering who God is, his goodness and his power. Trust in him more than in your own strength, and calmly hand over to him what worries you.
exp.4:18:
Jesus does not let the healed man go with Him in the boat. He tells him to return home, to his family and his people, and to tell them how great the Lord's work was for him and how He had compassion on him. The word "compassion" here means the kindness and pity that helps someone who suffers.

Jesus speaks with a man who had been tormented by demons. The people of the region, frightened, asked Jesus to leave. The man wanted to stay with Him, but Jesus gave him another task: to bear witness in his own land. He then went and proclaimed throughout the Decapolis, a region of ten cities, and the people were amazed.

For today: sometimes serving God does not mean going far away, but rather telling simply, at home and at work, what God has done in our lives.
exp.5:46:
Mark 6:47 says that when evening came, the disciples' boat was in the middle of the lake, far from the shore, while Jesus was alone on land.

The phrase "when even was come" means that evening had arrived. "The sea" refers to the Sea of Galilee, which is a large lake. "The ship" is the boat.

Mark is the one telling the story. Jesus had just fed a large crowd, and then he sent his disciples ahead in the boat while he dismissed the people. After that he went up the mountain to pray. The text does not explain everything he prayed, but it shows that he sought to be alone with the Father.

Even though Jesus seems far away, he does not lose sight of his own. The next verse says he saw them struggling against the wind. When you feel alone in the middle of a difficulty, remember that Jesus sees you and prays for you. Trust in him and keep moving forward.
exp.5:48:
This verse tells that the disciples saw Jesus walking on the sea and thought he was a ghost. Out of fright, they cried out. "Sea" here refers to the Sea of Galilee, and they "cried out" means they shouted loudly.

Mark is the one narrating. The disciples had been rowing through the night against a strong wind for hours, tired and afraid. Jesus had seen them from the land and went out toward them. Near dawn (the last stretch of the night), they did not recognize him. Right away Jesus spoke to them, and the wind died down.

For today: sometimes Jesus is near in the middle of the storm, but fear keeps us from recognizing him. When you feel tired and afraid, stop and listen for his voice: he has already seen you, and he has not left you alone.
exp.10:32:
The religious leaders answer Jesus: "We cannot tell." Then Jesus tells them that He will not tell them by what authority He does these things either. The word "authority" here means the right or power to act. The verb form used in the source is in the present tense, as if the scene were happening now.

The chief priests, scribes, and elders had asked Jesus by what authority He acted, after He drove out the sellers from the temple. Jesus put a question back to them: was John's baptism from heaven or from men? They weighed the consequences and chose to say they did not know. They were not seeking the truth but protecting themselves. That is why Jesus gave them no answer.

For today: let us be honest with God and with others. Before asking something, let us ask ourselves whether we truly want the answer, even if it requires us to change. Telling the truth is worth more than guarding our image.
exp.3:5:
It says that when the sun came up, the little plants that had sprouted quickly in the rocky ground were scorched. Since they had no root, they dried up. The earth with stones had little depth, so the plant grew up quickly, but it could not hold itself up.

Jesus is teaching a crowd beside the Sea of Galilee and uses this parable of the sower. Later in the same chapter, he explains that this seed represents those who receive the word with joy but have no root in themselves, and when affliction or persecution comes because of the word, they stumble.

For today: an initial enthusiasm for God is not enough; we need roots. Cultivate simple, steady habits, such as praying, reading the Bible, and spending time with other believers, so that your faith can endure when trials come.
exp.13:28:
Peter answers Jesus with great confidence: even though all the others may be made to stumble, he will not. The sentence about an old word is rewritten here, and the unusual quoted wording is removed from the explanation: "All shall be offended" in the verse means that they would fall away in their faith and turn from Jesus because of what was about to happen.

Jesus had just said that all the disciples would abandon him that night, quoting a prophecy about the struck shepherd and the scattered sheep (it seems to refer to Zechariah 13:7). He also promised that, after rising, he would go ahead of them to Galilee. Peter wants to show his loyalty, but Jesus warns him that he will deny him three times.

For today: loving Jesus truly does not mean trusting in our own strength, but recognizing our weakness. We can ask him for help with humility, knowing that even if we fail, he offers restoration.
exp.5:9:
Jesus tells his disciples that, whenever they enter a house, they should stay there until they leave that place. The word "abide" in the verse means to stay or lodge somewhere. The phrase "in what place soever ye enter" means "in any house you enter."

Jesus sends out the twelve two by two to proclaim the kingdom of God. He asks them to travel with little, trusting in God and in the hospitality of the people they meet. Staying in one house keeps them from searching for a better place or more comfort, and keeps their focus on the mission.

For today: learn to be content with what God gives you, and do not move from place to place for comfort. Be thankful for the help of others, and serve simply wherever you are, trusting that God cares for you.
exp.3:33:
This verse says that Jesus, when he taught the crowds, used parables, that is, simple stories taken from everyday life. But when he was alone with his disciples, he explained everything to them.

Mark closes here a long block of teachings beside the sea, with the sower, the seed, and the mustard seed. Jesus spoke according to what the people were able to hear, that is, according to their capacity to understand. The parables invited people to think, and whoever was interested would come forward to ask questions. The disciples did this, and for that reason they received more light.

For today: if something in the Bible is not clear to you, do not stay with the doubt. Draw near to Jesus in prayer, read with patience, and ask with sincerity. He delights in teaching those who want to understand.
exp.13:38:
He says that Jesus went away from his disciples once more and prayed again. The phrase about the same words means that he repeated the same request he had made before, the one he had made to the Father: that, if it were possible, the cup would pass from him, but that God's will would be done.

Mark tells what happened in Gethsemane, shortly before Jesus was arrested. He was deeply distressed. He had just found Peter, James and John asleep, and he had urged them to watch and pray. Then he went away again to seek the Father.

For today: when you are weighed down, do not be afraid to pray about the same thing many times. Repeating a prayer sincerely is not a lack of faith. It can be a way of continuing to trust God and surrendering your will to him.
exp.3:10:
Jesus tells his close followers that God has given them the ability to know the mystery of the kingdom of God. This mystery is not something strange, but a truth of God that was once hidden and is now being revealed. By contrast, those who are outside, meaning those who do not come near to Jesus to follow him, receive everything in parables.

Jesus speaks to the twelve and to the other disciples who stayed with him alone, after teaching the crowd with the parable of the sower. They asked him what it meant. Parables reveal the truth to those who seek it, but they leave in doubt those who do not want to listen from the heart. Scholars explain this in several ways.

For today: if we want to understand God, it is not enough to hear from a distance. Draw near to Jesus, ask him sincerely, and read his Word with humility.
exp.13:52:
Mark tells us that, after Jesus was arrested in Gethsemane, they led him before the high priest. There gathered the chief priests (the leading priests), the elders (the leaders of the people), and the scribes (experts in the Law). In other words, the most influential group in Israel came together.

The narrator is Mark, and what follows is a meeting of the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council. According to the account, they were looking for evidence against Jesus to have him condemned to death, though they did not find any. The high priest at that time was Caiaphas, according to the other Gospels (Matthew 26:57). Mark shows Jesus alone, while his disciples flee.

For today: Jesus faced injustice without responding with violence or deceit. When you are treated badly or accused without cause, you can trust God and keep your integrity, knowing that He sees everything.
exp.13:11:
This verse tells us that the day arrived when the Jewish people were preparing the feast of the Passover, the day when the lamb was sacrificed. The disciples ask Jesus where he wants them to go to prepare everything so that they can eat the Passover supper together.

The ones speaking are the disciples, who ask their Master for instructions. Just before this, Judas had already agreed to hand Jesus over to the chief priests for money. So while some were secretly plotting, the others were simply seeking to prepare a sacred meal. Some scholars discuss how the timing of this supper fits with other accounts in the Gospels, and there is no single explanation that everyone accepts.

For today: The disciples did not make plans on their own, but asked Jesus. We can follow their example by bringing our decisions and preparations to God in prayer before we act, and by waiting humbly for his guidance.
exp.5:5:
Jesus was amazed, or surprised, that the people of his hometown did not believe in him, as this verse says. The word "marvelled" in the reader's verse fits here: it describes a surprise at their lack of faith. After that, Jesus continued going through the nearby villages and teaching.

Mark tells what happened in Nazareth, where Jesus grew up. There people knew him as the son of the carpenter, and that made it hard for them to accept him. When the text says he could do no mighty work there, it shows that their lack of faith limited what happened in that place. Even so, Jesus did not stop: he kept teaching and then sent out his disciples.

For today: do not let rejection or indifference stop you. If someone close to you does not receive your faith, keep serving with love and trust God. And keep your heart open, so that you do not harden yourself against what God wants to do.
exp.3:20:
Jesus asks whether anyone brings in a lit lamp to cover it with a measuring bowl (a large container for measuring grain) or to put it under the bed. The answer is obvious: a lamp is placed on the lampstand, that is, on the high stand, so that it gives light. The word "lamp" here refers to an oil lamp.

Jesus speaks to his disciples, right after explaining the parable of the sower. The word of God is like a light that should not be kept hidden. Although he is now teaching in parables, his message is meant to be made known. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see an invitation to share the truth, others a promise that the kingdom will be revealed.

Today: if you have received the word of God, do not keep it only for yourself. Let it shine in the way you speak, work, and treat others.
exp.8:26:
Jesus took the boy by the hand and lifted him up, that is, he helped him to stand on his feet. And the young man got up. The word that describes this, which your reader's verse renders as "lifted him up," means he raised him or set him upright. After the crisis, the boy lay on the ground as if he were dead.

Here the narrator, Mark, is telling what happened after Jesus drove out an unclean spirit that had been tormenting a child. The people thought the boy had already died. Jesus gives no speech; he acts with tenderness and authority. Some see in this a sign of Jesus' victory over death, although the text does not state this directly.

For today: when someone is fallen, tired, or without strength, we can draw near with a firm and kind hand. Jesus lifts up, and he invites us to help others get up as well.
exp.7:18:
Jesus reminds his disciples of a miracle they had already seen: when he broke five loaves for five thousand people, twelve baskets full of pieces were left over. The disciples answer with exact precision: "Twelve."

Jesus speaks to the disciples in the boat. They were worried because they had only one loaf of bread. He confronts them with tenderness but also with firmness, because they had already seen his power to supply what was needed. His questions aim to help them remember and to understand who is with them.

For today: when you worry about what you lack, remember how God has already cared for you before. Write down some of those times and let them strengthen your trust in him.
exp.8:44:
It says that if a person's foot makes them stumble or fall into sin, it is better to cut it off than to end up in Gehenna. The word "Gehenna" is not quoted here in English; instead, the verse's own word "hell" carries that sense. The phrase about causing a fall means the thing that causes stumbling. "Halt" means someone who is missing a foot or walks with difficulty.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after teaching them about humility and about not causing little ones to stumble. He uses a deliberate exaggeration to show how serious sin is. Almost everyone understands that he is not asking for mutilation, but for a firm decision to remove whatever pulls us away from God.

For today: think about which path, habit, or friendship keeps leading you back into sin. Ask God for help and take one concrete step to move away from it, even if it costs you.
exp.12:22:
The explanation says that the disciples must be attentive and watchful. "But take ye heed" means "but you, take care, stay alert." "I have told you all things beforehand" means "I have warned you about all of this in advance." Jesus does not want anyone to be taken by surprise or deceived.

Jesus speaks on the Mount of Olives with Peter, James, John, and Andrew. They asked him about the signs of the future. Before this verse, he warned about false Christs and false prophets who would perform miracles to mislead. Afterward, he speaks of signs in the heavens. His warning seeks to protect his followers, not to frighten them.

For today: do not believe everything that sounds spiritual or impressive. Compare what you hear with what Jesus taught in the Bible, and ask God for wisdom so that you are not deceived.
exp.13:60:
This verse tells us that Jesus kept silent in the face of the accusations. Then the high priest asked him another direct question: whether he was the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah, the "Son of the Blessed." "Blessed" was a respectful way of saying "God," used to avoid speaking his name. The words "asked again" simply mean that he asked once more.

Jesus is being tried at night by the Jewish council. The false witnesses had contradicted each other, so the high priest sought to have Jesus himself incriminate himself. His silence matches the image of the suffering servant in Isaiah 53:7. When the question touched on his identity, Jesus did answer: "I am."

For today: not every attack deserves a defense, but when it comes to confessing who Jesus is, we must speak with courage and simplicity. Ask God for wisdom to know when to be silent and when to speak.
exp.5:23:
This verse tells how the young woman went out of the hall and asked her mother what she should request from the king. Her mother answered without hesitation: "The head of John the Baptist." The phrase about going out and the phrase about her mother are older ways of wording the verse, and the request itself is simply stated in the verse above. The word for asking is used in the sense of making a request.

Herod Antipas had just promised the girl, under oath, whatever she wanted. Herodias held a grudge against John, because he had said it was not right for Herod to be married to her. Mark does not give the young woman's name; other ancient sources call her Salome, but that comes from outside this text.

For today: let us not allow the resentment of others to guide us. Before asking for or deciding something, let us pause and seek God's counsel, so that we do not harm anyone out of spite.
exp.10:14:
He says that Jesus came to Jerusalem and went into the temple. There he began to drive out those who were selling and buying. He also overturned the tables of the moneychangers, who exchanged coins, and the seats of those who sold doves. Old words: "overthrew" means that he turned over or knocked down; the "seats" were benches or stools.

Mark tells this right after the fig tree that had leaves but no fruit. Many understand it as a sign: religious appearance without real fruit. Jesus acts in the court of the temple, where what was needed for the sacrifices was sold. Then he explains that God's house was meant to be a house of prayer for all nations. Some think the problem was the abuse, others that the trade got in the way of worship.

Today we can ask ourselves: does my life of faith only have leaves, or does it also bear fruit? Take a moment to pray sincerely, and remove whatever gets in the way of your worship.
exp.0:11:
This verse says that, right after his baptism, the Holy Spirit drives Jesus into the desert. "Immediately" is the word used here, and "drives" means pushes or forces him along. It was no accident: the Spirit himself directed it.

Mark tells this quickly. First the Father declares his love for Jesus and the Spirit descends on him. Then comes the desert, where Jesus is tempted by Satan for forty days. The narrator, Mark, shows that being loved by God does not exempt anyone from trials. Some think this recalls Israel's forty years in the desert, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: if you are going through a difficult time, do not conclude that God has forgotten you. Jesus was called the beloved Son and still passed through the desert. Trust that God can be with you in the trial, and remember his love before you face it.
exp.5:28:
This verse says that when John the Baptist's disciples heard about his death, they went and took his body and buried it. "Hearing it" is the phrase here, and "tomb" is the word used for the place where he was laid.

Mark is the one telling the story. John had been imprisoned and executed on the orders of King Herod Antipas, after a promise made at a banquet. John's disciples did not run away; instead, they gave their teacher a proper burial. Soon after, the apostles return to Jesus, and he invites them to rest. The text does not say more about their state of mind, but the contrast between John's death and the apostles' return is striking.

For today: when someone we love suffers a loss or an injustice, we can stand with them through simple and faithful acts, such as being present, helping, and honoring their memory, even when we cannot change what has happened.
exp.4:42:
Jesus strictly ordered them that no one should find out what had happened, and asked that the girl be given something to eat. The phrase "charged them straitly" means that he insisted firmly. "Them" refers to the parents and the disciples who were present.

Jesus had just raised the daughter of Jairus, a leader of the synagogue. In Mark, Jesus often asks for silence about his miracles. Scholars explain this in several ways: to avoid crowds who only wanted miracles, or to avoid misunderstandings about his mission. It is not certain what the exact reason was here. Asking for food shows that the girl was truly alive and well, and that Jesus paid attention to everyday needs.

For today: God does great things, but also cares about simple details. After a powerful moment of faith, attend to the practical: serve, accompany, give food to the one in need. And do not seek applause for what God does.
exp.3:18:
It says that there are people who hear the word of God, but other things take away the place that it should have. "The cares of this world" are the worries of this present life. The word for "world" here means the present age or era. "The deceitfulness of riches" is the false idea that money will give us security. "Lusts" are disordered desires to have more. All of that chokes the word, the way weeds choke a plant, and it no longer bears fruit.

Jesus is speaking and explaining the parable of the sower to his disciples. The seed is the word, and the different kinds of ground represent how people receive it. Here he describes the third ground, the one with thorns.

For today: check which worries or desires are taking up more of your time than God does. This week, set aside a moment each day to read the Bible without rushing, and ask God to help you let go of one specific worry.
exp.0:26:
