They were all amazed at what Jesus did. They asked one another what this was, and they called his teaching a "new doctrine," meaning something never heard before. Authority and power are what the word "authority" means here. Unclean spirits are evil spirits. Even they obeyed him.

These words are spoken by those who were in the synagogue at Capernaum on a Sabbath. They had just seen Jesus drive an evil spirit out of a man. Mark shows that Jesus did not only speak well; his word had real authority. For this reason his fame soon spread throughout all of Galilee.

Today we can trust that the word of Jesus has authority over whatever frightens us or dominates us. When you feel fear or find yourself bound to something, pray and place yourself under his word, believing that he has the power to help you.
exp.13:63:
Here the high priest says they have already heard the "blasphemy," that is, an offense against God. He asks them what they think, and all of them decide that Jesus is "guilty of death," meaning he deserves to die. "Condemned" means they declared him guilty.

The high priest is speaking before the Jewish council. Jesus had just said that he is the Messiah, the Son of God, and that they would see him seated at the right hand of the power of God. For them, those words made him equal to God. But they did not believe it was true. Mark shows that Jesus was condemned precisely for saying who he was.

For today: let us not be carried along by the crowd or by pride. Before judging anyone, let us listen with humility. And before Jesus, let us ask ourselves honestly: who is he to me?
exp.9:50:
Jesus asks the blind man, "What do you want me to do for you?" The man answers, "Lord, that I might receive my sight." The word "receive" here means "recover" or "have again" in the sense of getting back what was lost.

This man is Bartimaeus, who was sitting by the road asking for money. He had cried out for mercy, and the crowd tried to silence him. Jesus stopped and had him called. The blind man threw off his cloak, perhaps his only coat, and went to Him. Jesus already saw his need, but He wanted to hear his request.

For today: God invites you to tell Him clearly what you need, without going around the subject. Speak with Him honestly and with confidence, and set aside whatever hinders you from drawing near to Him.
exp.4:41:
She got up at once and began to walk. The text adds that she was twelve years old, perhaps to show that she was already walking normally.

The people there were overcome with amazement, almost beside themselves.

Jesus was in the house of Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, whose daughter had died. Some were mocking Him, so He sent everyone out and went in alone with the parents and three of His closest disciples. He took the girl by the hand and spoke to her in Aramaic. Mark tells this event to show that Jesus has authority even over death. Afterward He asked that the girl be given something to eat, a very human and down-to-earth gesture.

When everything seems lost, we can trust in Jesus. He does not give way before ridicule or before what seems impossible. He also cares about everyday things, like giving a girl something to eat. Bring Him your most difficult situation today, without fear.
exp.14:41:
It says that the evening was already falling on that Friday, the day of "preparation." It was the day before the Sabbath, the day of rest for the Jews. The word "preparation" refers to the day before, and that day people got ready what was necessary, because from sunset no one could work.

The one telling the story is Mark, who recounts the death of Jesus. Earlier he mentions the women who followed and served Jesus and who watched from a distance. Mark notes the hour because time was short: when night came the Sabbath would begin. That is why Joseph of Arimathea acts right away and asks Pilate for the body of Jesus in order to bury it.

For today: when time is short, we should not wait until we feel ready to do good. Joseph did not let the opportunity pass; he served with courage and respect. Ask yourself whom you can help today.
exp.3:17:
This verse speaks of the third kind of ground in the parable of the sower. The people represented here are those who hear the word of God, but that seed falls among thorns. The thorns are harmful plants that grow alongside the wheat and take away its space and strength.

Jesus is teaching a crowd beside the Sea of Galilee. Afterward, alone with his disciples, he explains the parable. He does this to show that not everyone receives the word in the same way, and that hearing alone is not enough.

For today: examine what fills your heart, such as worries or the desire to have more. Ask God to help you remove whatever chokes his word, and set aside a fixed time each day to read it calmly.
exp.6:16:
This verse tells us that Jesus withdrew from the crowd and went into a house. There his disciples asked him to explain the parable he had just spoken. "Withdrawn" means he was away from the crowd, and "parable" is a teaching that uses a simple comparison.

Jesus had been speaking with the Pharisees, who criticized the disciples for eating without carrying out their ritual washing. He said that what enters a person through the mouth does not defile them, but what comes out of the heart does. It was a hard idea, and the disciples, in humility, asked for clarification in private.

When we do not understand something in God's Word, we can come to Jesus with sincerity and ask him. He is not bothered by someone who truly wants to understand. Praying, reading calmly, and asking other mature believers are good steps.
exp.5:36:
Jesus says to his disciples, "Give ye them to eat." The disciples answer with a question full of astonishment: are they going to go and buy bread for two hundred pennyworth? A pennyworth was about the pay for a day's work, so it was an enormous sum.

A large crowd had followed Jesus to a remote place, and it was already late. The disciples asked him to send the crowd away so they could find food in the villages. Jesus challenges them to take on the responsibility themselves. They see only what they do not have, but Jesus is preparing them to see what he can do.

Many times God puts us before a need that seems greater than our resources. Instead of saying "I cannot," we can place in his hands the little we have and obey, trusting that he can do much with it.
exp.8:5:
What the passage says: Mark explains why Peter spoke as he did. He says Peter "did not know what to say," meaning he did not really understand what he was saying, because the disciples were "afraid," that is, full of fear and awe. The word "booths" refers to tents or shelters made of branches.

Context: Jesus was transfigured on the mountain before Peter, James, and John. Moses and Elijah appeared and were talking with Him. Mark himself, as narrator, makes clear that Peter's proposal came out of fright. Right after, the voice of the Father sets the course straight: Jesus is the beloved Son, and they must listen to Him.

For today: When we feel fear or strong emotion, we can speak or decide without thinking. Before acting, let us be still and listen to Jesus in His Word. He should have the first place in our decisions.
exp.5:16:
This verse explains why John the Baptist was in prison. Herod himself had sent his soldiers to arrest him and lock him up in jail. The reason was Herodias, who had been the wife of Philip, Herod's brother, but Herod had married her.

The narrator, Mark, recalls something from the past. Herod kept hearing people talk about Jesus, and his guilty conscience suggested that John, whom he had ordered put to death, had come back to life. Mark explains the origin of the conflict this way: John had spoken boldly about that marriage, which went against God's law.

For today: telling the truth out of love can cost a great deal, but it is the right thing to do. We also learn that ignoring our conscience does not silence it, so let us seek to live in such a way that we do not have to run from it.
exp.4:5:
This verse tells how a tormented man saw Jesus from a distance, ran to Him, and fell down before Him. The word translated here as "worshipped" can mean paying homage or bowing down before someone with reverence. The old spellings of "saw" and "to" in the source wording are not relevant to the English reader, so nothing further is needed on them.

The one who tells the story is Mark. He speaks of a man possessed by an unclean spirit, whom no one could control. Mark emphasizes the man's suffering to show the power of Jesus. What follows indicates that the spirit was speaking through him. For this reason, the reaction is understood to combine the man's desire to reach Jesus with his recognition of Jesus' authority. Interpreters explain it in different ways, and the text does not fully settle the question.

For today: even if you feel bound by fear, guilt, or addictions, do not stay far away. Run to Jesus with honesty and humility. He can do what no one else has been able to do.
exp.13:56:
This verse says that some people stood up in the trial and accused Jesus with lies. "Bearing false witness" means stating something that is not true in order to harm another person. Mark tells it plainly: these were not simple mistakes, they were false accusations.

Jesus is before the Jewish council, called the Sanhedrin, during the night he was arrested. The religious leaders already wanted to have him condemned to death, but they had no proof. So they looked for witnesses, and since their accounts did not agree, the accusation kept falling apart. Mark shows that the trial was unjust from the start.

For today: God values the truth, and lies hurt people. Before repeating a rumor or speaking badly about someone, ask yourself whether you are sure it is true. And if someone accuses you unjustly, remember that Jesus also went through that, and he understands you.
exp.13:27:
Jesus says that, after he rises, he will go ahead of his disciples into Galilee. "But after that I am risen" points to the time after his resurrection, and "I will go before you" means that he will lead them and wait for them there. It is a promise that death will not be the end.

Jesus speaks with his disciples after the last supper, on the way to the Mount of Olives. He has just warned them that they will all be made to stumble, that is, they will fall away from him, like scattered sheep when the shepherd is struck (a quotation of Zechariah 13:7). Even so, before they fail, Jesus promises that he will seek them out again. Galilee was the region where they had lived with him. Peter does not even take in this promise, for he immediately says that he will never leave him.

For today: when you fail or feel far from God, remember that Jesus already goes before you. His faithfulness does not depend on yours; return to him with confidence.
exp.7:11:
Jesus sighs deeply, with sorrow in his spirit, and asks why this generation is asking for a sign. Then he solemnly declares that no sign will be given to them. The word for sighing here means groaning with pain, and the phrase translated "verily I say unto you" is simply a solemn assurance; a sign is a miraculous proof.

Jesus speaks upon arriving at Dalmanutha, a place by the Sea of Galilee whose exact location is not known for certain. The Pharisees were arguing with him and asked him for a sign from heaven, but not out of faith; they were testing him. They had already seen healings and the multiplication of the loaves, so their hearts were closed. Jesus leaves them and goes away by boat.

For today: faith does not come from demanding proofs from God on our own terms. We can come to Jesus with humility, trusting what he has already shown us in his Word and in his work, rather than putting him to the test.
exp.6:27:
Here a Gentile woman answers Jesus with humility and quickness. She says "Yes, Lord" and accepts what he said, but adds that even the little dogs under the table eat the crumbs that fall from the children's bread.

The woman was a Syrophoenician, that is, from outside Israel, and she was asking Jesus to free her daughter. He had spoken about giving bread first to the children, probably referring to Israel. Scholars discuss Jesus' tone; many see it as a test of faith. She does not take offense and trusts that in his goodness there is room for her. Jesus healed the girl.

We can come near to God with humility and confidence, without feeling that we deserve much. Even when the answer seems slow or hard, persisting in prayer with simple faith is a way of trusting in his mercy.
exp.2:28:
It says that all sins can be forgiven, but whoever blasphemes against the Holy Ghost has no forgiveness and stands under judgment that lasts forever. "Blaspheme" means speaking with contempt or insult against God. The phrase "under eternal judgment" means that the person is guilty of a sin whose consequences last forever.

Jesus speaks to the teachers of the law, who said that He cast out demons by the power of Satan. Mark makes clear that they said this because they claimed, "He has an unclean spirit." In other words, they called the plain work of the Spirit evil. Christians understand this passage in different ways, but all agree that it speaks of a hardened and persistent rejection.

Today, if you are worried that you have committed this sin, that very concern shows a heart that is sensitive to God. Come to Christ with humility and trust, for He receives everyone who repents.
exp.3:28:
It says that when the grain is already ripe, the farmer immediately puts in the sickle, a curved tool for cutting, because the time of the harvest has come. The word "brought forth" means the fruit is already ready. "Harvest" is the same as the reaping.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd in parables. He tells of a man who sows and then goes about without worry, while the seed grows on its own, step by step. In this way he teaches how the kingdom of God works: it grows in a mysterious way and at its appointed time. Many understand the harvest as God's final moment, though some also see it as the fruit gathered in this life.

For today: sow God's word with faith in others and in yourself, and be patient. You do your part, and God makes it grow and decides the time of the harvest.
exp.13:42:
It says that, while Jesus was still speaking with his disciples in Gethsemane, Judas arrived, one of the twelve. He came with a large crowd armed with swords and clubs. They were sent by the chief priests, the scribes (teachers of the law), and the elders (leaders of the people). The word "immediately" in the verse means that the events happened right away.

Mark, who writes the account, shows that everything happens right after Jesus said: "The one who betrays me is near." Jesus already knew what was coming. The religious leaders wanted to arrest him, and Judas, who was one of the closest of the group, helped them find him at night.

For today: Jesus faced betrayal without fleeing and without losing his calm, because he trusted in the Father's plan. When someone close to us fails us, we can pray, ask for strength, and respond not with revenge but with the peace that comes from God.
exp.11:9:
Jesus asks his listeners whether they have never read this passage of Scripture: the stone that the builders rejected has become the chief stone. The stone at the corner is the key stone that joins and holds up two walls of the building. The word rejected means cast aside.

Jesus is speaking in the temple to the priests, scribes, and elders. He has just told the parable of the wicked tenants, who kill the son of the owner of the vineyard. He quotes Psalm 118 to show that, even though they reject him, God will exalt him. They understood that he was speaking about them, and they wanted to arrest him, but they feared the crowd.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we accept Jesus as the center of our lives or whether we set him aside when he makes us uncomfortable. Building on him gives us a firm foundation, even when others despise him.
exp.14:4:
It says that although the chief priests were accusing Jesus of many things and Pilate was asking him to defend himself, Jesus did not answer anything. The explanation of the old wording is removed here because the verse your reader sees already says Pilate marvelled, so there is no need to explain it further. Jesus is being tried before Pilate, the Roman governor of Judea. The religious leaders bring charges against him so that he will be condemned. Pilate expected an accused man to defend himself vigorously, yet Jesus kept silent. Many Christians see here a fulfilment of what Isaiah 53:7 foretold about the servant who does not open his mouth.

For today: when you are criticized or treated unfairly, you do not always have to respond with anger or long defenses. Ask God for wisdom to know when to speak and when to be silent, trusting that he cares for you.
exp.15:1:
Very early on the first day of the week, the women arrive at the tomb when the sun had already risen. Mark uses the present tense ("arrive") to make the scene feel alive. "Tomb" is the place where they laid Jesus.

The one speaking is the narrator of the Gospel, Mark. He tells what happened after Jesus died. The women waited until the Sabbath, the day of rest, had passed, and now they are going to anoint the body with perfumes, as an expression of love and respect. Some notice that "very early in the morning" and "the sun had already risen" seem different; many think it refers to dawn, when the sun was coming up.

Today: they went out of love, without knowing how the tomb would be opened. Take the step of faith you can, even if you cannot yet see the whole solution. God often opens the way while you walk.
exp.9:25:
The disciples were even more astonished and alarmed. Among themselves they asked, "Then who can be saved?" The word "astonished" here means that they were deeply struck and troubled, not that they feared some dangerous thing.

Jesus had just spoken with a rich man who was unwilling to give up his possessions to follow him. Then he said that it is very hard for those who trust in riches to enter the kingdom of God. For many Jews of that time, wealth seemed a sign of blessing, so his words sounded surprising to them. If even the rich man was finding it hard, who could have hope?

Today we can learn that no one is saved by their own effort, their money, or their merits. Jesus answers right away that what is impossible for people is possible for God. We can trust less in what we have and more in his grace.
exp.0:4:
Many people went out to meet John the Baptist: they came from all the land of Judea and also from Jerusalem. There, in the river Jordan, John baptized them, and they confessed their sins out loud. "They went out to him" means "they went toward him." "All the land" is a way of saying that a very large number of people came.

Mark, the author, presents John as the messenger who prepares the way of the Lord, just as the prophet had announced. John preached repentance, that is, turning back to God from the heart. Confessing sins and being baptized showed that the people wanted to change and to be ready to receive Jesus, who was coming after him.

For today: preparing your heart for God begins with being honest. Take a moment this week to tell God, without excuses, the ways you have fallen short, and ask him for forgiveness and for help to change.
exp.9:13:
This verse says that Jesus was greatly displeased when he saw his disciples pushing the children away. He told them to let the children come to him and not to stop them. "To hinder" means to place obstacles in the way, and "such as these" means "those who are like them." Jesus affirms that the kingdom of God belongs to those who are like children.

Jesus was speaking, and the disciples had kept quiet. Some parents were bringing their children so that Jesus would touch and bless them, but the disciples were scolding them. Then Jesus explains that one must receive the kingdom of God like a child: with trust and without boasting of merits. Then he embraces the children and blesses them.

Today we can take care that no one, neither children nor simple people, finds in us an obstacle to coming to Jesus. And we can learn to trust God with humility and simplicity.
exp.4:38:
Jesus enters the house and asks why there is so much commotion and weeping. He says the girl is not dead, but sleeps. "Why make ye this ado" refers to making a noisy fuss or disturbance.

Jesus speaks in the house of Jairus, whose daughter had died. The people were weeping, and they mocked Him. Some understand "sleepeth" as a way of speaking about death, which for Jesus is not final. Others think He meant to show that death would be temporary. The text does not clarify this further; what follows is that He raises her.

When a situation seems hopeless, do not measure it only by what you see. Bring your pain to Jesus with sincerity and trust that He has power and authority where we see only an end.
exp.13:13:
Jesus tells two of his disciples that, when they go into the house the man carrying a jar of water leads them to, they should speak to the owner. They are to ask him about the room, that is, the guest room or hall, where Jesus will eat the Passover with his disciples. The word translated as "Master" in the verse above is the one used here for Jesus, who calls himself "The Master."

Jesus speaks a few days before his death. It is the day when the Passover supper was being prepared, the feast that remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. He gives precise instructions, and he calls himself "The Master." Some think the owner already knew Jesus or that the arrangement had been made beforehand; the text does not make this clear.

For today: The disciples obeyed without understanding every detail, and everything happened as Jesus said. We can trust his word and take the next step of obedience, even when we cannot yet see the whole path.
exp.9:37:
Jesus answers James and John that they do not understand what they are asking. He asks them whether they can drink the cup that he drinks and be baptized with the baptism that he is baptized with. "Cup" and "baptism" are images of the suffering Jesus was about to go through. The "right hand" and the "left hand" are places of honor.

The two brothers, disciples of Jesus, had just asked him for the first places in his glory. Jesus had already announced his death, but they were thinking about honor and power. He shows them that the road to glory goes through suffering and service. Scholars agree that the cup and the baptism speak of his passion, although they are explained in several ways.

Today, before asking God for recognition or success, it is worth asking ourselves whether we are willing to follow Jesus also in what is hard: serving, forgiving, and persevering without seeking applause.
exp.6:23:
He says that Jesus left that place and went into the region of Tyre and Sidon, cities to the north of Galilee. There he entered a house and did not want anyone to know he was there, but he could not stay hidden. The phrase "went away" is simply the verb for leaving, and the word for the area is "borders," meaning the region or territory around those cities.

Mark tells this right after the argument with the Pharisees about what is clean and unclean, where Jesus taught that what defiles comes from the heart. Now Jesus leaves Jewish territory and moves toward an area where most people were not Jewish. Mark does not say why he wanted to pass unnoticed; some think he was seeking rest or time alone with his disciples, but that is an interpretation.

For today: Jesus also needed to withdraw to rest, and yet he attended to the one who sought him. Guard your times of rest, but keep your heart open to anyone who needs help.
exp.10:11:
It says that on the next day, as Jesus and his disciples were leaving Bethany, Jesus became hungry. Bethany is a village near Jerusalem where they had spent the night. The text shows Jesus as a real man, with physical needs like ours.

Mark is the one telling the story. The day before, Jesus had entered Jerusalem amid shouts of "Hosanna," and he had looked around the temple. Now he returns to the city in the morning. This hunger serves as the introduction to the account of the fig tree, which follows right after. Interpreters explain that account in several ways, and the story is linked to what Jesus will do in the temple.

For today: Jesus knows tiredness and hunger because he experienced them. You can come to him with your everyday needs, without feeling that they are small or that they bother him.
exp.9:45:
They came to Jericho, and as Jesus and his disciples left the city, accompanied by a large crowd, a blind man named Bartimeus, son of Timeus, was sitting by the side of the road, asking for alms. Begging here means asking those who pass by for help or money. Mark explains that the name Bartimeus means "son of Timeus."

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. Just before this, Jesus taught that the greatest is the one who serves, and that he came to give his life for many. Now Mark shows Jesus serving someone whom society ignored. Jesus is on his way to Jerusalem, and this encounter prepares the way for Bartimeus's cry in the verses that follow.

For today: God sees those whom others overlook. If you feel forgotten today, you can come to Jesus with confidence. And if you are on the road, look around you: whom could you serve or listen to?
exp.5:21:
The verse tells how the daughter of Herodias came in and danced, and her dancing pleased Herod and his guests. Then the king, very pleased, told the young girl to ask for whatever she wanted, and he would give it to her.

Mark narrates a birthday banquet of Herod Antipas, with important people from Galilee. Earlier, Herod had imprisoned John the Baptist, yet he respected him and listened to him with interest. Here Herod speaks, carried away by the moment, the applause, and the atmosphere of the feast. That hasty promise will become the path to a terrible decision.

For today: be careful with promises made out of pride or the emotion of the moment. Before we commit ourselves, it is wise to think calmly and ask God for wisdom, because a word spoken without reflection can have very serious consequences.
exp.6:17:
Jesus asks his disciples whether they too are without understanding, that is, whether they still do not grasp what he is teaching. He explains that nothing that comes from outside and enters a person can make that person unclean. "Make unclean" here means to make someone impure before God. "You" is the plural form of address.

Jesus speaks at home, away from the crowd, answering the disciples who ask him to explain his parable. Earlier, the Pharisees had criticized his disciples for eating without observing certain washing rituals. Jesus teaches that true impurity does not come from food, since food goes into the stomach, not into the heart. Mark adds that this made all foods "clean," and many understand this as a clarification by the evangelist himself.

For today: let us not measure our life with God only by external rules. Let us ask him to examine our heart, where our words and decisions come from, and to cleanse it.
exp.6:2:
This verse describes a custom of the Pharisees and of many Jews of that time. They followed "the tradition of the elders," that is, rules that had been handed down from generation to generation. According to that custom, they would not eat without washing their hands "oft," a phrase whose exact meaning is not entirely clear; some believe it refers to washing carefully or even up to the wrist.

Mark adds this comment in parentheses for his readers, who probably were not familiar with Jewish customs. The Pharisees and scribes from Jerusalem criticized Jesus' disciples for eating without that ritual washing. It was not a matter of hygiene, but of a human religious tradition.

For today: check whether you give more weight to your religious customs than to the heart and to the Word of God. Traditions can help, but they should never take the place of loving God and others.
exp.13:64:
Mark 14:65 tells how some of those present mocked Jesus after condemning him. They spat on him, covered his face, struck him with their open hands, and said to him, "Prophesy!" They were mocking him, daring him to name who had hit him. The servants, or temple guards, also struck him.

This happens on the night of the trial before the high priest. The leaders had just declared that Jesus deserved death for supposed blasphemy. Mark shows how Jesus is rejected and humiliated, just as he had foretold he would suffer. No one knows for certain who the "some" were, but the text suggests members of the council and their guards.

For today: when you are humiliated or treated unjustly, remember that Jesus went through this without returning evil for evil. Ask him to give you patience, and treat with respect even those who hurt you.
exp.9:35:
Jesus answers James and John with a simple question: "What would you have me do for you?" The old wording is minimal: the word for "would you have" is "would ye," and "me do for you" is "should do for you." Jesus lets them state clearly what they desire from Him.

Jesus had just announced for the third time his suffering, his death, and his resurrection. Even so, James and John come forward with a request for a place of honor. Jesus knows their hearts, but He invites them to express them. Then He shows them that they do not understand what they are asking: the road to glory passes through suffering and service.

For today: Jesus invites you to speak to him honestly, even about your desires. But ask yourself whether what you are asking for seeks personal honor or seeks to make you more like Him.
exp.11:41:
She put two small coins into the offering box, a poor widow, and together they were worth one farthing. Here the coins are described by their value in the verse itself, so no further explanation of the old names is needed.

Mark tells us what Jesus sees in the temple, as he sits across from the offering box. Shortly before, he had criticized the teachers of the law who took advantage of widows and pretended to be pious with long prayers. In contrast, he now shows us a real widow, with no power and no money, and teaches his disciples how God values what is given.

For today: God does not measure our giving by the amount, but by the heart and the sacrifice it costs. Give what you can with sincerity, whether money, time, or help, without comparing yourself to others or feeling ashamed of how little it seems.
exp.2:12:
It says that Jesus went up a mountain and called to his side the people he wanted. They answered his call and went to him. The phrase "called to himself" means that he called them so that they would be close to him. "Whom he wanted" indicates that Jesus himself chose them, by his own decision.

Mark tells what Jesus did. Earlier, many people were following him, and even evil spirits recognized him as the Son of God, but he ordered them to be quiet. Now Jesus withdraws from the crowd and calls a smaller, closer group. The verses that follow explain that he appointed the twelve apostles, so that they would be with him and then be sent out to preach.

For today: God first calls us to be with Jesus, and then to serve. Before doing anything for him, give time to his company: prayer, reading the Bible, and silence. Respond simply, as they did: "they came to him."
exp.7:26:
Jesus and his disciples set out toward the villages near Caesarea Philippi, a region north of Galilee. As they walk, Jesus asks them what people are saying about him. The word "villages" refers to small towns, and the old spelling is not something your reader needs to know.

It is Jesus who speaks, and he does so right after healing a blind man in Bethsaida, in two stages. With this question he begins to lead his disciples toward an important decision: to recognize who he truly is. The answers the people give, which come next, show that many admired him but did not fully understand him.

For today: it is not enough to repeat what others think about Jesus. Take a quiet moment to answer honestly who he is for you, and ask him to help you know him better.
exp.13:2:
Jesus was in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, sitting at the table. Then a woman came in carrying a jar made of alabaster, a fine stone used for keeping perfumes. It held pure nard perfume, very costly. She broke the jar and poured the perfume on Jesus' head.

Mark tells this while the religious leaders were looking for a way to arrest Jesus secretly and kill him, just before the Passover. He sets their wickedness against the act of this woman. Afterward, some of those present complained about the cost. The text does not give her name here; other gospels identify her in different ways, and there is debate about whether they describe the same event.

For today: Giving Jesus the best of ourselves, with sincere love, is never wasted, even when others do not understand.
exp.2:20:
His friends heard about it and went out to take hold of him. They were trying to bring him away with them, not arrest him like a criminal. They said, "He is beside himself," meaning that he had lost his mind.

Mark tells this right after the crowd gathered so thickly in the house that Jesus and his disciples could not even eat. His own people were probably his family, though the text does not give names here. They were surely worried about him, but they did not understand his mission. Soon afterward, some scribes from Jerusalem accuse him of something even worse.

Today, even people close to us may not understand our faith or our service. If that happens to you, follow Jesus' example: stay faithful with humility and patience, without becoming bitter. And take care not to dismiss what God is really doing as mere excess.
exp.3:22:
Jesus says that whoever has ears to hear should listen. He is not speaking only of the ear of the body, but of listening carefully, with a real desire to understand and to obey. In this text, "hear" means paying genuine attention.

Jesus is teaching the crowd right after the parable of the sower. He says that a lamp is not lit to be hidden, and that what is hidden will come to light. With this statement he invites his listeners not to hear out of habit, but with seriousness, because what they hear will have consequences.

For today: before reading the Bible or listening to a teaching, pray a brief prayer asking for an attentive heart. Then write down one thing God showed you, and decide how you will put it into practice this week.
exp.9:12:
This verse tells that some people were bringing little children to Jesus so that he would touch them, that is, so that he would bless them. The disciples rebuked those who brought them, meaning they scolded them and tried to keep them away. The word "brought" here means that they carried or led the children to Him.

Jesus had just been talking with the Pharisees about marriage and divorce, and then these children arrive. The disciples probably thought Jesus had more important matters to attend to. But the text says that Jesús was indignant when he saw this, and he corrected them: the kingdom of God belongs to those who are like children.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are, without meaning to, putting up barriers for those who want to come near to Jesus. Children, and every simple person, deserve to be welcomed with patience and affection. Furthermore, we ourselves must draw near to God with humility and trust.
exp.11:6:
The explanation says that the tenant farmers to whom the owner of the vineyard had entrusted his land spoke among themselves. They recognized that the son was the heir, and even so they decided to kill him in order to keep the inheritance for themselves.

Jesus tells this parable in Jerusalem, to the religious leaders who were questioning him. The owner represents God, the vineyard the people of Israel, the servants the prophets, and the son Jesus himself. Mark says that the leaders understood he was speaking about them (v. 12). Jesus anticipates his own rejection and death.

For today: let us not try to manage our lives as if they were our property. Everything we have comes from God. Let us ask ourselves whether we are receiving Jesus with humility or whether we want to keep control.
exp.13:6:
Jesus says that the poor will always be with you, and that his disciples can help them whenever they wish, but that they will not always have him. The words "whensoever ye will" are an older way of saying "whenever you want," and "do them good" means to help them or be generous to them.

Jesus speaks in Bethany, at a meal, after a woman poured very expensive perfume on him. Some of those present criticized her for the waste. Jesus defends her and explains that she acted at the right moment, since his death was near. He does not look down on the poor; he teaches that there are moments that do not come back.

Today we can care for those in need throughout the year and, at the same time, not put off time with God and with the people we love. There are opportunities that pass and do not return.
exp.3:19:
Jesus says that the good ground stands for people who hear the word of God, receive it, and bear fruit. That fruit is not the same for everyone: some bear thirtyfold, others sixty, and others a hundred.

Jesus is teaching the crowd and then explains the parable of the sower to his disciples. This verse closes that explanation. After speaking of those who do not bear fruit, he shows those who do. With this he invites us to listen carefully and not stop at merely hearing.

Today you might ask yourself: what do I do with what I hear from the Bible? Choose one teaching this week and put it into practice, for example by forgiving someone or helping a person in need. In this way the word begins to bear fruit.
exp.12:17:
Jesus asks his disciples to pray that their escape does not happen in winter. Words from the source wording that are not in this verse are explained only where needed; here the first two sentences are rewritten so they do not quote or explain those words. "Escape" is the hurried departure to get away from danger.

Jesus speaks to four of his disciples on the Mount of Olives, and he warns them about times of great suffering that will come upon Jerusalem. Many believe this refers to the destruction of the city in the year 70, though others also see a future fulfillment. Winter is mentioned because the roads and swollen rivers made escaping harder. Interpreters understand this in different ways.

For today: Jesus teaches us to bring God into our practical details. Pray about the difficult situations you might face, and trust that God cares for you.
exp.1:25:
Jesus recalls that David entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence (consecrated bread that was set out before God) and also gave it to his companions. According to the law, that bread was only for the priests. "Permitted" means allowed, and "high priest" means the chief priest.

The Pharisees were accusing the disciples of breaking the Sabbath. Jesus answers with a story from the Scriptures (1 Samuel 21). There, human need weighed more than a ceremonial rule. As for the name Abiathar, the account in Samuel mentions his father Ahimelech; scholars explain this in several ways, and there is no single certain answer.

Today: God gave us his commands for the good of people, not to make us hard toward them. Before judging someone, ask yourself whether you are caring for the heart of the law: loving God and helping the one who needs it.
exp.9:3:
The Pharisees answer Jesus that Moses allowed a husband to write a certificate of divorce and send his wife away. To "send away" here means to put a wife out of the marriage. A certificate of divorce was a written document that brought the union to an end.

The Pharisees are speaking in order to set a trap for Jesus. He asks them what Moses commanded, and they cite the law of Deuteronomy 24. Notice that Jesus speaks of what Moses "commanded," but they answer that Moses "allowed." Jesus will soon explain that this concession existed because of the hardness of the human heart, and he will lead them back to God's original plan for marriage.

For today: before asking what is the least that is permitted, let us ask what God desires. Let us guard our hearts and seek to honor our commitments, instead of using the law as an excuse.
exp.10:13:
Jesus speaks directly to the fig tree and says that no one will ever again eat fruit from it. His disciples hear this statement. "Answering" here does not mean that someone had asked him a question; it means he is reacting to what he has just found: a tree full of leaves, but without fruit.

Jesus was hungry and approached the tree expecting to find figs. Mark makes clear that it was not the season for figs, and for that reason there are different interpretations. Many see a symbolic act: the tree appears to be alive, but it bears no fruit, just as the temple does, which Jesus cleanses shortly afterward. Mark places both scenes side by side, as if each explained the other.

God looks for genuine faith, not mere appearance. Today we can ask ourselves whether our Christian life has only leaves, or whether it also bears fruit: love, honesty, and service to others.
exp.12:29:
Jesus says that "this generation" will not pass away before all these things happen. "Generation" is usually understood to mean the people living at that time, though some scholars think it refers to humanity in general, to the Jewish people, or to the generation that will see the final signs. The "things" are the events Jesus has just described.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They had asked him when the temple would fall and what the signs would be. He teaches them with the parable of the fig tree: just as the leaves announce that summer is near, certain events announce that something is approaching. But then he makes clear that no one knows the day or the hour.

For today: do not spend your energy trying to calculate dates. Instead, live with attention and faithfulness, trusting that Jesus' words will not pass away, even when everything else changes.
exp.6:1:
This verse tells how the Pharisees and some of the scribes saw that certain of Jesus' disciples were eating bread with hands that were defiled, that is, unwashed. The word defiled here means unclean, not set apart for God according to their custom. And they found fault with them, meaning they criticized and accused them.

The one speaking is Mark, the narrator. The religious leaders had come from Jerusalem, probably to keep watch over Jesus. This washing was not for hygiene but a tradition of the elders, a human rule added over time. The Pharisees treated it as if it were an obligation before God.

For today: before judging others by customs or outward forms, let us ask whether what we demand comes from God or only from our tradition. Let us care more for the heart than for appearances.
exp.6:20:
Jesus says that evil does not come from outside, but from within, from the heart. From there come evil thoughts, adultery, fornication (sexual relations outside of marriage), and murders (killings). In the Bible, the heart represents the deepest part of a person: their thoughts, desires, and decisions.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples. The Pharisees had criticized his disciples for eating without washing their hands according to tradition. Jesus teaches them that no food makes a person unclean, because it enters the stomach and not the heart. What truly defiles us is what comes out of a twisted heart.

Today, instead of caring only about appearances, we can ask God to examine and cleanse our hearts. Let us pause each day to pray: "Lord, change my thoughts and my desires."
exp.0:10:
A voice came from heaven and spoke to Jesus. It said, "You are my beloved Son," that is, my dear Son. It added, "in you I take delight," a phrase that means "I am well pleased with you" or "I am very glad with you."

The one speaking is God the Father, and he speaks right after Jesus' baptism, when the Spirit descends on him like a dove. With these words he confirms who Jesus is before his public ministry begins. Notice that this happens before his miracles and teachings: the Father is pleased with him from the very beginning. Soon comes the desert and the temptation.

For today: if you believe in Christ, you can remember that God's love is not earned only by what you do. Rest in that love, especially in times of trial.
exp.9:16:
As Jesus was setting out again on his journey, a man came running, knelt down before him, and asked him, "Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" The phrase "inherit" means to receive eternal life as something given, like an inheritance.

Just before this, Jesus had said that people must receive the kingdom of God like a child, with open hands and without pride. Now a man appears who asks what he must do, as someone who wants to earn something for himself. Jesus will answer by asking why he calls him good, and will lead him to think about God.

For today: before asking what more I must do to please God, I can ask him for a humble heart that receives his grace simply, like a child.
exp.3:36:
Mark says that suddenly a strong storm came up, with a great wind. The waves were breaking into the boat, and it was already almost full of water.

Mark tells this as the narrator. Jesus had been teaching the crowd all day, and he suggested to his disciples that they cross to the other side of the lake. They took him along in the boat just as he was, tired. The storm came while they were doing what he had suggested, and it shows that following Jesus does not always keep us from difficulties.

Today, this verse reminds us that we can go through storms even when we are on the right path. When something overwhelms us, we can bring Jesus our worry honestly, trusting that he is with us, even when he sometimes seems silent.
exp.11:11:
This verse says that the religious leaders wanted to arrest Jesus. They understood that the parable of the wicked tenants was speaking about them. But they were afraid of the crowd, which admired Jesus, so they left him and went away.

Jesus is speaking to the chief priests, scribes, and elders in the temple in Jerusalem. He has just told the parable of tenants who mistreat the owner's servants and kill his son. Then he quotes Psalm 118 about the stone that was rejected. The leaders recognize themselves in the story, but instead of repenting, they become angry.

For today: when the Word of God confronts us, we can either harden our hearts or humble ourselves. Let us ask the Lord for a heart willing to listen, even when the truth is uncomfortable, and not to fear people more than God.
exp.14:9:
This verse says that Pilate knew the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy. "Chief priests" are the leading priests, the leaders of the temple. Envy is the resentment felt when someone sees another person receiving more respect or influence than oneself.

Mark explains here what Pilate, the Roman governor, was thinking. Jesus had many people following him, and the religious leaders felt their position was threatened. That is why Pilate offers to release Jesus, since he could see there was no just reason to condemn him. Even so, the text does not say how he came to that conclusion.

For today: envy can lead us to harm others without our even noticing. Let us ask God for a heart that rejoices in another's good, instead of competing or wishing that others would fail.
exp.10:3:
They went and found things just as Jesus had told them: a colt, that is, a young donkey, tied at a door, outside, on a street or corner where two roads met. So they untied it. "Found" means they came upon it, and the old spelling of the word "to" is what appears in some older texts.

Jesús was approaching Jerusalem and sent two disciples with precise instructions. Mark tells us that the colt was one that no one had ever ridden. Jesus was going to enter the city riding on it, and many see here a fulfillment of the prophecy in Zechariah 9:9. The detail that everything happened just as Jesus said shows his knowledge and his authority.

For today: when God asks us for a step that seems strange, we can obey with confidence, remembering that Jesus already knows the way. Sometimes we will only see it clearly as we move forward.
exp.11:5:
This verse says that the owner of the vineyard still had one last person to send: his beloved son. He sent him last, thinking the tenants would respect him. "Last" is what the sentence means by the word "postrero," and "respect" means to honor and esteem.

Jesus is speaking in the temple to the religious leaders, and he tells this parable of the wicked tenants. The owner represents God, the vineyard represents Israel, the servants represent the prophets who were sent, and the son, as most Christians understand it, points to Jesus himself. The leaders understood that he was speaking about them (v. 12).

For today: God has been patient and generous with us. We can ask ourselves whether we respond to Jesus with sincere respect, listening to his voice and obeying him, or whether we prefer to keep running our lives as if they were ours alone.
exp.5:37:
Jesus asks his disciples to check how much food they have. The phrase "go and see" is the wording used here. When they found out, they answered that they had five loaves and two fish. The word "when they knew" means "after finding out."

Jesus speaks with his disciples in front of a hungry crowd, in a remote place. The disciples wanted to send the people away so they could buy food. Jesus, however, told them: "You give them something to eat." His question leads them to see how little they have, before he does something greater, as the following verses show.

For today: we often look at what we have and think it is not enough. Jesus invites us to offer him the little we have, with sincerity and trust. He knows what to do with what we give him.
exp.6:11:
Jesus says that such a person is no longer permitted to do anything more for his father or his mother. The word "suffer" in the verse means "allow," so the sentence is saying that once someone declared an offering, "Corban," the leaders released him from the duty to help his parents.

Jesus is speaking with the Pharisees and some teachers of the law. They were criticizing him because his disciples ate without following certain washing rituals. Jesus answers by showing that their human traditions were cancelling out a clear command from God: to honor one's father and mother. "Corban" refers to something dedicated to God. Scholars debate exactly how this practice was applied.

Today we can ask ourselves whether some religious custom or spiritual-sounding excuse is keeping us from caring for our family. Honoring God should never serve as a pretext for failing to love, visit, or help our parents.
exp.10:6:
It says the disciples brought Jesus the young donkey they had untied. A "colt" is a young donkey. They laid their cloaks on it, as an improvised saddle, and Jesus sat on it.

Mark is the one narrating. Jesus is drawing near to Jerusalem, and he had sent two disciples for this animal, which no one had ridden before. Many see here a fulfillment of Zechariah 9:9, where a king is announced who comes humbly, riding on a donkey. Mark does not quote that text here, so it is a connection that readers make. The people respond with praise.

Jesus chose to arrive with simplicity, not with force or luxury. Today we can ask ourselves whether we are willing to place what we have, our coats and our possessions, at his service, even when it seems little or ordinary. God can use what is simple.
exp.10:24:
Jesus says that when someone stands to pray, they should forgive anyone who has something against them. The reason is that the Father in heaven also forgives those who forgive. "Offenses" are the wrongs or bad deeds committed against others. The word "ye have" in the verse is an older way of saying "you have" or "you are."

Jesus speaks to his disciples after cursing the fig tree and cleansing the temple, when they are amazed at what happened. He teaches them about faith and prayer. Here he adds that praying with faith goes together with a heart that forgives. The following verse reinforces this with a serious warning. Some scholars explain it as a sign that the forgiveness received from God should be reflected in how we treat others.

Before praying, pause and ask God whether you are holding a grudge against someone. Hand it over to him sincerely and, if possible, take steps to be reconciled.
exp.4:13:
They say the men who tended the pigs ran off after seeing the whole herd drown in the sea. They went to report what had happened in the town and in the countryside, and people came out to see what had taken place.

Here the narrator, Mark, speaks. Jesus had just freed a man tormented by many evil spirits, called "legion." They asked to enter the pigs, and Jesus allowed it. The herdsmen, frightened, were the first witnesses and spread the news. Some think they fled out of fear or because they worried about losing their jobs; the text does not make this clear.

For today: when Jesus acts, people may react in different ways. We can ask ourselves whether we focus only on what was lost or whether we recognize what Christ gained: a free and restored life.
exp.6:5:
Jesus answers the Pharisees and calls them "hypocrites." That word was used for the actor who played a part on stage; here it means people who appear to be what they are not. He quotes the prophet Isaiah: the people honor God with their lips, but their heart is far from him.

The Pharisees and the scribes criticized the disciples because they ate without washing their hands, according to the tradition of the elders, a custom handed down by the teachers. Jesus does not speak against cleanliness, but against placing human rules above what God truly asks. He quotes Isaiah 29:13.

Today we can ask ourselves: do my prayers, my songs, and my religious customs come from a sincere heart? God wants real love and obedience, not just appearance. Today, take a moment to speak to him with honesty.
exp.4:22:
Here Jairus pleads with Jesus earnestly. He says his little daughter is at the point of death, that is, she is about to die. He asks Jesus to come and lay his hands on her that she may be healed and spared from dying, and that she shall live. It is clear that he believes Jesus' touch can restore her life.

The one speaking is Jairus, one of the rulers of the synagogue, a man respected in his community. Even so, he falls at Jesus' feet, setting aside his dignity. He does so out of desperation and a father's love. Jesus had just crossed the sea, and a great crowd surrounded him.

When you face a need you cannot resolve, come to Jesus with humility and without pretense. Tell him your pain, ask with confidence, and leave the outcome in his hands, even when you do not understand his timing.
exp.15:16:
The verse says that certain signs will accompany those who believe in Jesus. In his name, that is, with his authority, they will cast out demons and speak in new tongues, that is, languages they had not learned. The word "believe" refers to those who trust in Jesus, and "signs" are extraordinary events that point to his power.

The risen Jesus speaks to his disciples before ascending into heaven. He has just sent them to preach the gospel throughout the world. These signs would confirm their message. It should be said that many scholars point out that the oldest manuscripts of Mark end at verse 8, and that these final verses are debated, so some Christians interpret them with caution.

For today: trust that the power of Jesus supports his message, and focus on sharing the gospel with humility and love, rather than seeking the spectacular.
exp.13:59:
And the high priest stood up in the midst and asked Jesus whether he would answer nothing. He also wanted to know what the charges were that these witnesses were bringing against him.

Jesus is being tried at night before the Jewish council. The false witnesses contradicted one another, so they could not produce a firm accusation. The high priest, frustrated, tries to get Jesus himself to say something that would condemn him. Jesus keeps silent, which many connect with the suffering servant of Isaiah 53:7, though the text does not say this directly.

There are times when it is not necessary to defend yourself against every attack or lie. Jesus stayed silent before the false accusations, but he spoke clearly when it came to the truth about who he is. Let us ask for wisdom to know when to be silent and when to speak, trusting that God is our defender.
exp.8:19:
They brought the boy to Jesus. As soon as the spirit saw him, it threw the child into a violent convulsion. He fell to the ground and rolled about, foaming at the mouth. "Tare him" means to shake or convulse violently, and "foaming" refers to the foam that came from his mouth.

Mark tells this after the father explained that the disciples had not been able to cast out the spirit. Jesus, with sorrow, called the people a faithless generation and asked that the boy be brought to him. The spirit reacts immediately when it sees Jesus. Then Jesus will speak with the father, who has suffered for years.

For today: when a problem seems stronger than we can handle, let us not hide it. Let us bring it to Jesus as it is, with honesty and with our little faith. He is not frightened by our pain, and he can draw near to it with compassion.
exp.2:8:
Jesus asks his disciples to have a small boat ready for him. The word "ready" in this context means prepared or available. A "throng" is a large crowd, and the idea of being "pressed" or "crushed" means being squeezed or overwhelmed. So the boat was a safe way out in case the people pressed in on him.

Mark tells us that Jesus withdrew toward the Sea of Galilee, and a great many people from many places followed him, drawn by what they had heard about his healings. Jesus himself gives this instruction to his disciples. The verses that follow explain the difficulty: many sick people were pushing forward to touch him. The text does not say that the boat was used at that moment, only that he asked for it as a precaution.

For today: Jesus was compassionate, but also prudent. Looking after our strength and taking sensible precautions is not a lack of love; it helps us keep serving with peace and wisdom.
exp.9:9:
This verse tells us that, once they were inside a house, the disciples asked Jesus again about the same subject he had just been discussing. The word "again" points back to what had just happened, and "of the same matter" refers to the subject of marriage and divorce.

Jesus had just answered some Pharisees, who wanted to test him, by quoting that God joined man and woman together as one flesh. The disciples had heard his answer in public, but they were left with doubts or wanted to understand it better. So they waited until they were in private and asked. Afterward, Jesus explained it to them in more detail.

For today: when a teaching of Jesus is hard for us or leaves us with questions, let us not pass over it or avoid it. We can come to him with sincerity, in prayer and in reading his Word, and ask him to help us understand it and live it.
exp.7:25:
Jesus sends the man he has just healed of blindness straight home. He tells him not to enter the village and not to tell anyone there. The word "sent" in the verse is the one that appears in the King James text, and "village" is a small town.

Jesus speaks this just after healing the blind man of Bethsaida in two stages. Mark mentions several times that Jesus asked for silence about his miracles. Interpreters give different reasons: to avoid crowds who sought only signs, or to wait for the right moment for people to understand who he was. The text does not fully explain it. Right afterward, Jesus asks his disciples who they think he is.

For today: after receiving God's help, it is not always necessary to make noise. We can spend time at home, in quiet, letting his work transform us and helping us know him better.
exp.4:40:
Jesus takes the girl by the hand and speaks to her in Aramaic, the language of his people: "Talitha cumi." Mark himself translates it: "Damsel, I say unto thee, arise." The word "make a commotion" means to make noise and fuss, and the phrase "being interpreted" means "translated."

Jesus speaks in the house of Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, whose twelve-year-old daughter had fallen ill and died. Before entering, he said that the girl was "sleeping," and the people mocked him. Jesus put everyone outside and went in alone with the parents and his closest disciples. Some understand that "sleeping" stresses that death is not final before his power; others, that she had not yet died completely. The text narrates the event as a resurrection.

For today: when a situation seems lost and others mock your hope, draw near to Jesus with confidence. He speaks with tenderness and authority, and he still takes by the hand those who seek him.
exp.5:27:
It says that the guard sent by Herod went to the prison and killed John the Baptist by cutting off his head. Then he brought the head on a platter and handed it to the young woman, Herodias's daughter, and she gave it to her mother.

Mark tells this as the narrator. Herod had made a rash promise at a banquet, and Herodias, angry because John was criticizing her marriage, took the opportunity to ask for his death. Herod was saddened, but he gave in out of pride and to look good before his guests. The account appears while the apostles are on mission, and it foreshadows that following God can be costly.

For today: think before you promise something, and do not let the fear of looking foolish lead you to do what is unjust. Speaking the truth with courage, as John did, is worth more than the approval of others.
exp.8:29:
They left that place and traveled through Galilee, a region in the north of Israel. Jesus did not want anyone to know where they were. The phrase "he would not that any man should know it" means that he was trying to pass through without being noticed.

Mark tells this after Jesus healed a boy and explained to his disciples why they had not been able to help him. Now Jesus withdraws from the crowds because, according to the next verse, he wanted to spend time teaching his disciples, and he spoke to them about his death and resurrection.

For today: sometimes God invites us to step away from the noise and the rush so that we can listen to him calmly. Find a quiet time each day to pray and read the Bible, and let him teach you.
exp.2:14:
He says Jesus gave the twelve disciples "power," that is, authority, to heal the sick and to cast out demons. The word "power" we would today call "authority." "Cast out" means to drive out.

Mark tells us that Jesus went up into the mountain, called those he wanted, and chose twelve. They had a threefold purpose: to be with him, to be sent out to preach, and to have authority over sicknesses and demons. That authority was not their own; it came from Jesus. Then Mark lists their names, beginning with Simon, whom Jesus named Peter.

Today not all of us receive the same calling as the twelve, but we can still learn the order: first to be with Jesus, and then to serve. When we care for the sick, comfort the afflicted, and help those who suffer, we do so depending on Christ, not on our own strength.
exp.11:20:
This verse continues the story of seven brothers. The second brother married the widow of the first, and he too died without leaving children. The same thing happened with the third. The word "seed" means offspring, that is, children. To "take" the woman means to marry her.

The ones speaking are the Sadducees, a religious group that did not believe in the resurrection. They approach Jesus with this case in order to make him look foolish. They rely on the law of Moses about a brother marrying the widow, which was meant to keep the name of the dead man from being lost. Jesus will answer that they do not truly know the Scriptures or the power of God.

For today: sometimes we ask questions not to seek the truth, but to defend what we already think. Let us come to the Bible with humility, willing for God to correct our ideas and enlarge our faith.
exp.14:30:
This verse shows the religious leaders mocking Jesus while he is on the cross. The word translated here as "mocking" means jeering at someone with contempt, though this sentence explains a source-language term, so I will rewrite it: the verse says the chief priests were mocking, speaking among themselves with the scribes. The chief priests were the principal priests, and the scribes were the teachers of the law. They said to one another: "He saved others; himself he cannot save."

These are the religious leaders who wanted to see Jesus condemned. Earlier, the people passing by had also mocked him. Without meaning to, they admit that Jesus saved others, but they do not understand that he stays on the cross out of love, to save many.

For today: sometimes love costs something and does not look like success. When you serve or forgive and others do not understand, remember that Jesus was also misunderstood. Ask God for strength to love without depending on the approval of others.
exp.13:35:
Jesus prays to God calling him "Abba, Father," a very close and familiar word, like saying "daddy." He acknowledges that God can do all things and asks him to take away from him this cup, meaning the suffering that awaits him. But he ends by surrendering: let what God wills happen, not what he himself desires.

Jesus is in Gethsemane, shortly before being arrested. He has just said that his soul is very sorrowful, even to death. The disciples are nearby, but they fall asleep. Many understand that the "cup" refers to the cross and what it involved; the text does not explain further details.

You can be honest with God about your fear or your pain, as Jesus was. And then, with the confidence of a child, you can say: "Not what I will, but what you will." Praying this way is not giving up reluctantly, but trusting in a good Father.
exp.12:9:
It says that before the final events arrive, the good news must be proclaimed to all nations. Here "must" means it is necessary and has to happen. "Nations" means peoples or nations, and "first" indicates that this happens before the end.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he warns them about wars, earthquakes, and persecutions. He tells them that these things are only the beginning of sorrows. In the middle of trials, their testimony before rulers will become an opportunity to make the message known. Christians understand in different ways when and how this will be fulfilled.

For today: when the news or our difficulties frighten us, let us remember that God continues working so that his message reaches everyone. We can share the gospel with courage and trust that the Holy Spirit will help us speak.
exp.11:24:
Jesus says that when the dead rise, there will be no marriage: no men marrying and no women being given in marriage. They will be "as the angels which are in heaven." Note: it does not say they become angels, but that they resemble them in not marrying.

The phrases "shall rise" and "are given in marriage" are older forms of wording; today we would say "rise" and "are given in marriage."

Jesus is speaking with the Sadducees, a group that denied the resurrection. They brought him the case of a woman who married seven brothers, one after another, to mock that belief. Jesus answers that their error comes from not understanding the Scriptures or the power of God.

For today: trust that what God prepares is greater than what we imagine. Live your relationships with love, but do not forget that your final hope is in God.
exp.7:8:
This verse says that about four thousand people ate and that Jesus sent them away, meaning he let them go home. The word "sent them away" does not mean he drove them off; it means he dismissed them calmly after caring for them. The verse also mentions large baskets, and the explanation describes them as big baskets woven from wicker or palm.

Here the one acting is Jesus, and Mark is the one telling the story. A crowd had followed him for several days and had nothing to eat. Jesus felt compassion, broke the bread and the few small fish, and there was enough for everyone, with seven baskets left over. Right after this, the Pharisees ask him for a sign, even though they had already seen a miracle.

For today: God cares for our real needs, even when what we have seems small. Place what you have in his hands and trust that he will provide, without demanding further proof.
exp.15:12:
They told the others about it, but the others did not believe them either.

Mark tells here how Jesus' followers reacted to the news of his resurrection. First Mary Magdalene had told them, and they did not believe her. Now two disciples bear witness, and again there is doubt. Mark writes this honestly: the first witnesses did not come to belief easily. Afterward Jesus himself rebukes them for their unbelief and sends them out to preach.

For today: if you have doubts, do not hide from God. Jesus did not reject his doubting disciples; he sought them out and transformed them. Bring your questions to him honestly, and also listen to the testimony of other believers.
exp.5:8:
It says the disciples could wear sandals, that is, simple footwear tied to the foot, but they were not to take two tunics, that is, one spare set of the clothing worn close to the body. The archaic forms of the verbs in the source wording are dropped here, since the reader's verse uses "be shod" and "put on" instead.

Jesus speaks to the twelve before sending them out two by two to proclaim his message. He asks them to travel light, without extra supplies, so that they depend on God and on the hospitality of the people. Some think this also showed urgency; the text does not say so with certainty.

Today we might ask what things hinder us from serving God. Perhaps the point is not to give up everything, but to live simply, trust that God cares for us, and be ready to obey without so much baggage or excuses.
exp.4:1:
Mark tells us that Jesus stepped out of the boat, and immediately a man came to meet him from among the tombs. This man had an unclean spirit, which in the Bible means an evil spirit that enslaves and harms the person. "Immediately" is the word used here, and "came to meet him" means to go out to receive or run into someone.

Here it is not a character speaking, but Mark narrating. Jesus and his disciples have just crossed the Sea of Galilee, after calming the storm. They arrive in the region of the Gerasenes, a territory that was mostly non-Jewish. Tombs were places of death and uncleanness, and the account shows how far this man's ruin had reached.

For today: Jesus does not turn away from people whom others consider lost or beyond help. We can approach those who suffer with compassion, and trust that Christ can bring hope where it seems there is none.
exp.14:24:
Mark says it was "the third hour." Jews counted the hours from sunrise, so this would be around nine in the morning. "They crucified him" refers to the Roman soldiers who carried out Jesus' execution.

Here the narrator, Mark, tells the events simply. He notes the hour with care, like a precise memory of a day no one forgot. John 19:14 mentions a different hour during Pilate's trial, and scholars explain the difference in several ways, without full agreement. The central point is that Jesus did not die by accident, but at a real moment in history.

Today we can remember that Jesus truly entered into our suffering. If you are going through a hard day, pray with confidence: He knows what pain is, and He is close to you.
exp.2:29:
This verse explains why Jesus spoke so strongly about blaspheming against the Holy Spirit. Mark tells us that Jesus said this because they said, He hath an unclean spirit. Unclean means impure, evil. To blaspheme means to speak with contempt against God.

Mark tells how some scribes who had come down from Jerusalem were saying that Jesus cast out demons by the power of the prince of the demons. Jesus warns them that calling the work of the Holy Spirit a work of evil is something extremely serious. Many understand this to mean stubbornly rejecting the work of God and holding to that rejection until the end, and not a passing stumble.

Today, if you are afraid that you have committed this sin, notice that Jesus was speaking of a hardened heart. Keep your heart humble, and when God is at work, do not call it evil; draw near to Him with confidence and repentance.
exp.12:35:
This verse says that the master of the house may return at any time, and if he arrives suddenly, he must not find his servants asleep. "Coming" is the plain word for the return, and "find" means to come upon them. Here "asleep" speaks of carelessness, not only of physical sleep.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, shortly before his arrest. He teaches them about staying alert through this parable. The man who travels is a picture of Jesus, and the servants with their tasks and the doorkeeper represent his followers. Christians understand this to refer to his return, a day no one knows.

For today: live with your eyes open, faithfully doing what God has entrusted to you. Today you can pray, serve someone, or correct something you have neglected, without waiting for tomorrow.
exp.0:36:
The disciples find Jesus after searching for him. "When they had found him" simply means that they found him, and "they say to him" is how the verse reads. They tell him that everyone is looking for him.

Simon Peter speaks, along with those who were with him. The day before, Jesus had healed many people in Capernaum, and the crowd wanted more. But Jesus had left early for a solitary place to pray. His answer, in the following verse, shows that he was not swayed by popularity: he decided to go to other towns to preach, because that was why he had come.

For today: before we respond to what everyone asks of us, it is good to set aside a moment to pray. In this way we can tell the difference between what seems urgent and what God is truly calling us to do.
exp.8:40:
It says that whoever does a small act of kindness, such as giving a cup of water to Jesus' disciples, and does it because they belong to Christ, will surely receive a reward. "Verily I say unto you" is a solemn way of affirming something; it means "I assure you." The reward is the prize or payment that God gives.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. John had just complained because he saw someone casting out demons in Jesus' name who was not part of the group of twelve. Jesus teaches them not to be jealous or exclusive, and to value those who help his people. Then he firmly warns against causing believers of simple faith to stumble.

For today: do not despise small acts. A simple help to a brother or sister in the faith, such as a meal, a visit, or a kind word, is valuable to God. And rejoice when others serve Christ, even if they are not from your church.
exp.9:34:
James (Jacobo) and John, the sons of Zebedee, come to Jesus and say to him, "Teacher, we want you to grant us whatever we ask." The phrase "we would" and "we shall desire" is the older form; today we would say "we want" and "we ask." It is like asking for a blank check before saying what they want.

Jesus had just announced for the third time that he would be handed over, mistreated and killed, and that he would rise again. Right after that, these two disciples ask for the places of honor beside him in his glory. This shows that they had not understood his message of suffering and service. Jesus answers them patiently, asking them what they want.

For today: before asking something of God, examine your heart. Are you seeking to be served or to serve? You can pray with sincerity, and ask him to align your desires with his.
exp.15:7:
The verse tells that the women went out quickly from the tomb, filled with trembling and amazement. They said nothing to anyone, because they were afraid. The words "fled" and "amazed" show a very strong fright, mixed with wonder at what they had seen and heard.

The one who speaks before is a young man dressed in white, who told them that Jesus had risen and charged them to tell the disciples and Peter. Here the Gospel of Mark ends in the oldest manuscripts; the verses that follow do not appear in them, and many scholars think they were added later. The accounts in Matthew, Luke and John show that the women did in fact report it later.

Fear can paralyze us before something from God, but it does not have the last word. Even when we doubt or tremble, God keeps moving forward with his work and can give us courage to tell what we have received.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that Jesus withdrew with his disciples toward the sea (the Sea of Galilee). There a great crowd followed him, coming from Galilee and from Judea.

Mark is the one telling the story. Just before this, Jesus healed a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees joined with the Herodians to plan his death. Jesus moves away from that conflict, but the people keep looking for him. The verses that follow show that they came from many other places, drawn by what he was doing.

For today: when there is opposition or tension, we do not always have to stay and fight. Jesus withdrew, yet he kept serving those who sought him. We can step away from conflicts with wisdom and keep doing good.
exp.9:10:
Jesus says that if a man "divorces" his wife (that is, he sends her away and breaks the marriage) and marries another, he commits adultery against her. Jesus considers that new marriage to seriously wound the first wife, because the first covenant remains valid before God.

Jesus speaks at home, alone with his disciples, who ask him again about what he had taught the Pharisees. There he had recalled that God joined man and woman together from the beginning. In that time a divorced woman was left very unprotected, and Jesus defends her dignity. Christians understand some details and particular cases of this subject in different ways.

For today: value your marriage as a serious covenant and care for your spouse with faithfulness and respect. If you have gone through a divorce, remember that God offers forgiveness and comfort; seek support in a church or a trusted counselor.
exp.9:44:
This verse says that Jesus, called "the Son of man," did not come into the world to be served by others, but to serve others. Moreover, he came to give his life as a ransom for many. A ransom was the price paid to free a slave or a prisoner. Here "not even" works like "also": not even he came to be served.

Jesus is speaking with his disciples. James and John had just asked him for the places of greatest honor, and the other ten became angry. Jesus teaches them that among them, greatness is not measured by ruling, but by serving. He himself is the example. Shortly afterward he serves Bartimaeus, a blind beggar.

Today we can ask ourselves: "Whom can I serve this week without expecting recognition?" It might be helping at home, listening to someone, or supporting the church, remembering that Jesus served us first.
exp.0:43:
