Jesus tells the man he has just healed: "See that you say nothing to anyone. Instead, go, show yourself to the priest, and offer for your cleansing what Moses commanded, as a testimony to them." The word "cleansing" refers to being declared clean after leprosy.

Jesus speaks just after healing a leper. According to the law of Moses (Leviticus 14), only the priest could declare someone clean and allow them to return to the community. That is why Jesus sends him there. Why he asked for silence is not known for certain; some think he wanted to avoid crowds who sought only miracles. The man did not obey, and Jesus had to stay in deserted places.

For today: obeying God in simple things matters more than doing what seems best to us. That man wanted to help by telling the news, but obedience would have better honored what Jesus asked.
exp.3:15:
He says that another group of people is like the seed that falls on stony ground, that is, on soil with little earth and many rocks. These people hear the word of God and immediately receive it with joy. Stony ground is land full of rocks, and joy means happiness.

Jesus is speaking and explaining to his disciples the parable of the sower. The sower represents the one who shares God's message, and the different kinds of ground show how each heart responds. The next verse makes clear that this initial joy has no root and does not endure hardship.

For today: being moved by the word of God is good, but it is not enough. We can put down roots by reading the Bible faithfully, praying, and seeking a Christian community that walks with us. That way, when trials come, our faith will not depend only on what we feel.
exp.5:47:
This verse tells that Jesus saw from the shore his disciples worn out from rowing, because the wind was blowing against them. Around the fourth watch of the night (between three and six in the morning, according to the Roman way of counting the night), Jesus went toward them walking on the sea. "Toiling in rowing" means rowing with great effort. "Would have passed by them" can be understood as meaning that he was going to pass them by; commentators explain it in several ways.

Here the narrator is Mark. Jesus had just sent away the crowd he fed with the bread and the fish, and he had gone off alone to pray. The disciples were in the boat, and although Jesus was far away, he saw them and knew their difficulty.

For today: when you feel you are struggling against the wind and are exhausted, remember that Jesus sees you even when you do not notice it. Pray with confidence and keep doing what is yours to do, trusting that he will come near in time.
exp.7:28:
Jesus now asks his disciples what they themselves think of him. The word "you" here refers to them, those who followed him closely. Peter answers: "You are the Christ." "Christ" is a Greek word that means "the Anointed One," the same as "Messiah" in Hebrew: the King God promised to his people.

Jesus was with his disciples near Caesarea Philippi. First he asked them what people were saying, and the answers were good but incomplete: John the Baptist, Elijah, a prophet. Then he asked for their own answer. Peter speaks and confesses who Jesus is. Right after this, Jesus tells them that he will suffer and die, and that he will rise again. In this way he shows them what kind of Messiah he is.

It is not enough to repeat what others say about Jesus. Today he also asks us personally: "But whom do you say that I am?" Take a moment to answer him honestly in prayer.
exp.14:22:
It says they offered Jesus wine mixed with myrrh, a bitter, aromatic resin, and that he did not take it. Many understand that this mixture was meant to ease the pain, although the Bible does not explain this in detail.

Mark, who is narrating, describes the moment just before the crucifixion, at Golgotha. Some think the drink was a gesture of compassion; others think it was part of the usual treatment of the condemned. We do not know for certain who offered it. What is clear is that Jesus refused it. Many believe he wanted to face the cross with full awareness, although the text does not give the reason.

For today: Jesus did not run away from the suffering he had accepted out of love for us. When you face something difficult, ask God for clarity and strength not to avoid it, but to go through it trusting that he goes with you.
exp.5:6:
He called the twelve to him and began to send them out two by two, and he gave them authority over the unclean spirits, that is, the evil spirits that harmed people.

Mark tells this right after the people in Nazareth did not believe in Jesus, and he marveled at their unbelief. Even so, Jesus kept teaching in the villages, and now he multiplies his work by sending out the twelve. He is the one who speaks and acts; they go with the authority he gives them, not with their own. The text does not say why he sent them two by two, though many think it was to support one another and to give a firmer witness.

For today: do not serve alone or by your own strength. Look for someone to walk with you in what God entrusts to you, and trust that he is the one who gives the ability.
exp.13:16:
This verse says that, when evening came, Jesus arrived at the prepared place and gathered with his twelve disciples. The phrase "when evening came" means at nightfall, when the day of the Passover was beginning according to the Jewish way of counting time.

Mark tells this as part of the account of Jesus' final days. His disciples had already prepared the Passover supper, which remembered Israel's deliverance from Egypt. Jesus arrives with the twelve, and soon he will tell them that one of them will betray him. Mark calmly presents a scene that will soon be filled with sorrow.

For today: Jesus sought out the table and the company of his own, even knowing what was coming. We can follow his example by making time to be with other believers, to share a meal and to pray, especially before difficult trials.
exp.2:21:
The explanation says that some teachers of the law, called scribes, came down from Jerusalem and accused Jesus. They claimed that he had Beelzebub, a name used for the chief of the demons, and that by the power of that chief he drove out the other demons. The phrase "casteth he out" means that he drove them out of people.

Mark tells us that Jesus was surrounded by crowds, with no time even to eat. His relatives thought he had lost his mind. Now religious leaders arrive from the capital, with authority, and they cannot deny the miracles, so they look for another explanation to take away his credit. Jesus answers at once with a logical question: a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand.

Today we can ask ourselves whether, when something does not fit our ideas, we humbly recognize the good that God does, or whether we dismiss it out of pride or prejuice. Let us pray for an open heart to see the work of God.
exp.13:8:
Jesus says that wherever the gospel is preached anywhere in the world, what this woman did will also be told, so that she will be remembered. The phrase "Verily I say unto you" means "I assure you." The words that would be translated as "shall be spoken of for a memorial of her" mean that her act will be remembered always.

Jesus speaks in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper. A woman has just poured a very expensive perfume over his head, and some people criticized her for the waste. Jesus defends her: she did what she could and, without knowing it, prepared his body for burial. Right after this, Judas goes to betray him, and the contrast is strong.

God values sincere love, even when others see it as excessive. Today we can offer Jesus the best we have, with humility, without expecting applause. A simple act of love done for Him is never lost.
exp.5:24:
She returned quickly to King Herod and made her request. "Quickly" means in a hurry, right away. She did not want to wait: she demanded, "at once," the head of John the Baptist, and that it be given to her on a platter.

Here the young woman speaks, following the advice of her mother, Herodias. John had told Herod that it was not lawful for him to have his brother's wife, and Herodias held a grudge against him. Herod, in the middle of a banquet, had made a rash oath, and she seized the moment to ask for that death.

For today: let us guard our words and promises, especially when we are surrounded by applause or pressure. A commitment made without thinking can drag us into doing wrong. Let us ask God for the courage to speak the truth, as John did, and for the wisdom not to let pride or the opinions of others lead us to decide badly.
exp.0:35:
Simon Peter, along with those who were with him, went after Jesus. The word "followed" here means that they set out to look for him, perhaps in a hurry, because Jesus had gone away alone. It is a short phrase, but it shows that they missed him when they could not find him.

Mark tells this after a day full of healings and the casting out of demons in Capernaum. Jesus got up very early to pray in a quiet place. The narrator is Mark, and he wants to show Jesus' pattern: prayer, then service. The disciples find him and tell him that everyone is looking for him, but Jesus decides to go to other towns to preach.

For today: before you attend to the demands of the day, look for a moment alone with God. There, what is important becomes clear and direction is received, even when others expect something different from you.
exp.5:18:
It says that Herodias was lying in wait for John the Baptist, that is, she was waiting for the right moment to harm him. She wanted to kill him, but she could not. The explanation about the two words quoted from the source wording is removed, since the reader's verse does not contain them.

Here the narrator, Mark, speaks. John had told Herod that it was not lawful, or permitted, for him to have his brother's wife. This left Herodias deeply resentful. For this reason Herod had John put in prison. Even so, the following text explains that Herod feared John, respected him and listened to him, and this held back her plan for a time.

For today: when someone tells us an uncomfortable truth, we can respond with anger or with humility. Let us ask God for a heart willing to receive correction, without holding a grudge against the one who speaks to us sincerely.
exp.4:23:
Jesus went with Jairo, and a large crowd followed him. The crowd pressed in around him so tightly that people nearly pushed and squeezed against him. Jesus responded at once to the plea of that father.

Here the narrator of the Gospel speaks. Jairo was a leader of the synagogue, and he humbled himself at Jesus' feet, asking for desperate help for his daughter who was dying. Jesus makes no excuses and does not delay; he goes with him. But the road is full of people, and this prepares what follows: the sick woman who will touch his cloak in the middle of the crowd.

For today: Jesus allows himself to be interrupted and attends to people's needs, even in the middle of the throng. When you carry a heavy burden, come to him with confidence, as Jairo did. And when others need you, try to keep a heart ready to walk alongside them.
exp.3:16:
Some people receive the word with joy, but they do not put down roots within themselves. Their faith lasts only a short while. When affliction (suffering) or persecution comes because of the word, they quickly stumble and fall away from the faith.

Jesus explains the parable of the sower to his disciples. The seed is the word, and the different kinds of ground represent the ways people receive it. Here he speaks of the rocky ground, where the soil is shallow and does not allow deep roots to grow.

For today: it is not enough to be moved emotionally when we hear the word. It is wise to put down roots through steady reading of the Bible, prayer, and fellowship with other believers, so that when difficulties come, our faith does not wither but remains firm.
exp.10:17:
Mark reports that the scribes and the chief priests heard about what Jesus had done and said in the temple. They were looking for a way to kill him. "Sought" means they were trying to do it, and his "teaching" is what he taught. They feared him because all the people were astonished at what he taught.

Mark is the narrator. Jesus had just driven the sellers out of the temple and quoted the Scriptures: the temple was to be a house of prayer for all nations. The religious leaders were losing authority and influence, and that is why they reacted with violence. Their fear was of the people, not of God.

For today: when the truth of Jesus makes us uncomfortable, we can harden ourselves or let it correct us. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that loves his will more than our own comfort or reputation.
exp.6:18:
Jesus explains that food does not reach the heart, meaning the deepest part of a person, but goes into the stomach, and then the body eliminates it. "Belly" refers to the stomach and intestines; "goeth out into the draught" means it goes out of the body. "Meats" are foods. The last phrase, "purging all meats," is added by Mark as a comment: Jesus was declaring all foods clean.

Jesus speaks privately with his disciples, who did not understand his earlier teaching. The Pharisees had criticized them for eating without performing the ritual washings. Jesus clarifies that what defiles a person is not what is external, but what comes out of the heart.

For today: it is not enough to take care of religious appearances. We can ask God to examine our hearts and change our thoughts, words, and desires, because that is where who we really are is decided.
exp.9:1:
Mark says that some Pharisees came to Jesus to test him. They asked him whether it was lawful for a husband to divorce his wife. To divorce means to send her away, end the marriage, and put her out of the home. Here, to test him means to examine him or set a trap for him, not to lead him into wrongdoing.

Jesus was in Judea and across the Jordan, teaching the people as he usually did. The Pharisees were teachers of the law who often questioned Jesus. Their question was meant to make him say something he would regret. Scholars discuss what political or religious consequences his answer might have had, but the text only says they wanted to test him. Jesus answers by asking them what Moses commanded.

For today: when we have hard questions about the Bible, let us ask them with a sincere desire to learn and obey, not to win an argument. On the subject of marriage, let us first turn humbly to what God says.
exp.14:10:
The chief priests, the leading religious figures, persuaded and stirred up the crowd so that they would ask for Barabbas to be set free instead of Jesus. To "stir up" means to push or encourage someone to act; the chief priests were the most senior priests.

Pilate, the Roman governor, had just offered to release Jesus, because he could see that they had handed him over out of envy. It was the custom at the feast to free a prisoner, and Barabbas was a man held for an uprising and a murder. Mark shows how the pressure of the leaders changed the mood of the people.

For today: Before following the majority or an influential voice, it is wise to stop, think, and pray. Crowds can be wrong, and I must seek the truth honestly, without letting envy or the pressure of others carry me along.
exp.12:10:
Jesus says that when his followers are arrested and handed over to the authorities, they should not worry beforehand about preparing their defense. The word "premeditate" in the verse means to plan or think something out in advance. In that moment, the Holy Spirit will give them what to say, and it is the Spirit who will speak through them.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he warns them about hard times before the end. He tells them they will be beaten and brought before rulers because of him. Those trials would also be an opportunity to bear witness to the gospel. Some understand this as a promise for specific moments of persecution, not for every speech.

For today: when you face pressure or mockery because of your faith, trust that God is with you. Pray, remain faithful, and do not freeze up from fear of not knowing what to say.
exp.12:24:
The explanation says that the stars will fall from heaven and that the "powers" of the heavens will be shaken. "Powers" here refers to the forces or powers of the heavens. "Shaken" means moved with great force. It is language describing a great upheaval throughout the cosmos.

Jesus speaks on the Mount of Olives with his disciples. They had asked him about the future of the temple and the signs of the last times. Jesus uses images that the prophets also used to speak of judgment and the end. Some believe these are literal events; others, that they are symbolic language. What is clear is what follows: the Son of Man will come with power and glory, and will gather his own.

For today: when the world seems unstable, we can live with calm and alertness, trusting that Christ has the final word and cares for his own.
exp.0:20:
It says that Jesus and his first disciples arrived in Capernaum, a town by the Sea of Galilee. When the Sabbath came, which was the day of rest for the Jews, Jesus went into the synagogue and began to teach. The word translated "straightway" is very common in Mark and means "immediately" or "at once." The synagogue was the place where the Jewish community gathered to pray and to hear the Scriptures.

Here the narrator, Mark, speaks, telling how the ministry of Jesus began. He had just called Peter, Andrew, James and John. Now he takes them with him and shows them what his work is like. What follows shows that the people were astonished, because he taught with an authority unlike that of the scribes.

For today: Jesus had the habit of meeting with the community of faith and teaching the Word. We can seek out, with steady commitment, a place where we hear the Scriptures together with others, and come with an open heart to whatever God wants to say to us.
exp.2:10:
This verse says that when the evil spirits saw Jesus, they fell down before him and cried out that he was the Son of God. The words "unclean" and "fell down" in the earlier wording are explained here by their plain sense: "unclean" meaning the spirits were impure, and "fell down" meaning they bowed low to the ground. [Note: the sentence explaining these two words is rewritten to refer to "unclean spirits" and "fell down," which appear in the verse.]

Mark tells this while great crowds were coming to Jesus to be healed. The evil spirits recognize his identity and authority, but they do not speak out of faith or love. For this reason, in the next verse, Jesus firmly orders them not to make him known. Many interpret that he did not want a testimony from those voices, nor for his mission to be misunderstood before its time.

For today: it is not enough to know who Jesus is; we must trust in him and follow him. We can ask him that our faith be not only correct information, but a sincere surrender of our lives.
exp.11:38:
This verse continues Jesus' warning about the scribes. He says they seek the "chief seats" in the synagogues, that is, the places of honor, and the "uppermost rooms" at feasts, meaning the best places at banquets. The feasts mentioned here refer to important, festive meals.

Jesus speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, teaching a crowd that listened to him gladly. He warns against teachers of the law who sought prestige and public recognition. What is serious, according to the verses that follow, is that they combined that vanity with injustice toward the most vulnerable, such as widows, and with an outward show of religiousness.

For today: examine your motives when you serve. Ask yourself whether you are looking to be seen and admired, or whether you truly want to honor God and help others. A good step is to do some simple service without anyone finding out.
exp.15:3:
Mark tells us that the women looked up and saw that the stone had already been rolled away to one side. He says it was "very great." The word about the stone being moved aside is the one that matters here. Where the explanation says "removed" or "rolled," the reader's verse says "rolled away," so I will use that wording.

Mark tells what happened early on the Sunday. The women were going to Jesus's tomb and wondering how they would move that huge stone. When they arrived, the problem had already been taken care of, without anything they did. The text does not say here who moved it; the account that follows shows that the tomb was open and empty.

We often worry about obstacles that seem impossible. The women kept walking despite their doubt, and they found that God had already acted. Take the step of obedience that you can take today, and trust that God can open paths you cannot see.
exp.12:19:
Jesus says that God set a limit on those days of great suffering. If he had not shortened them, no one would survive. The phrase "no flesh" means no human being. And he shortened them for the sake of the chosen ones, that is, those who belong to God.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives and warns them about difficult times. Many think he is first referring to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70, while others also see a future fulfillment. Christians understand this in several ways.

For today: in the midst of distress, remember that God is still in control and that the suffering will not last forever. Rest in his care, stay alert, and do not be carried away by voices that promise easy answers.
exp.5:45:
He sent the crowd away, and then he went off alone up the mountain to pray. "Sent away" here means that he sent them home. "Went" is the plain word we use today, and the explanation's old spelling needs no mention.

Mark tells this right after Jesus fed five thousand people. He himself had told his disciples to cross the lake by boat while he was sending the people away. Mark does not explain why Jesus prayed, but John 6:15 says the people wanted to make him king, and some think that influenced him. That is an interpretation, not something Mark states here.

After a day full of people and miracles, Jesus looked for a moment alone with the Father. Today too we can set aside a quiet time, even a brief one, to pray before facing what comes next.
exp.9:19:
Here a man answers Jesus: "Master, all these have I observed from my youth." The word "mocedad" is an old way of saying youth. He claims he has obeyed the commandments Jesus has just mentioned since he was young.

The one speaking is the man who came to Jesus asking how to inherit eternal life. Jesus reminded him of the commandments, and he responds with sincerity and confidence. Then Jesus looks at him with love and points out what he still lacks: letting go of his riches and following him. The text does not say that his answer was false, but that it was not enough to reveal what he had in his heart.

Today we can ask ourselves honestly: beyond doing what is right, is there something I find hard to surrender to Jesus? He looks at us with love, and invites us to follow him with all our heart.
exp.9:11:
The verse says that if a woman leaves her husband (to divorce means to formally reject or send him away) and marries another man, she commits adultery. The word "adultery" refers to breaking the faithfulness of marriage. Jesus applies the same standard to the man and to the woman.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples, now at home, after the Pharisees had tested him about divorce. In that time, Jewish law and custom gave a man much greater ease in sending away his wife. Jesus, by contrast, places both on the same level and reminds them that God designed marriage as a serious and lasting union. Some believers debate how this applies in cases of abuse or abandonment; the text does not detail these.

Today we can value marriage as a sacred commitment and treat our spouse with faithfulness, respect and patience, asking God for help to forgive and to be reconciled.
exp.8:3:
This verse says that, on the mountain, Elijah and Moses appeared before the three disciples, and that they were talking with Jesus. The word "appeared" means that they suddenly became visible. Jesus was already transfigured, with his clothes very white.

Mark tells the scene as Peter, James, and John saw it. Moses represents the Law and Elijah the prophets, so their presence shows that all of Scripture points to Jesus. Mark does not say here what they were talking about; Luke 9:31 mentions that they spoke of his departure. Peter, frightened, proposes making three shelters, but he did not really know what he was saying.

For today: when you read the Bible, look for Jesus in it. All of Scripture, from the Law to the prophets, leads us to Him. Before speaking with fear or haste, as Peter did, first listen to Him.
exp.6:0:
This verse tells us that the Pharisees and some of the scribes gathered around Jesus. They were not from the region: they had come from Jerusalem. The phrase "came together unto him" in the verse above means that they drew near to Jesus, and the scribes were the teachers and interpreters of the Law.

Here it is not Jesus who speaks, but the narrator, Mark. Jerusalem was the religious center of the Jewish people, so the arrival of these men suggests that they came to examine or watch over Jesus. The following verses show that they soon question him because his disciples ate without observing a washing custom that came from the tradition of the elders.

For today: before judging others, let us examine our attitude. One can go to see Jesus with a humble heart that wants to learn, or with a desire to criticize. Let us ask God for an open heart.
exp.12:12:
Jesus says that his followers will be hated by everyone because of his name, that is, because they belong to him. But he promises that whoever keeps going, staying firm and not giving up, until the end will be saved. The word "hated" here means hated or rejected.

Jesus speaks to four disciples on the Mount of Olives, and he prepares them for hard times. He warns them of persecution, betrayal by family members, and trials, but he also assures them that the Holy Spirit will be with them. Some understand "the end" as the end of life or of the trial, and others as the end of the age; Christians have interpreted it in several ways.

Today, if people criticize you or leave you out because you follow Christ, do not lose heart. Ask the Holy Spirit for strength, and take one more faithful step today, trusting that God sustains those who belong to him.
exp.13:54:
This verse says that the chief priests and the whole council (the Sanhedrin, the Jewish court) were looking for evidence against Jesus so they could have him put to death. They wanted to bring about his execution. But they were not finding any valid testimony.

The narrator, Mark, describes the night of the trial before the high priest. The leaders had already decided the outcome and were only looking for an excuse. The verses that follow explain that many gave false statements, but their accounts contradicted each other. Even an unjust trial could not make its accusations stand. Mark also presents Jesus as innocent.

For today: when someone has already decided what they want to believe, they look for reasons that support it instead of looking for the truth. Let us ask God for an honest and just heart, one that listens with humility and does not use lies to get its own way.
exp.7:35:
Jesus asks what good it does a person to gain the whole world if in the end they lose their soul. The words "gain" and "profit" are what the reader sees in the verse, so the sentence explaining the old wording is rewritten: "gain" means to get or obtain, and "profit" means to be of use or benefit. The word "soul" here can also be understood as life itself, that is, the whole person. No wealth or success can be compared with the worth of a life.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, after announcing that he will suffer and die. He explains that following him means denying oneself and carrying the cross. Some scholars emphasize eternal life, others the whole life of the person, but both see a serious warning.

Today we can ask ourselves what we are pursuing most strongly: money, fame, or comfort. Before an important decision, ask yourself whether it brings you closer to Christ or takes you further from him. Seek first what cannot be lost.
exp.2:9:
This verse explains why so many people sought out Jesus. He had healed many, and so those who were suffering from some illness rushed toward him, pressing forward to touch him. The word "plagues" in the verse means serious illnesses or ailments, and the phrase "pressed upon him" describes a crowd surging toward him.

Mark is the narrator. He explains why Jesus asked his disciples to have a small boat ready: the crowd was coming from many places, even from distant regions, and could crush him. The reputation of his works had spread, and people were seeking him out with real and urgent need.

For today: people learned that Jesus could help, and they came to him without hesitation. We can do the same with our wounds and burdens, bringing them to him in prayer with confidence. But it is also worth seeking him himself, and not only his blessings.
exp.6:15:
He says that whoever has ears to hear should truly listen. Here, "hear" means more than simply perceiving sounds. It means paying attention and understanding. Jesus uses this phrase to invite people to think seriously about what he has just said.

Jesus speaks to the crowd after debating with the Pharisees about the traditions of washing hands and about foods. He teaches that what defiles a person is not what goes into the mouth, but what comes out of the heart. Later, at home, the disciples do not understand well and ask him to explain it. Some early manuscripts do not include this verse, which is why it does not appear in certain Bibles.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we listen to the Word only out of habit or with a real desire to change. Before judging others by what is external, let us ask God to examine our heart and our words.
exp.2:17:
Here the list of the twelve apostles that Jesus chose continues. Andrew, Philip, Bartholomew, Matthew, Thomas, James the son of Alphaeus, Thaddaeus, and Simon the Canaanite are named. The word "Canaanite" does not refer to the town of Cana, but probably means "zealous" or "Zealot," a name tied to a group with great fervor for their nation. Some scholars debate this.

Mark tells here how Jesus formed his closest group. Jesus does not speak in this verse; the narrator, Mark, lists those chosen to be with Jesus and sent out to preach. They were men very different from one another: fishermen, a tax collector, and someone of zealous spirit.

Jesus calls ordinary and different people. Today too he invites us to serve him together, regardless of our past or character. Ask yourself how you can value and work with those who are different from you in your church.
exp.1:7:
This verse says that Jesus perceived, "in his spirit," what the scribes were thinking silently. He asked them a question: "Why reason ye these things in your hearts?" The word "immediately" means "at once," and "reason" is "think" in modern usage. In the Bible, the "heart" is the center of thought and decision.

Jesus is in a house in Capernaum, and four men have lowered a paralyzed man through the roof. Jesus told him that his sins were forgiven. The scribes thought this was blasphemy, because only God forgives sins. Jesus responds to what they did not say out loud, and so he shows that his authority is real.

For today: God knows what we think and feel even when we do not say it. Instead of hiding our doubts, we can bring them to him honestly in prayer, and ask him to give us a humble heart willing to believe.
exp.13:49:
This verse says that when Jesus was arrested, all his disciples abandoned him and ran away. The word "forsook" means leaving him alone, and "fled" means they escaped out of fear.

Mark, the narrator, tells the scene in the garden of Gethsemane. Jesus had just said that he was not a thief and that the Scriptures had to be fulfilled. Shortly before, Peter and the others had promised not to abandon him (Mark 14:31). Jesus had already warned them that they would be scattered (Mark 14:27), and here what he said comes true.

For today: we can all fail when we feel afraid, even those who truly love Jesus. We can acknowledge our weakness with humility, ask him for strength, and remember that he does not reject us for having failed, but seeks us out to restore us, as he did with his disciples.
exp.4:39:
They laughed at Jesus when he said the girl was only sleeping. Then Jesus sent out everyone who was causing a disturbance. He took the girl's father, her mother, and the disciples who were with him, and went into the room where the girl was lying.

Mocking him means laughing at him with scorn. Sending them out means he made them leave the house.

The father, Jairus, was a leader of the synagogue, and he had asked Jesus to help his daughter. Meanwhile, the house was full of weeping. Jesus had said that the girl was "sleeping," and the people, knowing she was dead, laughed. He did not act to impress anyone, but cared for the faith and grief of the family.

For today: when others mock your hope in God, do not lose heart. Jesus does not need applause. Come to him with your pain, in trust and in quiet, and let him do his work.
exp.9:49:
He says that the blind man, on hearing that Jesus was calling him, threw off his cloak, leaped to his feet and went to Jesus. The word for throwing off means to cast something away. The cloak was his outer garment, the loose piece of clothing he wore over everything else.

Mark tells us what Bartimaeus, a blind beggar, did. He kept crying out for mercy while the people told him to be quiet. Jesus stopped and had him called. Some think the cloak was in his way and slowed him down; others see in it a gesture of leaving behind his life as a beggar. The text does not explain this, so these are only interpretations.

When Jesus calls you, respond without delay. Perhaps you should let go of something that holds you back, such as fear, a habit, or a false sense of security, so that you can come to Him with confidence and simplicity.
exp.3:30:
Jesus compares the kingdom of God to a grain of mustard seed. He says that, when it is sown in the ground, it is the smallest of all the seeds. Here the point is size: something that begins almost unseen.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd, beside the sea, teaching with parables, which are comparisons drawn from everyday life. He has just explained how the seed grows and bears fruit. Now he wants to show that the kingdom of God usually begins in a small and humble way. The verses that follow say that this seed becomes a large plant. Scholars debate whether the phrase "the smallest" is a popular expression of his time or an exact botanical fact, but the central idea is clear.

For today: do not despise small beginnings. An act of kindness, a prayer, or a word of faith may seem like very little, but God knows how to make it grow.
exp.5:14:
Some people said he was Elijah. Others said he was a prophet, or one of the prophets of long ago. The phrase "or as one of the prophets" means "one like the prophets of old."

These were ordinary people speaking, while Jesus' fame kept growing because of his miracles and because he had sent out the twelve disciples. Herod thought he was John the Baptist risen from the dead, and others had their own ideas. Everyone sensed that something extraordinary was happening, but none of them yet saw that Jesus was the Messiah, the Son of God. Later Jesus himself will ask his disciples who they believe he is.

For today: it is not enough to have a respectful opinion about Jesus, such as saying he was a good teacher. Ask yourself honestly: "Who is Jesus to me?" Read it in the Gospels and let him answer you himself.
exp.3:24:
What it says: Jesus teaches that whoever has something will receive more, and whoever does not have will lose even the little they seem to have. "Has" here refers to what a person has received from God's teaching and how they receive it. "Will be taken away" means they will lose it.

Context: Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples after the parable of the sower. He has just asked them to listen carefully and to pay attention to what they hear. Many understand "has" to mean receiving the word with faith and obedience; whoever despises it loses it. Afterward, Jesus speaks of the kingdom growing like a seed.

For today: Listen to the Word of God with attention and put it into practice, even in small things. When what we understand is obeyed, God gives more understanding. If we ignore it, it fades away in us.
exp.11:36:
Jesus asks a simple question: if David, guided by the Holy Spirit, calls the Christ "Lord," how can the Christ be merely his son, that is, his descendant? The phrase "the common people" refers to ordinary folk, and "heard him gladly" means they listened to him with pleasure.

Jesus is teaching in the temple in Jerusalem, and he quotes Psalm 110. The scribes taught that the Messiah would be a son of David, which is true but incomplete. Jesus suggests that the Messiah is more than a human king: he is also Lord. He does not fully explain this here; he lets the people think it through. Right after, he warns against the proud scribes.

For today: listen to Jesus with a simple and open heart, as those people did. Do not be satisfied with knowing facts about him; acknowledge him as your Lord and let his word teach you every day.
exp.12:21:
Jesus warns that people will appear who claim to be the Christ (the Messiah) or prophets of God, but they will be false. They will perform signs and wonders, that is, miracles and astonishing things, in order to deceive people. The phrase that they would deceive even the elect, those who belong to God, shows that they will try to mislead even those who are God's own.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. He is explaining the difficulties that will come before his return, and he speaks of times of great distress. He wants them to be prepared, which is why he tells them that he has already told them everything. Interpreters differ on how much of this discourse refers to the destruction of Jerusalem and how much to the end of the age.

Today, do not be impressed simply because something seems miraculous or because a leader is charismatic. Compare what you hear with what Jesus taught in the Bible, and stay close to Him in prayer.
exp.14:35:
Here it is told that someone ran, dipped a sponge in vinegar, put it on the end of a reed, and held it up to Jesus so that he would drink. While doing so, he said: "Wait, let us see whether Elijah comes to take him down." "To take him down" means to take him down from the cross. The word "took" in the verse is an old form of "gave," and it is spelled differently today.

Vinegar was a sour and cheap drink. It is not known for certain whether the gesture was compassion, mockery, or both. Mark does not make it clear.

When someone suffers, others often misunderstand their pain. Today we can listen carefully, without mocking or rushing to judge, and offer simple and real help.
exp.5:19:
Herod feared John and respected him, because he knew that John was a righteous and holy man. The explanation says that "feared" here means that Herod held John in deep respect. "He held him in respect" can also be understood as meaning that Herod protected him or looked after him. Herod would listen to John gladly, even though John's words left him troubled, and he would even do some of the things John said.

Mark explains why Herodias wanted to kill John: John had said that it was not lawful for Herod to live with his brother's wife. Herod had imprisoned John, but something in him resisted putting him to death. In this way Mark prepares the account of the banquet, where that weakness will become evident.

We can hear the truth with pleasure and still not obey it. Listening to God is not enough; we must let his word change our decisions, even when it costs us.
exp.8:12:
Jesus says that Elijah has already come, and that they treated him however they wanted, just as it is written about him. The words "but" and "I tell you" are the ones he uses here, and the sentence about the first of those means that Jesus speaks of Elijah as someone who has already fulfilled his role, yet was mistreated.

Jesus speaks with Peter, James, and John as they come down from the mountain of the transfiguration. They ask why the scribes teach that Elijah must come first (Malachi 4:5). Jesus answers that this forerunner has already come. From the parallel in Matthew 17:13, it is understood that he refers to John the Baptist, whom Herod had put to death. Jesus connects him with his own coming suffering. How "as it is written" is fulfilled is not explained precisely, and it has been interpreted in different ways.

God sometimes works in ways we do not expect, and we do not always recognize them. Let us ask him for open eyes and a humble heart to receive his message, even when it comes simply or at a cost.
exp.2:22:
Jesus calls the people who were accusing him and speaks to them in parables, that is, in simple comparisons. He asks them a question: how can Satan cast out Satan? Put another way, does it make sense for evil to fight against itself?

Jesus is speaking. The scribes, teachers of the law who had come down from Jerusalem, were saying that he cast out demons by the power of Beelzebub, the ruler of the demons. Also, his family thought he was beside himself, that is, out of his mind. Jesus answers that accusation with clear reasoning.

For today: before judging what we do not understand, it is wise to think with humility and to look at the fruits. What sets people free and draws them closer to God deserves to be received with gratitude, not with hasty suspicion.
exp.13:4:
It says the perfume the woman poured out could have been sold for more than three hundred pence, and that the money could have been given to the poor. A penny was the normal pay for a day's work, so this was about a year's wages. The text says they "murmured against her," which means they criticized her angrily and in low voices. The perfume was "spikenard," a very expensive ointment.

Mark tells this in the house of Simon the leper, in Bethany, shortly before Jesus' death. Those speaking are some of those present, who saw the woman's gesture as a waste. Their concern for the poor seemed good, but Jesus defended the woman and called what she did a "good work."

For today: before criticizing another person's generosity or devotion, it is wise to stop and ask what is in their heart. We should help the poor, without forgetting to worship Jesus with sincere love.
exp.2:0:
This verse tells that Jesus went back into a synagogue, the place where the Jews gathered every Sabbath to pray and hear the Scriptures. There was a man there with a hand that was withered, meaning shrunken, with no strength or movement.

The phrase "again" shows that Jesus had already been in that place before.

Here the narrator, Mark, presents a brief scene before the conflict. The verses that follow say that some were watching Jesus to see whether he would heal on the Sabbath, so that they could accuse him. Thus the sick man stands in the middle of a tension between compassion and religious rules.

For today: do not walk past someone who suffers near you, not even in places that seem holy. Ask yourself whether your faith leads you to look with mercy and to do good, rather than to watch over or judge others.
exp.5:20:
This verse tells us that a convenient day arrived, that is, the moment Herodias had been waiting for. It was Herod's birthday, and he gave a supper for his lords (high officials), his captains (military commanders), and the chief men of Galilee (the important men of the region).

The one who narrates is Mark. Earlier he explained that Herodias hated John the Baptist because he had pointed out her marriage to Herod. She wanted to kill him, but Herod protected him, since he respected him. This banquet opens the door to the trap that will end in John's death.

For today: let us be watchful in settings where we lower our guard, such as celebrations or moments of pride. There a hasty decision can cause serious harm. Let us ask God for wisdom before we promise anything.
exp.5:10:
If in some place people do not receive the disciples or want to listen to them, the disciples are to leave and shake the dust off their feet as a sign against that place. Jesus adds that the punishment for that city will be harsher than the one for Sodom and Gomorrah.

The words "receive" and "listen" are rendered here in plain modern English; the sentence about the old wording is removed because the reader's verse does not contain it, and "testimony" is explained as a sign or warning.

Jesus speaks to the twelve apostles, whom he sends out two by two to proclaim repentance. Shaking off dust was a gesture that showed separation. Some understand it as a serious warning that rejecting the message has consequences. The Bible does not detail here what that judgment will be like.

For today: share the truth with love and without pressure. If someone does not want to listen, do not become bitter or discouraged. Keep going, trust God with that person, and look for those who are open.
exp.4:16:
The explanation says that the people of that region began to ask Jesus to leave their territory. The word "coasts" in the verse means the region or borders, and "pray" here means to ask earnestly.

The ones speaking are the inhabitants of the area of the Gerasenes. They had just seen the man who had been tormented before, now calm and clothed, and they had also heard about the loss of the pigs. The text says they were afraid. It does not fully explain their motives; it may have been fear of Jesus' power, concern over their financial loss, or both. What we do see is that they preferred distance rather than drawing near to Him.

For today: sometimes Jesus changes things that trouble us or cost us. Before asking Him to go away, it is good to ask ourselves what truly frightens us. We can hand that fear over to Him and trust that His work is for our good, as that healed man experienced.
exp.4:34:
While Jesus was still speaking with the woman he had healed, some people came from the house of Jairo, the ruler of the synagogue, the official in charge of the local synagogue. They told Jairo that his daughter had died. They asked, "Why bother the Teacher any further?" In other words, why keep troubling Jesus? To them, there was nothing more to be done.

The ones speaking are messengers or people from Jairo's household. He had asked Jesus to heal his sick daughter. The delay in attending to the woman seemed to have come too late. Jesus would answer right away: "Do not be afraid; only believe."

For today: when the news seems to close every door, do not let despair have the last word. Before giving up, bring your situation to Jesus and keep trusting in him, even when you do not understand what is going to happen.
exp.10:30:
This verse shows what the religious leaders were thinking while Jesus asked them a question. They reasoned among themselves: "If we say that John's baptism came from heaven, that is, from God, he will say: Why then did you not believe him?"

Jesus was in the temple, and the chief priests, the scribes, and the elders were asking him by what authority he did his works. He answered with another question about John the Baptist. They were not seeking the truth, but an answer that would protect them from looking bad.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are seeking the truth or only the most comfortable answer. Being honest with God means acknowledging what we already know, even when it makes us uncomfortable or asks us to change.
exp.5:34:
This verse says that it was already very late when the disciples approached Jesus. They told him the place was deserted, meaning there were no shops or houses nearby, and that the day was already ending. The phrase "far spent" means the afternoon was well advanced.

The ones speaking are the disciples. Jesus had been teaching a crowd that had followed him for hours, and he had felt compassion for them because they were like sheep without a shepherd. The disciples see a practical problem: the people are hungry and there is nowhere to buy food. They ask that the crowd be sent away. Jesus will answer with something unexpected: "You give them something to eat."

For today: when you see a need that seems bigger than your resources, do not stop at the problem. Bring it to Jesus and ask him what he wants you to do with the little you have.
exp.11:15:
Jesus receives the coin they bring him and asks whose face and writing are stamped on it. They answer that it belongs to Caesar. The old wording "whose" is the same question, and the "face" is the emperor's likeness, while the "writing" is the inscription around it.

Some Pharisees and Herodians want to trap Jesus with a question about paying the tax to Caesar. If he says yes, he would anger the people; if he says no, they would accuse him before Rome. Jesus, knowing their hypocrisy, uses the coin to answer them with simplicity and wisdom.

For today: fulfill your civic responsibilities with honesty, but remember that your whole life belongs to God, since you were made in his image. Ask yourself today: am I giving God first place?
exp.11:26:
Jesus says that God is not the God of the dead, but of the living. For this reason he declares that the Sadducees are greatly mistaken. The phrase "greatly err" in the verse above is the point being made here, meaning that they are quite wrong.

Jesus is speaking with the Sadducees, a group that denied the resurrection. They had put to him a difficult case about a woman married to seven brothers. Jesus answers them from the Scriptures: God revealed himself to Moses as the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, who had already died. Jesus understands that this relationship with God continues to live, and so he points toward the resurrection.

For today: if God is the God of the living, your life and your hope are secure in him, even in the face of death. Today you can trust God with your loved ones who died in the faith, and live without fear, knowing that your relationship with him does not end.
exp.14:14:
Pilate, the Roman governor, wanted to please the crowd. So he released Barabbas, a well-known prisoner, and handed Jesus over to be crucified. Before that, he ordered Jesus to be flogged. To "content" the people means to please them, to give them what they wanted. Releasing Barabbas means that Pilate set him free.

The narrator is Mark, who tells the story of Jesus' trial. Pilate had already asked what wrong Jesus had done, but the crowd, stirred up by the chief priests, kept shouting for him to be crucified. Mark shows that Pilate gave in to the pressure, even though he did not find a clear reason to condemn him.

For today: sometimes it is easier to please others than to do what is right. Before deciding something important, ask yourself whether you are seeking approval or seeking what is just. Jesus, who was handed over unjustly, gives us courage to act with integrity.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that everything that is now hidden will, sooner or later, come out into the open. To "manifest" means to make known, and to "uncover" means to take off the covering from something. Nothing will stay hidden forever.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd and to his disciples right after the parable of the sower. He has just spoken about the lamp, which is not lit to be covered up but set up high. Many understand that the message of the kingdom, which now seems veiled, will be revealed completely. Others add that it also applies to what is hidden in the heart. Both readings are possible.

Today we can live with sincerity, knowing that God sees everything. Furthermore, if we have received his word, let us not keep it hidden away: let it shine through our actions and words.
exp.14:7:
This verse tells how a crowd came before Pilate and began to ask him to do what he had always done. The phrase "to do as he had ever done unto them" means that he should release a prisoner, as he customarily did at the festival.

Mark recounts Jesus' trial before Pilate, the Roman governor. The crowd reminds him of a custom at the Passover: releasing a prisoner. Pilate knew that the chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy. The texts do not state clearly why the crowd asked for this, but the account shows how the pressure of the people influenced the outcome.

Today we might ask ourselves whether our decisions come from habit or from what others loudly demand. Before following the crowd, it is wise to stop, pray, and seek what is just and true.
exp.7:22:
This verse tells how Jesus took a blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. There, he spit on his eyes, put his hands on him, and asked whether he could see anything. A village is a small town. Spitting was a gesture that at that time was associated with healing.

This happens in Bethsaida. Some people bring the blind man and ask Jesus to touch him. Shortly before, Jesus had rebuked his disciples for not understanding. Mark is the only one who tells this healing in two steps. It is not known for certain why Jesus took him out of the town; some think he sought a more personal and quiet setting.

For today: Jesus treats each person with care and patience. If your faith or your understanding is growing slowly, do not be discouraged. He takes you by the hand and keeps working with you.
exp.1:15:
This verse tells how the scribes and Pharisees saw Jesus eating with tax collectors and sinners. The tax collectors worked for Rome, and many people looked down on them.

The scribes were teachers of the law, and the Pharisees were very strict about religious purity. For them, sitting at the table with people like this was a sign of approving of them. Jesus had just called Levi, a tax collector, and Levi held a meal in his house. Jesus replies right away that he came to call sinners.

Today, Jesus invites us to draw near with love to those others reject. Before judging someone, we can ask ourselves: would I treat them with the same grace with which Christ treated me?
exp.13:39:
He returned and found them sleeping again, Peter, James and John. Their eyes were heavy with sleep and weariness. When Jesus looked at them, they did not know what to say to him, probably out of shame.

This happens in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before Jesus was arrested. He was praying with deep anguish and had asked his friends to stay awake with him. Mark tells the story simply: they could not keep themselves awake. Jesus had already told them that the spirit is willing, but the flesh is weak.

For today: recognize your limits without making excuses for yourself. If you want to be faithful to God, make prayer a habit, and ask him for help in your moments of weakness. Jesus understands our frailty and continues to call us with patience.
exp.0:8:
In those days John was preaching, and Jesus came from Nazareth, a town in the region of Galilee, and John baptized him in the Jordan River.

Mark, the author, introduces Jesus here for the first time in his account. John had said that someone more powerful than he was coming after him. Now Jesus appears, simple and humble, among the people. Some scholars think he was baptized to identify himself with the people; the text gives no further explanation, which is why it is interpreted in different ways. What follows shows the Father's approval.

For today: Jesus began his path with humility, without seeking privileges. Today we can imitate him by taking the first step of obedience to God simply, without waiting for anyone's recognition.
exp.4:25:
This verse says that the woman with a flow of blood had suffered greatly at the hands of many doctors. She spent all her money seeking healing, but she did not get better; on the contrary, she kept getting worse. The verse's wording "was nothing bettered" means that the treatments did her no good at all, and "but rather grew worse" means that, instead of improving, her condition became worse.

Here Mark, the narrator of the Gospel, is speaking. Jesus was on his way to Jairo's house, surrounded by a crowd. Mark describes this woman's desperate situation to show that she no longer had any human way out. Her illness, moreover, probably kept her apart from social and religious life, according to the law of Moses (Leviticus 15), although Mark does not mention this directly.

For today: when you have exhausted your resources and your strength, do not give up or shut yourself away. Bring your need to Jesus honestly. He is not troubled by your desperation; there your hope can begin.
exp.0:27:
This verse says that the news about Jesus spread very quickly. "Immediately" means "right away," and "fame" means what people were saying about Him. It spread "throughout all the region round about Galilee," that is, to the territory surrounding that area.

Mark, who is telling the story, has just related that Jesus taught in the synagogue in Capernaum and drove an unclean spirit out of a man. The people were amazed at His authority. That amazement became conversation, and the conversation carried the news further. Mark thus shows how Jesus began to make Himself known at the start of His ministry.

For today: when God works in your life, do not keep it all in silence. Sharing simply what Jesus has done for you can awaken faith in others. No great speech is needed; it is enough to be honest and thankful.
exp.12:13:
Jesus says that when his disciples see the abomination of desolation spoken of by Daniel standing where it ought not, they must act quickly. The words "but" and "see" in the older wording are simply "but" and "see" in the verse your reader has, and "was" is "was." The word "desolation" means destruction or devastation. Those who are in Judea must flee to the mountains.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after announcing the destruction of the temple. He warns them of difficult times. Interpreters differ on exactly which event he has in mind: some think of the fall of Jerusalem in the year 70, others of a fulfillment still in the future, and others of both. What is clear is his call to be watchful.

For today: God asks us for discernment and prompt obedience. Ask him for wisdom to recognize spiritual dangers in time, and do not delay what you know you should do.
exp.5:2:
The people of Nazareth knew Jesus very well: they remembered him as the carpenter, the son of Mary, with brothers and sisters who lived there. That is why they were offended at him, that is, they stumbled and took offense, because they could not accept that someone so ordinary could have such wisdom and power.

The ones speaking are the neighbors of Nazareth, in the synagogue, on a Sabbath. They were amazed by his teaching, but their amazement turned into rejection because they saw him only from the familiar. Jesus answers that a prophet is little honored in his own country, and Mark says that he could not do many miracles there because of their lack of faith. Some debate whether the "brothers" were sons of Mary or close relatives; the Bible does not clarify this here.

For today: let us not dismiss God or people because they seem ordinary to us. God often works through simple means; let us ask him for a humble heart that is willing to believe.
exp.12:34:
Jesus says: "Watch," that is, stay awake and alert. The reason is that no one knows when the master of the house will return. The four times he mentions (evening, midnight, the cockcrowing, and morning) were the four watches into which the night was divided. Together they cover the whole night, so he could come at any moment.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, after telling them about difficult things that would come. With the parable of the man who travels and leaves his servants in charge, he teaches that his return is certain, but the date is not known. Each person has a task and must carry it out faithfully.

For today: live each day as if you were going to give an account to the Lord. Do your work honestly, care for your family, pray, and serve others, without anxiety about dates, but with a heart that is awake.
exp.6:6:
Jesus says that the worship of these people is of no use. "In vain" means "without value." "Honor me" means they praise or respect him. The problem is that they teach as if things that only people invented were commands from God.

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees and the scribes, who criticized him because his disciples ate without performing the ritual washing required by the tradition of the elders. Jesus answers them by quoting the prophet Isaiah: they speak well of God, but their heart is far away. He shows them that they placed their customs above what God commanded.

For today: check whether your faith is only habit or pretty words. Ask yourself whether what you practice comes from the Bible or from human habits, and ask God for a sincere heart that truly loves him.
exp.8:24:
This verse tells that Jesus saw the crowd running together and gathering around. Then he spoke with authority to the evil spirit, which he called the foul spirit, meaning unclean or impure. He called it a dumb and deaf spirit because the boy could neither speak nor hear. Jesus commanded it to come out and never enter him again.

Jesus speaks. He has just talked with the boy's father, who confessed: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." Jesus acts quickly, perhaps to avoid a spectacle, though the text does not say so. His word is enough, without rituals or effort. Afterward the boy lies as if dead, and Jesus lifts him up by the hand.

For today: you can come to Jesus with imperfect faith. If your trust is weak, tell him honestly what that father said: "Lord, I believe; help thou mine unbelief." He continues to listen and has authority over whatever oppresses you.
exp.14:26:
Mark tells us that Jesus was not crucified alone. Two robbers were crucified with him, one on his right hand and the other on his left, that is, one on each side.

Mark is the one telling the story, and he does it with a simple but powerful detail. Shortly before, the sign had read "The King of the Jews." So Jesus appears as king, yet surrounded by criminals. The next verse, which some early manuscripts add, recalls the prophecy of Isaiah 53:12: "he was numbered with the transgressors." In other words, Jesus was treated as one of the wrongdoers.

For today: Jesus placed himself beside those who were in shame and guilt. If you feel unworthy or far from God, remember that he was not ashamed to be in that place. You can draw near to him with sincerity, without pretending.
exp.8:21:
Here the father describes how serious his son's situation is. The spirit that torments him has thrown him many times into the fire and into the water, intending to kill him. The word "cast" means to throw, and the phrase "have compassion" is a plea for mercy on them. The father asks for help, but with doubt in his request: "if you can do anything."

The one speaking is the boy's father, who has spent years suffering alongside his son, since the boy was a child. He had already gone to Jesus' disciples earlier, and they could not help him. That is why his request comes out tired and uncertain. Jesus will answer by speaking about faith, and the man will cry out honestly: "I believe; help my unbelief."

For today: when your faith is mixed with weariness or doubt, do not pretend. Bring your need to Jesus just as it is, fears included, and ask him to strengthen your trust. He receives with compassion those who come to him with sincerity.
exp.12:18:
Jesus says that those days will bring suffering and distress greater than anything that has happened since God made the world, and that nothing like it will happen again.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives and warns them about what is coming. Many understand this as referring to the destruction of Jerusalem in the year 70 AD; others think it also looks toward the end of time, and some see both. Christians interpret this in different ways. He speaks so that they will stay alert and not be deceived.

For today: even when times are hard, God cares for his people. Trust his words, stay awake in prayer, and do not follow anyone who promises easy answers.
exp.11:10:
It says that what God did with the rejected stone is his own doing, and that it is something astonishing in our eyes. It is part of a quotation from Psalm 118, which speaks of the stone that the builders threw away and that ended up becoming the cornerstone of the building.

Jesus is speaking in the temple with the religious leaders, after telling the parable of the wicked tenants. With this quotation he shows them that, although they reject him, God will exalt him. They understood that he was speaking about them, and that is why they wanted to arrest him, although they feared the crowd.

For today: when you feel rejected, discarded, or undervalued, remember that God can work in unexpected ways. Trust in him, and do not reject Christ out of pride or out of habit.
exp.2:26:
Jesus says that no one can enter the house of a strong man and carry off his belongings unless he first ties up the strong man. Only after tying him up can he plunder his house. The word "goods" means possessions or valuable things, and "strong man" is the one who holds them.

Jesus speaks to the scribes, who were saying that he cast out demons by the power of the prince of demons. He answers that Satan would not fight against himself. With this picture, Satan is the strong man, and Jesus is the one who overcomes him and sets the captives free.

For today: if Christ has already overcome evil, you can trust him when you feel bound by fear or harmful habits. Ask for his help in faith, and seek support in your Christian community.
exp.0:12:
It says that Jesus spent forty days in the wilderness, and that there Satan tempted him. He was also with the wild beasts, that is, wild animals, and the angels ministered to him. The phrase "ministered to him" means that they took care of him and helped him with what he needed.

Mark, the narrator, tells this right after Jesus' baptism, when the Father said: "You are my beloved Son." Then the Spirit led him into the wilderness. Mark is brief and does not detail the temptations, as Matthew and Luke do. Some think the mention of the wild beasts shows how dangerous the place was; others see a sign of peace and dominion, but the text does not make this clear. After this, Jesus begins to preach.

Being loved by God does not free us from trials. But in the middle of them, God does not abandon us: Jesus overcame them and understands us when we go through difficult moments.
exp.13:62:
What it says: The high priest, hearing Jesus, tore his clothes in a sign of great anger and grief. Then he asked: "What need do we have of more witnesses?" By this he was implying that Jesus' own declaration was already enough to condemn him.

Context: Jesus is being tried before the Jewish council. The false witnesses did not agree with one another, so the high priest asked him directly whether he was the Christ. Jesus answered "I am" and spoke of the Son of Man in glory. To the high priest, this was blasphemy. Ironically, what they called blasphemy was the truth.

For today: Sometimes we react with anger to a truth that makes us uncomfortable, without examining it honestly. Let us ask God for a humble heart, willing to listen to Jesus instead of hardening itself.
exp.1:2:
This verse tells that some people came bringing a man who was paralyzed, carried by four men. The phrase "came to him" in the original is rendered in the verse above as "come unto him," so the explanation's quoted phrase is translated as "come unto him," meaning they came to Jesus. "Paralyzed" describes someone who cannot move his body, or part of it. Four friends were carrying him because he could not get there on his own.

Mark recounts this in Capernaum, in a crowded house where Jesus was teaching the word. The one speaking here is the narrator, Mark, who presents the scene. Nothing is said about what these men were thinking, but later the account shows their determination was great, because they broke through the roof to reach Jesus.

Today we can learn to bring others before Jesus. Perhaps someone close to us is tired, sick, or without strength to pray. We can accompany them, help them, and present them to God in prayer with love and perseverance.
exp.5:44:
Jesus immediately made his disciples get into the boat and go ahead of him to Bethsaida, to the other side of the lake. Meanwhile, he stayed behind to send the crowd away, that is, to tell the people to go home.

Mark tells what happened right after Jesus fed five thousand people. He does not explain why there was such a hurry. The Gospel of John says the people wanted to make him king by force, and many believe that helps explain the urgency. Jesus separates the disciples from the crowd's excitement and stays behind to send the people away calmly.

Today, sometimes Jesus sends us ahead when he is not in sight. Obey even when you do not understand everything. What follows in the text shows that he does not forget us: he goes off to pray, and from there he watches over his disciples.
exp.0:38:
This verse says that Jesus traveled through all of Galilee proclaiming God's message in the synagogues, which were the places where Jewish people gathered each Sabbath to pray and hear the Scriptures. He also cast out demons, that is, he freed people from evil spirits that oppressed them.

The phrase "their synagogues" refers to the synagogues of the Jewish people in that region.

Mark, the narrator, tells us that the crowds were looking for Jesus in Capernaum, but he chose to go to other towns, because he said that was why he had come. His priority was preaching, and his works showed that the kingdom of God was drawing near with power.

For today: do not stay only where you feel comfortable or where you are applauded. Ask God what your purpose is and share it with others, both in words and through concrete help.
exp.14:20:
They forced a man passing by, Simon of Cyrene, to carry Jesus' cross. He was coming in from the countryside, and Mark names him as the father of Alexander and Rufus. The word "forced" here means that they compelled him, and "Cyrene" was a city in North Africa.

Mark tells this right after the soldiers mocked Jesus and before they reached Golgotha. It was common for the condemned man to carry his own cross, but Jesus, already badly beaten, needed help. Mark names the sons, perhaps because his readers knew them, though the Bible does not make this clear. Some think Rufus is the one mentioned in Romans 16:13, but this is not certain.

Simon did not choose that moment; it was an uncomfortable interruption. Even so, he ended up following Jesus closely. Sometimes God leads us to serve in situations we did not seek. Today we can help someone who is carrying a burden, even when it gets in our way, and there discover Jesus.
exp.13:50:
This verse tells of a young man who was following Jesus, wearing only a linen cloth over his naked body. Some men tried to seize him. The sentence explaining the meaning of the old word for "young man" and the word for "arrest" has been removed, since those words do not appear in the verse your reader sees.

Mark is describing what happened in Gethsemane, when Jesus was arrested. The disciples had already fled. The text does not say who this young man was. Some think it may have been Mark himself, but that is a guess, not something certain. The detail shows the fear and confusion of that night, since the young man ended up running away naked.

For today: following Jesus can be easy when everything is going well, but pressure reveals how firm we are. If we fail, it is not the end. Jesus keeps moving forward for us and calls us back again with grace.
exp.9:23:
Jesus calls his disciples "Children" with affection, and they were alarmed by what he said about the rich. He clarifies that it is hard to enter the kingdom of God for those who trust in riches. "Were astonished" means they were amazed and troubled. "Again" means he repeated it.

Jesus has just spoken with a rich young man who would not give up his possessions to follow him, and he went away sad. Then Jesus teaches his disciples. In that time many people thought wealth was a sign of God's blessing, which is why they were surprised. Jesus makes clear that the problem is not having money, but trusting in it.

Today we can ask ourselves: where do I find rest when I think about my future? Having possessions is not sin, but God desires our trust. We can practice generosity as a way of remembering that God is our true provision.
exp.13:19:
Jesus answers his disciples' question and says that the betrayer is one of the twelve, someone who eats with him and dips bread into the same dish. The phrase "dips with me in the dish" speaks of sharing a meal up close, like friends. He does not give a name, but he makes it clear that it is someone very near to him.

Jesus is at the Last Supper with his disciples. He has just said that one of them will betray him, and they all become sad and ask, "Is it I?" He already knew what was going to happen, and what he says agrees with what the Scriptures had foretold. His grief is real: the betrayal comes from the table they share.

This scene invites us to examine our own hearts, as the disciples did, instead of pointing at others. We can ask God to keep us from disloyalty and to help us remain faithful to Christ, even when it is hard.
exp.1:12:
This verse says that Jesus went out again by the seaside, that is, the Sea of Galilee. There a large crowd came to him, and he taught them. Here "sea" refers to that large lake, and the old spelling in the source is simply the word "a" written in an older form.

Mark tells this right after Jesus healed a paralyzed man in Capernaum, and everyone was amazed. The one speaking is the narrator, Mark. He shows that, after the healing, Jesus does not stay with the fame of the miracle, but returns to his main work: teaching. Soon he will call Levi, a tax collector, to follow him.

For today: it is not enough to admire the works of God; we need to sit down and listen to his word. Find a quiet moment today to read the Bible and let Jesus teach you.
exp.9:18:
Jesus reminds this man of some of the commandments of the law of Moses: do not commit adultery, do not kill, do not steal, do not bear false witness against another in a trial or an accusation, do not defraud (that is, do not cheat or take from someone what is rightfully theirs), and honour your father and mother.

Jesus speaks with a man who came running and knelt to ask him how to receive eternal life. Jesus first directs him to the commandments, which concern how we treat others. The man says he has kept them since he was young. Then Jesus, looking at him with love, points out what he still lacks: to trust fully in Him, even above his riches.

For today: it is not enough to do well on the outside. Ask God whether there is something you love more than Him, and give that place to Jesus with sincerity and obedience.
exp.5:31:
This verse tells us that Jesus and his disciples got into a boat and went off to a lonely place, away from the crowds. The word "desert" here does not necessarily mean sand and heat, but an uninhabited, quiet place. "Privately" means they went alone, without the crowds.

The apostles had just returned from their mission, and they told Jesus everything they had done and taught. So many people were coming and going that they did not even have time to eat. That is why Jesus invited them to rest for a while. What follows shows that the people saw them leave and arrived before them.

Resting is not laziness; Jesus himself proposed it. After serving or working hard, setting aside time to be quiet, to eat, and to be with God renews us. Look for a brief moment of quiet today, even though your responsibilities are still there.
exp.3:23:
Jesus says: "Take heed what you hear." He uses the image of a measure, like when grain is weighed or measured out. By the measure you use, it will be given back to you. And to those who listen carefully, more will be given.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples and the crowd, right after the parable of the sower. He has just said that what is hidden will come out into the light. His teaching is a treasure that must be received with seriousness. Whoever listens with interest gains more understanding; whoever does not loses even the little they had. Some interpret the "measure" as the attention we give when we hear, others as the way we treat other people; both ideas fit.

Today, when you read or listen to the Word, do so with attention and a desire to obey. Before opening the Bible, ask God for a willing heart.
exp.9:22:
Jesus looks around and tells his disciples that it is very hard for rich people to enter the kingdom of God. The phrase "very hard" means "with great difficulty," and "wealth" refers to goods and money in abundance.

Jesus had just spoken with a rich man who wanted eternal life. Jesus looked at him with love and asked him to let go of his possessions to follow him, but the man went away sad. Then Jesus uses that moment to teach his disciples. He then explains that the problem lies in trusting in riches, and his disciples are amazed.

Today we can ask ourselves: in what do I rest my security? Having things is not a sin, but Jesus invites us not to depend on them. A practical step: give generously to someone in need this week, to train the heart to trust in God.
exp.9:42:
Jesus says that among his followers things must not work the way they do in the world. Whoever wants to be great must be a "minister", that is, someone who attends to and helps others. "But" is the word that marks the contrast here, and "whosoever will" means "whoever wants." Greatness is measured by service, not by authority.

Jesus speaks with his twelve disciples on the way to Jerusalem. James and John had just asked him for places of honor in his kingdom, and the other ten became angry. Jesus takes the opportunity to correct them all: the rulers of the nations lord it over others, but his community must live differently. He himself is the example, for he came to serve and to give his life for many.

Today we can ask ourselves, at home, at work, or in church: "Whom can I help today without expecting recognition?" Do one concrete act of service, even if no one notices.
exp.4:30:
The disciples tell Jesus that it is ridiculous to ask who touched him, because the crowd is pressing against him from every side.

The ones speaking are the disciples, and they do so with some amazement. To them, the bumping of so many people made it impossible to know who had touched him. But Jesus was speaking of a different kind of touch: that of a sick woman who came near in faith and was healed. He noticed the difference between a simple push and a touch of trust.

Today we may be close to Jesus in a casual way, as part of the crowd, or we may come to him with sincere faith. He knows the one who truly trusts in him. Today, come to him with an honest prayer, even a simple one.
exp.9:21:
