What it says: The rich man heard Jesus' invitation and became very sad. He left with a downcast face, because he had many possessions and did not want to give them up. "Youth" means the early years of life, and "possessions" are his property and wealth.

Context: This man ran to Jesus to ask how to inherit eternal life. He said he had kept the commandments since he was young. Jesus looked at him with love and pointed out what he was still missing: to let go of his security in money and follow him. Afterward, Jesus explained to his disciples how hard it is to enter the kingdom when a person trusts in riches. The text does not say whether this man came back later.

For today: Ask yourself honestly what you find hard to surrender to God: money, comfort, success, or some other security. Ask Him to help you trust Him more than these, and take one concrete step of generosity today.
exp.8:34:
Jesus sits down, calls the twelve disciples, and tells them that whoever wants to be first will have to be last of all and servant of all. "Last" means finally, at the back of the line, and a "servant" is someone who attends to and helps others. The verse is told in the present tense, as if the account were placing us right there in the scene.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples in a house in Capernaum. On the road they had been arguing about who was the greatest, and when he asked what they had been discussing, they fell silent, most likely from shame. With this gesture of sitting down and teaching, he corrects the way they were thinking. Then he takes a child and places him in the middle of them as an example.

For today: instead of seeking recognition, look for one concrete way this week to serve someone without anyone finding out, at home, at your work, or in your church.
exp.12:28:
Jesus says that when his disciples see these things happening, they should recognize that it is near, even at the doors. The words "see these things" are the phrase that appears in the verse, and "know" carries the sense of "be aware" or "understand." It is like someone who is already standing behind the door, about to come in.

Jesus speaks to four of his disciples on the Mount of Olives. He has described hard times and his coming. He uses the fig tree as an example: just as its tender leaves announce summer, certain signs announce that something is near. Christians have understood in different ways what is near: the fall of Jerusalem, the return of Christ, or both.

For today: live attentive and at peace, without living in fear or becoming preoccupied with dates. Trust the words of Jesus, which do not pass away, and keep your heart prepared each day.
exp.7:24:
He put his hands on the man's eyes again and told him to look up. Then the man was healed and saw everything far off and clearly.

Mark tells this in Bethsaida. Jesus took the blind man out of the village and healed him in two stages: first he saw blurry, then clearly. The text does not explain why he did it this way. Some think it illustrates how the disciples gradually came to understand who Jesus was, since right after this comes the question: "Who do people say I am?" That is one interpretation, not something the text states directly.

For today: if your faith or your understanding of God is still blurry, do not be discouraged. Jesus is patient and can keep working in you until he gives you clarity.
exp.3:26:
This verse describes a man who scatters seed and then goes on with his ordinary life: he sleeps and gets up, night and day. Meanwhile the seed sprouts and grows without him understanding how it happens.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, using parables to teach about the kingdom of God. Here he tells the parable of the seed that grows on its own, which appears only in Mark. Many understand it to teach that the kingdom advances through the mysterious work of God, not only through human effort. Then comes the harvest, which is usually seen as the final fulfillment.

For today: do faithfully what is yours to do, such as praying, serving, or sharing the Word, and trust that God makes grow what you cannot control. You can rest without anxiety, even though you do not see immediate results.
exp.7:6:
It says they had a few small fish. Jesus gave thanks to God for them, blessed them, and commanded that they also be distributed to the people. "Small fish" refers to little fish, and "blessed" here means he gave thanks to God for the food.

Jesus is in a remote area with a crowd of about four thousand who had been with him for three days and had nothing to eat. He feels compassion and does not want to send them away hungry. With the seven loaves and these few fish, he makes it enough for everyone. His disciples only put out what they have and distribute it.

For today: do not despise what little you have. Give it to God with gratitude and serve others with it. God can do much with the small, and our part is to offer it with confidence.
exp.8:8:
He says that as Jesus and three of his disciples were coming down from the mountain, he ordered them not to tell anyone what they had seen. They could speak about it only after the Son of man had risen from the dead. The words "to no one" are the same in meaning as "to anyone," and "Son of man" is a title Jesus used for himself.

Jesus speaks with Peter, James, and John after the transfiguration, where they saw his glory and heard the voice of the Father. He asked for silence, probably because his glory could not yet be understood apart from the cross and the resurrection. The disciples did not understand what it meant to rise from the dead, as the following verse shows.

For today: God sometimes shows us truths that we will only fully understand over time. Trust him, follow Jesus with humility, and let him teach you step by step.
exp.11:27:
This verse tells us that a scribe, that is, an expert teacher of the law of Moses, came up to Jesus. He had heard the debate with the Sadducees and noticed that Jesus had answered well. So he asked him which commandment was the first of all.

Jesus had just answered the Sadducees, who denied the resurrection. He showed them that God is the God of the living, not of the dead. The scribe, impressed, asked a sincere question about what is central to the law. In Mark, this scribe seems to be truly seeking, unlike others who wanted to trap Jesus. Other parallel passages present the intention in a different way.

Today we too can come to Jesus with honest questions. If we want to know what matters most in life, he answers us with clarity. Ask him with humility and listen to his answer in the Bible.
exp.5:40:
He took the five loaves and the two fish, looked up to heaven, and gave thanks to God. Then he broke the loaves and gave them to his disciples so they could set them before the people. He also divided the two fish among everyone. "Blessed" means that he gave thanks to God for the food. "Gave to" is the same as "gave them to," and "should set" is the same as "might set."

The account tells of Jesus and a crowd that had followed him to a remote place. It was late, and there was not enough food. Jesus ordered the people to sit down in orderly groups on the grass. The disciples had little, but Jesus used what they had. Mark tells us that everyone ate and that there was plenty left over.

For today: when what you have feels very small, place it in God's hands with thankfulness. He can use the little we have, and often he does so through people willing to serve and share.
exp.0:22:
In the synagogue at Capernaum, Mark says, there was a man with an unclean spirit, that is, an evil spirit that had hold of him. That man cried out loudly. The word that was once spelled differently in the older text is simply "cried" in modern English.

Mark tells this right after the people were amazed at Jesus' teaching, because he taught with authority. Now that authority is shown in the face of evil. The spirit speaks through the man and recognizes Jesus as the Holy One of God. Jesus does not listen to it as an ally, but rebukes it and commands it to come out.

For today: Jesus has authority over whatever oppresses us. We can come to Him with confidence in our fears and struggles, knowing that His word has power and that His care for us is real.
exp.3:38:
Jesus stood up and spoke with authority to the wind and the sea. "Rebuked" means that he sternly corrected them. "Peace, be still" is a command for the storm to stop and grow quiet. The wind stopped and everything became calm.

The disciples were in a boat crossing the Sea of Galilee when a strong storm arose. Jesus was sleeping in the stern, the back part of the boat. Frightened, they woke him and complained that he did not care about their danger. Mark tells us that Jesus acted, and then asked them about their fear and their little faith. They were filled with awe.

When you feel your life sinking in a storm, do not think that Jesus has forgotten you. Speak to him honestly, even with your fears, and trust that his power and his care are still present, even when he does not always calm everything at once.
exp.13:5:
Jesus says to those who were criticizing the woman: "Leave her alone. Why are you bothering her? What she did for me is a good thing."

Jesus is in Bethany, in the house of Simon the leper, a few days before his death. A woman poured a very costly perfume over him. Some of those present became angry and scolded her, because they thought that money could have helped the poor. Jesus defends her and recognizes her act of love.

For today: do not despise or quickly judge the sincere acts of love toward God that others make. And you too can offer Jesus something valuable, such as your time, your attention, or your affection, without fear of criticism.
exp.5:26:
It says that King Herod, as soon as he heard the girl's request, sent a soldier from his guard with orders to bring back the head of John the Baptist. The word "immediately" in the verse means right away, and the guard was a soldier from his personal bodyguard.

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. Herod had made a vow in front of his guests, and Herodias's daughter, pushed on by her mother, asked for John's death. John had criticized Herod's marriage to Herodias. Herod was saddened, but he gave in out of pride and out of fear of losing face before the others.

For today: do not let the pressure of other people or pride lead you to do something unjust. It is better to admit a mistake and correct it in time than to keep a bad promise. Ask God for the courage to act justly, even when it costs you.
exp.10:7:
It says that many people laid their cloaks on the road, and others cut branches from the trees and also laid them on the ground. "Cloaks" here means outer garments, such as coats or capes. "Spread" can mean "laid out" or "put on the ground."

Mark recounts Jesus' entry into Jerusalem, riding on a young donkey (a colt). It is not a character speaking; it is the narrator describing the crowd's reaction. Spreading cloaks was a way of honoring someone important, such as a king. Afterward the people shout "Hosanna!", an expression of praise that is also a cry of "save us." Scholars debate how much the people understood about who Jesus really was.

Today we can ask ourselves what things we are willing to lay at the feet of Jesus: our time, our pride, or our comforts. Honoring him is not only shouting praises, but giving him something real.
exp.6:25:
This verse introduces the woman who came to Jesus. It says she was a "Greek," that is, of Greek culture and language, and a Syrophoenician by nation, meaning born in Phoenicia, a region that at that time belonged to the Roman province of Syria. She begged him to cast the demon out of her daughter, that is, to drive it out.

Mark, the author, tells us that Jesus had gone to the area of Tyre and Sidon, territory inhabited by non-Jewish people. The woman was a foreigner, but she heard about Jesus and came humbly, falling at his feet. Then Jesus speaks to her about the children's bread, and she responds with a simple and persistent faith.

For today: when a need overwhelms us, we can come to Jesus with humility and trust, regardless of our background or the barriers we face. She persisted out of love for her daughter, and we too can pray with perseverance for those we love.
exp.7:12:
Jesus left the Pharisees, got back into the boat, and crossed to the other side of the lake. The phrase "left them" means that he walked away from them, without continuing the argument. Going to the other side means he went to the opposite shore.

The Pharisees had come to test him, asking him for a sign from heaven. Jesus had already done many miracles, so their request did not come from sincere faith. He sighed deeply and refused to give them another sign. Then he left, and shortly afterward he warned his disciples about the influence of the Pharisees, using the image of bad influence spreading like yeast through dough.

For today: not every argument deserves our energy. When someone wants to fight and is not seeking the truth, sometimes the wisest thing is to withdraw in peace and continue forward with God.
exp.1:9:
Jesus says that he wants people to know that the Son of man has authority here on earth to forgive sins. The word "authority" here means the right and power to act. "Son of man" is a title Jesus uses for himself. Then he turns to the paralytic to speak to him.

Jesus speaks with some teachers of the law who were accusing him in their hearts of blasphemy, because only God forgives sins. Jesus knows their thoughts and answers them with a visible fact: healing the paralytic in front of everyone. In this way he shows that his word has power over the body and also over the soul.

Jesus cares not only for our visible wounds but also for our deepest need: forgiveness. Today you can come to him with confidence, without hiding your guilt, and receive his forgiveness and his help to rise up and go on with your life.
exp.9:17:
Jesus answers with a question: "Why do you call me good?" Then he states that no one is good except God. Here "good" means morally perfect, without any stain. Old words: "kneeling" means getting down on the knee; "youth" means a young man's years.

A man came running, knelt down, and called Jesus "Good Teacher," asking how to inherit eternal life. Jesus does not deny being good; he wants the man to think about what he is saying. Some believe he is inviting him to recognize who Jesus really is; others, that he is preparing him to see that no one is saved by their own merits. The text does not fully settle the matter.

Today we can avoid boasting about our goodness and comparing ourselves with others. All true goodness comes from God. Let us humbly ask him to transform us and trust in his mercy, not in our achievements.
exp.10:4:
Mark says that some people who were standing nearby asked the disciples why they were untying the colt. A colt is a young donkey. To untie is to loose what had been tied fast. It was a natural question, since they were taking an animal that did not belong to them.

Jesus was approaching Jerusalem, and he had sent two disciples to get this colt. He had told them what to say if anyone questioned them. The ones speaking here are the owners or those present, who saw something that seemed strange. The disciples answered as Jesus had told them, and the people let them go. Mark does not explain why they agreed so quickly; some think they knew Jesus, but the text does not say so.

For today: Jesus knows what he needs and can take care of every detail. When we obey his words, even when we do not understand everything, we can trust that he goes before us.
exp.7:15:
The explanation says that the disciples were arguing among themselves because they had no bread. The word "reasoned" in the verse above means that they were debating or discussing with some tension. They were worried because they had forgotten to bring food, and they had only one loaf of bread in the boat.

Jesus had just warned them to watch out for the yeast of the Pharisees and of Herod, that is, for an influence that spreads and corrupts, like dough that rises. The disciples understood his words in a literal way, thinking about bread. That is why Jesus rebukes them patiently, reminding them that they had already seen him multiply the loaves.

For today: when we worry about what we lack, it is easy not to hear what is most important. Let us remember how God has already cared for us, and ask him for attentive ears to understand what he is truly saying to us.
exp.4:6:
He says that the man, crying out loudly, asked Jesus what he had to do with him. He calls him "the Son of the Most High God." The man was asking Jesus not to torment him.

The demon-possessed man is from the region of the Gadarenes, though the voice that comes out is that of the unclean spirit that controlled him. Jesus had already commanded the spirit to come out of him. The spirits recognize who Jesus is and fear his authority. Their recognition is not faith or repentance; they only admit that Jesus has power over them.

For today: it is not enough to know who Jesus is; one must trust in him and follow him. And if there is something that dominates or binds you, you can turn to him, because his authority is greater than any oppression.
exp.2:18:
This verse ends the list of the twelve apostles whom Jesus chose. The last one named is Judas Iscariot, and he is said to have been the one who betrayed him. "Betrayed" means that he handed Jesus over, putting him into the hands of his enemies. The verse then says that they went into a house, meaning Jesus and his disciples returned to a house. "Iscariot" probably indicates where Judas came from, although there are different opinions about its exact meaning.

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. He has just told how Jesus went up the mountain and called twelve to be with him and to be sent out to preach. Mark mentions the betrayal already at this point, although it will happen later. Right after this, the house fills with people, and Jesus is hardly able to eat.

For today: Jesus called imperfect people, even the one who would betray him. This reminds us that being close to Christ calls for a sincere heart, not merely a position. Let us ask him to keep us faithful each day.
exp.9:40:
The other ten disciples heard about the request that James and John had made to Jesus, and they became indignant with the two brothers. Here "became indignant" means feeling strong displeasure. The ten are the rest of the apostles, not counting these two brothers.

James and John had just asked Jesus for the places of honor at his right and his left in his glory. Jesus had spoken to them about his suffering, but they were thinking about power and position. Mark tells us the others were upset, perhaps because they also wanted those places. The text does not say this clearly, so it is a possibility. Right after this, Jesus gathers them all together and corrects them all.

For today: the anger we feel at the ambition of others can reveal our own ambition. Before we criticize, let us examine our hearts and ask: do I seek to be served or to serve? Jesus invites us to greatness that is lived out in service.
exp.14:13:
Pilate asks them, "Why, what evil hath he done?", that is, what crime Jesus had committed. The crowd does not answer with reasons but shouts even louder: "Crucify him." The word "cried out" means shouted.

Pilate was the Roman governor and had the authority to decide. The chief priests had handed Jesus over out of envy (Mark 15:10), and the crowd was calling for Barabbas to be released. Pilate seems to recognize that Jesus is innocent but, as the following text says, wanted to "please the crowd" and gave in to the pressure.

For today: often knowing what is right is not enough; it takes courage to do it. Let us ask God for firmness not to be swept along by group pressure, and to defend truth and justice, even when it costs us.
exp.6:21:
Jesus keeps listing the evil that comes out of the human heart. Stealing is the first item, and greed is the desire to have more and more. Evil intentions and deceit, which is lying to gain an advantage, are also part of the list, along with shameless conduct. The evil eye points to envy or a selfish way of looking at others. Slander and insults come next, then pride, and finally foolishness, which means living without wisdom.

Jesus speaks to the crowd and to his disciples, after arguing with the Pharisees, who were concerned about washing their hands and about what foods were clean. He teaches that what truly defiles a person is not what goes into the mouth, but what comes out of the heart.

For today: instead of focusing only on outward appearances, we can ask God to examine our hearts. If you notice envy, pride, or dishonesty in yourself, acknowledge it honestly and ask him to cleanse you and change you from within.
exp.14:2:
This verse says that the most important religious leaders, called the chief priests, kept bringing many accusations against Jesus. "Accused him of many things" means they kept presenting charges against him over and over, with insistence.

Mark tells us that at daybreak the Jewish council handed Jesus over, bound, to Pilate, the Roman governor. Pilate asked him whether he was the King of the Jews, and Jesus answered, "You say so." Afterward, the priests kept accusing him, and Jesus remained silent. Mark does not detail the accusations here, but he shows the pressure against Him and the calm with which Jesus faced it.

When someone accuses us unjustly, we do not always have to defend ourselves with many words. Jesus trusted the Father and kept his peace. We can ask God for wisdom to know when to speak and when to be silent.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that from the beginning, when God created everything, he made human beings as male and female. The word "hembra," an old word, here simply means "woman." Jesus points out that the difference between them and their union was God's idea from the beginning.

Jesus is speaking with some Pharisees who are testing him by asking about divorce. They cite Moses, who allowed a certificate of divorce. Jesus answers that this was a concession because of the hardness of the people's hearts. Then he takes them further back, to God's original purpose in creation, which is the basis of what he teaches about marriage.

For today: when we have doubts about marriage or relationships, let us think not only about what is permitted or convenient, but about what God intended from the beginning. We can care for our promises with humility, patience, and a heart willing to forgive.
exp.13:40:
Jesus returns for the third time and finds his disciples asleep. He tells them to sleep on and take their rest, but then immediately adds "it is enough," which means "that is enough." He says the hour has come and that the Son of man is about to be handed over into the hands of sinners. Some understand his first words as a question or as a gentle rebuke; the text does not make this entirely clear.

Jesus is speaking in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before his arrest. He was distressed and had asked his friends to keep watch with him. Overcome by weariness, they could not. Even so, Jesus had already prayed and was ready to face what was coming.

For today: when you fail or give in to tiredness, do not stay in guilt. Return to Jesus, who understands you, and seek strength in prayer before the trials arrive.
exp.2:32:
Jesus responds with a question: "Who is my mother, or my brethren?" He does not deny his family. He uses the question to draw attention to something deeper.

Jesus is teaching in a house full of people. His mother and his brothers arrive and wait outside. Shortly before this, Mark tells us that some people thought Jesus was out of his mind (Mark 3:21), so the family may have come out of concern, although the text does not give every detail. Jesus looks at those sitting around him and explains that his true family is those who do the will of God.

For today: being part of Jesus' family does not depend only on human ties, but on listening to God and obeying him. Today you can take one concrete step of obedience and welcome other believers as brothers and sisters, even if you have not known them before.
exp.0:25:
This verse tells the end of the scene. The evil spirit shook the man violently, cried out loudly, and finally came out of him. "Having torn him" means that it convulsed him or shook him hard. "Crying out" means shouting. "Unclean" refers to something impure.

Jesus is in the synagogue in Capernaum, teaching on a Sabbath. The spirit had recognized Jesus as "the Holy One of God," and Jesus commanded it to be silent and come out. Mark presents this event as a sign of Jesus' authority, which then leaves the people amazed.

For today: when you feel that something is controlling you, such as fear, a vice, or guilt, you do not have to face it alone. Jesus has authority over every evil. Come to Him in prayer and seek the support of your community of faith.
exp.5:54:
It says that, after recognizing Jesus in Genezaret, the people ran through the whole surrounding region. They began to bring the sick lying on beds to any place where they heard that Jesus was. Some old words: the word for "a" is simply "to," and "heard" means that they found out by what they were hearing.

Mark is the one telling the story. Jesus and his disciples had just crossed the lake, after a difficult night in which Jesus walked on the water. On arrival, the people recognized him right away. Mark shows that his reputation as a healer had spread, and that many came to him with hope.

For today: just as those people brought their sick to Jesus, we can bring those who suffer to him in prayer, without waiting until everything is resolved. And if you know someone who is tired or sick, accompany them with a visit, a favor, or a sincere prayer.
exp.13:46:
This verse tells that, at the moment of Jesus' arrest, one of the bystanders drew his sword and struck the servant of the high priest, cutting off his ear. Mark does not say who used the sword, nor does he give the servant's name. The word "struck" here means that he hit him with the weapon.

This happens in the garden of Gethsemane, right after Judas betrays Jesus with a kiss and the guards seize him. It is a defensive reaction in the midst of fear and confusion. Other Gospels give more details: John says it was Peter and that the servant's name was Malchus. Jesus responds afterward that He is giving Himself up so that the Scriptures may be fulfilled, not because of the force of His enemies.

For today: when we feel fear or injustice, a violent reaction is not the way of Jesus. Let us ask God for calm and confidence so that we may respond with peace and firmness.
exp.3:2:
Jesus asks the crowd to pay attention: "Hearken," that is, "listen." Then he says that a sower went out to sow. The word "Behold" is an old way of saying "look" or "take notice." With it Jesus stirs up curiosity and prepares his hearers for something important.

Jesus is teaching beside the Sea of Galilee. So many people gathered that he got into a boat and sat down in it, while the crowd listened to him from the shore. Mark says he was teaching them many things in parables, that is, simple stories with a deeper meaning. This is the first of them, and later Jesus explains its meaning.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God in passing. Today you can read a passage of the Bible calmly, ask God to speak to you, and stop to think about what he is saying to you.
exp.4:35:
Here is the explanation. It says that Jesus, as soon as he heard the message that the girl had died, spoke directly to Jairo, the ruler of the synagogue. He asks him two things: not to be afraid, and only to believe, that is, to trust without adding any conditions.

Jesus is speaking with a distressed father. He had just healed a woman along the way, and in the meantime messengers arrived saying it was no longer worth troubling the Teacher. Jesus does not ignore the bad news; he simply invites Jairo to keep trusting in the middle of it.

Today, when news arrives that seems to close every door, we can pause and bring it to Jesus in prayer. He does not ask us to pretend it does not hurt, but to trust that he remains with us.
exp.7:32:
Jesus turns around, looks at his disciples, and rebukes Peter firmly. He says to him, "Get thee behind me, Satan," because Peter is thinking the way people think, and not the way God thinks. "Rebuked" means that he reprimanded him. The words "get thee behind me" can be put as "get behind me" or "get out of my way." The word "Satan" means "adversary" or "opponent."

Jesus had just announced that he would suffer, be rejected, die, and rise again. Peter, with good intentions, wanted to stop him. But his idea of a Messiah without the cross was an obstacle to God's plan. Jesus speaks in front of all the disciples, because the lesson was for them too.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we want a comfortable faith or a faithful one. Sometimes we think the way the world thinks and avoid every sacrifice. Let us ask God to teach us to trust his ways, even when we do not understand them.
exp.2:27:
Jesus says that God forgives all the sins of people, including blasphemies, which are words that offend or speak evil against God. The phrase "to the sons of men" means to human beings. The word "wherewith soever" means of any kind.

Jesus speaks with the teachers of the law, who had come down from Jerusalem and were saying that he drove out demons by the power of Satan. He answers them that a divided kingdom cannot stand. This verse opens a serious warning that continues in the next one: harshly rejecting the work of the Spirit and calling it evil. Christians have explained that sin in several ways.

For today: no one is too far from God's forgiveness. If you feel guilt, come to him with humility and trust, and do not harden your heart.
exp.9:36:
James and John ask Jesus for a place of honor: to sit at his right and at his left when he reigns in his glory. The right side and the left side were the places of greatest authority next to a king.

Jesus had just announced for the third time that he would be handed over, mistreated, and killed in Jerusalem. The two brothers, who were among his closest disciples, seem to be thinking of a kingdom of power and prestige, without yet understanding the path of suffering. Jesus answers that they do not know what they are asking, and he speaks of drinking the cup and of the baptism, images of his own suffering. The other ten disciples later became angry with the two brothers.

Before we ask anything of God, it is good to examine our motives. Am I seeking to serve, or to be recognized? Jesus invites us to follow him with humility, trusting him even when the path is difficult.
exp.13:1:
The chief priests and the teachers of the law wanted to arrest Jesus secretly and kill him. But they said, "Not on the feast day," because they feared that the people would riot. A riot means a tumult or disturbance.

The religious leaders are speaking two days before the Passover. Jerusalem was full of pilgrims, and many people admired Jesus. The leaders feared a reaction from the people, so they looked for a quieter moment. What they planned, however, ended up happening during the Passover, which shows that they did not control everything.

For today: there are those who care more about their image and their convenience than about truth and justice. Let us examine our hearts and ask God to give us courage to do what is right, without hiding our decisions out of fear of what others think.
exp.8:0:
Jesus says that some of those standing there will not die before they see the kingdom of God come with power. "To taste death" is an old way of saying "to die." "Power" means strength or might.

Jesus speaks to his disciples and the crowd, right after teaching that following him means carrying the cross. He gives them a promise of hope. Interpreters understand it in different ways: some see it fulfilled in the transfiguration, which the text describes right after; others think of the resurrection, Pentecost, or the spread of the church. The text does not fully make this clear.

For today: when following Jesus costs you something, remember that his kingdom is real and his power is greater than your difficulties. Be encouraged to keep going with hope and confidence.
exp.7:19:
Jesus reminds his disciples of the second miracle of the loaves: with seven loaves he fed four thousand people. He asks them how many baskets full of leftover pieces they picked up, and they answer: seven.

Jesus speaks with the disciples in the boat, after they had worried because they had no bread. He warns them about the yeast of the Pharisees, but they think about food. With these questions he shows them that they had already seen his power to provide abundantly. Their lack of understanding is what Jesus points out.

For today: when you worry about what you lack, remember how God has already cared for you before. Recalling his past works strengthens trust and helps you listen better to what he wants to teach you.
exp.15:15:
Jesus says that whoever believes the message of the gospel and is baptized will be saved, that is, rescued from condemnation and brought into a new life with God. On the other hand, whoever does not believe will be condemned. Note that condemnation is tied to lack of faith, not to lack of baptism.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, speaking to the eleven disciples. He has just rebuked them for their unbelief and commands them to carry the gospel to the whole world. This verse explains the weight of that message: believing in it decides the destiny of each person. Some scholars point out that the oldest manuscripts do not include the final verses of Mark, and for that reason their origin is debated.

For today: if you already believe in Jesus, take the step of baptism as a public confession of your faith, and share the good news you have received with someone close to you.
exp.8:43:
The verse says that in that place their worm does not die, and the fire is never put out. It is language of strong images, taken from Isaiah 66:24.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. He has just warned against causing the little ones who believe in him to stumble. He uses deliberate exaggerations, such as cutting off a hand, to show how serious sin is and how much life with God is worth. Christians understand in different ways whether the images are literal or symbolic.

Today we can take seriously what makes us fall. Without going to extremes, it is wise to ask ourselves what habit or friendship is pulling us away from God, and to turn away from it with determination and humility.
exp.2:1:
These verses say that some people in the synagogue were watching Jesus closely. The word "watched" here means observing someone closely, with bad intent, waiting for a mistake. They wanted to see whether Jesus would heal the man on the sabbath, the day of rest, so that they would have a reason to accuse him.

Here the narrator, Mark, is speaking. Jesus is in a synagogue and sees a man with a withered hand, that is, a hand that is paralyzed or shrunken. Those who were watching him were probably religious leaders (the text does not name them here). For them, the law of the sabbath weighed more than compassion. Jesus confronts them with a question that leaves them silent.

For today: let us examine our hearts. Sometimes we watch others in order to judge them, instead of seeking their good. Let us ask God for a faith that loves and helps, and that does not use rules as a weapon against others.
exp.6:14:
Jesus says that what a person eats or touches from outside does not make them impure before God. What does defile them is what comes out of them, that is, what springs from the heart. "Defile" here means to make impure, in a moral and spiritual sense.

Jesus is speaking to the crowd after arguing with Pharisees and teachers of the law. They were criticizing his disciples for eating without performing certain ritual washings that came from human tradition. Jesus shows them that these customs had been placed above the word of God. Then he calls everyone to understand what really matters: the condition of the heart. Later he explains the meaning to his disciples in private.

Today we can ask ourselves not only which things we avoid on the outside, but what is in our hearts. Before we speak in anger or criticize, let us ask God to cleanse our attitudes and our words.
exp.8:49:
Jesus says that salt is good, but if it loses its taste, there is no way to restore it. The word for losing taste, here, means becoming tasteless, and seasoning means giving food its flavor. Then he tells his disciples to have salt in themselves and to live at peace with one another.

Jesus speaks to his disciples after warning them with strong words about sin and judgment. Talk of being salted with fire and of sacrifices recalls purification and giving oneself to God. Scholars interpret the salt in several ways: tested character, faithfulness, or the effect of preserving and seasoning. What is clear is that he connects that dedicated life with living in peace.

For today: make sure your faith has flavor in everyday life. Before answering in anger, choose a kind word, and seek peace with someone you have tension with.
exp.13:29:
Jesus tells Peter, with great certainty, that this very night, before the rooster crows twice, he will deny him three times.

Jesus speaks with his disciples after the Last Supper, shortly before he is arrested. He has just said that they would all abandon him. Peter, with good intentions, insists that he never would. Jesus, who knows him well, warns him clearly. He also promises that after he rises, he will go before them into Galilee, showing that there will be restoration.

For today: do not put too much trust in your own strength. Recognize your weaknesses, pray, and depend on Christ. And if you fail, remember that Jesus still offers forgiveness and a new beginning.
exp.15:17:
It says that those who believe in Jesus will see signs around them. "They shall take up serpents" means they will pick up or remove snakes without being harmed; "any deadly thing" refers to something capable of killing, such as poison. It also promises that, when they lay hands on the sick, the sick will recover.

Jesus speaks after his resurrection, giving his final words to the disciples before he ascends to heaven. He charges them to carry the gospel to everyone, and the signs confirm the message. It should be said that many ancient manuscripts do not include Mark 16:9-20, and scholars debate it. Furthermore, the book of Acts shows Paul bitten by a viper without harm, but it never commands anyone to bring on danger.

For today: do not test God with unnecessary risks. Rather, pray for the sick with faith, lovingly help those who suffer, and trust that God cares for those who proclaim his word.
exp.9:51:
Jesus tells the blind man to go on his way, because his faith has made him whole. At that very moment the man regains his sight and, instead of leaving, follows Jesus along the road.

Regained his sight means he could see again. Whole can be understood as healed, and also as reached by God's saving power; the text allows both ideas. And immediately means at once.

Jesus is speaking as he leaves Jericho on the way to Jerusalem. The blind man, named Bartimaeus in the passage, had cried out asking for mercy, even though the crowd wanted him silenced. He threw off his cloak, came near, and asked clearly for what he needed. Jesus responds to that trust.

For today: come to Jesus with confidence, even when others try to get in your way, and tell him honestly what you need. And when you receive his help, do not simply go your own way: respond by following him with gratitude.
exp.3:3:
It says that, as the sower was scattering the seed, some fell by the way side. There it could not enter into the ground, and the birds came and ate it up. The word "devoured" here means they ate it completely. The phrase "it came to pass" means "it happened."

Jesus is speaking to a crowd by the Sea of Galilee, and he teaches in parables, or simple stories with a spiritual message. Later he explains that the seed is the word of God, and that the wayside represents those who hear it but do not understand or keep it, and the adversary takes it away (Mark 4:14-15).

For today: it is not enough to hear the Word of God; we must receive it with attention. We can read the Bible calmly, think about what we have read, pray over it and put it into practice, so that it is not lost in the busyness of the day.
exp.6:19:
Jesus says that what comes out of a person is what defiles them. The quoted phrases in the original cannot be carried over here, so the sentences about them are removed. Defiling means making someone impure or staining them from the inside, not only on the outside.

Jesus speaks with his disciples and with the crowd, after arguing with the Pharisees, who criticized the disciples for eating without following the ritual washings. He teaches that food does not stain the heart; what does harm comes from within: evil thoughts, words, and actions, as he explains in the verses that follow. Some understand that by this he declared all foods clean.

Today, instead of looking only at outward appearances, we can ask God to heal our heart. Before we speak or act, it is good to ask ourselves what is inside us, and to pray sincerely for a clean heart.
exp.0:0:
Mark opens his book by saying that it begins "the gospel" of Jesus Christ. "Gospel" means "good news." He calls him Jesus Christ, that is, the Messiah, the promised one sent by God, and also the Son of God. From the very first line he tells us who Jesus is.

The author is Mark, according to ancient Christian tradition, although the text itself does not give his name. He writes without any introduction, and right away he quotes the prophet Isaiah to show that the coming of Jesus was no surprise, but part of God's plan announced long before. Some understand "the beginning" as the start of the story; others understand it as the beginning of God's work in Christ.

Today we can read the Gospels not only as history, but as personal good news. Before asking what I should do, let us start by recognizing who Jesus is and trusting in Him.
exp.13:70:
Peter began to curse and to swear. With this he wanted to convince everyone that he was telling the truth when he said, "I do not know this man you are talking about." The words "curse" and "swear" here probably mean that Peter called down a curse on himself if he was lying, or that he swore emphatically. Scholars understand this in somewhat different ways.

Mark tells this on the night of Jesus' arrest. Peter is in the courtyard of the high priest, and several people recognize him as a follower of Jesus because of his Galilean accent. This is the third denial. Jesus had already told him that he would deny him, and shortly afterward Peter remembers those words and weeps.

For today: when we fail, let us not hide in shame. Peter wept with repentance and returned to Jesus. We can do the same, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.0:24:
Jesus speaks firmly to the unclean spirit. "Rebuked" means that he sharply corrected it, and "Hold thy peace" means "be quiet." Then he orders it to come out of the man. He does not argue or bargain; he simply commands.

This happens in the synagogue at Capernaum. The spirit had cried out that it knew who Jesus was, the Holy One of God. Jesus does not want that testimony, and he silences it. Some think he was preventing people from announcing him in a distorted way or too soon, though the text does not explain this. The people are amazed because his authority is seen in deeds, not just in words.

For today: when you feel fear, guilt, or confusion pressing down on you, go to Jesus and trust his authority. He can bring order where you cannot, and his voice should carry more weight than any other.
exp.9:29:
Jesus says that whoever gives up something for his sake and for the gospel will receive "a hundredfold," that is, a hundred times as much, in this present life: houses, brothers, sisters, mothers, children, and lands (fields). But this comes "with persecutions." And in the age to come, he will receive eternal life.

Peter has just said that the disciples left everything to follow Jesus. After seeing the rich young man walk away sorrowful, Jesus responds with a promise. Many understand the "family" and the possessions to refer to the community of believers who share what they have. Others see it in a broader way. Even so, the text joins the reward with suffering.

For today: if following Christ costs you something, you are not alone. Look for a church where you can give and receive love and support, and trust that God cares for those who obey him.
exp.13:44:
This verse tells how Judas came straight up to Jesus and went to him at once. He said "Master, Master," which was a greeting of respect, and he kissed him. The kiss was the agreed signal so that the armed crowd would know whom to arrest.

It is the night Jesus was arrested, in the garden of Gethsemane. The narrator, Mark, shows that Judas, one of the twelve, handed Jesus over. He did it on behalf of the religious leaders, who wanted to seize him quietly. A gesture of affection was used to betray.

For today: let us make sure our words and gestures are sincere. It is possible to speak with respect and still have our hearts far from God. Let us ask him to give us an honest and faithful trust, not just an outward appearance.
exp.5:15:
Herod hears about Jesus and reaches a frightened conclusion: "It is John, whom I beheaded, and he has risen from the dead." The word "beheaded" means having the head cut off.

The king speaking is Herod Antipas. People had various ideas about Jesus: some said he was Elijah, others that he was a prophet. Herod, however, was not thinking about God but about his own guilt. He had imprisoned John because John had told him that it was not lawful to have his brother's wife. His conscience gave him no peace.

For today: unresolved guilt pursues us and makes us see everything with fear. Instead of hiding it or justifying it, we can bring it to God with humility, ask for forgiveness, and correct our course.
exp.11:34:
Jesus is teaching in the temple and asks everyone a question: why do the teachers of the law say that the Christ, the promised Messiah, is "son of David"? The word "scribes" refers to the experts who copied and explained the Scriptures. The phrase "son of David" means a descendant of King David.

Earlier, a scribe had answered wisely about loving God and loving one's neighbor, and no one dared to ask Jesus anything more. Now Jesus takes the initiative. He does not deny that the Messiah comes from David, but he is going to show that this idea, though true, does not say everything. The verses that follow explain this with a psalm of David.

For today: let us not be satisfied with ideas that are correct but small about Jesus. He is more than a figure from the past or a good teacher. Let us ask the Spirit to help us know him and honor him as Lord.
exp.1:24:
Jesus answers the Pharisees with a question: have you never read what David did when he was in need and hungry, he and those with him? It is a way of saying: you know the Scriptures well, so remember this case.

The Pharisees were accusing the disciples of breaking the Sabbath by picking heads of grain as they walked. Jesus answers them with the story of David, who ate the sacred bread from the sanctuary when he was fleeing and hungry (1 Samuel 21). In this way he shows that human need and mercy weigh more than a rule applied with rigidity.

God gave his commandments for the good of people, not to burden them. Before judging someone by a rule, ask yourself whether you are caring for the heart of God: compassion toward the one who is in need.
exp.13:34:
He went a little way off from his disciples and threw himself face down on the ground. There he asked God that, if it were possible, he would not have to go through that hour. That "hour" refers to the time of suffering and death that was drawing near. The word "fell" here means that he bowed down until he touched the earth.

Mark records this in the garden of Gethsemane, shortly before Jesus was arrested. He had just said that his soul was very sorrowful. He had taken Peter, James, and John along so they would keep him company. His prayer shows his true humanity and also his trust in the Father, for right after it he says: "not what I will, but what you will."

For today: you can be honest with God when you are afraid or in pain. Tell him exactly what you feel, and then ask him to help you trust him.
exp.6:13:
Jesus calls all the people around him and asks them to pay attention. He says, "Hearken unto me every one of you, and understand." Some of the wording in the older text is worth noting: where the earlier version has a word for "calling," the modern reading is "calling to," and where it has a word for "hear," the modern reading is "hearken." The point is not only to hear, but to understand.

Jesus speaks after arguing with the Pharisees and the teachers of the law. They criticized him because his disciples ate without going through certain ritual washings. Jesus showed them that their human traditions sometimes overrode what God commanded. Now he turns to the whole crowd to teach them something deeper: what truly makes us unclean comes from the heart, not from outward things.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give more importance to religious customs than to obeying God with sincerity. Before we pray or read the Bible, we can ask him: "Lord, help me to hear and to understand."
exp.15:6:
Here the young man dressed in white tells the women to go and inform the disciples, and especially Peter, that Jesus is going ahead of them into Galilee. There they will see him, just as he had told them.

The one speaking is a young man, that is, a youth, who is in the empty tomb. Many understand him to be an angel, although the text only calls him a young man. Jesus had already announced this meeting in Galilee. Naming Peter in particular draws attention, since he had denied Jesus; for this reason many see here a gesture of care and forgiveness.

If you have failed, Jesus does not leave you behind. He goes ahead of you and calls you by your name. Approach him with confidence, and if you can, encourage others too who feel unworthy.
exp.14:11:
Pilate speaks again to the crowd and asks them what they want him to do with Jesus, whom they call "the King of the Jews." The word "again" shows that he had already asked them before. "Chief priests" are the leaders of the priests in the temple.

Pilate was the Roman governor. He knew that the religious leaders had handed Jesus over out of envy, not justice. They had persuaded the crowd to ask for Barabbas to be set free. Pilate tries to leave the decision in the hands of the people, but that question ends up pushing the crowd toward the shout of "Crucify him!" Some scholars see here a weak Pilate who avoids his responsibility.

Today, this verse invites us not to let ourselves be swept along by the pressure of the crowd. When we know what is right, let us ask God for the courage to do it, even when it is difficult or unpopular.
exp.6:29:
She says that when the woman returned to her house, she found that the demon had already left her daughter. The girl was lying on the bed.

Mark tells what happened after Jesus told this woman, a Greek woman of Syrophoenician origin, that her daughter was already free. She had pleaded with humility and faith. Now the narrator confirms that Jesus' word was fulfilled, even though He was not present in the house. Some see here a sign of his authority from a distance.

Today we can trust the word of Jesus even when we do not see results right away. The woman believed, went away, and found that it was true. We can pray with humility and perseverance, and rest in what He says.
exp.8:31:
This verse says that the disciples did not grasp what Jesus had just announced about his death and resurrection. Moreover, they were afraid to ask him to explain it. The word "saying" here refers to what Jesus said, that is, his message.

Jesus was walking with his disciples through Galilee and wanted to teach them in private. He told them that he would be handed over and killed, and that he would rise on the third day. They expected a different kind of Messiah, so the idea of suffering was hard for them to accept. The Bible does not say exactly why they feared to ask; perhaps they did not want to hear something painful, or they thought he would rebuke them. Shortly afterward, they were arguing about who was the greatest.

When we do not understand something from the Word of God, we should not remain silent out of fear or shame. We can bring our doubts to Jesus in prayer, and also ask humbly of mature believers.
exp.12:23:
Jesus says that, after a time of great tribulation, the sun will be darkened and the moon will not give its light. "But" is the ordinary word for "however," and "tribulation" means great suffering or anguish. These are images of extraordinary signs in the sky.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives. They asked him about the future of the temple and the signs of the end. He warns them about deception and false teachers, and then announces that his coming will be visible and powerful. Some believe the language is literal; others believe it is symbolic, as in the prophets of the Old Testament. Christians understand it in different ways.

For today: do not live in fear, and do not be carried away by anyone who promises dates or secrets. Trust in the words of Jesus, stay watchful, and keep doing good with faith and calm.
exp.0:16:
Jesus invites Simon and Andrew. "Come after me" means "follow me," that is, follow me as disciples. He promises that he will make them "fishers of men," that is, people who help others come close to God. The word "I will make" shows that Jesus himself is going to form them.

Jesus has just begun his ministry in Galilee, announcing that the kingdom of God is near and calling people to repent and believe. He walks along the sea and speaks to two fishermen who are at work. He speaks to them using words from their trade. The text says that at once they left their nets and followed him.

Following Jesus is a personal invitation, and he does not expect us to be perfect before we begin. Today we can ask him how to use our work and our relationships to encourage someone to know him.
exp.4:21:
Here it is told that a man named Jairus arrived, one of the leaders of the synagogue, the place where the Jews gathered to pray and to hear the Scriptures. As soon as he saw Jesus, he fell down and bowed low at his feet.

The one telling the story is Mark. Jesus had just crossed the lake, and a large crowd was waiting for him. Jairus was a respected man, but his daughter was seriously ill. The verses that follow show that this is why he humbled himself and asked Jesus for help.

For today: when pain overwhelms us, pride and position stop mattering. We can come to Jesus with humility, without pretense, and honestly tell him what hurts us most.
exp.13:24:
Jesus says with seriousness that he will not drink wine again until a future day, when he will drink it new in the kingdom of God. "I tell you the truth" means "I assure you." "New" suggests a different and renewed celebration.

Jesus speaks with his disciples at the Last Supper, shortly before his arrest. He has just given them the cup and spoken of his blood being poured out. With these words he looks beyond the cross: his death will not be the end. Interpreters often see this as a promise of a future banquet with his people, though not all agree on exactly what it will be like.

For today: even in difficult moments, we can live with hope. When you take part in the Lord's Supper or pray, remember that Jesus promised a future shared table. That promise encourages you to remain faithful and not give up.
exp.6:30:
Jesus went out again from the region of Tyre, passed through Sidon, and came to the Sea of Galilee, crossing through the middle of the territory of the Decapolis. Some older wording in the verse: "the sea" refers to the lake of Galilee, and "coasts" means region or territories. The Decapolis was a group of ten cities, mostly with a non-Jewish population.

Here the narrator, Mark, speaks. Jesus has just healed the daughter of a foreign woman, and now the account continues on its way. Mark does not explain why he took this roundabout route, and we do not know his reasons for certain. What we do see is that Jesus was in Gentile lands, and there he soon meets another person in need.

For today: Jesus does not stay in one place or with only one kind of people. Ask him to make you attentive to those near your path, even those who seem different from you, and help whoever you can.
exp.7:7:
It says that all the people ate until they were satisfied. Afterward, the disciples gathered up what was left over and filled seven baskets. A basket here is a large container made of woven fiber or wicker. The phrase "they were filled" means they ate enough, without being left hungry.

Mark tells this as a fact; Jesus is not speaking in this verse. Jesus had seen a crowd that had been with him for three days and had nothing to eat. He felt compassion and did not want to send them away hungry. He took seven loaves and a few small fish, gave thanks, and distributed them through his disciples. It shows his care and his power.

Today we can trust that God cares for our real needs. Even when what we have seems small, if we offer it to him with gratitude, he can do much with it. We can also learn to be generous and to share what we have with those who need it.
exp.4:28:
It says that as soon as the woman touched Jesus' clothes, her bleeding stopped completely. The phrase "the fountain of her blood" is an old way of speaking about the source of her bleeding. "Plague" here means a sickness that strikes and punishes the body. She did not just feel better: she felt it in her body, she knew she was well.

Mark tells this as a narrator. This woman had been sick for twelve years, had spent everything on doctors, and kept getting worse. Because of her condition, under the law of Moses, she was kept apart from others. That is why she came up from behind, afraid, but trusting that Jesus could heal her.

For today: when you are tired or have no way out, come to Jesus with your need, even if your faith is small and timid. He sees your trust and hears you.
exp.2:13:
He appointed twelve, that is, named or designated twelve men. He had two purposes: that they would "be with him," meaning that they would accompany him closely, and that he would "send them forth to preach," meaning to proclaim the message of the kingdom of God. First came the companionship, and after that the mission.

Mark presents this as an act of Jesus, the main character. He goes up the mountain and calls those he wanted, showing that the initiative is his. Shortly before, crowds were following him and unclean spirits recognized him, but he told them to keep quiet. Now he forms a close group who will learn from him and then carry on his work. Many see in the number twelve a connection with the twelve tribes of Israel, although the text does not explain this here.

Before serving God, we need to spend time with Jesus: praying, reading his Word, and learning from him. From that closeness comes a healthy service with strength.
exp.11:42:
Jesus called his disciples to pay attention, and with authority he told them that the poor widow had given more than all the others. Verily I say unto you means "I assure you" or "I tell you the truth." The treasury chest was the box or container where people placed their offerings in the temple. The two mites were two coins of very little value.

Jesus was sitting opposite the place of the offerings, watching how the people gave. Many rich people put in large amounts, but a widow came and gave almost nothing. Jesus wants to teach his disciples that God does not measure an offering by the amount, but by what it costs the heart that gives. The following verse explains that she gave everything she had to live on.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we give only what we have left over or whether we give with sacrifice and trust in God. Even if your offering, your time, or your help seems small, God sees it and values it.
exp.5:49:
They all saw him and were terrified. But right away he spoke to them. Where the explanation mentions the words that begin "be of good cheer" and "I am," it can be read as the same encouragement and the same identity: "Take courage" and "It is I, not a ghost." "Do not be afraid" is the same as "do not be afraid" in the verse.

Jesus speaks. His disciples had been rowing through the night against the wind, exhausted. Seeing him coming over the water, they thought he was a spirit and cried out. Jesus calms them with his voice and his presence. Then he gets into the boat and the wind dies down. The text says they still struggled to understand, since they had not grasped what the feeding of the bread had meant. Some scholars see in "I am" an echo of the name of God, but the passage does not explain this; it is one possible interpretation.

When you are tired and feel that everything is against you, remember that Jesus draws near to you. Listen for his voice in his Word and in prayer, and answer him with trust, not fear.
exp.0:34:
He rose very early, while it was still dark, and left the house for a lonely place. There he began to pray. The words "went out" and "departed" describe him leaving the house and going into a solitary place, which here means a quiet, unpopulated spot away from people, not necessarily a sandy wilderness.

The one acting is Jesus, and Mark, who tells the story, shows him after a very busy day in Capernaum, where he healed the sick and cast out demons. The whole city was looking for him. Even so, Jesus withdraws to pray before going on. Then Simon and the others arrive, telling him that everyone is looking for him, and he decides to go to other towns to preach.

For today: even when life is full of tasks and people who need us, it is good to set aside a little time, even a short one, to speak with God before starting the day. That prayer helps us remember what matters most.
exp.11:13:
The Pharisees and Herodians come to Jesus with flattery: they say he is sincere, that he is not swayed by anyone, and that he teaches the way of God in truth. Then they ask him whether it is permitted by the law to pay the tax to Caesar, the Roman emperor.

They speak, but their intentions are wicked. They wanted to trap him with his own words. If he said yes, the people who hated Roman rule would be angry; if he said no, they could accuse him before Rome. Jesus, as the following text says, saw their hypocrisy.

Today we can learn to be wary of flattery that hides ulterior motives, and to speak with sincerity. Before praising someone, let us ask ourselves whether we are doing it from the heart or to gain something.
exp.0:40:
Mark tells us that Jesus felt compassion for a man with leprosy. Then he stretched out his hand, touched him, and said: "I will; be thou clean." The word "clean" here means healed of leprosy and also welcomed back into the community.

The leper had knelt before Jesus and said to him: "If you are willing, you can make me clean." He believed in Jesus' power, but he was not sure of his willingness. At that time, according to the law of Moses, lepers lived apart from others and were considered ritually unclean (Leviticus 13). Touching them was something people avoided. Jesus responds with both words and touch, and so shows that he is willing to help.

Today we can approach Jesus with sincerity, even with our doubts and shame. He does not turn away from our need. His response invites us to trust his compassion and to treat with closeness those whom others reject.
exp.8:10:
The disciples ask Jesus a question: why do the scribes, the teachers of the Law, teach that Elijah must come first? The word "scribes" refers to the experts in the Scriptures. That teaching came from Malachi 4:5.

Jesus has just come down the mountain with Peter, James and John, where they saw Elijah with Him. He had asked them to keep quiet about what they had seen until He rose from the dead. They did not understand what rising from the dead meant, and perhaps the appearance of Elijah made them remember what the scribes taught. Jesus answers that Elijah has already come, and most readers understand that He is speaking of John the Baptist.

When something about God does not fit with what we expect, we can do as they did: bring our honest questions to Jesus and listen to His answer in the Bible.
exp.10:12:
Jesus sees a fig tree in the distance, covered with leaves, and goes toward it, hoping that perhaps he would find something on it, that is, fruit in case he found any. But there are only leaves, because it was not the season for figs, meaning it was not the time when the fruit was ready.

Mark tells us that Jesus was hungry and had just seen the temple. This scene surrounds the account in which Jesus drives out the sellers from the temple. For this reason many believe the fig tree shows a religion that only looks alive, without fruit. That Jesus would look for figs out of season is difficult, and scholars explain it in several ways.

For today: do not be content with looking good on the outside. Ask God that your faith be seen in real fruit, such as love, honesty and service, and not only in words or customs.
exp.9:48:
This verse tells us that Jesus stopped, stood still, and asked for the blind man to be brought to him. Then the people called him and said, "Be of good comfort", that is, "take heart, do not be afraid." They also said to him, "Rise, he calls you." The word "standing still" means that Jesus came to a halt.

Here Mark is speaking, telling what happened on the road out of Jericho. The blind man, named Bartimaeus in the verse before this passage, was crying out and asking for mercy. Many wanted to silence him, but Jesus heard him. The same people who had rebuked him now encourage him, because Jesus has called him.

For today: Jesus stops for the one who cries out to him in faith. If you feel your need is too small, or if others try to keep you quiet, keep drawing near to him in prayer. And if you can, encourage others to come to Jesus as well.
exp.13:67:
Peter answers the servant girl with a denial: he says he does not know Jesus and does not understand what she is talking about. Then he moves away toward the entrance of the courtyard, and at that moment the rooster crows.

Jesus is already under arrest and is being tried inside the house of the high priest. Peter had followed him from a distance and mixed in with the people by the fire. A servant girl recognizes him and points him out. Peter, out of fear of meeting the same fate as his Master, denies being his disciple. It is the first of three denials, and the crowing of the rooster recalls what Jesus had warned him.

We can all fail just when we thought we were firm. Peter teaches us that fear can make us silent about our faith. If you stumble today, do not stay in shame: remember that Jesus restored Peter, and he can also raise you up.
exp.11:16:
Jesus says that there are things owed to Caesar, that is, to the government, and things owed to God. The old-fashioned spelling "Á" is the earlier form of "a". The phrase "they marvelled" means that they were astonished by his answer.

Some Pharisees and Herodians asked him whether it was lawful to pay taxes to Caesar. It was a trap: if he said yes, he would upset many Jews; if he said no, they could accuse him before Rome. Jesus asked for a coin, which bore the image of the emperor, and answered with wisdom. Scholars explain in various ways how far what belongs to Caesar extends, but it is clear that God is above all.

We can fulfill our civic responsibilities, such as paying taxes and respecting the laws, without forgetting that our whole life belongs to God. Today you might ask yourself: am I giving God my trust, my time, and my obedience?
exp.8:4:
Peter speaks to Jesus, whom he calls "Master." He says it is good for them to stay in that place and to make three shelters, which were simple huts or booths made of branches. He wants one for Jesus, another for Moses, and another for Elijah.

Jesus has been transfigured before Peter, James, and John, and Moses and Elijah appear talking with him. Peter responds with amazement and fear. The text immediately says that he did not know what he was saying. Perhaps he wanted to prolong that glorious moment. Then the voice from heaven corrects the scene: Jesus is the beloved Son, and it is to him that they must listen.

For today: it is natural to want to hold on to beautiful spiritual moments, but God calls us above all to listen to Jesus and obey him in everyday life, not only when we feel something extraordinary.
exp.12:0:
Mark tells us that Jesus was leaving the temple in Jerusalem when one of his disciples said to him, "Master, see what manner of stones and what buildings are here!" He was amazed at the size and beauty of the structure. The word "buildings" refers to the buildings that make up the temple complex as a whole.

The disciple who speaks is not named, and he is amazed as any visitor would be. Jesus replies at once that all of it will be thrown down. This begins his teaching about the future, to which Mark gives the whole of chapter 13. Many believe that Jesus is announcing the destruction of the temple, which happened in the year 70 AD, although the rest of the discourse is interpreted in several ways.

For today: it is easy to be impressed by what is big and showy. Let us ask God to teach us to place our trust in Him and not in what looks firm but passes away.
exp.8:47:
It says there is a place where the worm does not die and the fire is not put out. Jesus uses these images to speak of Gehenna, which was the name of the Valley of Hinnom, near Jerusalem, used as a picture of God's judgment. "Occasion to fall" means whatever makes us stumble or sin. "Season" means to add flavor.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. He has just taught them that sin is very serious, and he deliberately uses exaggerations: cutting off the hand or plucking out the eye. He is not asking anyone to hurt themselves, but to decisively cut off whatever leads to sin. The phrase comes from Isaiah 66:24. Christians understand in different ways how these images should be interpreted.

Today we can ask ourselves what habit, friendship or custom makes us stumble. With God's help, let us make a concrete decision to move away from that, because entering the kingdom of God is worth more than anything else.
exp.0:5:
This verse describes how John the Baptist lived and dressed. He wore clothing made of camel's hair, with a leather belt around his waist. The word for "loins" here means the waist or the lower part of the back, so it refers to his belt. His food was locusts, which were edible insects, and wild honey, that is, honey found in nature. Some think the locusts might instead refer to carob pods, but most understand them to be insects.

Mark is the one telling the story. He wants to present John as the messenger who prepares the way for Jesus. His simple clothing recalls the prophet Elijah (2 Kings 1:8), and it shows that John lived with simplicity, focused on his mission.

For today: John did not seek attention for himself, but pointed to Christ. We can ask ourselves what things distract us from what is essential, and live with more simplicity, so that our lives point to Jesus.
exp.6:33:
Jesus looks up to heaven, sighs deeply, and speaks to the deaf man with a word in Aramaic, which means "be opened." The word "sighed" here means that he breathed out a deep sigh or groan.

Jesus is in the region of the Decapolis, away from the crowd. Some friends bring him a man who is deaf and can barely speak. Jesus takes him aside, touches his ears and tongue, then prays and commands that he be opened. Scholars think the sigh shows his prayer or his compassion for the man's suffering; this is not stated with certainty.

When something in your life seems closed, such as forgiveness, faith, or words, bring it to Jesus with sincerity. And like this man's friends, bring others before him through your prayer and your help.
exp.0:2:
This verse speaks of a voice crying out in the wilderness. "Prepare" means to get ready, and "paths" are the ways or roads. "Make straight" means to make straight what was crooked. The message is: get the road ready for the coming of the Lord.

Mark quotes the prophets (Isaiah, and also a phrase that recalls Malachi) to present John the Baptist as that messenger. He preached in the desert and called people to repentance. People confessed their sins and were baptized, thus preparing their hearts to receive Jesus. Mark wants to show that Jesus was expected and announced from long ago.

Today we can ask ourselves what is crooked in our lives and gets in the way of our relationship with God: a resentment, a lie, a habit. This week, acknowledge it honestly before God and take one concrete step to make it straight.
exp.9:0:
He got up from there and went into the region of Judea and across the Jordan. Again crowds gathered around him, and, as he was accustomed to do, he taught them again.

The narrator here is Mark, who describes Jesus' journey toward Jerusalem. The phrase "as he was accustomed to do" shows that teaching was his regular practice. This verse sets up the scene that follows: some Pharisees approach to test him with a question about divorce. Even in the midst of that tension, Jesus keeps teaching calmly and answers them by leading them back to the Scriptures.

For today: just as Jesus taught with constancy, we can make God's Word a daily habit. Setting aside a fixed time to read and listen prepares us to respond wisely when difficult questions or moments of pressure arrive.
exp.10:9:
The explanation says that the people were praising God because the kingdom of David, their ancestor, the great king of Israel, was coming. "Blessed" means praised or blessed. "Hosanna" was a cry that means "save us," and it was also used as praise. "In the highest" is understood as "in the highest place," that is, in heaven.

The speakers are the crowd that accompanied Jesus when he entered Jerusalem riding on a young donkey. They spread cloaks and branches as a sign of honor to a king. They expected God to restore the kingdom promised to David. Scholars debate how much they understood of Jesus' mission, since soon he would go to the cross.

For today: We can praise Jesus, but it is worth asking ourselves whether we receive him as he is and not only as we want him to be. Today you can bring your expectations to him in prayer and ask him to reign in your life in his own way.
exp.5:25:
King Herod was deeply distressed when he heard the girl's request. But because of the oath he had made, and out of regard for the guests who were dining with him, he did not want to refuse her. The word "refuse" in the verse means to turn down or deny the request.

Mark tells this during Herod's birthday banquet. He had sworn an oath to give Herodias's daughter whatever she asked for. Herodias held a grudge against John, because he had told her that her marriage to Herod was not lawful. Herod respected John, but his pride and his fear of looking bad before others weighed more heavily.

For today: let us not make promises lightly, and let us not allow shame or the opinion of others to lead us into doing wrong. It is better to correct a mistake in time than to hold on to it out of pride.
exp.10:18:
The verse says that, when evening came, Jesus went out of Jerusalem. The word "when even was come" means that the day was ending and it was growing dark.

Mark is the one telling the story. Jesus had just cleansed the temple and taught with authority, and the religious leaders wanted to kill him, but they feared the crowd. Each evening, when Jesus left the city, he withdrew from danger and noise. Mark does not say where he went; from the nearby account, many think he returned to Bethany, although this verse does not make it clear.

Today we can learn from Jesus to close the day with calm. After working, facing tensions, or doing what God asks of us, it is also wise to withdraw, rest, and entrust our worries to God.
exp.8:9:
It says that Peter, James, and John kept in their hearts what Jesus had ordered them to keep quiet about. But among themselves they were discussing what "rising from the dead" meant. The words "kept that saying with themselves" mean that they held on to it privately, and "questioning one with another" means arguing it out or asking one another about it.

Jesus was coming down from the mountain where the disciples had seen him transfigured, and he asked them to keep silent until the Son of Man had risen from the dead. They knew about the hope of a final resurrection, but they did not understand that Jesus himself would die and rise before that. That is why his words were hard for them to grasp. Then they ask him about Elijah.

Today, when we do not understand something about God, we can do as they did: hold on to his word, stay close to Jesus, and ask him sincerely. Understanding may take time, and God is patient with someone who truly wants to learn.
exp.7:31:
Jesus was speaking openly, that is, without parables or indirect language, about his suffering and death. Then Peter took him aside and began to rebuke him, that is, to correct him firmly.

Jesus had just been recognized by Peter as the Christ. Then he explained to them that the Son of Man must suffer, be rejected by the religious leaders, die, and rise again. Peter, like many of his time, expected a victorious Messiah, without the cross. That is why he was distressed and spoke up. Jesus then answered him sharply, because Peter was thinking as men think and not as God does.

For today: sometimes we want a faith without difficulties or sacrifices. Let us ask God for humility to accept his way, even when it does not match our expectations, and trust that his plan is better than ours.
exp.8:15:
Jesus asks the crowd and the scribes, "What are you arguing with them about?" The word "arguing" means discussing or debating with force. "Them" refers to the disciples, who were in the middle of the crowd. It is a simple question that invites an explanation of the reason for the conflict.

Jesus had just come down from the mountain with Peter, James, and John. When he arrives, he finds the other disciples surrounded by a crowd and by scribes, who were teachers of the law. It is later revealed that a father had brought his son to be set free, and the disciples had not been able to do it. The scribes were probably using that failure to argue. Jesus asks calmly, although he already knows what is happening.

When there is tension or failure, instead of arguing with others, let us bring the problem to Jesus and tell him honestly what we are going through.
exp.3:7:
It says that another part of the seed fell on good ground and produced fruit. The plant came up and grew, and gave an abundant harvest: some seeds yielded thirty, others sixty, and others a hundred times as much.
