Jesus is teaching the crowd with the parable of the sower. He contrasts the earlier soils, where the seed did not thrive, with this one, where it does bear fruit. Then he says, "He who has ears to hear, let him hear," and afterward, in private, explains the parable to his disciples. There he makes clear that the seed is the word of God.

For today: ask God for a willing and humble heart to receive his word. Listening is not enough; it must be obeyed in concrete things, such as forgiving, being honest, or serving someone. Do not compare yourself with others, since Jesus recognizes different levels of fruit.
exp.8:39:
Jesus says that whoever is not against them is for them. The phrase "for he that is not against us is on our part" is a short statement that works as a simple rule: not everyone who does not belong to our group is an enemy.

Jesus is speaking to his disciples. John had just told him that they saw a man casting out demons in Jesus' name, and they forbade him because he was not following with them. Jesus corrects them: whoever does a work in his name will hardly speak evil of him soon after. It is a teaching about not thinking of ourselves as the owners of God's work.

Today, when you see other believers serving Christ in a way different from yours, in another church or with another style, rejoice instead of criticizing. Ask yourself: does it exalt Jesus? If so, celebrate and pray for them.
exp.5:30:
Jesus invites his disciples: "Come ye yourselves apart into a desert place and rest a while." The reason is that there were so many people coming and going that they did not even have time to eat. "Desert place" means a solitary, uninhabited spot, not necessarily a desert of sand.

Jesus speaks to the apostles, who have just returned from their mission and are telling him everything they did and taught. They were tired and surrounded by crowds. He cares for them: he sees their exhaustion and offers them a chance to rest. The text that follows shows that the people reached them, so the rest did not turn out as they had planned.

For today: resting is not laziness. After serving, set aside a little time to eat, be quiet, and be with Jesus. If your rest is interrupted, you can trust that he is still attentive to your weariness.
exp.1:11:
What it says: The paralyzed man stood up at once, picked up the mat (the "bed" was a woven mat or pallet) and walked out in plain view of everyone. The people were all astonished, praised God, and said, "We never saw anything like this." The word "at once" means "right away."

Context: Four men had lowered this sick man through the roof to where Jesus was. Jesus first forgave the man's sins, and some teachers of the law criticized him in their hearts. Then Jesus healed the man to show that he has authority to forgive. Mark tells the account.

For today: Jesus cares about your deepest need, forgiveness, as much as your visible needs. When He helps you, do not keep it to yourself: give thanks and glorify God before others, as these people did.
exp.6:35:
He told them to tell no one about what he had done for the deaf and mute man. But the more he urged them, the more they spread the news everywhere. Some older words: "charged" means ordered, "so much the more a great deal" means even more, and "published" means made it known publicly.

Mark tells us what happened after Jesus healed this man. The people who were present were the ones who received the command. It is not known for certain why Jesus asked for silence. Many think he wanted to keep people from following him only for the miracles, or from misunderstanding him. Others see in this a sign of his humility.

For today: when God does something good in your life, it is natural to want to share it. But ask him for wisdom to speak with humility, so that the attention does not stay on you, but on Christ and his work.
exp.8:27:
This verse tells us that Jesus went into a house, and his disciples came to him privately. They asked him an honest question: why had they not been able to drive out the evil spirit from that boy? "Privately" means alone, apart from the crowd.

The ones speaking are the disciples. They had tried to help the boy and could not, and that left them puzzled. Jesus did heal him. Once they were alone, they looked for an explanation. Jesus answered that this kind of spirit comes out only by prayer and fasting. Some scholars understand this as a deep dependence on God, not as a magic formula.

For today: when we fail or do not understand something, we should not hide it. Let us bring the question to Jesus honestly. And let us remember that our strength comes from God, so it is good to seek him in prayer before and during our service to others.
exp.3:32:
He taught the word, that is, the message of the kingdom of God, using many parables like the ones he had just told. A parable is a simple comparison taken from everyday life. The phrase "as they were able to hear it" means that he spoke according to what the people were able to understand and receive. "Hear" here does not mean only listening with the ears, but understanding.

Jesus is teaching a crowd beside the Sea of Galilee. He had just told the parable of the mustard seed, and before that the parable of the sower. Afterward, in private, he explained everything to his disciples. Scholars understand in several ways why he used parables: to make things clear, to stir reflection, and to distinguish those who truly wanted to understand.

Today, God teaches us with patience and at our own pace. Do not be discouraged if you do not understand everything; keep listening to his word, ask with sincerity, and let it grow little by little.
exp.6:3:
This verse continues to explain the customs of the Pharisees and of many Jews. When they came back from the marketplace, they did not eat without first washing. They also kept other traditions, such as washing the cups they drank from, the pitchers, the metal utensils, and the couches where they reclined to eat. Some early manuscripts do not include the last of these, and its text is debated.

The one speaking here is the evangelist Mark, who explains these customs to readers who were perhaps not Jews. The Pharisees criticized Jesus' disciples for not following this tradition of the elders. It was a human rule, not a written command from God, and Jesus will answer by pointing to the problem of the heart.

For today: examine whether your religious practices bring you closer to God or only make you look good. Ask Him that your heart be near to Him, not just your lips.
exp.14:16:
They dressed Jesus in a purple robe and placed on his head a crown woven from thorny branches twisted together. The explanation of "dressed" means that they put clothes on him, and "woven" means twisted or intertwined. Purple was a color associated with kings and powerful people.

Mark, as the narrator, tells what happened after Pilate, wanting to please the crowd, released Barabbas and handed Jesus over to be crucified. The Roman soldiers gathered the whole company and made a cruel mockery, pretending to crown Jesus as king. Without knowing it, they were mocking the one who truly is King.

For today: Jesus accepted being humiliated out of love for us. When you feel despised or misunderstood, remember that he knows that pain. You can bring him your shame in prayer and trust in his presence.
exp.12:11:
Jesus says there will be betrayal within the very families. A brother will hand over his brother to be killed, a father will do the same with his child, and children will rise up against their parents and cause their deaths. The word "betray" means to hand someone over to the authorities, knowing that they could die.

Jesus speaks to his disciples on the Mount of Olives, when he announces what will come before the end. He warns them that following him will bring persecution, even from those closest to them. He says this so that they will not be surprised, and he promises that the Holy Spirit will give them what to say. Some believe this speaks of the times of the apostles, others of a time still to come, and others of both.

For today: if following Jesus brings rejection from your family, you are not alone. Keep loving and forgiving, trust in the Spirit, and persevere with hope.
exp.0:6:
John the Baptist announces that after him comes someone far greater. He says this person is mightier than he is, and that he is not even worthy to stoop down and unloose the thong of his sandals. In that time, sandals were the footwear people wore, and loosening them was the work of a servant.

John preaches by the river Jordan, and many people from Judea and Jerusalem come to confess their sins and be baptized. His simple life, with clothing of camel's hair and food from the wilderness, draws attention. But John does not want people to admire him. His mission is to prepare the way for Jesus, so he points toward Him and places himself in a humble position.

For today: serve and teach with humility, without seeking applause. Ask yourself whether what you do directs others' eyes toward Christ and not toward you.
exp.13:69:
Peter denies Jesus for a second time. A little later, other people who were standing there tell him that he is surely one of Jesus' followers. They give two reasons: he is a Galilean, and his way of speaking gives him away. The word "speech" here means accent or way of talking.

This happens on the night of Jesus' arrest, in the courtyard of the high priest. The ones speaking are ordinary people who were warming themselves there. The Galileans had an accent of their own, different from that of Jerusalem. Peter is afraid and denies knowing Jesus, just as Jesus had foretold.

Today, Peter teaches us that fear can make us silent about our faith. But his story also shows that failure is not the end: Peter wept, repented, and Jesus restored him afterward. If you have failed, return to Him with a sincere heart.
exp.8:6:
This verse tells how a cloud covered Jesus and the three disciples on the mountain. From the cloud came a voice that said, "This is my beloved Son: hear him." The cloud's covering them is the picture of being enveloped or wrapped in its presence.

Peter had just seen Jesus shining beside Moses and Elijah. Frightened and not knowing what to say, he proposed building three shelters. Then God himself speaks from the cloud. His message gently corrects Peter: Jesus is not just one more figure alongside Moses and Elijah, but the beloved Son. Afterward, the disciples see only Jesus.

For today: when there are many voices and opinions, take some time to read the Gospels and listen to Jesus first. Ask yourself, "What did Jesus say about this?" and try to follow him in one concrete step today.
exp.0:7:
John says that he baptizes with water, but that Jesus will baptize with the Holy Spirit. The water was a visible sign of repentance. The Spirit is the presence and power of God himself in a person. "Indeed" is the sense of "surely" or "in truth."

The one speaking is John the Baptist, a prophet of simple life who was preparing the people for the coming of the Messiah. Just before this, he said he was not worthy even to untie the sandals of Jesus. By saying this, he wants no one to mistake him for the Savior. Believers have understood in different ways when and how this baptism with the Spirit is fulfilled, but all agree that it comes from Christ.

For today: do not be content with rituals or good habits. Ask Jesus to have his Spirit transform you from within, and humbly recognize that he is the center, not you.
exp.1:26:
Jesus says that the sabbath was made as a gift for people's good. God did not make human beings to serve the sabbath, as if it were a burden, but made the sabbath to serve human beings, giving them rest and renewal.

Jesus speaks with the Pharisees, who were criticizing his disciples for picking heads of grain on the sabbath. He reminds them of the story of David, who, when he was hungry, ate the bread that had been set apart. Human need mattered more than a ceremonial rule. Then Jesus declares himself Lord of the sabbath, meaning he has authority over its true purpose.

Today we can remember that the rules of faith exist to lead us to God and to care for people. Set aside time each week to truly rest, and when you serve someone in need, do not see it as a fault, but as the heart of God.
exp.14:0:
Early in the morning, this verse tells us, the religious leaders of Israel met to decide what to do with Jesus. The chief priests were the leading priests. The elders and scribes were leaders and teachers of the law, and the council was the Sanhedrin, the Jewish court. Then they bound Jesus, led him away, and handed him over to Pilate, the Roman governor.

Mark tells this as the author, not as a character in the story. During the night, Jesus had already been questioned by the Jewish leaders. At dawn they brought him before Pilate, probably because under Roman rule they needed his authority to carry out a death sentence. Mark shows that Jesus was not arrested by chance, but handed over by those who should have recognized him.

For today: let us watch that religion or pride does not close our hearts to Jesus. Before defending our own ideas, let us ask for humility to truly listen to him.

sum.8: Jesus is transfigured before Peter, James, and John, and a voice from heaven says, "This is my beloved Son. Listen to him." Afterward he heals a boy who was possessed by a spirit that made him mute, when the boy's father cries out, "I believe; help my unbelief." He announces his death and resurrection, and teaches that the greatest person is the one who serves everyone.
sum.3: In Mark 4, Jesus teaches using parables. The parable of the sower shows how different people receive the word of God in different ways. Other parables compare the kingdom to a seed that grows on its own and to a mustard seed. Then, during a storm at sea, Jesus calms the wind and the waves, and the disciples are amazed.
sum.15: The women go to the tomb and find the stone rolled away. A young man dressed in white tells them that Jesus has risen and that they will see him in Galilee. Jesus appears to Mary Magdalene and to others, but the disciples doubt, and then he sends them out to preach the gospel to everyone. After this he goes up into heaven, and they preach everywhere.
sum.7: Jesus feeds about four thousand people with seven loaves and a few small fish, and the Pharisees ask him for a sign. Then he heals a blind man in Bethsaida, and Peter says that Jesus is the Christ. Jesus announces that he will suffer, die, and rise again, and he calls his followers to deny themselves and take up their cross.
sum.12: As Jesus was leaving the temple, he announced that it would be destroyed, and his disciples asked him when this would happen. He warned them not to be led astray by false messiahs, and said there would be wars, persecutions, and great distress, but that God would take care of his chosen ones. He assured them that the Son of Man would return, and that no one knows the day or the hour, so they must stay alert and be ready.
sum.13: Jesus is anointed in Bethany, shares the Last Supper with his disciples, and foretells Judas's betrayal and Peter's denial. He prays in anguish in Gethsemane, is arrested and taken before the council, where he declares himself to be the Christ and is condemned. Peter denies him three times and weeps.
sum.10: Jesus enters Jerusalem riding on a young donkey while the people praise him as the one who comes in the name of the Lord. Then he clears the temple, saying it should be a house of prayer, and he teaches about faith, prayer, and forgiveness after the fig tree dries up. In the end, the leaders question his authority, and he does not answer them.
sum.14: The religious leaders hand Jesus over to Pilate, who, giving in to the crowd, releases Barabbas and has Jesus sent off to be crucified after the soldiers mock him. Jesus dies on the cross; the curtain of the temple is torn, and a centurion says that he was the Son of God. Joseph of Arimathea buries him while some women look on.
sum.6: Jesus rebukes the Pharisees for putting human traditions above the word of God, and he teaches that what defiles a person comes out of the heart, not from what they eat. Then he sets free the daughter of a Syrophoenician woman because of her faith, and he heals a man who was deaf and had a speech impediment.
sum.5: Jesus is rejected in his hometown because the people there do not believe, and then he sends the twelve out two by two to preach, heal, and drive out demons. The death of John the Baptist at the hands of Herod is recounted. Jesus feeds five thousand people, walks on the sea, and heals many sick people.
sum.2: Jesus heals a man with a withered hand on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees begin plotting to kill him. Then he chooses twelve disciples to be with him and to preach, while some think he has lost his mind and the scribes accuse him of acting by the power of Beelzebul. He answers that a divided kingdom cannot stand, and he says that his true family is made up of those who do God's will.
sum.9: In Mark 10, Jesus teaches that God joined man and woman together in marriage, blesses the children, and says that the kingdom is received with the simplicity of a child. He shows that riches get in the way of someone who trusts in them, announces his death, teaches that greatness comes through serving others, and heals the blind man Bartimaeus.
sum.1: Jesus forgives the sins of a paralyzed man whom four friends lowered through the roof, and he heals him to show his authority. He calls Levi, eats with sinners, and explains that he came to call the sick, not the healthy. He also teaches about fasting and the Sabbath, and says that he is Lord of the Sabbath.
sum.4: Jesus frees a man who was tormented by many unclean spirits, and the man tells people throughout the region what God had done for him. Then Jesus heals a woman who touched his clothes in faith, and he raises Jairo's daughter from the dead. Jesus has power over evil, sickness, and death.
sum.0: John the Baptist prepares the way, and Jesus is baptized. The Father calls him his beloved Son, and then he is tested in the desert. After that, Jesus announces that the kingdom of God is near, calls his first disciples, and shows his authority by casting out demons and healing the sick, including a man with leprosy.
sum.11: Jesus tells the parable of the wicked tenants who kill the owner's son, and he wisely answers questions about paying taxes to Caesar, the resurrection, and the most important commandment: to love God and your neighbor. He warns against proud scribes and praises the poor widow who gave everything she had.
